Hyperfocus: How to Be More Productive in a World of Distraction

cheatsheet.md

Hyperfocus — Cheatsheet

The two modes (know which you need)

HYPERFOCUSSCATTERFOCUS
DirectionAttention outward, one thingAttention inward, nothing in particular
Best mode forProductivityCreativity
Fills attentional space withone complex taskfree space to connect dots
Fueled bymental energy (drains it)rest (restores it)
Boost withcaffeine, Biological Prime Timelow energy, Creative Prime Time, (occasional) alcohol

The Four Types of Tasks — where should you be?

AttractiveUnattractive
Productive✅ Purposeful (sweet spot; ~3–4 tasks)✅ Necessary (push yourself)
Unproductive⚠️ Distracting (small doses)❌ Unnecessary (active laziness)

Live in the top row. Sort your tasks here first.

Decision rules

  • What to focus on? → the most consequential task (the domino toppling a hundred others), not the most urgent/stimulating.
  • Analytical problem? → hyperfocus (+ caffeine). Creative/insight problem? → scatterfocus (low energy).
  • Am I productive? → Did I accomplish what I intended? (Busy ≠ productive. A planned lazy day = productive.)
  • Should I break? → If you're switching a lot, rereading, or drifting to mindless work — yes, and take it before you feel fatigued.
  • Worth consuming? → Treat it as a "pitch" for your attention. Useful > balanced > entertaining > trashy.

Hyperfocus in 4 stages

1. Choose a purposeful object → 2. Eliminate distractions (in advance) → 3. Focus for a preset time → 4. Draw back when you wander (you will, 47% of the day).

Intention precedes attention. Make it an implementation intention (when/where/which action) → 62% vs 22% follow-through.

Key numbers (thresholds & defaults)

  • Attentional space: ~4 chunks / ~40 conscious bits per second.
  • Focus lasts ~40 seconds at a computer before interruption.
  • Never pair two complex tasks; only complex + habitual.
  • Task-switching makes work ~50% slower (attention residue).
  • Breaks: at least every 90 min, ~15 min per hour worked.
  • Sleep: 1 hr missed ≈ 2 hrs lost productivity; deficit shrinks attentional space up to 60%.
  • Caffeine: benefit up to ~200mg; avoid >400mg.

Where the wandering mind goes → why scatterfocus is productive

Past 12% · Present 28% · Future 48% (prospective bias). In scatterfocus you're 14× more likely to plan the future than when focused.

Three scatterfocus styles

  • Capture — roam free, write it down → clears the mind.
  • Problem-crunching — circle one problem → for a big decision (sparingly).
  • Habitual — simple enjoyable task + notepad → most powerful; recharges + connects most dots.

Tells you need to recharge

Frequent switching · losing grip on intentions · slower pace (rereading) · drifting to mindless work · slipping into scatterfocus unintentionally.

Master habit

Meta-awareness — hourly, ask "what's in my attentional space, and is it what I intended?" Meditation is the one proven way to enlarge that space.

glossary.md

Hyperfocus — Glossary

Active laziness — Staying busy with unnecessary work that produces nothing (Ch 1).

Attention residue — Fragments of a previous task lingering in attentional space after switching; makes work ~50% slower (Sophie Leroy) (Ch 2).

Attentional space — Bailey's term for working memory; the mental scratch pad ("RAM") holding what you're aware of now (~4 chunks, ~10-second lifespan) (Ch 2).

Autopilot mode — Managing attention reactively, without deliberate choice; fine for habits, toxic for attention (Ch 1).

Biological Prime Time (BPT) — Your peak-energy hours; best for focus/hyperfocus work (Ch 10).

Boredom — The restlessness of transitioning from high to low stimulation; "unwanted scatterfocus" (Ch 6).

Capture mode — Scatterfocus style: let the mind roam and write down whatever surfaces (Ch 6).

Chunking — Grouping information into meaningful units to hold more in attentional space (Ch 2).

Clustering — The brain's grouping of related dots; builds expertise and frees attentional space (Ch 9).

Creative Prime Time (CPT) — Your low-energy hours; best for creative/scatterfocus work (least-inhibited brain) (Ch 10).

Default network — The brain network active when unfocused; scatterfocus lights it up to connect dots (Ch 6).

Distraction-free mode — Eliminating every controllable distraction in advance to enable hyperfocus (Ch 4).

Dot — Any idea or piece of information in your mind; creativity = connecting dots (Ch 6, 8).

Flow — Total immersion when challenge ≈ skill (Csikszentmihalyi); often produced by hyperfocus (Ch 3, 5).

Four types of distractions — 2×2 of in/out-of-control × annoying/fun (Ch 4).

Four types of tasks — 2×2 grid: necessary, unnecessary, distracting, purposeful (Ch 1).

Hyperfocus — Keeping one important, complex object of attention filling your attentional space; the brain's most productive mode (Ch 3).

Habitual scatterfocus — The most powerful scatterfocus style: do a simple enjoyable task and capture rising ideas (Ch 6).

Hourly awareness chime — An hourly timer prompting you to check what's in your attentional space (Ch 3, 10).

Implementation intention — A specific when/where/which-action plan; doubles/triples follow-through (Gollwitzer) (Ch 3).

Insight trigger — A cue (from environment or wandering mind) that sparks a solution to an incubating problem (Ch 8).

Intention precedes attention — Decide what to accomplish before you begin; attention without intention is wasted (Ch 3).

Jobs to be done — Asking what "job" you "hire" each device to do (Christensen); redundant jobs = unnecessary device (Ch 4).

Meta-awareness — Noticing what's occupying your attentional space; the master attention skill (Ch 2).

Novelty bias — The prefrontal cortex rewards task-switching with dopamine, so busyness feels productive (Ch 2).

Open loops — Unresolved tasks/commitments held in your head that hijack attentional space (Ch 4).

Parkinson's Law — Work expands to fill available time; busywork can signal a lack of real work (Ch 5).

Positive affect — How good you feel; a good mood expands attentional space (Ch 10).

Problem-crunching mode — Scatterfocus style: hold one problem loosely and let thoughts circle it (Ch 6).

Productivity — Accomplishing what you intend to (not being busy) (Ch 2).

Prospective bias — The wandering mind's tendency to think about the future (48% of the time) (Ch 6).

Purposeful work — Attractive + productive tasks; the sweet spot; your ~3–4 highest-impact tasks (Ch 1).

Reduced-distraction mode — Taming the biggest distractions while staying reachable for collaboration (Ch 4).

Rule of 3 — Choose the three things you want accomplished by day's end (Ch 3).

Scatterfocus — Intentional mind-wandering; the brain's most creative mode (Ch 6).

Ten-thousand-hour rule — Rough length of deliberate practice to build expert-level dots (Ch 9).

Zeigarnik effect — Unfinished tasks weigh more heavily on the mind than finished ones (Ch 8).

40 bits / 4 chunks — We consciously process ~40 of 11M sensory bits/second, and hold ~4 chunks in short-term memory (Ch 2).

40 seconds — Average time we focus at a computer before being interrupted or self-interrupting (Ch 0, 2).

90/15 break rule — Break at least every 90 minutes, ~15 minutes per hour of work (Ch 7).

patterns.md

Hyperfocus — Patterns & Techniques

Sort Tasks into the Four Quadrants

When to use: Whenever you feel busy but unproductive.

How: Map monthly tasks by productive/unproductive × attractive/unattractive → necessary, purposeful, distracting, unnecessary. Live in the top two.

Trade-offs: A "stepping-back" activity — you must remove yourself from the trenches to do it (5–10 min).

The Four Stages of Hyperfocus

When to use: Any complex, purposeful task.

How: (1) Choose a meaningful object; (2) eliminate internal + external distractions in advance; (3) focus for a preset time; (4) draw attention back each time it wanders.

Trade-offs: For complex tasks only — full attention on a habit makes you choke.

Rule of 3

When to use: Every morning.

How: Pick the three things you want done by day's end; keep them visible. Optionally set 3 weekly and 3 personal intentions too.

Most Consequential Tasks

When to use: A long to-do list.

How: Rank by second/third-order consequences — which task is the domino that topples a hundred others? Combine with the quadrant grid.

Implementation Intentions

When to use: Any difficult or important intention.

How: Specify when/where/which-action ("Go to the gym" → "go on my lunch break"). Name the situational cue.

Trade-offs: Overkill for trivial goals; essential for hard ones. You must actually care about the goal.

Hourly Awareness Chime

When to use: To stay intentional moment-to-moment.

How: Set an hourly timer; when it rings, check whether you're on autopilot, how full your attentional space is, and whether you're on the most consequential thing. Pick 2–3 prompts.

Distraction-Free Mode

When to use: Before any hyperfocus block.

How: Block distracting sites/apps (Freedom, Cold Turkey, RescueTime), phone in Do Not Disturb in another room, noise-canceling headphones, maybe caffeine. When a new distractor slips through, add it to the block list.

Trade-offs: Impulsive people may find blockers stressful — use for the hardest tasks and treat yourself after.

Tame the Five Pain Points

When to use: Ongoing, to reduce baseline distraction.

How: Notifications (disable nonessential) · Phone (treat as "a more annoying computer"; stow it; second "distractions device"; phone swap) · Email (batch at set times, five-sentence rule, delete phone app, external to-do list, 20-min hyperfocus bursts) · Meetings (no agenda→no meeting; question recurring; challenge attendee list) · Internet (disconnect periodically).

Clear Your Mind (Externalize Open Loops)

When to use: When nagging thoughts fragment your focus.

How: Offload to a to-do list, calendar, distractions list, waiting-for list, worry list (Getting Things Done). Removes guilt (past), worry (future), doubt (present).

The Three Styles of Scatterfocus

When to use: To plan, recharge, or connect ideas.

How: Capture (roam free, write what surfaces — clear the mind); Problem-crunching (circle one big problem — use sparingly, 30–60 min); Habitual (simple enjoyable task + capture ideas — most powerful, most often). Keep a notepad.

Refreshing Breaks (90/15 Rule)

When to use: Throughout the workday.

How: Break at least every 90 min, ~15 min per hour; make it low-effort, wanted, and not a chore ("pleasurably effortless"). Not email/news. Take breaks before you need them.

Connect More Dots

When to use: Stuck on a creative or nonlinear problem.

How: Scatter in a richer environment; write the problem down; sleep on it; step back/unfocus; leave the task unfinished (stop mid-sentence); consume more valuable dots.

Consumption Audit

When to use: Periodically, to upgrade your inputs.

How: Log everything you consume into useful/balanced/entertaining/trashy. Cut trash, add a valuable item for each cut, veg out with intention, invest in serendipity.

Match Mode to Problem (with Substances)

When to use: Choosing how to attack a task.

How: Analytical → hyperfocus at Biological Prime Time (+ caffeine). Creative/insight → scatterfocus at Creative Prime Time (low energy; occasional drink for pure-creative). Caffeine narrows focus; alcohol widens wandering.

How to Win Friends and Influence People

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — How to Win Friends & Influence People

The 30 Principles at a Glance

Part 1 — Handling People

1. Don't criticize, condemn, or complain.

2. Give honest and sincere appreciation.

3. Arouse in the other person an eager want.

Part 2 — Make People Like You

1. Become genuinely interested in others. 2. Smile. 3. Use the person's name. 4. Be a good listener; let them talk about themselves. 5. Talk in terms of their interests. 6. Make them feel important — sincerely.

Part 3 — Win to Your Thinking

1. Avoid arguments. 2. Never say "You're wrong." 3. If wrong, admit it fast. 4. Begin friendly. 5. Get "yes, yes" early. 6. Let them talk most. 7. Let the idea be theirs. 8. See their viewpoint. 9. Sympathize with them. 10. Appeal to nobler motives. 11. Dramatize ideas. 12. Throw down a challenge.

Part 4 — Be a Leader

1. Begin with praise. 2. Criticize indirectly. 3. Admit your own faults first. 4. Ask, don't order. 5. Let them save face. 6. Praise every improvement. 7. Give a reputation to live up to. 8. Make the fault seem easy to fix. 9. Make them happy to comply.

Decision Rules

SituationDo thisBecause
Tempted to point out a faultStop — say nothing, or correct indirectlyCriticism triggers defense, never change
Need someone to actReframe around their wantNo one is motivated by your want
Someone says "You're wrong" is on your lipsSay "I may be wrong — let's check"Contradiction locks the mind shut
You are wrongAdmit it loudly, first, before they doDisarms the critic completely
Facing resistance / an early "no"Open with questions earning "yes"Momentum carries them to your view
Must give feedbackPraise + "and" (never "but") + easy fix"But" cancels the praise
DelegatingPhrase as a questionPreserves initiative and pride
Someone is losing/wrong publiclyGive them a face-saving exitHumiliation costs the relationship
Want the idea adoptedLet them think they thought of itPeople back their own ideas
First meetingAsk about them, listen, use their nameInterested beats interesting

Tells & Smells

  • You feel the urge to say "Actually..." → you're about to trigger ego defense. Stop.
  • Your praise contains "but" → it will read as a set-up. Swap for "and."
  • You're explaining what you need → you've lost them. Reframe to their interest.
  • You "won" the argument → check whether you just lost the person.
  • Praise feels generic → it will read as flattery. Name the specific thing or don't say it.

The One-Line Test

Before any interaction: "What does the other person want, and how do I make them feel important — sincerely?" If you can't answer, you're not ready to persuade.

glossary.md

Glossary — How to Win Friends and Influence People

Appeal to the nobler motives — persuade by attributing a fine, unselfish reason to the other person and letting them live up to it (Ch 3, P10).

Appreciation (honest and sincere) — genuine, specific recognition of what is admirable in someone; the second Fundamental Technique. Opposite of flattery (Ch 1, P2).

Arouse an eager want — frame any request around the other person's desires so they want to act (Ch 1, P3).

Bait the hook to suit the fish — metaphor for speaking to the other person's self-interest, not your own (Ch 1).

Begin in a friendly way — open persuasion with warmth, not confrontation; "a drop of honey" (Ch 3, P4).

Creatures of emotion — Carnegie's premise that people are driven by pride and vanity, not logic (Ch 1).

Dramatize your ideas — make points vivid and showmanlike so they land and stick (Ch 3, P11).

Face-saving — protecting another's dignity even when they're wrong; a core leadership move (Ch 4, P5).

Flattery — insincere, generic praise; "from the teeth out." The counterfeit of appreciation (Ch 1).

Fundamental Techniques (the three) — don't criticize; give sincere appreciation; arouse an eager want (Ch 1).

Importance hunger — the deepest human craving to feel important and appreciated; root of most behavior (Ch 1).

"...and" not "...but" — replace "but" with "and" after praise so correction reads as encouragement, not a set-up (Ch 4, P2).

Indirect criticism — calling attention to a mistake by inference rather than direct rebuke (Ch 4, P2).

Nobler motives — the reason that "sounds good" (vs. the real reason); appeal to it to move people (Ch 3, P10).

Praise every improvement — reinforce the slightest progress specifically and lavishly (Ch 4, P6).

Reputation to live up to — assign someone a virtue so they strive to embody it (Ch 4, P7).

Save face — see Face-saving (Ch 4, P5).

Secret of Socrates — chain of small "yes" agreements that builds momentum toward your conclusion (Ch 3, P5).

Show respect for opinions — never say "You're wrong"; invite a joint look at the facts (Ch 3, P2).

Six Ways to Make People Like You — interest, smile, names, listening, their interests, feeling important (Ch 2).

Smile — low-cost signal of gladness; "act as if" until the feeling follows (Ch 2, P2).

Spotlight rule — aim attention at the other person, not yourself (Ch 2).

Throw down a challenge — spur people via competition and the desire to excel (Ch 3, P12).

"Yes, yes" response — see Secret of Socrates (Ch 3, P5).

patterns.md

Patterns — Carnegie's Techniques in Practice

Bait-the-Hook Reframe

When to use: any request or "ask" (email, delegation, sales, parenting).

How: delete every "I/we want" framing; rewrite the ask around what the other person already wants and show the path from their want to your request.

Trade-offs: requires genuinely knowing their interests — guessing wrong reads as manipulation.

Sincere Appreciation (not Flattery)

When to use: opening a relationship, motivating, before a hard conversation.

How: find something specific and genuinely admirable; name it concretely ("the way you handled X" not "good job"). Must be true.

Trade-offs: fails instantly if insincere or generic; over-use dilutes.

The "Yes, Yes" Ladder (Secret of Socrates)

When to use: overcoming resistance or an early "no"; onboarding, sales, negotiation.

How: begin with questions the other person cannot help but agree to; chain agreements toward the conclusion you want. Never open on the point of dispute.

Trade-offs: transparent if the questions are leading or gimmicky; keep them honest and relevant.

Admit-Your-Own-Fault-First

When to use: correcting a peer or junior; defusing a critic.

How: name your own similar mistake before mentioning theirs ("I got this wrong for years myself..."); or beat a critic to the punch by condemning yourself first.

Trade-offs: requires humility; loses power if the shared-fault claim is fabricated.

"And" Instead of "But"

When to use: any praise-then-correct message (feedback, reviews, coaching).

How: give sincere praise, then join the improvement with "and" — never "but," which cancels the praise.

Trade-offs: subtle; still needs the correction phrased as a forward-looking possibility, not a veiled criticism.

Order-as-a-Question

When to use: delegating, directing a team, changing behavior.

How: convert commands into questions — "Would it work to...?", "What do you think about trying...?" — so the person keeps initiative and ownership.

Trade-offs: slower than a direct order; unsuitable in true emergencies where speed > buy-in.

Reputation-to-Live-Up-To

When to use: motivating improvement, building trust, turning someone around.

How: publicly attribute a virtue to the person ("you've always been reliable"), then hand them the task that lets them prove it.

Trade-offs: manipulative if the virtue is fictional; works only when the person can plausibly own it.

Idea-Ownership Transfer

When to use: pushing a proposal that meets resistance.

How: plant the seed via question or partial suggestion; let the other person develop and voice the conclusion so it becomes their idea.

Trade-offs: requires ego restraint — you don't get public credit for the idea.

The Face-Saving Exit

When to use: someone is wrong, is losing, or must reverse course.

How: give them a dignified way out — attribute the error to circumstances, offer a graceful reframe, correct privately.

Trade-offs: means forgoing the satisfaction of being visibly right.

Interested-Not-Interesting Listening

When to use: any first meeting, networking, relationship-building.

How: ask about the other person's favorite subject and listen with full attention; talk about yourself as little as possible.

Trade-offs: none, provided the interest is genuine; feigned interest eventually shows.

The Certainty Illusion: What You Don't Know and Why It Matters

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Certainty Illusion

Triage: which illusion is this?

  • Claim leans on research, mechanism, or "studies show" → Science Illusion → run Scienceploitation Detection + Body-of-Evidence Test (ch01–ch05)
  • Claim leans on a virtuous adjective (natural, clean, safe, sustainable, manly) → Goodness Illusion → run Health Halo Deconstruction + separate goal from intervention (ch06–ch10)
  • Claim leans on what other people think (stars, rankings, polls, "everyone says") → Opinion Illusion → run the Review Escape Plan + Four Poll Questions (ch11–ch13)

Core decision rules

  • When a guidepost feels unusually trustworthy, raise suspicion, because distortion follows value. Trust level is a risk indicator, not a safety indicator.
  • When you feel the urge to share, pause and ask "is this accurate?" — the single highest-return habit in the book.
  • When content makes you feel politically self-righteous, do not share yet. Misinformation is measurably easier to process, more emotional, scarier, and more moralized than accurate content.
  • When a claim rests on one study, refuse it. One study rarely changes anything — most of all when it flatters your priors or offers a contrarian thrill.
  • When a claim is extraordinary, scale the proof bar to the improbability and keep the onus on the claimant (Sagan standard).
  • When someone invokes Galileo or persecution, treat it as a last-resort defence, not an argument, and return to the body of evidence.
  • When jargon appears with no plain-language mechanism, the language is there to impress, not inform.
  • When a label carries a virtuous adjective, read the ingredient list instead. Assume health-halo terms are meaningless or misleading.
  • When you can't answer who reviewed, how many, and how selected — the number is not evidence.

Thresholds & defaults

SignalThreshold / default
Clinical trials reaching clinical application~10% — calibrate "breakthrough" headlines down hard
Submission-to-acceptance for real biomedical papers91–639 days, ~100 avg. Two weeks = no real peer review
National survey sample size~1,000 respondents is reasonable; self-selecting internet polls are worthless
Unreliable share of online reviewsAssume 25–30%; no platform is at zero
Fake-review target band4.2–4.5 stars with minor complaints — a manipulation zone, not a credibility signal
Incentivized reviewsInflate ratings 40–70%
Your ability to detect fake reviewsAssume ~zero; AI-generated fakes are detected at chance
Biomedical abstracts containing spin~40%
Post-retraction citations acknowledging retraction5.4% — retraction status will not reach you passively
Predatory journals in existence11,000–16,000; 750,000+ articles/year
Default food strategyReal food — fruits, veggies, nuts, legumes, whole grains

Tells & smells — fast red flags

Science-y bunk

  • The word quantum attached to a health product → stop, walk away
  • Riding a hot topic: stem cells, regenerative medicine, genomics, nanotech, microbiome, quantum, AI
  • No stated risks or limitations (only 19% of stem-cell clinic sites mentioned any)
  • Science-y word salad in place of a mechanism; "scientifically proven" with no relevant research
  • Scientific trappings inside a field already tied to pseudoscience (quantum + astrology)
  • "Immune-boosting" — a near-reliable scam marker
  • Vagueness sold as profundity: consciousness, resonance, paradigms, optimal levels, transformational
  • Fear + jargon together (the science-y/scary dyad) — strip each and test alone; neither usually survives

Bad publication

  • Vague or institution-mimicking author affiliations; two-week acceptance; no ethics review
  • Editorial board publishing itself; journal built to support one predetermined position
  • Nobody else cites it (check PubMed / Google Scholar)
  • One weak paper carrying an entire commercial industry's proof of efficacy

Goodness marketing

  • The Devious Dozen: natural, holistic, healthy, organic, non-GMO, gluten-free, chemical-free, toxin-free, locally grown, the colour green, immune-boosting, personalized
  • Halo stacking, or halos fused with science jargon — the incoherence is the tell
  • Halo appearing where the claim is logically inapplicable (gluten-free water)
  • The pitch first manufactured the insecurity it now sells the fix for
  • Challenge met with retreat to an unarguable truism (motte-and-bailey)
  • "Toxin-free" → substitute "evil-spirits-free" and re-read

Opinion

  • All five stars (depresses sales — real profiles aren't that clean); balanced-sounding minor gripes (the faker's credibility texture)
  • Aggregates you can't decompose: who reviewed, how many, how selected
  • Physician/professional ratings — knowledge asymmetry means they track experience, not clinical quality
  • Poll with no named methodologist, no sample size, or a sponsor with a stake

Evidence-source preference order

1. Scientific consensus via responsible aggregators (science journalists, university and government resources, credible professional bodies)

2. Independent expert review with side-by-side comparative testing under standardized conditions (Consumer Reports, Wirecutter)

3. Multiple independent expert sources cross-checked (experts can also be incentivized)

4. Actual humans you know, face to face

5. — hard stop —

6. Consumer star ratings and aggregate scores (ignore for anything with objective quality)

When consensus is genuinely unsettled

  • Consensus well known (smoking, exercise, vaccines, climate, flat Earth) → act on it
  • Consensus findable but less known (GMO safety, most supplements, homeopathy) → look it up via aggregators
  • Consensus in flux (psychedelics for mental health, probiotics, parabens) → seek independent expert advice; do not let a single study or a confident podcaster settle it
  • Assume you underestimate how strong consensus is — the public reliably does, because contrarians are overrepresented

Judging a contrarian claim

  • Was it raised and tested in a scientific venue, or proclaimed on podcasts and cable news? → venue is the discriminator
  • Plate tectonics and bacterial ulcers won because data eventually supported them, not because the proponents were disbelieved
  • Does the claimant have relevant expertise, something to sell, and a story about what thousands of researchers missed?

glossary.md

Glossary — The Certainty Illusion

Accuracy nudge — A prompt shifting attention to accuracy before sharing; measurably raises the quality of news people share (Pennycook & Rand) (Ch 14)

AI as "weapon of mass disruption" — Eurasia Group's 2023 designation: content volume rising past most citizens' ability to sort fact from fiction (Ch 5)

Anchoring effect — An inflated average rating becomes the reference point pulling honest reviewers' own ratings upward (Ch 11)

Animal magnetism — Mesmer's 1779 magnets-and-magnetic-fluid pitch; the historical prototype of scienceploitation (Ch 1)

Appeal to nature fallacy — Presuming what is natural is inherently good, safe, or better; refuted by arsenic, venom, lightning (Ch 6)

Attentional bias — Focusing on some elements and ignoring others, obscuring alternative explanations (Ch 8)

Backlash — The "it's all so confusing, I give up" effect; conflicting health information causes outright rejection of new recommendations (Ch 10)

Body-of-evidence test — Judging a claim against the weight of existing literature and the scientific consensus rather than any single study (Ch 3, Ch 14)

Bro-science — Cherry-picked data, anecdote, and guru testimonial offered in place of real science (Ch 9)

Catastrophizing — Overstating the potential harms of emerging science; the mirror image of hype (Ch 3)

Certainty grift — Selling false certainty about both a virtuous goal and the path to it, monetizing the gap between wanting to do good and doing it (Ch 10)

Certainty illusion — The book's thesis: the more we seek certainty, the harder it becomes to find, because valued guideposts attract distortion (Ch 0)

Certainty Six — Caulfield's six personal strategies: pause for accuracy; watch for scienceploitation; resist hype; scrutinize goodness marketing; consult the body of evidence; like what you like (Ch 14)

Chemophobia — Fear of "chemicals," where the word has drifted from all physical matter to a stand-in for artificial and unsafe (Ch 6)

Choice supportive bias — Post-purchase rationalization; verified reviewers already paid, so they are motivated to report liking it (Ch 11)

Clean beauty — An undefined, circular market category promising safety without specifying a standard (Ch 7)

Confirmation bias — Finding, favouring, and remembering information that supports pre-existing belief (Ch 2, Ch 8)

Devious Dozen — Caulfield's list of pervasive health-halo terms: natural, holistic, healthy, organic, non-GMO, gluten-free, chemical-free, toxin-free, locally grown, the colour green, immune-boosting, personalized (Ch 6)

Dose makes the poison — Anything harms at some dose and is safe at a low enough one, making "toxin-free" content-free (Ch 6)

Dunning-Kruger effect — Overestimating one's knowledge because lacking knowledge impedes recognizing the lack (Ch 2, Ch 12)

Faux research — Frank Graves' term for flawed or fabricated polling that corrodes the public interest (Ch 13)

Fake review cycle — Business buys fakes, sells more, buys platform ads with the gain; platform, business, and faker all profit, only consumers lose (Ch 11)

Fear marketing — Selling by manufacturing anxiety about conventional products; the cosmetics industry's fallback (Ch 7)

Galileo gambit — Answering the weight of evidence with a persecution narrative: "they laughed at Galileo too" (Ch 2)

Goldilocks zone (4.2–4.5 stars) — The believably-good rating band that sophisticated fakers target, adding small complaints for credibility (Ch 11, Ch 12)

Goodness bias — Perceived moral worthiness warping judgment, evidence evaluation, and research conduct (Ch 8)

Goodness illusion — A messaging strategy making a choice feel like the right thing without close examination (Ch 0, Ch 6)

Great flattening of knowledge — A race to the bottom in which real science, worthy goals, and valued opinion become equally meaningless (Ch 0)

Health halo — A word or phrase creating an immediate impression of health or virtue that the evidence does not support (Ch 6)

Hijacked journal — Criminal cloning of a legitimate journal's name and domain to harvest publication fees; fraud, distinct from predatory publishing (Ch 4)

Hot stuff bias — Grant applications converging on whatever field is currently fundable (Ch 3)

Hype — Exaggerated claims of potential benefit and social impact, generated at every stage of the knowledge pipeline (Ch 3)

Illusory superiority — Believing fakes fool other people but not you (Ch 12)

Impact merchants — How senior academics describe themselves; "marketizing" research as a survival requirement (Ch 3)

Incentivized review — A review paid or discounted into existence; inflates ratings 40–70%; FTC requires disclosure (Ch 11)

Incidental similarities — Non-political common ground that increases closeness and openness to opposing political views (Ch 13)

Infodemic — The WHO's term for harmful misinformation spreading like an infectious disease (Ch 0)

Intention-behaviour gap — Wanting to do good without converting it into behaviour; only ~2.7% of Americans live a healthy lifestyle (Ch 10)

Knowledge asymmetry rule — The more expertise separates you from a provider, the less any review tracks actual quality (Ch 12)

Knowledge production crisis — Degradation of the methods and institutions that make knowledge, distinct from downstream misinformation (Ch 0)

Literature pollution — Fake and low-quality papers entering databases, then systematic reviews, guidelines, and policy (Ch 4, Ch 5)

Marketing placebo effect — Price and brand altering measured experience; pricier wine tastes better (Ch 11)

Masculinity as a health halo — "Manly" functioning as an unargued proxy for good, lending certainty to unproven interventions (Ch 9)

Motivated reasoning — Selecting evidence and arguments to endorse a preferred outcome (Ch 5, Ch 8)

Motte-and-bailey fallacy — Advancing a weak controversial claim, then retreating to an unobjectionable truism when challenged (Ch 7)

Negativity bias — Encoding and remembering negative information more strongly (Ch 1)

Paper mill — A multi-million-dollar industry selling authorship on publications with faked or poor-quality data (Ch 5)

Pareidolia — Seeing meaningful patterns in random data; amplified by prior belief (Ch 8)

Post-retraction citation — Continued citation of retracted work; only 5.4% of such citations acknowledge the retraction (Ch 5)

Precarious manhood principle — Men devaluing feminine-coded brand names to defend masculinity (Ch 11)

Predatory journal — A publication charging author fees with lax or nonexistent peer review; est. 11,000–16,000 exist (Ch 4)

Pseudoarchaeology — Origin myths dressed as research; the ancient alien narrative and its extremist linkages (Ch 8)

Pseudo-profound bullshit — Syntactically coherent but meaningless word salad deployed to impress through vagueness (Ch 2)

Publish or perish — The pressure regime creating the market for predatory journals, paper mills, and salami science (Ch 4, Ch 14)

Retraction attention paradox — Retracted papers drawing more attention over ten years than never-retracted ones (Ch 5)

Sagan standard — Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence; scale required proof to improbability (Ch 2)

Salami science — Slicing one project into many small papers to manufacture apparent productivity (Ch 14)

Science washing — Deploying "science" as a generic legitimizing badge — graphs, numbers, jargon (Michelle Wong) (Ch 1)

Science-y — Sounding scientific without being scientific; jargon as celebrity endorsement (Ch 1)

Science-y / scary dyad — Science-sounding jargon plus a fear message; the most durable misinformation engine (Ch 1)

Scienceploitation — Using scientific verbiage and hot research topics to market unproven or harmful products and agendas (Ch 0, Ch 1)

Scientism — Inappropriately deferential attitude to science; treating it as inherently good and infallible (Ch 1)

Scientific consensus — Solid pieces of evidence all pointing the same direction; emerges slowly, iteratively, unglamorously (Ch 14)

Single study syndrome — Treating one study as decisive, especially when it flatters priors or supplies a contrarian thrill (Ch 5, Ch 14)

Social influence bias — Prior positive reviews raising subsequent ratings via positive herding (+32% likelihood, +25% final ratings) (Ch 11)

Spin — Distortion in the reporting of results; ~40% of biomedical abstracts contain some (Ch 3)

Spiral of silence — Withholding opinions believed to be in the minority, so visible consensus silences dissent (Ch 13)

Substitution risk — Replacing a well-studied ingredient with a poorly studied "natural" one is information loss, not a safety gain (Ch 7)

Super contributor — A high-volume reviewer for whom reviewing is identity and brand; disproportionately influential (Ch 11)

Transportation — Narrative immersion producing emotional investment that persists after viewing (Ch 10)

Vanity / agenda-driven journal — A purpose-built pretend journal created to legitimize a predetermined position (Ch 4)

White hat bias — Distortion of research-based information in the service of perceived righteous ends (Allison & Cope) (Ch 8)

Wishful thinking — The perception traps that let us construct the certainty we want (Ch 8)

Zombie science — Discredited or retracted findings that keep circulating and influencing debate after correction (Ch 5)

patterns.md

Patterns — Techniques from The Certainty Illusion

The Certainty Six

When to use: As a standing checklist for any consequential claim you encounter or are about to share.

How: (1) Pause and recognize the information ecosystem isn't rigged for accuracy — ask "is this accurate?" before sharing. (2) Watch for scienceploitation. (3) Resist the allure of science hype. (4) Take a closer look when goodness is used as a marketing strategy. (5) Always consider the existing body of evidence. (6) Like what you like.

Trade-offs: Deliberately low-effort by design, so it will not catch sophisticated fraud. It is a filter for the 90% of everyday claims, not an audit.

The Accuracy Pause

When to use: The instant before sharing, forwarding, or acting on any headline, meme, or post.

How: Take a beat and ask yourself whether this is accurate before you hit share (David Rand's phrasing). No fact-checking required — the attentional shift alone does the work.

Trade-offs: Highest return per unit of effort in the book, but it only counters the impulsive channel; motivated, deliberate belief is untouched by it.

Scienceploitation Detection

When to use: Any claim leaning on scientific vocabulary to persuade.

How: (1) Is the claim riding a hot topic — stem cells, regenerative medicine, genomics, nanotech, microbiome, quantum, AI? (2) Does actual research support it, or is the buzzword itself doing the persuading? Does the mechanism make conceptual sense, or is it science-y word salad? (3) Are the scientific trappings appearing inside a field already associated with pseudoscience? (4) Are risks and limitations stated — absence is diagnostic. (5) Check what the field's own governing body says is actually clinic-ready.

Trade-offs: Produces false positives on genuinely novel legitimate work, which also uses new vocabulary. Resolve with the range-of-sources test.

The Quantum Test

When to use: A health product or procedure is explained using the word quantum.

How: Stop evaluating. Assume pseudoscience and a fraudster nearby. Physicist Mark Freeman has never seen quantum used accurately in a health product claim.

Trade-offs: A blunt heuristic with essentially no false-negative cost in the consumer-health domain; do not export it to physics contexts.

The Sagan Standard

When to use: Evaluating any contrarian, fringe, or "they don't want you to know" claim.

How: Assess plausibility against the existing knowledge base; assess the claimant (relevant expertise? selling something? claiming to know what thousands of researchers and mountains of data missed?); scale the required proof to the improbability. Onus stays with the claimant.

Trade-offs: Conservative by construction — it will slow acceptance of the rare valid revolution. Caulfield accepts this: real revolutions survive testing.

Dismantling the Galileo Gambit

When to use: Someone answers evidence with a persecution narrative.

How: (1) Galileo faced a religious orthodoxy, not a scientific consensus. (2) Sagan's rebuttal — they laughed at Bozo the Clown too. (3) Real revolutionaries produced data tested against the conventions of their time. (4) Classify it as a defence of last resort, not an argument, and return to the body of evidence.

Trade-offs: Rhetorically satisfying but rarely persuades the claimant; its value is protecting the audience.

The Humility Inventory

When to use: Before forming or publicly defending a position on contested evidence.

How: List areas in your personal and professional life where evidence evolved and you changed position. Separately list the grey areas where you are still gathering information. An empty list is itself the finding.

Trade-offs: Self-report, so it is gameable — but the exercise is diagnostic precisely because most people find it harder than expected.

The Red-Flag Audit for a Single Study

When to use: Someone waves one paper at you as proof.

How: Check (1) the publisher — known predatory operator? (2) author affiliation — vague or mimicking a real institution? (3) submission-to-acceptance interval — biomedical papers average ~100 days; two weeks means no real review. (4) ethics review conducted? (5) methods — control group, blinding, standardization, sample size. (6) the author's regulatory history. (7) retraction status. (8) citation pattern — do a breadth of other academics cite it?

Trade-offs: Time-consuming and requires some literacy in academic publishing. Reserve it for claims that actually matter to a decision.

The Body-of-Evidence Test

When to use: Any extraordinary, contrarian, or personally flattering claim.

How: (1) Refuse single study syndrome. (2) Name your own bias on the topic first. (3) Check venue and retraction status. (4) Ask what the scientific consensus is and find it via responsible aggregators — good science communicators, science journalists, university resources, credible professional organizations, competent governments, mainstream media.

Trade-offs: Consensus is slow-moving and genuinely lags on emerging topics; for those, seek independent expert advice rather than a settled answer.

The Range-of-Sources Breakthrough Test

When to use: A dramatic scientific result is being reported.

How: Ask whether you are hearing it from a range of independent reputable sources or from exactly one commercially interested channel — a clinic's website, a wellness influencer, a podcaster. Real breakthroughs propagate broadly.

Trade-offs: Introduces lag; you will be late to genuine news. That lag is the point.

Health Halo Deconstruction

When to use: Any product label or wellness claim leaning on a positive-sounding adjective.

How: (1) Ask what the word actually means — is it defined by any regulator? (2) Ask what it implies — usually "healthier/safer." (3) Check whether the implied claim is supported. (4) The gap between (1) and (3) is the halo. For food: assume health-halo terms are meaningless or misleading, read the ingredient list, and default to real food.

Trade-offs: Some halo terms encode real production facts (organic means something about farming) — the error is inferring nutrition or safety from them.

The Evil-Spirits-Free Substitution

When to use: A product claims to be "toxin-free," "chemical-free," or similar.

How: Substitute "evil-spirits-free" and re-read. If the claim still feels persuasive, you are responding to vibe rather than content.

Trade-offs: A rhetorical check, not an ingredient assessment; it will not tell you whether a specific ingredient is a problem.

Separating the Goal from the Intervention

When to use: Any pitch framing a product as serving an obviously virtuous end — safety, sustainability, masculinity, doing right by your kids.

How: (1) Isolate the goal. (2) Ask whether the goal was argued for or merely assumed. (3) Ask what evidence supports this intervention for that goal. (4) Check whether the pitch first manufactured insecurity in order to sell the fix.

Trade-offs: Watch for the motte-and-bailey retreat — challenge the specific claim, and expect a fallback to the unarguable truism.

The Emotional-Signal Check

When to use: Before sharing anything politically or morally charged.

How: Kate Starbird's rule — when content makes you feel politically self-righteous, that is precisely the moment to be extra careful about sharing. Misinformation is measurably easier to process, more emotional, scarier, and more focused on morality than accurate content.

Trade-offs: Requires honest introspection in exactly the moment when you least want to slow down.

The Review Escape Plan

When to use: Any purchase, booking, or professional choice driven by ratings.

How: (1) Be very skeptical of online reviews. (2) Seek side-by-side comparisons under standardized conditions. (3) Go to independent expert outlets — Consumer Reports, Wirecutter, professional video reviews. (4) Use multiple comparative sources, since experts can also be incentivized. (5) Ignore star ratings and aggregate scores. (6) Assume you cannot detect fakes; watch legacy red flags but never conclude the rest are genuine. (7) For professionals and physicians, know the profound limitations and use with extreme caution. (8) Ask who is doing the reviewing and whether their tastes are relevant to yours. (9) Talk to actual humans, face to face. (10) Keep an open mind, try things, and like what you like.

Trade-offs: Expert comparatives don't exist for every category, and don't apply to genuinely subjective goods — for those, find critics whose taste consistently matches yours.

The Four Poll Questions

When to use: A survey or poll result is being cited at you.

How: (1) How big is the sample — ~1,000 respondents is reasonable for a national survey. (2) Is it representative — random selection, or a self-selecting open internet poll? (3) Who did the research — survey experts or an influencer? (4) Any obvious biases, such as a sponsor with a vested interest? Plus: check question wording for leading phrasing.

Trade-offs: You often cannot get answers to all four; inability to answer them is itself a verdict. Standard: sound survey research should mirror public opinion, not shape it.

Bridge-Building via Incidental Similarities

When to use: Trying to reach someone across a political or ideological divide.

How: Establish non-political common ground first — shared interests, experiences, tastes. Incidental similarities increase felt closeness and, in turn, openness to opposing political views.

Trade-offs: Slow, individual-scale, and not a substitute for correcting the record; but it works where argument does not.

Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Atomic Habits (decision aid)

The core decision: build or break?

StepTo BUILD a good habitTo BREAK a bad habit
1. CueMake it ObviousMake it Invisible
2. CravingMake it AttractiveMake it Unattractive
3. ResponseMake it EasyMake it Difficult
4. RewardMake it SatisfyingMake it Unsatisfying

Which law do I reach for? (diagnose the failing step)

  • "I keep forgetting / never get around to it" → 1st Law: implementation intention, habit stacking, environment cue.
  • "I don't feel like doing it" → 2nd Law: temptation bundling, join a culture where it's normal, reframe "get to."
  • "It's too much effort / I start too big" → 3rd Law: Two-Minute Rule, reduce friction, prime the environment.
  • "I do it once then drop it" → 4th Law: immediate reward, habit tracking, never miss twice, accountability.

Fill-in formulas (memorize these)

  • Implementation intention: "I will [BEHAVIOR] at [TIME] in [LOCATION]."
  • Habit stacking: "After [CURRENT HABIT], I will [NEW HABIT]."
  • Temptation bundling: "After [HABIT I NEED], I will [HABIT I WANT]."
  • Identity: "I am the type of person who [does X]." → prove with small wins.

Rules of thumb & thresholds

  • 1% better/day ≈ 37× in a year; 1% worse/day ≈ near zero.
  • Two-Minute Rule: any new habit must start in < 2 minutes.
  • Never miss twice: one miss = accident; two = new habit. Recover next day.
  • Goldilocks / sweet spot: aim for ~50% success rate; flow ≈ ~4% beyond current skill.
  • Immediacy > magnitude: a small instant reward beats a big delayed one.
  • Frequency > time: count reps, not days, to build automaticity.

Tells & smells (recognize the trap)

  • You're reading/planning/researching a lot but not doing → motion, not action (Ch 11).
  • "I'll start Monday / when I'm ready" → readiness is a byproduct of reps, not a prerequisite.
  • Relying on willpower to resist a visible cue → self-control is short-term; remove the cue instead.
  • "No thanks, I'm trying to quit" → still the old identity; say "I'm not a [X]."
  • One slip → "I've blown it" → all-or-nothing thinking; apply never-miss-twice.
  • Habit feels boring so you seek novelty → boredom is the threshold pros push through, not a stop sign.

Goals vs. Systems

  • Goal = direction (fine for setting aim). System = the process (what actually moves you).
  • "You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems."
  • If you keep resetting the same goal → fix the system/inputs, not the outcome.

The three questions to find your fit (Ch 18)

1. What feels like fun to me but work to others?

2. What makes me lose track of time?

3. Where do I get greater returns than the average person?

→ If you can't win by being better, win by being different.

Sustaining loop (Advanced)

Mastery = Habits + Deliberate Practice, kept honest by Reflection & Review (Annual Review + midyear Integrity Report). Keep identity flexible so growth doesn't threaten who you are.

glossary.md

Glossary — Atomic Habits

Aggregation of Marginal Gains — the philosophy of improving every component of a system by ~1%; small gains compound into decisive results (Ch 1).

Annual Review — yearly reflection: what went well, what didn't, what I learned (Ch 20).

Atomic Habit — a tiny, easy routine that is also a building block of a larger system of compound growth (Ch 1).

Automaticity — the state where a behavior runs without conscious thought, reached through repetition (Ch 3, 11).

Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change — what is immediately rewarded is repeated; what is immediately punished is avoided (Ch 15).

Commitment Device — a present choice that controls your future actions, locking in good behavior in advance (Ch 14).

Craving — the motivational force behind a habit; the anticipation of a reward / desire for a change in state (Ch 3, 8).

Cue — the trigger that initiates a habit by predicting a reward (Ch 3).

Decisive Moments — small daily forks (cook vs. takeout) that set the options available to your future self (Ch 13).

Deliberate Practice — focused effort to improve specific weaknesses; paired with habits it produces mastery (Ch 20).

Diderot Effect — obtaining something new spirals into further consumption/behaviors; behaviors chain (Ch 5).

Environment Design — arranging surroundings so good-habit cues are obvious and bad-habit cues invisible (Ch 6, 7).

Explore/Exploit Trade-off — sample options early (explore), then double down on the best fit (exploit) (Ch 18).

Fall in Love with Boredom — pros stick to the schedule when it's dull; boredom is the main threat to lasting habits (Ch 19).

Fit — the match between a habit/field and your natural temperament; good fit multiplies returns (Ch 18).

Flow State — full immersion "in the zone," reachable when challenge is ~4% beyond current ability (Ch 19).

Four Laws of Behavior Change — Make it Obvious, Attractive, Easy, Satisfying (build); invert to break (Ch 3).

Frequency, Not Time — habits form from number of repetitions, not days elapsed (Ch 11).

Gateway Habit — the ≤2-minute entry point on the path to a larger goal (Ch 13).

Goldilocks Rule — peak motivation comes from tasks of just manageable difficulty — not too hard, not too easy (Ch 19).

Habit — a behavior repeated enough to become automatic; a reliable solution to a recurring problem (Ch 3).

Habit Contract — a written, witnessed agreement stating a habit and the penalty for failing (Ch 17).

Habit Loop — Cue → Craving → Response → Reward, the neurological feedback cycle of every habit (Ch 3).

Habit Shaping — scaling a two-minute habit up in stages, mastering the first two minutes of each level (Ch 13).

Habit Stacking — pairing a new habit with a current one: "After [CURRENT HABIT], I will [NEW HABIT]" (Ch 5).

Habit Tracking — measuring whether you did a habit; obvious, attractive, and satisfying at once (Ch 16).

Habits Scorecard — listing daily habits and scoring each +/–/= against your desired identity (Ch 4).

Identity-Based Habits — habits chosen from who you wish to become rather than what you want to achieve (Ch 2).

Immediate-Return vs. Delayed-Return Environment — ancestral rewards were instant; modern good habits pay off later (Ch 15).

Implementation Intention — a pre-set plan: "I will [BEHAVIOR] at [TIME] in [LOCATION]" (Ch 5).

Integrity Report — midyear reflection on core values and whether you're living them (Ch 20).

Inversion of the Four Laws — Make it Invisible, Unattractive, Difficult, Unsatisfying (to break habits) (Ch 3, 7, 10, 14, 17).

Lagging Measure — an outcome (weight, net worth) that trails the habits producing it (Ch 1).

Law of Least Effort — behavior gravitates to the option requiring the least energy (Ch 12).

Motion vs. Action — motion is planning/preparing; action is the rep that produces results (Ch 11).

Never Miss Twice — a slip is fine; two in a row starts a bad habit — recover immediately (Ch 16).

One Space, One Use — give each context a single association so cues don't compete (Ch 6).

Plateau of Latent Potential — the phase where effort is "stored" before results appear (Ch 1).

Pointing-and-Calling — saying actions aloud to make automatic behavior conscious (Ch 4).

Priming the Environment — pre-arranging surroundings so the next good action is ready to go (Ch 12).

Reflection and Review — periodic review that prevents habits from becoming mindless and off-course (Ch 20).

Reward — the end of the loop that satisfies the craving and teaches the brain to repeat the cue (Ch 3).

Sweet Spot of Desire (50/50) — motivation peaks near a 50/50 split of success and failure (Ch 19).

Systems vs. Goals — goals set direction; systems drive progress. "You fall to the level of your systems" (Ch 1).

Temptation Bundling — linking a wanted action to a needed one: "After [NEED], I will [WANT]" (Ch 8).

Three Layers of Behavior Change — Outcomes → Processes → Identity; change from the inside out (Ch 2).

Three Social Groups We Imitate — the Close, the Many, the Powerful (Ch 9).

Two-Minute Rule — a new habit should take less than two minutes to start (Ch 13).

Valley of Disappointment — the stretch where effort feels wasted before results surface (Ch 1).

Votes (for an identity) — each habit is a piece of evidence for the type of person you're becoming (Ch 2).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Atomic Habits

Concrete, reusable techniques with their fill-in formulas. Organized by which Law they serve.

Implementation Intention (1st Law)

When to use: any habit you keep forgetting or postponing.

How: write I will [BEHAVIOR] at [TIME] in [LOCATION].

Trade-offs: requires specificity up front; vague versions don't fire.

Habit Stacking (1st Law)

When to use: you have reliable daily habits to anchor to.

How: After [CURRENT HABIT], I will [NEW HABIT]. Chain several into a routine.

Trade-offs: the anchor habit must itself be rock-solid, or the chain breaks.

Environment Design / Make the Cue Obvious (1st Law)

When to use: any good habit you want automatic.

How: place the cue in your line of sight; give each space one dedicated use.

Trade-offs: only as strong as the most obvious competing cue.

Habits Scorecard (1st Law — awareness)

When to use: before changing anything.

How: list every daily habit → mark +/–/= vs. your desired identity.

Trade-offs: awareness only; no change without follow-through.

Pointing-and-Calling (Inverted 1st Law)

When to use: catching an automatic bad habit in the act.

How: say the action and its consequence aloud.

Trade-offs: works in the moment; doesn't remove the cue.

Remove the Cue / Make It Invisible (Inverted 1st Law)

When to use: breaking an environment-triggered bad habit.

How: delete the trigger — phone in another room, snack out of the house.

Trade-offs: requires controlling the environment; harder in shared/public spaces.

Temptation Bundling (2nd Law)

When to use: a good habit that isn't intrinsically appealing.

How: After [HABIT I NEED], I will [HABIT I WANT]. Allow the craved thing only with the needed thing.

Trade-offs: pick a "want" that doesn't cancel the habit's benefit.

Join the Right Culture (2nd Law)

When to use: making a habit socially attractive.

How: join a group where the desired behavior is normal and you share common ground.

Trade-offs: the same force works against you in the wrong group.

Reframe / Highlight Benefits (2nd Law & inverted)

When to use: making good habits attractive, bad habits unattractive.

How: "get to" not "have to"; associate a bad habit with its true hidden costs.

Trade-offs: mindset shift takes repetition to stick.

Reduce Friction / Prime the Environment (3rd Law)

When to use: any good habit.

How: cut steps and decisions; set up in advance (clothes out, gear ready).

Trade-offs: setup effort now for effortlessness later.

Two-Minute Rule (3rd Law)

When to use: starting or reviving any habit.

How: scale it to <2 minutes (the gateway habit); master showing up, then use habit shaping to scale up.

Trade-offs: risk of staying at two minutes forever — shape upward once established.

Add Friction / Commitment Device (Inverted 3rd Law)

When to use: bad habits you'll rationalize away in the moment.

How: increase steps for bad habits; lock in good ones with a present decision (auto-transfer savings, delete the app, one-time purchases).

Trade-offs: must set it up while willpower is high.

Add an Immediate Reward (4th Law)

When to use: good habits with delayed payoff (saving, exercise).

How: attach a small instant reward that reinforces your desired identity.

Trade-offs: reward must not contradict the habit (no ice cream after the gym).

Habit Tracking / Don't Break the Chain (4th Law)

When to use: sustaining consistency.

How: mark each completion (calendar X, jar, app); keep the streak alive.

Trade-offs: don't let the metric become the goal; keep it simple.

Never Miss Twice (4th Law)

When to use: recovering from a slip.

How: the day after a miss, do at least the two-minute version.

Trade-offs: none — the key defense against all-or-nothing collapse.

Habit Contract / Accountability Partner (Inverted 4th Law)

When to use: high-stakes bad habits needing external teeth.

How: write the habit, schedule, and immediate penalty; have partners co-sign.

Trade-offs: needs a trustworthy partner who'll enforce it.

Explore/Exploit + Pick the Right Game (Advanced)

When to use: choosing which habits/fields to commit to.

How: sample broadly, then double down where you have natural fit; if you can't be better, be different.

Trade-offs: over-exploring delays mastery; over-exploiting too early risks the wrong game.

Goldilocks Tuning (Advanced)

When to use: sustaining long-term motivation.

How: keep difficulty at just-manageable (~50% success); raise the bar in small steps.

Trade-offs: too easy → boredom; too hard → discouragement.

Habits + Deliberate Practice + Review (Advanced)

When to use: pursuing mastery, not just consistency.

How: automate fundamentals via habit, deliberately push weaknesses, run Annual Review + Integrity Report.

Trade-offs: reflection takes scheduled time; skipping it invites complacency.

Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Changing World Order (Dalio's judgment, distilled)

Decision Rules (if X → do/expect Y, because Z)

  • If all three big cycles are in good phases → country is strong and rising; if all three are bad → weak and declining. (The 3: debt/money, internal order, external order.)
  • If a government has bankrupt finances AND big wealth gaps → treat civil war/revolution as the single most likely lead outcome — a broke government can't save the system.
  • If a country runs big deficits producing more debt than non-central-bank buyers will absorb → it's the Stage-5 trigger toward Stage 6 (must raise taxes/cut spending, or print heavily).
  • If debt is in your own currency → expect devaluation, not default (repay 50–70% in real terms). If in a currency you can't print → expect true default.
  • If real interest rates are deeply negative late in the debt cycle → don't hold cash/bonds; buy "any stuff" that keeps pace with inflation (the payback period is the longest ever).
  • If you see capital controls on a currency during a domestic debt problem → run from that currency.
  • If money/credit is being printed cheaply → own assets (asset value is the reciprocal of money's value; money's value is the reciprocal of its quantity).
  • If a rival's power ≈ yours AND differences are existential/irreconcilable → highest war risk; trade red lines to avoid it.
  • If your relative power is declining → fight/negotiate EARLY; if rising → LATER.
  • If you don't want to be in a civil war → get out late in Stage 5, while the doors (and capital) are still open.
  • If a great power cuts off a rival's ESSENTIAL imports (oil, chips, rare earths) → major escalation toward a shooting war.

Cycle Clocks (rough durations — read conditions, not the calendar)

CycleTypical length
Short-term debt ("business") cycle~8 years
Long-term debt cycle~50–75 years (6–10 short cycles)
Internal order cycle~100 years
Big Cycle of an empire~250 years (±150)
Bad destruction/restructuring period~10–20 years
Peaceful prosperous period~40–80 years
Left/right political swings~10 years

The 6 Internal-Order Stages → the leader each needs

StageConditionBest leader
1New order, consolidate powerConsolidator of power
2Build systems/bureaucracyCivil engineer
3Peace & prosperity (sweet spot)Inspirational visionary
4Excess / bubbleDisciplined restrainer (rare)
5Bad finances + conflictStrong peacemaker (ideal) or fighter
6Civil war / revolutionInspirational general

Stage-5 → Stage-6 Tells (watch these on any country, esp. the US)

Decadence · high bureaucracy blocking good decisions · populism & polarization (moderates vanish) · class warfare + scapegoating · loss of truth in media · rules disregarded · blood spilled = Stage 6 has begun.

The 4 Debt-Reduction Levers (order of use)

1. Austerity (deflationary, brief) → 2. Defaults/restructurings (deflationary, painful) → 3. Transfers/taxes (political) → 4. Print & devalue (most expedient, most common).

The Rise Sequence (and it reverses in the same order)

Education → innovation/tech → competitiveness → output & trade share → military → financial center → reserve currency (last to rise, last to fall).

Reserve-Currency Reserves Snapshot (~2019)

USD 51% · EUR 20% · Gold 12% · JPY 6% · GBP 5% · CNY 2%. No attractive alternative to the dollar — but a currency devalues anyway as capital flees to gold/commodities/stocks/property.

Current Readings (as of the book, 2021)

  • US: ~70% (±10%) through its Big Cycle; internal order Stage 5; ~30% civil-war-dynamic odds in 10 yrs.
  • China: internal order Stage 3 (peace/prosperity); rising fast; roughly tied with US in trade/output/innovation.
  • US-China: in 4 of 5 wars (trade/tech/capital/geopolitical), not military; ~35% odds of a big war in 10 yrs; MAD holds it down.
  • Biggest long-run risk: currency-value-of-money (creditors' assets devalued below inflation), not debtor default.

Portfolio Rules of Thumb

  • Risk = failing to meet your needs (unmet-needs, ruin, confiscation) — not volatility.
  • All markets driven by: growth, inflation, risk premiums, discount rates.
  • Diversify so no environmental bias; tilt tactically. Beware survivorship bias (don't extrapolate US/UK only).
  • In war: sell debt, buy gold (printing devalues money/debt; credit isn't accepted).
  • Ask constantly: does the interest compensate for the devaluation risk?

One-Line Principles

  • "Peace is profitable and war is costly." · "Power rules; tests of power reveal who rules."
  • "All currencies devalue or die." · "Debt eats equity — but central banks feed debt by printing."
  • "Bet on evolution's upside, but not so much that a bump knocks you out."
  • "In war, the ability to withstand pain matters more than the ability to inflict it."
  • The best way to win a war: get strong and show it, so the opponent won't fight. "Deserve Victory!"

glossary.md

Glossary — Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order

Acts of Nature — Droughts, floods, pandemics; historically bigger killers than wars/depressions and a determinant of decline (Ch 2, 14).

Anti-capitalist phase — Decline-era backlash blaming capitalism, capitalists, and elites; drives redistribution and populism (Ch 1, 5).

Balance of Power Cycle — The timeless allies-and-enemies dynamic driving struggles for power, internal and external (Ch 2, 6).

Beautiful deleveraging — Creating enough money/devaluation to offset a deflationary depression without triggering an inflationary spiral (Ch 3).

Big Cycle — The self-reinforcing rise-and-decline arc of an empire (~250 yrs), composed of the three cycles + 18 determinants (Ch 1).

Big Five — The five most important forces: the 3 cycles + innovation/technology + acts of nature (Ch 2).

Bretton Woods (1944/45) — The post-WWII monetary system linking the dollar to gold and other currencies to the dollar; start of the current long-term debt cycle (Ch 3, 11).

Capital war — Conflict via sanctions, asset freezes, and blocking capital-market access ("no money = no power") (Ch 6, 13).

Classic Toxic Mix — Bad finances + large wealth/values gaps + a severe negative economic shock; ignites big internal conflict (Ch 5).

Culture is destiny — Cultural differences in how people believe they should treat each other matter enormously (Ch 2).

Debt eats equity — Debt is senior and must be paid first, forcing asset sales — "but central banks can feed debt by printing money" (Ch 3).

Decadence — Late-cycle shift of time/money from productive investment to luxury/consumption; reduces productivity, breeds resentment (Ch 5).

Determinant — A single causal factor (e.g., money supply); a cycle is a self-reinforcing chain of determinants (Ch 2).

Determinants (18) — The measurable + qualitative forces explaining rises/declines; 8 headline powers + inherited + human/cultural factors (Ch 2).

Eight measures of power — Education, competitiveness, innovation/technology, economic output, share of world trade, military, financial-center, reserve-currency status (Ch 1).

Evolution + cycles (the upward corkscrew) — Steady productivity uptrend with pendulum cycles around it (Ch 1).

Exorbitant/extraordinary privilege — A reserve-currency issuer's ability to borrow cheaply and abundantly — which sows the seeds of its decline (Ch 1, 3).

Fiat money (Type 3) — Money not linked to anything of intrinsic value; printable without restriction (Ch 3).

Financial economy vs. real economy — Two systems with separate supply/demand; central banks move money/credit to steer the real economy imperfectly (Ch 3).

Financial wealth — Promises to deliver money (cash, bonds, stocks); no intrinsic value — only what it buys is useful. Invented ~1350 in Italy (Ch 2, 7).

Guns and butter — A country must fund both military strength and domestic living standards without excess (Ch 6, 11).

Hard money (Type 1) — Money with intrinsic value (gold, silver, copper coins) (Ch 3).

Human capital / "self-sufficient plus" — People (or countries) who produce more than they spend; the most sustainable capital (Ch 2).

Inflationary depression — Monetary inflation (currency devaluation) coexisting with real-economy deflation (Ch 3).

Internal order cycle (6 stages) — New order → build systems → peace/prosperity → excess → bad finances/conflict → civil war → repeat (~100 yrs) (Ch 5).

Legalism — Chinese philosophy favoring autocratic conquest and strict obedience; Western equivalent = fascism (Ch 12).

Linked currency system (Type 2) — Paper notes convertible to hard money at a fixed rate (Ch 3).

Long-term debt cycle — ~50–75 yr arc across 6 stages ending in debt/monetary restructuring; contains 6–10 short-term (~8 yr) cycles (Ch 3).

Mandate of heaven — The Chinese conception of legitimate rule that persists while the dynasty's approach works (Ch 12).

Monetary Policy 1/2/3 (MP1/MP2/MP3) — MP1 = interest rates; MP2 = printing to buy assets (QE); MP3 = fiscal-monetary coordination (govt spends, central bank buys the debt) (Ch 4, 11).

Monetary systems (Type 1/2/3) — Hard money → paper claims on hard money → fiat; countries rotate 1→2→3 then back (Ch 3).

New world order — The system of power set by the winners after a big war (Westphalia 1648, Vienna 1815, Versailles 1919, 1945) (Ch 6, 8).

Populism — Anti-elite politics of ordinary people; of the left or right; a Stage-5 marker (Ch 5).

Prisoner's dilemma — Game-theory reason rivals attack first; peace requires mutually assured protections (Ch 2, 6).

Real wealth — Goods with intrinsic value (house, car) — distinct from financial wealth (Ch 2).

Reserve currency — A widely saved/traded currency; grants cheap borrowing; the last strength to fade in a decline (Ch 1, 3).

Resulting / survivorship bias — Judging by (limited, winner-only) samples; using US/UK returns as "representative" distorts perspective (Ch 7).

Run (on the bank) — More claims on hard currency than the bank can satisfy; forces default or devaluation (Ch 3, 4).

Short-term debt cycle — "The business cycle," ~8 years (Ch 3).

Systemically beneficial vs. destructive devaluation — Debt relief that flows into productivity (beneficial) vs. one that wrecks the credit system but wipes out debt (destructive) (Ch 4).

Three big cycles — Money/credit/debt; internal order/disorder; external order/disorder (Ch 2).

Win-win vs. lose-lose — Relationship types both parties choose; win-win (grow and divide the pie) beats fighting (Ch 2, 6).

World order — The prevailing system of power domestically and internationally; changes when leading powers change (Ch 1).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — The Changing World Order

Concrete, reusable methods from the book for diagnosing and acting on Big Cycle conditions.

Rate a Country on the 18 Determinants (1–10 Scorecard)

When to use: To gauge whether a country is likely to rise or decline on a relative basis.

How: Score the country 1–10 on each of the 8 headline powers (education, competitiveness, innovation/tech, output, trade share, military, financial center, reserve currency) plus the other determinants. Sum them. Higher total → higher probability of relative rise; lower → decline. The average reading, not any single one, defines the Big Cycle stage.

Trade-offs: Approximate, not precise; strengths are mutually reinforcing so they move together.

Locate the Internal-Order Stage (Disease-Diagnosis Method)

When to use: To assess civil-conflict risk and the right policy response.

How: Match symptoms to Stage 1–6 (new order → build → peace → excess → bad finances/conflict → civil war). Watch the Stage-5 markers: decadence, bureaucracy, populism/polarization, class warfare/scapegoating, loss of truth in media, rule-following fading into raw fighting. Stage 6 begins when people die in the fighting.

Trade-offs: Being in a stage doesn't make the next inevitable — but it sets the risk profile.

Red-Flag Count → Civil-War Probability

When to use: Quantifying internal-conflict risk.

How: Count economic red flags (high inequality, high debt/deficits, inflation, bad growth). 60–80% present → ~1-in-6 chance of severe internal conflict; >80% → ~1-in-3.

Trade-offs: Base rates from ~2,200 yrs of nine powers; probabilistic, not deterministic.

The Financial Safety-Margin Projection

When to use: Assessing any entity's (your own, a company's, a country's) true financial health.

How: Project income vs. expenses and assets vs. liabilities forward. Ask: if income disappeared and assets fell by half, how long would you last? Distinguish "looks rich" (high spending on borrowed money) from "is rich." For countries, check surplus/deficit, assets/liabilities, own-vs-foreign-currency debt, and who funds it.

The 4 Levers to Reduce Debt Burdens

When to use: Diagnosing how a debt crisis will be resolved.

How: Expect the progression — (1) austerity (deflationary, brief), (2) defaults/restructurings (deflationary, painful both sides), (3) transfers/taxes (politically hard, part of the mix), (4) print & devalue (most expedient, most common). Aim for a "beautiful deleveraging" (enough printing to offset deflation, not enough to spiral into inflation).

Read the Monetary System Type (1/2/3) and Its Transition

When to use: Judging currency/devaluation risk.

How: Identify Type 1 (hard money), 2 (paper claims on hard money), or 3 (fiat). Countries move 1→2→3 for printing flexibility under stress/war, then back to 1 after hyperinflation. Transitions happen under financial stress + military conflict and precede runs and devaluations.

Spot a Reserve-Currency Decline

When to use: Anticipating a currency's fall.

How: Watch for chronic devaluations, falling net central-bank reserves (often years ahead), suspended convertibility, claims-on-gold exceeding reserves, and a war/defeat with large debts. Reserve status lags all other strengths, then plunges "slowly then suddenly" once the interest rate can't offset the decline.

The Win-Win Point-Allocation Negotiation

When to use: Resolving conflicts (personal to geopolitical) without a lose-lose fight.

How: Each party ranks its top-10 wants, allocating 100 points. Identify and trade items that are low-priority for you but high for them (and vice versa). Know and respect each other's existential red lines. Winning = getting what's most important without losing what's most important.

Power Timing (When to Fight vs. Negotiate)

When to use: Deciding whether to press a conflict now or later.

How: Use power when it's greatest. Fight early if your relative power is declining; fight later if rising. Have power, respect power (don't fight a war you'll lose), use power wisely (soft power/generosity often beats bullying; hide the knife until needed).

Watch the Escalation Ladder of the 5 (+2) Wars

When to use: Tracking how a great-power rivalry could turn hot.

How: Trade → technology → capital → geopolitical wars typically precede military war by ~5–10 years. The escalation marker is cutting off essential imports (oil, tech, rare earths). Also add culture war (what each will die for) and the war with ourselves (internal strength). Identify each side's red lines and trip wires.

The "Dropped into 1900" Portfolio Stress Test

When to use: Testing an investment strategy against tail risk.

How: Simulate your strategy across every decade and many countries since 1900, not just US/UK since the 1950s. Because 7 of 10 great powers of 1900 saw wealth wiped out at least once, always hold protections against big adverse moves and against being wrong. Define risk as failing to meet your needs — not volatility.

The 4-Determinant Market Read

When to use: Connecting the world to the markets.

How: All markets are driven by growth, inflation, risk premiums, discount rates. Forecast how each will move (given fiscal/monetary policy) and balance assets as building blocks so the portfolio has no environmental bias, then tactically tilt. When money/credit is printed cheaply, assets rise — own them; ask always whether interest compensates for devaluation risk.

Death by Meeting: A Leadership Fable About Solving the Most Painful Problem in Business

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Death by Meeting — Cheatsheet

Diagnose first: which problem is this?

SymptomRoot problemFix
Meeting is boring, disengaged, politeLack of dramaMine for conflict; add the hook
Meeting is ineffective, nothing decidedLack of contextual structureSplit into the four meetings
People want different things from one meetingMeeting stewSeparate by purpose/format/timing
Lots of post-meeting email/hallway clarifyingSneaker timeGet clarity/closure/buy-in in the room

The Four Meetings — pick by purpose

If you need to…UseTimeCadence
Coordinate today's activitiesDaily Check-in5 min, standingDaily
Resolve this week's tacticsWeekly Tactical45–90 minWeekly
Decide a big long-term issueMonthly Strategic~2 hrs/topicMonthly
Decide a big issue that can't waitAd Hoc Strategicas neededOn demand
Step back & review the whole businessQuarterly Off-Site1–2 daysQuarterly

Weekly Tactical — run it in this order

1. Lightning Round — each person, 2–3 priorities, ≤60 sec (~10 min)

2. Progress Review — 4–6 key metrics, clarify only (~5 min)

3. Real-Time Agenda — set now, from what's actually happening (~15 min in)

Rule: strategic topic raised? Park it for the Monthly Strategic. Don't discuss.

Decision rules

  • When a meeting feels flat → mine for conflict. Surface the disagreement everyone

is avoiding; politeness is the disease, not the cure.

  • When first conflict gets tense → grant real-time permission. Interrupt: "this is

exactly the debate we need — keep going."

  • When a strategic issue erupts in a tactical meeting → park it, don't solve it.
  • When a strategic issue truly can't wait → call an Ad Hoc Strategic, separate from

the Weekly Tactical.

  • When tempted to pre-write the Weekly agenda → don't. Use disciplined spontaneity.
  • When someone says "too many meetings" → count the sneaker time the bad meetings

create. Better meetings save net time.

  • When the Daily Check-in runs long → stay standing, end hard, park the rest.

Thresholds & defaults

  • Daily Check-in: 5 min (hard-cap ~10), standing, never cancel.
  • Lightning round: 60 sec/person; 2–3 priorities.
  • Progress review: ~5 min, 4–6 metrics max.
  • Monthly Strategic: ≥2 hrs/topic, 1–2 topics only, prep required.
  • Off-site: 1–2 days, ~1 hour's drive away (not Hawaii), no outsiders

(except a trusted facilitator).

  • New meeting type: commit ~2 months before judging it.

Tells & smells (you're in trouble if…)

  • The leader optimizes for ending on time and avoiding tension.
  • The agenda was emailed 48 hrs early and no one replied.
  • One 2–3 hour "staff meeting" covers tactics + strategy + admin + culture.
  • People lobby to end the meeting to "go do real work."
  • Disagreements happen in the hallway, never in the room.
  • The off-site is mostly slides or mostly golf.

Off-Site: four reviews to cover

Strategy · Team · Personnel (stars & poor performers) · Competition/Industry

Genre cheat (for buy-in)

Headline News = Daily · Sitcom/Crime Drama = Weekly · Feature Film = Monthly ·

Mini-Series = Quarterly

glossary.md

Glossary — Death by Meeting

Ad Hoc Strategic Meeting — a separately convened strategic meeting for a critical

issue that can't wait for the next Monthly Strategic; kept distinct from the Weekly

Tactical so minds reset and enough time is allotted (Ch 5).

Boondoggle — a self-indulgent, socially-driven off-site that wastes the

opportunity for critical conversations; an anti-pattern for the Quarterly Off-Site (Ch 5).

Cascading Messages — agreeing at meeting's end on what to communicate downward to

the rest of the organization; a field on the Weekly Tactical guide (Ch 5).

Contextual Structure — clearly distinguishing the purpose, format, and timing of

each meeting type so participants know what mode they're in; the cure for Problem #2 (Ch 4).

Daily Check-in — ~5-minute, stand-up daily meeting to share schedules/activities

and keep priorities aligned; genre: Headline News (Ch 5).

Disciplined Spontaneity — planning the meeting's structure while letting the

agenda emerge live from real activity and progress; basis of the Real-Time Agenda (Ch 5).

Drama — legitimate, constructive ideological conflict that keeps people engaged;

its absence makes meetings boring (Problem #1) (Ch 2–3).

Fear of Conflict — reluctance to engage in unfiltered ideological debate; a named

challenge that undermines Monthly Strategic and Off-Site meetings (Ch 3, 5).

The Four Meetings — Daily Check-in, Weekly Tactical, Monthly Strategic, Quarterly

Off-Site Review; the structural solution to meeting stew (Ch 5).

The Hook — jolting participants in the first ten minutes by making the stakes

vivid, so they have a reason to care (Ch 3).

Huddle — Verne Harnish's term (from Mastering the Rockefeller Habits) for the

short daily meeting Lencioni adapted into the Daily Check-in (Ch 5).

Ideological Conflict — disagreement about ideas/issues (productive), as opposed to

personal or political conflict (destructive) (Ch 3).

Lightning Round — opening segment of the Weekly Tactical where each person states

their 2–3 weekly priorities in ≤60 seconds; sets the tone and surfaces issues (Ch 5).

Lack of Contextual Structure — Problem #2: cramming all issue-types into one
