meeting, leaving no clear context for any discussion → ineffective meetings (Ch 4).

Lack of Drama — Problem #1: removing conflict, the ingredient that makes meetings

engaging → boring meetings (Ch 3).

Magnitude Mismatch — the difficulty of shifting between decisions of very

different weight (e.g., travel policy vs. a merger) in one meeting (Ch 4).

Meeting Paradox — meetings are simultaneously critical and painful; resolvable by

fixing attitude and design, not by avoiding meetings (Ch 2).

Meeting Stew — the structural error of throwing every issue-type into one

undifferentiated staff meeting "like a bad stew" (Ch 4).

Meetings vs. Movies — meetings should beat movies for engagement because they're

interactive and directly relevant, while movies are passive and irrelevant (Ch 2–3).

Mining for Conflict — the leader's deliberate act of seeking out and surfacing

buried disagreements, even at the cost of being temporarily unpopular (Ch 3).

Monthly Strategic — 2+ hours/topic meeting (monthly or biweekly) to debate and

decide a few critical long-term issues; genre: feature film (Ch 5).

Parking Lot — capturing an out-of-context (usually strategic) issue raised in a

tactical meeting so it gets the right forum later; the Monthly Strategic is the

standing parking lot (Ch 4–5).

Progress Review — Weekly Tactical segment reviewing a handful (4–6) of key metrics

quickly, without deep discussion (Ch 5).

Quarterly Off-Site Review — 1–2 day quarterly meeting to review strategy, team,

personnel, and competition holistically; genre: mini-series (Ch 5).

Real-Time Agenda — setting the Weekly Tactical's agenda only after the lightning

round and progress review, based on actual current activity (Ch 5).

Real-Time Permission — the leader interrupting a first tense exchange to affirm the

conflict is good and wanted, separating ideological passion from fear of rejection (Ch 3).

Sneaker Time — uncounted hours spent after bad meetings clarifying via email,

voicemail, and hallway visits; the hidden cost good meetings eliminate (Ch 6).

TV/Film Genre Analogy — mapping each meeting type to a media format (Headline News,

sitcom, feature film, mini-series) so context sets expectations (Ch 1).

Weekly Tactical — 45–90 minute weekly meeting to review activities/metrics and

resolve tactical obstacles; goals: resolution of issues + reinforcement of clarity (Ch 5).

Will's White Board — the fable's artifact where Will maps the four meetings to TV/

film genres and diagnoses the missing elements of meetings (Ch 1).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Death by Meeting

The Hook (First Ten Minutes)

When to use: opening any important meeting, especially a dry-sounding one.

How: in the first ~10 minutes, make the stakes vivid — name a competitive threat,

the cost of a bad decision, or the mission's impact on customers/employees/families.

Give people "a reason to care."

Trade-offs: requires the leader to prepare a genuine stake; overuse or manufactured

urgency reads as manipulation. The conflict/stakes must be legitimate.

Mining for Conflict

When to use: real disagreement exists but is being politely buried.

How: as leader, prioritize uncovering unresolved disagreements; when people dodge,

force the issue onto the table. Both leaders and participants should act as "miners."

Trade-offs: temporarily unpopular; risks tipping into personal conflict if not kept

ideological. The cost of not doing it is worse — buried conflict returns as politics.

Real-Time Permission

When to use: the tense moment a team unaccustomed to conflict first debates openly.

How: interrupt, name that the conflict is exactly what's wanted, encourage both

parties to continue, remind them questioning each other improves the outcome.

Trade-offs: feels "paternal," but is "remarkably effective" at separating

ideological passion from interpersonal fear so debate can continue.

The Lightning Round

When to use: opening of every Weekly Tactical.

How: go around the table; each person names 2–3 priorities for the week in ≤60

seconds. ~10 minutes total even for a large team.

Trade-offs: strict 60-second cap can feel rushed, but over-detail loses the room

and obscures the real issues. Sixty seconds is "a lot longer than it seems."

Progress Review

When to use: right after the lightning round in the Weekly Tactical.

How: quickly review a handful (4–6) of key metrics; clarifying questions only.

~5 minutes. Avoid deep discussion of underlying issues here.

Trade-offs: reviewing too many metrics drowns the signal; pick the few that define

success.

Real-Time Agenda (Disciplined Spontaneity)

When to use: setting the Weekly Tactical agenda.

How: do not pre-set the agenda. After the lightning round + progress review

(~15 min in), let the agenda emerge from what people are actually working on and how the

company is actually performing. Plan the structure; improvise the content.

Trade-offs: sacrifices some control and predictability; requires leader discipline

to resist preparing an agenda 48 hours early. Payoff: the meeting addresses what

actually matters this week.

Parking Lot (Park Strategy in Tactical Meetings)

When to use: a strategic/long-term issue surfaces during a Weekly Tactical.

How: take it off the table and add it to a list for the next Monthly (or Ad Hoc)

Strategic. Don't discuss it now.

Trade-offs: feels like deferring something important, but mixing magnitudes wrecks

both topics; a trusted parking lot gives people confidence to table issues.

Ad Hoc Strategic Meeting

When to use: a critical strategic issue genuinely can't wait for the next Monthly

Strategic.

How: convene a separate, clearly delineated meeting (even later the same day);

allot enough time for real analysis. Keep it distinct from the Weekly Tactical.

Trade-offs: disrupts schedules — justified only for truly critical issues, but

those are exactly when great teams outmaneuver competitors.

The Trial-Period Commitment

When to use: introducing a new meeting type (especially the Daily Check-in).

How: commit to running it consistently for a set period (~2 months) before judging

whether it works; keep time/place consistent and never cancel.

Trade-offs: forces persistence through early awkwardness when abandonment is

tempting.

Outside Facilitator (Off-Site Exception)

When to use: a Quarterly Off-Site where the leader wants to participate fully.

How: bring in a trusted facilitator who knows the business and serves the team's

objectives — not an outsider who changes team dynamics.

Trade-offs: the only sanctioned exception to "no outsiders at the off-site";

choose someone driven by the team's goals, not their own.

Genre-Tagging Meetings (TV/Film Analogy)

When to use: teaching/enforcing the four-meeting structure.

How: label each meeting by its genre so attendees bring the right expectations —

Headline News (Daily), sitcom (Weekly), feature film (Monthly), mini-series (Quarterly).

Trade-offs: an explanatory device, not a rule; useful for buy-in and for keeping

meetings in their lane.

Six Thinking Hats

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Six Thinking Hats

The Six Hats at a Glance

ColorModeFocusSignature questionTypical time
WhiteNeutral / informationFacts & figures; what we have vs. need"What do we know? What do we need?"~1 min/person; extend
RedFeelingEmotions, hunches, intuition — no justification"What do I feel about this?"Briefest; often 1 min total
BlackCautionRisks, dangers, why it won't work, fit"What could go wrong? Why won't it work?"~1 min/person; extend
YellowBenefitValue, optimism, feasibility (with reasons)"What are the benefits? Why will it work?"~1 min/person; extend
GreenCreativeNew ideas, alternatives, provocation "po", movement"What new ideas are possible?"Set block (e.g. 10 min)
BlueControlProcess, agenda, focus, summaries"What thinking is needed next?"Bookends + interjections

Pairs: white/red, black/yellow, green/blue. Always name the colour, never the function.

Recommended Sequences

  • Initial idea exploration: Blue → White → Green → (Red) → Blue
  • Evaluating a proposal / assessment: Blue → White → Yellow → Black → (Green to fix difficulties) → Red → Blue
  • Quick decision: Blue → White → Yellow → Black → Red → Blue
  • Problem solving: Blue → White → Black (define the problem) → Green (options) → Yellow + Black (assess) → Blue
  • Resolving conflict / charged topic: Blue → Red (vent feelings) → White → Yellow → Black → Green → Red → Blue

Rules for sequences: blue always bookends; any hat may repeat; you need not use every hat; use pre-set (planned up front) not evolving until experienced.

Decision Rules

  • When a meeting turns adversarial or ego-clogged → call Red Hat (surface the feelings), then Blue Hat (reset structure).
  • When an idea is dismissed on first sight → "Let's have some yellow hat on it" before any black hat.
  • When assessing a NEW idea → Yellow before Black, so difficulties become problems worth solving.
  • When strong feelings pre-exist → open with Red — UNLESS the boss's feeling would make everyone conform, or no feelings pre-exist.
  • When an objection is "I don't like it" → that's Red, not Black; ask for the logical Black-hat reason.
  • When stuck in the same old ideas → Green Hat, deliberate effort from everyone, judgement deferred.
  • When you need to break a fixed pattern → put an idea forward as "po" and use it for movement, not judgement.
  • When green produces too many ideas → fast Red Hat to pick those fitting a frame; park the rest.
  • When someone won't switch hats → only the Blue-hat leader changes hats; staying critical after a switch = refusing to play the game.
  • When a decision won't come at the final Blue → name why (missing info / clashing values), design a way covering both, or make an honest Red-hat decision — all decisions are finally red hat.

Never

  • Never use the Black Hat to attack a person's idea to win — it's caution, not argument.
  • Never assign one person a fixed hat for the whole meeting — everyone wears every hat.
  • Never label people by hat ("she's black hat") — hats are directions, not descriptions.
  • Never demand justification under the Red Hat.
  • Never state a believed fact as a checked one under the White Hat — frame the likelihood.

glossary.md

Glossary — Six Thinking Hats

Assessment hats — Red, yellow and black: the hats used to evaluate (feelings, benefits, cautions), not merely gather information — why a decision follows exploration (Ch 8).

Backward effect — Judging an idea by how well it fits past experience and existing patterns; the mode of the black and yellow hats, deliberately set aside under green (Ch 6).

Black Hat — Caution mode: risks, dangers, difficulties, why something won't work or doesn't fit; the most used and most valuable hat, but not for winning arguments (Ch 4).

Blue Hat — Process-control mode: thinking about thinking — orchestration, agenda, focus, discipline, summaries and conclusions; the conductor (Ch 7).

Blue-hat bookends — The rule that an initial blue hat opens and a final blue hat closes every structured session (Ch 1, Ch 7, Ch 8).

Directions not descriptions — A hat asks what is about to happen (a direction to think in), never labels what already happened or who a person is (Ch 0, Ch 1).

Discipline — Members stay with the indicated hat; only the leader changes hats; the rule that keeps parallel thinking from collapsing into argument (Ch 1, Ch 8).

Ego, removal of — In argument the ego is tied to being right; under the hats you show off by performing well as a thinker in every direction (Ch 0).

Evolving sequence — Choosing each next hat as you go; not recommended until experienced — wastes time and looks manipulative (Ch 1, Ch 8).

Facts, first-class vs. second-class — Checked/proven facts vs. facts believed true but not yet verified; kept distinct under the white hat (Ch 2).

Focusing questions — Narrowing an information request to draw out exactly what is needed and avoid being drowned in data (Ch 2).

Green Hat — Creative mode: new ideas, alternatives, possibilities, provocation and movement; deliberate scheduled creative effort (Ch 6).

Lateral thinking — A set of attitudes, idioms and techniques (movement, provocation, po) for cutting across patterns in a self-organising asymmetric patterning system to generate new concepts (Ch 6).

Likelihood frame — Labelling information by its degree of truth ("always," "by and large," "sometimes," "believed") so nothing is stated more firmly than known (Ch 2).

Map-making — Exploring and laying out the whole terrain before choosing a route, versus picking a conclusion first and defending it (Ch 0, Ch 7).

Mismatch mechanism — The brain's natural flagging of anything that doesn't fit expected patterns; the basis of easy black-hat caution (Ch 4).

Movement — Active green-hat idiom: using an idea for its forward effect (where it leads), not judging its fit; more than merely suspending judgement (Ch 6).

No-justification rule — Under the red hat, feelings are expressed as they are and never explained or justified (Ch 3).

Operacy — The "doing" skill of thinking — concern with effectiveness and making things happen, associated with the yellow hat (Ch 5).

Parallel thinking — Everyone thinks in the same direction (wears the same hat) at the same moment, laying views side by side, instead of adversarial argument (Ch 0).

Po (provocative operation) — A word marking an idea put forward as a provocation for its movement value; acts as a flag of truce protecting it from black-hat judgement (Ch 6).

Provocation — A deliberately illogical or reversed idea used as a stepping stone to jerk thinking out of fixed patterns (Ch 6).

Red Hat — Emotion mode: feelings, hunches, intuition, expressed without justification and on an individual basis (Ch 3).

Reversal — A simple provocation technique: state how something usually happens, then reverse it ("po, the store pays the customer") (Ch 6).

Sensitisation — The brain tunes chemically in one direction at a time (danger vs. benefit); you can't be optimally sensitised two ways at once — the basis for separating hats (Ch 0, Ch 4).

Sequence, pre-set — A hat order laid out in advance under the initial blue hat and then followed, with minor variations (Ch 1, Ch 8).

Signalling — A hat can request thinking of others, indicate a mode, signal your own mode, or (key for green) signal to yourself to make deliberate effort (Ch 1, Ch 6).

Single use — Invoking one hat on demand within an ordinary discussion to request a mode of thinking (Ch 1).

Six hats / six directions — White (facts), Red (feelings), Black (caution), Yellow (benefit), Green (creativity), Blue (control); paired as white/red, black/yellow, green/blue (Ch 0, Ch 1).

Speculative-positive — De Bono's name for the yellow hat: looking forward for value and feasibility as a deliberate choice (Ch 5).

Value sensitivity — A trained habit of being as alert to value as we naturally are to danger; needed because the yellow hat has no natural brain support (Ch 5).

White Hat — Information mode: neutral, objective facts and figures — what we have and what we need — like a computer (Ch 2).

Yellow Hat — Benefit mode: optimism, value, feasibility, logically-based; harder to wear than the black hat (Ch 5).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Six Thinking Hats

Reusable ways to deploy the hats in real discussions, meetings, and solo thinking.

Single-Hat Request

When to use: A live discussion drifts into one register too long, or needs a specific mode injected right now.

How: Name the colour, not the function — "I think we need some green hat thinking here"; "Let's have some black hat on this"; "Yes, that's fine black hat; now let's try the yellow hat." You need not specify a hat every time you speak.

Trade-offs: Depends on everyone knowing the idiom; feeble if the group hasn't been trained. Great for steering without personal friction.

Blue-Hat Bookends

When to use: Any structured session, and especially thinking alone (which needs structure most).

How: Open with an initial blue hat (why we're here, definition and alternative definitions, goal, background, planned hat sequence). Close with a final blue hat (outcome, conclusion, decision, next steps; or, if stuck, define a new focus).

Trade-offs: Adds a little ceremony up front; pays back in focus and a clean, harvestable outcome.

Pre-Set Sequence

When to use: Group exploration or problem-solving you want mapped without mid-meeting arguments over what to do next.

How: Lay the whole hat order out at the start under the initial blue hat, then follow it (minor variations allowed by output). Any hat may repeat; no need to use every hat.

Trade-offs: Less adaptive than evolving on the fly — but evolving sequences waste time and look manipulative until the group is experienced.

Opening Red Hat (Vent / Surface Emotion)

When to use: When strong feelings already exist on the subject and are distorting the "logic."

How: Immediately after the first blue hat, go round the group for a brisk red-hat feeling each — no explanations. Get the emotion into the open early.

Trade-offs: Skip it if the boss's stated feeling would make everyone conform, or if no strong feelings pre-exist (nothing to surface). Consider a second red hat later to check for shifts.

Yellow-Before-Black (New-Idea Assessment)

When to use: Appraising a new idea or proposal.

How: Run the yellow hat first to find and reason out the value; only then run the black hat for difficulties. If no value appears under yellow, stop — no point proceeding.

Trade-offs: Feels counter-intuitive (we default to criticism), but seeing benefit first turns difficulties into problems worth overcoming rather than reasons to quit.

Timeboxing Each Hat

When to use: Every hat, to force concentration and cut waffle.

How: Set a short time — about one minute per person present — and extend only while genuine points still flow. Keep the red hat briefest (often one minute total, since no justification is given).

Trade-offs: Under-allotting risks cutting a productive vein — hence "extend while real points come." Far better than long slots with people sitting idle.

One-Minute Green-Hat Effort

When to use: To break "same old ideas" fixation, or to build creative confidence.

How: Deliberately put on the green hat and require a creative effort from everyone (or keep quiet). Even a barren effort counts — signalling to yourself sets aside the time and raises future yield.

Trade-offs: May produce nothing on a given round; the value is cumulative habit, not guaranteed instant ideas.

Provocation with "Po"

When to use: Thinking is trapped in existing patterns and needs jerking out.

How: Put forward a deliberately illogical idea marked "po" ("po, a polluting factory should be downstream of itself"), or use reversal (state the norm, then reverse it). Then use it for movement — where does it lead? — not judgement. Po protects it from black-hat attack.

Trade-offs: Uncomfortable for judgement-minded people; requires discipline to defer criticism until after movement.

Solo / Individual Thinking Within a Group

When to use: To get more and deeper ideas, especially under green, yellow or black.

How: The chair pauses a hat for two minutes of silent individual thinking, or goes round person by person for each one's thinking under the current hat.

Trade-offs: Slows the flow briefly; worth it when group cross-talk is crowding out real thought.

Green → Red Triage

When to use: The green hat has produced more ideas than there's time to assess.

How: Use a fast red hat to pick the ideas that fit a frame ("low-cost," "easy to test"); park the rest for later. Keeps the creative energy usable.

Trade-offs: Feeling-based selection may drop a slow-burn idea — so park, don't discard.

Final Red Hat (Reflect on the Thinking)

When to use: After the final blue hat, to appraise the session itself.

How: One quick round — "What do we feel about our thinking? Are we happy with the outcome? Did we do a good job?"

Trade-offs: Optional; useful for teams building the habit and for catching lingering unease before acting.

The Defining Decade: Why Your Twenties Matter

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Defining Decade

Meg Jay's decision rules, thresholds, and tells — the judgment behind the frameworks.

Core Decision Rules (if → then)

  • Choosing between options → take the one with the most identity capital (skills + connections + a door-opening story), even if it's less fun or lower-paid now.
  • "I don't know what I want" → it's a defense; assemble your real six-flavor table and choose from those. There is no 24-flavor table.
  • Speech full of "should / supposed to / less-than" → you're in a search for glory; separate goals (inside, energizing) from shoulds (outside, oppressive) and drop the shoulds.
  • Seeking a job/intro/opportunity → work your weak ties with a specific, researched favor, not your close friends and not a vague "coffee???"
  • Rejecting a path because it's "ordinary" → that's the should-not; ask "What am I for?" and claim it. Different is simple; affirmative is brave.
  • Applying/interviewing → lead with a coherent story (past→present→next) that makes sense, not a list.
  • Considering moving in together → decide, don't slide; have the commitment conversation first. Ideally don't cohabit before engagement.
  • A work/relationship jolt makes you catastrophize → reappraise: "What about the facts?" A feeling isn't a command. Jobs/relationships usually aren't that fragile.
  • Low confidence at a new job → you can't feel it before you earn it; bank mastery experiences, count toward 10,000 hours, seek feedback.
  • Feeling stuck / "at loose ends" → life transplant: make concrete adult commitments; don't wait to feel like an adult before acting.
  • Future feels far off / goals tossed decades away → do the math with a timeline, working backward from what you want.

What to Be Picky About in a Partner (Being in Like)

Be picky about (20-year things)Let go of (everyday things)
Extreme differences in values / goalsUnread book on the nightstand
Personality mismatch (esp. high Neuroticism)"Not funny enough at parties"
Whether you love each otherForgot the lilies / corny in-law gifts
Whether you genuinely like who they areDifferent taste in weekend activities

Rule: Obvious similarities (age, religion, politics) are deal breakers, not match makers. Personality is the real match maker — and where couples are least alike.

Red flag: High Neuroticism predicts breakup more than any dissimilarity. How you handle differences > the differences.

Tells & Smells (recognize the situation fast)

  • Shame story running the show → secrecy: they won't mention a partner/job until it blows up; never even thought to tell a best friend.
  • Dating/working down → choices that contradict who the person actually is now.
  • A self-cure gone bad → a coping habit (music, hookups, numbing) that once helped now isolates. "Every problem was once a solution — put the raft down."
  • Sliding, not deciding → "it just happened"; no conversation, ring, or decision behind a big life change.
  • Present bias → love/work described as "way far off," lots of distraction, hanging with people who don't talk about the future.
  • Availability heuristic → reasoning from a couple of anecdotes / Hollywood headlines instead of base rates.
  • Leaf in the wind → mood tracks the last thing a boss said; work taken intensely personally.

The Big Five (low ↔ high)

FactorLowHigh
Opennesspractical, routine, skepticalcurious, creative, adventurous
Conscientiousnesseasygoing, careless, spontaneousdisciplined, organized, dutiful
Extraversionreserved, energized aloneoutgoing, energized by others
Agreeablenessantagonistic, suspiciouscooperative, warm, trusting
Neuroticismsecure, resilientanxious, moody, sees the negative

Numbers & Thresholds to Remember

  • Frontal lobe matures between ~20 and 30.
  • ~10,000 hours to expertise ≈ 5 yrs focused full-time (or 10 yrs part-time).
  • Marriage age: past ~25, age at marriage no longer predicts divorce. Divorce rate ~40%.
  • Fertility vs. your twentysomething self: ~½ at 30, ¼ at 35, ⅛ at 40. Per-cycle odds ~20–25% to 35, ~5% at 40.
  • Miscarriage: ~¼ after 35, ~½ after 40.
  • Cohabitation effect is pre-engagement only — living together after a public commitment carries no penalty.
  • Wage growth: ~⅔ of lifetime wage growth happens in the first 10 years of a career.
  • Weak ties: >¾ of new jobs come from contacts seen "occasionally" or "rarely."

The One-Line Ethos

"Claim your adulthood. Be intentional. Get to work. Pick your family. Do the math. Make your own certainty. You are deciding your life right now."

glossary.md

Glossary — The Defining Decade

Age Thirty Deadline — The nagging twentysomething worry "I'd better not be alone at thirty" (Ch 6).

Age Thirty Bait and Switch — At thirty, the deadline flips to panic; commitment goes from "something for later" to "something for yesterday," driving rushed choices (Ch 6).

Availability heuristic — Judging how likely something is by how easily an example comes to mind; e.g. overestimating late-40s fertility from anecdotes and headlines (Ch 15).

Big Five — The five personality factors: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism; ~50% inherited, relatively stable; the real "match maker" (Ch 10).

Borrowing an ego — Reaching out so someone else's frontal lobe does your emotional calming; fine occasionally, harmful if overused (Ch 12).

Claiming (vs. conforming) — Committing to a concrete interest/career; feels like conforming but is what makes a life distinctive (Ch 5).

Cohabitation effect — Couples who live together before engagement are, on average, less satisfied and more likely to divorce (Ch 8).

Customized life — An authentic, unique life assembled from standard "parts" over time, like a custom bike (Ch 5).

Deal breakers, not match makers — Obvious similarities (age, religion, politics) filter out mismatches but don't create happiness (Ch 10).

Elaborated speech — Fuller, more organized communication required with weak ties who don't share your assumptions (Ch 2). See restricted speech.

Falling up — Being successful young as a survival strategy that hides real pain (Ch 7). See YAVIS.

Fixed mindset — Believing abilities are innate ("you have it or you don't"), so mistakes become verdicts (Ch 13). See growth mindset (Carol Dweck).

Flashbulb memory — A vivid, "frozen" memory of a surprising or emotional moment; the twenties produce more than any stage (Ch 12).

Forward thinking — Frontal-lobe function of anticipating consequences and planning under uncertainty; comes with practice, not just age (Ch 11).

Frontal lobe — The brain's "executive functioning center," last to mature (between ~20 and 30) (Ch 11).

Getting along and getting ahead — Making adult commitments (jobs, partners, leases) that drive positive personality change in the twenties (Ch 14).

Growth mindset — Believing people can learn and grow, so failures are opportunities, not verdicts (Ch 13).

Helper's high — The happiness/health boost from being generous; underlies goodwill toward twentysomethings (Ch 2).

Homophily — "Love of the same"; similarity breeds connection, which makes strong-tie clusters homogeneous (Ch 2).

Identity capital — Your collection of personal assets (résumé and personal) that you use to "purchase" jobs and relationships (Ch 1).

In like — Being alike in ways that matter and genuinely liking who your partner is (Ch 10).

Lock-in (consumer lock-in) — Decreased likelihood of switching to a better option after an investment; built from setup and switching costs (Ch 8).

Mastery experience — An actual lived success at something difficult; the true source of confidence (Ch 13).

Memento vivi — A reminder that you are going to live — that life continues, and can be great, past the twenties (Ch 16). Cf. memento mori.

Microtrauma — An everyday jolt of the twentysomething workweek (a public "screwup") taken intensely personally (Ch 12).

Negative / positive identity — Knowing yourself by what you're not vs. the braver, affirmative sense of what you are (Ch 5).

Neuroticism — Big Five factor (anxious, moody, critical); high Neuroticism is "toxic" — more predictive of breakup than dissimilarity (Ch 10).

Person, place, and thing — An adult life is built from who you're with, where you live, and what you do — start with whichever you know (Ch 4).

Positivity effect — With age, greater interest in positive information and weaker reaction to the negative (Ch 12).

Present bias — Discounting the future in favor of today's rewards; strong in twentysomethings (Ch 16).

Restricted speech — Encoded in-group shorthand used among similar strong ties (Ch 2). See elaborated speech.

Search for glory — Striving toward an ideal rather than your real potential (Karen Horney) (Ch 4).

Self-cure — An old coping solution that outlives its usefulness and becomes the new problem; "the most difficult thing to cure" (Ch 9).

Self-defining memory / life story — The narratives (often shame-laden) formed in adolescence/twenties that shape identity and choices; highly changeable (Ch 9).

Self-efficacy — One's trusted ability to produce a desired result; the precise term for confidence (Ch 13).

Setup cost — The initial investment (furniture, lease, pets) that contributes to lock-in (Ch 8).

Six-flavor table — Your real, limited set of viable options (vs. the mythical "24-flavor table" of infinite choice), from the jam experiment (Ch 3).

Sliding, not deciding — Drifting into cohabitation (or a shared life) gradually, without a conscious decision (Ch 8).

Social recovery — Relearning frontal-lobe skills through regular routines (Phineas Gage driving a stagecoach) (Ch 11).

Strength of weak ties — Acquaintances (not close friends) most often bridge us to new jobs and opportunities (Mark Granovetter) (Ch 2).

Survival of the busiest — "Neurons that fire together, wire together"; the brain keeps connections you use, prunes those you don't (Ch 11).

Switching cost — The time/money/effort to change course; underestimated upfront, larger up close; rises with age (Ch 8).

10,000-hour rule — Expertise comes mostly from time in (~5 yrs focused full-time); "naturals" are largely myths (K. Anders Ericsson) (Ch 13).

Tyranny of the should — Paralyzing outside judgments ("shoulds") that masquerade as goals but oppress (Karen Horney) (Ch 3–4).

Tyranny of the should-not — The mirror image: rejecting every conventional path in the name of being different (Ch 5).

Unthought known — Something you know about yourself but forget or won't say out loud (Christopher Bollas) (Ch 3).

Urban tribe — The makeshift family / weekend friends; supportive but insular, helps us survive not thrive (Ch 2).

Weak ties — People you've met or are connected to but don't currently know well (Ch 2). See strength of weak ties.

YAVIS — Young, Attractive, Verbal, Intelligent, Successful; high-functioning clients whose polish can hide real pain (Ch 7).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — The Defining Decade

Concrete moves Meg Jay uses (or teaches) to help twentysomethings act. Each is a repeatable technique, not just a concept.

Take the Job With the Most Capital

When to use: Choosing between twentysomething options (jobs, programs, moves).

How: Rank options by identity capital gained — skills, connections, door-opening stories — not by comfort or short-term pay. Reframe "paying dues" as "investing in your dream."

Trade-offs: The high-capital option is often less fun/lower-paid now; the payoff is compounding and delayed.

Assemble Your Six-Flavor Table

When to use: When you (or someone) claim to have "no idea" what to do.

How: List your actual viable options (usually ~6, shaped by your history), not the mythical infinite menu. Then choose among those. Ask the real question: What could I do well enough to support the life I want, and enjoy enough to keep at for years? — not the lottery question.

Trade-offs: Choosing opens you to work, failure, and heartbreak — but not-choosing has worse, delayed consequences.

Surface the Unthought Known

When to use: Vague "I just want things to work out" talk that avoids what the person already knows.

How: Have them recount real experiences and history; reflect back the patterns; let them "stumble onto" the choice they were avoiding. Name the vagueness as a defense.

Trade-offs: Requires patience (listening first); the surfaced truth may be scary to act on.

Ask a Weak Tie for a Specific Favor (the Franklin method)

When to use: Seeking a job, intro, reference, or informational interview.

How: Research the person's expertise → make yourself interesting and relevant → ask for a clearly defined favor (not "coffee???"). Doing a favor makes them like you (Ben Franklin effect); one favor begets larger ones.

Trade-offs: Some will say no; vague or oversized asks (deciding your whole career) overwhelm and fail.

Sort Shoulds From Goals

When to use: Speech full of "should," "supposed to," "less-than."

How: For each ambition, ask: does this direct me from inside (goal) or judge me from outside (should)? Trace each should to its source (parents, friends, Facebook) and test it against what's real and authentic for you.

Trade-offs: Dropping a prestigious "should" can feel like failing others' expectations.

Build From Person, Place, and Thing

When to use: Overwhelmed about how to construct an adult life.

How: Start with whichever of who-you're-with / where-you-live / what-you-do you already know something about, and build outward.

Trade-offs: Committing to one anchor (e.g. a city) can feel like foreclosing options; usually it opens them.

Tell a Coherent Story (Customized Life)

When to use: Applications, interviews, coffee dates.

How: Make yourself the protagonist with an arc — past → present → intended next. Balance complexity and cohesion; it must make sense (not necessarily be linear). Move from "what I'm not" to "what I'm for."

Trade-offs: A too-simple story reads inexperienced; too-complex reads disorganized. Aim for the middle.

Don't Slide — Decide (avoid the cohabitation effect)

When to use: Considering moving in together.

How: Before combining lives, have an explicit conversation about each person's commitment level and what it means. Ideally don't cohabit before engagement; if you do, anticipate and regularly re-evaluate the setup/switching costs that could lock you in. Test the relationship other ways (variety, travel).

Trade-offs: The convenient/economical path (sliding) is easy now but raises later switching costs.

Run the Nicaragua Test

When to use: Assessing a serious relationship's real compatibility.

How: Do something stressful and inescapable together (third-world travel is "the closest thing to being married and raising kids") and watch whether you become better or more extreme versions of yourselves.

Trade-offs: Reveals mismatches you'd rather not see — which is the point.

Assess the Big Five (and check Neuroticism)

When to use: Evaluating a partner's fit beyond obvious similarities.

How: Rate both of you high/medium/low on Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism. Personality similarity smooths the early years; be especially wary of high Neuroticism (it drives criticism and contempt). Be picky about 20-year things (values, goals, personality, love), not daily discrepancies.

Trade-offs: Some difference is inevitable; over-filtering on minor traits (a high-N habit) sabotages good relationships.

Edit Your Life Story (stop dating/working down)

When to use: Choices that contradict who the person actually is now; secrecy/shame tells.

How: Get the untold story out of the back of the mind by telling it aloud; treat it as a first draft from adolescence and revise it through new conversations and experiences. Replace old internal voices with new ones. Shift from being wanted to wanting.

Trade-offs: Naming a shame story is painful; it's the precondition for change.

Reappraise ("What about the facts?")

When to use: A work/relationship jolt triggers catastrophizing ("I'll be fired and waiting tables").

How: Answer the emotional brain (amygdala) with the frontal lobe — reevaluate based on facts. Jobs/relationships usually aren't that fragile; a feeling isn't a command to act. Avoid the failure modes: flight (quitting), chronic worry, suppression, over-borrowing an ego.

Trade-offs: Reappraisal is a learned skill — slower and harder than calling mom, but it builds self-soothing.

Bank Mastery Experiences (confidence outside-in)

When to use: Low confidence at a new job.

How: Seek challenging work done without too much help; count hours toward ~10,000; take stock of hours already earned; adopt a growth mindset (failures are feedback); seek feedback instead of avoiding it; stop self-deprecating talk.

Trade-offs: Requires tolerating not-going-well days — but easy successes build only fragile confidence.

Prescribe a Life Transplant

When to use: Feeling stuck, anxious, "at loose ends," waiting to feel like an adult before acting.

How: Make concrete adult commitments (a job, a steady place, a goal you actually want) — "getting along and getting ahead." Even working toward good work/love raises happiness; goals alone boost well-being.

Trade-offs: Feels like it will "add to your problems"; the evidence says the opposite.

Do the Math With a Timeline

When to use: The future feels far off and abstract; goals get tossed "decades away."

How: Work backward from what you actually want (career milestones, marriage, kids), counting the required steps and years. Bring the future close (like seeing your future self). Distinguish having a life at thirty from starting one then.

Trade-offs: Timelines provoke anxiety — that discomfort is what converts distance into action.

HBR Guide to Persuasive Presentations

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Duarte's Judgment Calls

Thresholds & Defaults

DecisionDuarte's number
Content vs. slot lengthPlan for 60% (40 min of a 60-min slot)
Audience patience ceiling30–40 min before squirming
Executive summary slides~10% of appendix length (50 appendix → 5 summary)
Executive rehearsal frameBuild for 30, rehearse as if cut to 5
Slide comprehension3 seconds (glance test)
Text field costDefault text box ≈ 80 words ≈ 20 sec of lost listening at 250 wpm
Typefaces per deck1, at most 2
Colors per deck3 complementary + 2 neutrals
Quote slide length≤ 30 words, one quote at a time
Cutting an hour to 40 minCut ~1/3 of slides
Slide count, high-energy style~5/min (145 slides in 40 min); moderate = 1–2/min
Remote slide change interval~20 seconds
Interpreter (any type)Prepare half the material for the slot
Interpreter lead timeNotes sent 1 week ahead; hiring up to 1 month ahead
Tech setup minimum30 minutes, walkthrough preferred
Calming breath cycle4 deep hold-and-slow-release breaths (<1 min)

Decision Rules

  • If it's a topic, not a sentence with POV + stakes → you don't have a big idea; don't generate content yet.
  • If an idea doesn't support the big idea → cut it, however interesting. If you don't filter, the audience will — and resent you.
  • If the audience is senior → lead with conclusions and recommendations; a big reveal at the end will be interrupted away.
  • If the content is understandable without a presenter → it's a document. Circulate it; don't project it.
  • If a slide takes more than 3 seconds → it's a document, a build, or two slides.
  • If bullets on a slide don't need to be associated → give each its own slide. Slides are free.
  • *If bullets do feel related* → circle the verbs/nouns, name the relationship, replace with a diagram.
  • If the data has no z-axis → no 3-D. Ever.
  • If one number carries the message → show that number, huge, with no chart.
  • If you're deemphasizing chart context → you must supply it out loud; don't redistribute that slide.
  • If you don't know a Q&A answer → say so and commit to follow up. Never fake it; they see through it.
  • If a question seems trivial → look for the question behind the question before dismissing it.
  • If the room's body language turns → change course mid-talk; enduring it costs more than admitting it.
  • If the backchannel turns hostile → engage and acknowledge; make people feel heard rather than ignoring or defending.
  • If you're tempted to flag your own sound bite for sharing → don't. Overt flagging reduces sharing.
  • If your first visual metaphor arrives instantly → discard it; it's everyone's first idea.
  • If you're running long → drop to the false ending. That's why you planted it.

Choosing the Vehicle

  • Two direct reports, informal → conversation or whiteboard, no deck
  • Venture capitalists, small room → formal stand-up presentation
  • Analysts → a carefully written memo may outperform slides
  • Young professionals / broad reach → video, streamed or posted
  • Decision still open, want input → sketch live; a slick deck signals "final"
  • Commencement, eulogy, wedding toast, layoff announcement → no slides
  • Status update → distribute a document; don't hold a meeting to read it

Analytical vs. Emotional Mix

TopicAudienceLean
Layoffs, launchesAnyEmotional, but never sentimental
Science, engineering, financeSpecialistsAnalytical + at least one human anchor
Cost cuttingManagers who must fire peopleEmotional first, numbers second, or you read as inhumane
Cost cuttingExecutives owning the bottom lineNumbers first — but acknowledge the human cost

Resistance Diagnosis

SignalTypeResponse
Counterarguments, competing data, "have you seen X?"LogicalRead the opposition; build a nuanced POV
Bias, dogma, moral objection, raw nerveEmotionalProceed carefully; explicitly honor the value at risk
"We can't afford / reach / staff that"PracticalName the sacrifice; visibly shoulder part of it

Tells & Smells

  • Deck ends with a "why it matters" slide → self-focused structure; move it to the front.
  • You can describe the talk as a noun phrase → no big idea.
  • Middle of the talk is all one side of the contrast → tension collapsed; add toggles.
  • Ending is a task list → the new bliss is missing.
  • Slide won't fit on a sticky note → concept too complex for one slide.
  • Eye doesn't know where to start on a slide → hierarchy failure, not content failure.
  • Audience leaning back, arms crossed → resistance. Fidgeting, checking e-mail → boredom.
  • No laughs, no nods, no notes across several minutes → you're not connecting; intervene.
  • You can't find the verbal tic → you haven't watched yourself on video yet.
  • Nobody asks a question → they've disengaged, or you never made room; either is a problem.

glossary.md

Glossary

Analytical/emotional balance — the deliberate mix of logical and emotional content, set by topic and audience; no presentation should be devoid of emotion (Ch 3)

Anti-cliché rule — discard the first visual concept you think of, since it occurs to everyone else too (Ch 8)

Appropriate drama — matching a story's emotional scale to the stakes of the room, so you don't read as manipulative (Ch 6)

Audience as hero / presenter as mentor — the stance that the audience is the protagonist and the presenter is the Yoda-like mentor giving a gift, a tool, and a way to get unstuck (Ch 1)

Backchannel — the stream of online chatter before, during, and after a talk (Ch 12)

Backchannel revolt — coordinated online rejection of a speaker's message (Ch 12)

Big Idea — the one key message, stated as a complete sentence containing your point of view and what's at stake (Ch 2)

Build — animating a list so each item appears as you cover it, controlling pacing (Ch 8, Ch 9)

Clean surface — a blank slide with master prompts turned off, used as the starting point for design (Ch 8)

Comfort monitor — the presenter-facing teleprompter screen showing notes the audience never sees (Ch 7, Ch 10)

Common ground tiers — lots / moderate / minimal, describing how much overlap you share with an audience (Ch 1)

Concrete comparison — a simile or metaphor used as a sound-bite device, or a physical analogue used to convey magnitude (Ch 3, Ch 9)

Consecutive interpretation — the interpreter shares the stage and translates after each point (Ch 11)

Controlling idea — screenwriting's term for the big idea (Ch 2)

Convergent thinking — the elimination phase: sorting and filtering generated ideas against the big idea (Ch 3)

Curator of content — the presenter's role once the highest-leverage audience subgroup is chosen (Ch 1)

Divergent thinking — the generation phase, where new options emerge (Ch 2, Ch 3)

Dynamic opposites — canonical contrast pairs (sacrifice/reward, stagnation/growth, budget/quality) used to build tension (Ch 2)

Emotional texture — emotion layered onto an otherwise analytical case, usually via story (Ch 3, Ch 6)

Emotive anecdote — a gripping personal story used as a S.T.A.R. moment (Ch 6)

Executive summary slides — front-loaded summary at roughly 10% of deck length, with the rest as appendix (Ch 1)

False ending / real ending — two rehearsed exit points allowing a graceful early close (Ch 7)

Five arrangement principles — flow, contrast, white space, hierarchy, unity (Ch 9)

Five segmentation lenses — politics, demographics, psychographics, firmographics, ethnographics (Ch 1)

Four calls to action — the audience acts as doers, suppliers, influencers, or innovators (Ch 2)

Glance test — the standard that any slide be comprehensible in three seconds (Ch 8)

Grandmother test — rework language until a non-expert would understand the central terms (Ch 3)

Graphic recorder — a practitioner who visually synthesizes a talk in real time on a large mural (Ch 7)

Inventory of Personal Stories — a catalog of remembered events and the emotions they summon, built from prompts and reused across talks (Ch 6)

Mind mapping — solo associative brainstorming producing a web of concepts and connections (Ch 2)

New bliss — the rewarded state the audience reaches by adopting your idea; the destination of the ending (Ch 4, Ch 5)

Physical cues — involuntary audience body language read as live feedback (Ch 12)

Planted question — a question a facilitator raises because the audience is too intimidated to ask it (Ch 11)

Pre-selling — meeting tough critics in advance so their objections don't surface as roadblocks (Ch 2)

Pressure-testing — handing your big idea to someone else to attack (Ch 2)

Reciprocity — the currency of social media; spreading others' ideas so yours will spread (Ch 12)

Reexperiencing — narrating a story from inside the moment rather than reporting it (Ch 11)

Resistance types — logical, emotional, practical (Ch 2)

Resonance / resonant frequency — the physics metaphor for tapping something already inside the audience so they move on their own (Ch 1)

Rhythmic repetition — a sound-bite device repeating a phrase across sentences or slides (Ch 3)

Simultaneous interpretation — booth-based real-time translation delivered to audience earphones (Ch 11)

Slide cemetery — a holding area at the end of the file for cut slides, available during Q&A (Ch 7)

Slideument — Garr Reynolds' term for a text-dense document masquerading as a slide deck (Ch 7)

Slogan — a concise, memorable statement engineered for pickup (Ch 3)

Sound bite — a crafted, repeatable phrase delivered without fanfare (Ch 3)

S.T.A.R. moment — Something They'll Always Remember: a climactic shocking statistic, evocative visual, memorable dramatization, or emotive anecdote (Ch 6)

Subtext (in Q&A) — the larger issue or unspoken motive behind a surface question (Ch 11)

Toggling — alternating between what is and what could be through the middle of a talk (Ch 4, Ch 5)

Transformation arc — the mapped move from where the audience starts to where you want it to end up (Ch 1)

Verbal tic — a filler word substituting for a pause (Ch 11)

Visual taxonomy — the five diagram relationship types: network, segment, join, flow, stack (Ch 9)

Walk-in / walk-out slide — the slide displayed as people arrive, and the one left up as they leave (Ch 8)

What is / what could be — the juxtaposition of status quo and better way that generates a presentation's conflict (Ch 4, Ch 5)

Whispering interpretation — the interpreter whispers audience comments to the presenter (Ch 11)

White space — open space around elements; raises perceived value and sharpens focus (Ch 9)

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques

Audience-as-Hero Reframe

When to use: Any draft that reads as a list of things the audience must do for you.

How: Recast yourself as mentor. Deliver a gift (insight that improves their lives), a magical tool (a skill or mind-set serving their objectives and yours), and a way to get unstuck (a solution to a painful situation). Rewrite the opening so "why this matters to you" precedes the nitty-gritty.

Trade-offs: Takes longer to prepare and cedes the spotlight; in exchange you get willing advocates instead of grudging compliance.

Audience Segmentation and Curation

When to use: Mixed-role rooms; internal decision meetings.

How: Profile along politics, demographics, psychographics, firmographics, ethnographics. Identify who most affects adoption. Write mostly to that subgroup, keeping enough general content to avoid alienating the rest. Prepare responses for known objectors and pre-sell the saboteurs.

Trade-offs: Over-specialize and you lose the room; under-specialize and you move no one.

The Executive Compression

When to use: Senior executives, short slots, decision meetings.

How: Build for the allotted time, then rehearse as if cut to 5 minutes. Lead with findings, conclusions, recommendations, and call to action. Set expectations up front ("5 minutes of summary, then discussion"). Front-load executive summary slides at ~10% of deck length; the rest is appendix you pull from on demand. Rehearse with someone who succeeds at that level.

Trade-offs: You surrender narrative suspense — which executives don't want anyway.

Big Idea Sentence Construction

When to use: Before generating any content.

How: Start from the topic. Add your point of view. Add what's at stake. Result must be one complete sentence with a subject (often "you") and a verb. Use pain words to make the status quo uncomfortable and reward words to lure.

Trade-offs: Committing to a POV invites disagreement — which is the point.

Divergent–Convergent Brainstorm Loop

When to use: Content generation for any substantial talk.

How: Alone (mind map on paper), then group (fast facilitation, one idea per sticky note, no judgment), then alone again to develop latent ideas. Then converge: filter every idea against the big idea and cut mercilessly.

Trade-offs: Slow, and produces material you'll discard — quantity is the mechanism, not waste.

Resistance Triage

When to use: Before finalizing content; again before Q&A prep.

How: Classify likely objections as logical (read the opposing literature), emotional (identify the bias, dogma, or moral code your idea violates and address the value at risk), or practical (name the sacrifice, share the burden visibly). Pre-empt in the talk; pre-sell the loudest critics privately.

Trade-offs: Raising objections yourself risks planting doubt — but it demonstrates an open mind and invites reciprocity.

What Is / What Could Be Toggle (Sparkline)

When to use: As the skeleton of any presentation meant to change belief or behavior.

How: Establish what is until heads nod. Introduce what could be, opening a gap. Toggle repeatedly through the middle, drawing rows from your dynamic-opposite pairs. End in the new bliss. Never announce the transition.

Trade-offs: More work than a linear report; the only structure that reliably moves people.

Three-Level Ending

When to use: The close of any persuasive talk.

How: Describe future rewards at three levels — benefits to them, to their sphere (peers, reports, customers), and to the world. Then, and only then, action items.

Trade-offs: Can read as grandiose if the third level is a stretch; skip it rather than inflate it.

Emotional-Impact Story Template

When to use: Converting a dry supporting point into something that lands.

How: When/who/where → context → conflict → proposed resolution → complication → actual resolution. Place discomfort stories on the what-is side and awe/inspiration stories on the what-could-be side.

Trade-offs: Costs time in a tight slot; buys retention and retelling.

S.T.A.R. Moment Design

When to use: Once per talk, at the climax.

How: Choose one of four — amplified shocking statistic, evocative visual contrast, memorable dramatization (props, live demonstration), or emotive anecdote. Tie it directly to the big idea.

Trade-offs: Two S.T.A.R. moments dilute each other; a S.T.A.R. moment serving showmanship rather than the idea reads as manipulation.

Vehicle Selection Before Software

When to use: Before opening PowerPoint or Keynote.

How: Match medium to how the audience processes information and to the venue: memo, video, whiteboard conversation, props, handouts, demo, or deck. Use low-tech deliberately when you want to signal that thinking is still formative.

Trade-offs: A polished deck signals finality — sometimes desirable (investors), often not (collaborative decisions).

The 60% Time Budget

When to use: Every talk with a defined slot.

How: Plan content for 60% of the slot. Cut deck by a third, moving slides to a slide cemetery. Rehearse with the clock counting up while trimming; switch to counting down once in range, with quarter-mark time stamps. Plant a false ending and a real ending.

Trade-offs: Feels like leaving value on the table; nobody has ever been faulted for ending early.

Glance Test Pass

When to use: On every slide.

How: Can it be understood in three seconds? Start from a clean surface with master prompts off, justify each added element, limit and enlarge text, unify typeface and palette, align and size deliberately.

Trade-offs: Sparse slides carry less standalone information — which is why documents exist.

Sticky-Note Storyboarding

When to use: After the title outline, before building anything.

How: Sketch each idea on a 1.5″ × 2″ note. One idea per slide. Concepts that overflow the note are too complex — eliminate and re-brainstorm.

Trade-offs: Feels like a detour; it saves more time than it costs and surfaces reusable diagram ideas.

Bullets-to-Diagram Conversion

When to use: Any slide with a related bullet list.

How: Circle the verbs or nouns and identify the relationship. Match it to network, segment, join, flow, or stack. Replace the list with a diagram from that category.

Trade-offs: Diagrams take longer to make and can over-formalize a loose grouping.

Data Clarification Pass

When to use: Every data slide.

How: Decide the one thing to be remembered and give it visual emphasis; gray out the rest; mute gridlines, borders, axes, labels. Kill 3-D where there's no z-axis; keep axis proportions honest. Choose the chart for the argument (matrix for relationships, line for trajectory). Consider showing one huge number instead. Explain why and how, not just what. Anchor big magnitudes in concrete comparisons.

Trade-offs: Deemphasized context must be supplied by you, so it doesn't survive redistribution — send a document for that.

Rehearsal Stack

When to use: Every talk that matters.

How: Honest feedback from a skilled presenter on a printed deck; a rehearsed short version; continued slide tweaking as familiarity-building; runs in slide-show mode; and on-camera recording reviewed for presence, gestures, and tics.

Trade-offs: Time-expensive. Memorizing instead is cheaper and worse — it produces stiffness.

Technology Walkthrough Checklist

When to use: 30+ minutes before every in-person talk.

How: Befriend the AV person; test projector, clicker, audio; bring your own backups plus cloud, drive, and paper copies; prerecord demos; click through every slide in-room; verify comfort monitor legibility from the stage; confirm all media files transferred and play; confirm aspect ratio and projection direction, taping the floor; check for remote attendees.

Trade-offs: Pure overhead when nothing breaks; the one time it does, it's the whole talk.

Q&A Control

When to use: Every business presentation — trim content to make room.

How: Decide up front when questions come. Prepare answers to mundane through hostile questions. Answer the subtext, not just the surface. Admit ignorance and commit to follow up. Use a moderator or a one-question-per-person rule; acknowledge hostile questioners while answering to the rest of the room; use a filtering facilitator for charged topics. Close with a summary that recaps the new bliss.

Trade-offs: Taking questions throughout breaks your build; saving them all risks a pile-up.

Remote Presence Manufacturing

When to use: Any webinar, teleconference, or streamed talk.

How: Camera at eye level, stand, eyes on the lens, gestures kept in frame. Break content into small bites and change slides ~every 20 seconds. Build in interactivity and rewards. Vary voices with a co-host. Pause strategically to cut through white noise. Picture (or photograph) real faces. Test slides on the presenting machine — webinar software breaks builds and animations. Suppress personal, environmental, visual, and communal noise. Use a facilitator.

Trade-offs: High preparation cost for an audience whose attention you only partly control.

Backchannel Engagement

When to use: External talks with broad audiences (never confidential or client meetings).

How: Create and display a hashtag; invite use before, during, and after. Assign a quick-witted moderator to tweet key phrases, raise questions, redirect drift, and post slide links. Repeat and validate audience sentiment. Stream the talk. Post photos live. Invite bloggers. Don't flag your own sound bites, and be novel.

Trade-offs: The channel that spreads your idea can also organize against it; participation is the mitigation.

Structured Follow-Up

When to use: Immediately after every talk that asked for something.

How: Handwritten notes; thank-you e-mail recapping big idea, key points, call to action, and new bliss; open-door or lunch accessibility; promised materials sent immediately; one-on-one calls with people carrying the burden; a next-steps working meeting; and further presentations to other groups.

Trade-offs: Sustained effort long after the adrenaline stops — which is exactly why most presenters skip it and lose the adoption.

Thinking in Bets: Making Smarter Decisions When You Don't Have All the Facts

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Thinking in Bets

Decision rules and tells to keep beside you while deciding, learning, and communicating under uncertainty.

Core reflexes

  • Bad outcome? Ask first: bad decision or bad luck? Judge the bet given what was knowable, not the roll. (Avoid resulting.)
  • A non-0%/100% prediction can't be "wrong" from one result. A 2% event happening doesn't refute "2%." Judge calibration over many bets.
  • Replace "Am I sure?" with "How sure?" State a % or a range; update in small increments, never a right↔wrong flip.
  • Nearly nothing is 0% or 100%. If you're saying "always/never/certain," you're probably miscalibrated.
  • You're already guessing whenever you decide. So make the probabilities explicit — a wide range beats no estimate.

Tells → what's happening → countermove

If you notice…You're probably…Do this
Grading a decision by how it turned outResultingReconstruct what was knowable; judge the bet, not the result
Crediting your wins to skill, blaming losses on luckSelf-serving bias / fielding errorAsk "would this repeat?"; take the other's perspective
"So unlucky," "I always get screwed"Motivated outcome fieldingField into luck and skill buckets; look for a controllable
Dismissing an idea because of who said itShooting the message (universalism fail)Judge the claim on merit; imagine a source you respect
"I knew it all along," "it was bound to happen"Hindsight biasRebuild the tree; the outcome was one branch of many
"Worst day ever," reacting to the last half hourTicker watching / zoom lens / tiltRun 10-10-10; take the long view; step away
Everyone in the room agrees with youEcho chamber / confirmatory driftSeek dissent; add someone who disagrees
The detail you want to leave outCommunism fail (spinning a narrative)Share it — hesitation is the signal it matters

CUDOS checklist (rules of engagement for a truthseeking group)

  • Communism — is all the data on the table? "More is more."
  • Universalism — am I judging the idea, not the messenger?
  • Disinterestedness — did I hide the outcome and my own opinion so I don't infect them?
  • Organized Skepticism — am I asking "why might this not be true?" civilly?

Are you on tilt? (don't decide if yes)

Verbal tells: "Seriously? Again?", swearing, "why do I bother." Physical tells: flushed cheeks, racing heart, fast breathing.

→ Precommit to walk away, take ten breaths, sleep on it. Ask: "Will this matter in the long run?"

Which time-travel tool?

SituationTool
Hot, in-the-moment choice10-10-10
Map the path to a goalBackcasting (positive space)
Stress-test a plan before committingPremortem (negative space) — pair with backcast; the two sum to 100%
Predictable future temptationUlysses contract (raise or lower a barrier)
Choosing among uncertain futuresScenario planning + expected value
Catch yourself veering liveDecision swear jar

Talking to people who haven't opted in

1. Express uncertainty first ("I'm not sure, but…").

2. Lead with assent, then "and" — never "but."

3. Ask permission: "Want to vent, or looking for advice?"

4. Focus on the future: "What could you do so it turns out better next time?"

Life is poker, not chess — and it's one long game. Take satisfaction in making good bets; outcomes will vary. Calibrate a little better each time.

glossary.md

Glossary — Thinking in Bets

10-10-10 — A decision routine (Suzy Welch): weigh the consequences of each option in 10 minutes, 10 months, and 10 years to recruit future-self and defuse in-the-moment emotion (Ch 6).

Accountability — A willingness or obligation to answer to others for our beliefs and actions; a bet is a form of accountability that makes us hypervigilant about our confidence (Ch 4).

All decisions are bets — Every choice commits resources to one uncertain future while foreclosing others; "not betting" is itself a bet (Intro, Ch 2).

Backcasting — Imagining you've already achieved a goal ("We Achieved Our Goal!") and working backward to identify how you got there; reveals the positive path (Ch 6).

Belief-formation flaw — We don't hear→vet→believe; we hear→believe→(maybe) vet. Default is to believe what we hear (Gilbert) (Ch 2).

Bet — A decision about an uncertain future that risks resources on one outcome; the book's core reframe (Intro, Ch 2).

Blind-spot bias — Spotting bias in others but not ourselves; larger the smarter/more numerate we are. A group helps fill in our blind spots (Ch 2, Ch 4).

Calibration — Holding beliefs as probabilities and updating in small increments toward accuracy, instead of flipping between right and wrong (Ch 1, Ch 2).

Confirmatory thought — One-sided reasoning that rationalizes a held view; amplifies bias and breeds groupthink (Ch 4).

CUDOS — Merton's four norms for a truthseeking group: Communism, Universalism, Disinterestedness, Organized Skepticism (Ch 5).

Communism (Mertonian) — Data belong to the group; share everything, "more is more" (Ch 5).

Decision-interrupt — The stop-and-think moment a precommitment creates when you consider breaking it (Ch 6).

Decision quality ≠ outcome quality — A good process can yield a bad result (bad luck) and vice versa; judge the bet, not the roll (Intro, Ch 1).

Decision swear jar — A precommitment to flag words/thoughts signaling irrationality ("I'm sure," "so unlucky," "wrong"), triggering reflection (Ch 6).

Devil's advocate — An assigned role to argue against a position, raising alternative hypotheses (from the Church's canonization process) (Ch 5).

Disinterestedness (Mertonian) — Vigilance against conflicts of interest; use outcome/belief blindness so evaluators aren't infected (Ch 5).

Dissent Channel / red team — Institutional mechanisms (State Dept., CIA) that protect and reward dissenting views (Ch 4, Ch 5).

Echo chamber — A homogeneous group that repeats and confirms its own views; the natural drift of confirmatory thought (Ch 4).

Expected value — Probability-weighted worth of an option (a $50k grant at 70% beats a $200k grant at 10%) (Ch 6).

Exploratory thought — Even-handed consideration of alternative viewpoints; moves a group toward accuracy (Tetlock & Lerner) (Ch 4).

Fielding outcomes — Deciding whether a result came from skill (your decisions) or luck (outside your control); the mechanism of learning (Ch 3).

Hindsight bias — After an outcome, seeing it as inevitable ("I should have known"); the chainsaw that lops off unrealized branches of the tree (Ch 1, Ch 6).

Learning loop — Outcomes → field into luck/skill → update beliefs → better bets; fielding errors sever it (Ch 3).

"Lettermanning" — Offering a truthseeking challenge to someone who hasn't agreed to it, so it lands as an attack (Ch 4).

Loss limit — A preset stop-loss enforced by accountability to a group; a check against chasing losses while irrational (Ch 4, Ch 6).

Luck — The influence on outcomes of things outside our control (others' actions, weather, genes, hidden cards) (Intro, Ch 3).

Mental contrasting — Oettingen's finding that imagining obstacles (not just success) makes goals more achievable; basis of the premortem (Ch 6).

Mental time travel — Recruiting past- and future-selves as decision buddies to engage deliberative mind (Ch 6).

Motivated reasoning — Processing information to protect existing beliefs — seeking confirmation, discrediting the rest (Ch 2).

Organized skepticism (Mertonian) — Engaging dissent through civil discussion; asking "why might this not be true?" (Ch 5).

Outcome blindness — Presenting a decision up to the decision point, omitting the result, so it's judged on process not outcome (Ch 5).

Path dependence — Emotional response driven by the recent path, not the overall result (win $100 and feel sad, lose $100 and feel happy) (Ch 6).

Poker vs. chess — A model of decision environments: chess = perfect info, little luck; poker = hidden info, real luck (Ch 1).

Premortem — Imagining you've failed ("We Failed to Reach Our Goal") and listing why; reveals the negative space (Klein, Oettingen) (Ch 6).

Rashomon Effect — Different people give drastically different accounts of the same event; no one version is complete (Ch 5).

Reconnaissance / scenario planning — Mapping the range of possible futures of a decision and assigning probabilities (Ch 6).

Redefining "wrong" — A non-0%/100% prediction can't be proven wrong by a single outcome; judge calibration over many bets (Ch 1).

Resulting — Judging a decision's quality by its outcome; the core error to avoid (Ch 1).

Self-serving bias — Fielding wins into the skill bucket and losses into the luck bucket to protect self-image (Ch 3).

SnackWell's Phenomenon — Consuming more of something with less of a "bad" ingredient; a case of how hard it is to work backward from outcome to cause (Ch 3).

Temporal discounting — Overvaluing a reward now versus a bigger reward later (Night Jerry vs. Morning Jerry) (Ch 6).

"They saw a game" effect — Prior beliefs change how we experience the same event (Ch 2).

Tilt — Emotionally unhinged decision-making caused by recent outcomes; the limbic system shuts down the prefrontal cortex (Ch 6).

Truthseeking pod / buddy system — A small chartered group that helps you fight bias and field outcomes honestly (Ch 4).

Truthseeking charter — The explicit agreement for a productive group: accuracy, accountability, openness to diverse views (Ch 4).

Truthseeker — Someone who wants to know what's true regardless of whether it flatters existing beliefs (Intro).

Ticker watching — Reacting to moment-by-moment fluctuations instead of the long-term trend (Ch 6).

Ulysses contract — A precommitment by past-self to bind present-self against a predictable irrational impulse (Odysseus at the mast) (Ch 6).

Universalism (Mertonian) — "Don't shoot the message": judge a claim on its merits regardless of its source (Ch 5).

"Wanna bet?" — A challenge (real or imagined) that triggers vetting of a belief (Ch 2, Ch 3).

"Yes, and" — The improv rule for offering dissent: accept the construct, then add ("and" not "but") (Ch 5).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Thinking in Bets

Concrete, reusable practices Duke endorses for making smarter decisions under uncertainty.

The "Wanna Bet?" Self-Challenge

When to use: Whenever you catch yourself stating something as certain.

How: Imagine a credible person says "Wanna bet?" Then run the vetting questions — How do I know this? How good is my source? What am I missing? What are the plausible alternatives? Why might I be wrong? — before committing to the belief.

Trade-offs: Slows down snap judgments; the payoff is beliefs calibrated closer to the truth and fewer over-confident bets.

Express Confidence as a Percentage or Range

When to use: Any belief or prediction you state to yourself or others.

How: Replace "I'm sure" with a number ("I'm 60%") or a range ("Elvis died between 40 and 47"). Update in small increments as evidence arrives rather than flipping right↔wrong.

Trade-offs: Feels less authoritative, but it's more credible and invites others to add information and dissent.

Field Outcomes into Luck vs. Skill

When to use: Any result you want to learn from.

How: Ask "Would the same decision predictably produce this result again?" If yes → skill; if it hinged on things you couldn't control → luck (most outcomes are a blend). Treat the fielding itself as a bet, and use perspective-taking ("What if this had happened to someone else?") to reach the truthful middle.

Trade-offs: Fights self-serving bias, which credits wins to skill and blames losses on luck; requires honesty that stings.

Build a Truthseeking Pod with a CUDOS Charter

When to use: To sustain truthseeking that willpower alone can't; habits hard to change.

How: Recruit as few as three people (two to disagree, one to referee) who opt into a modified social contract. Charter it on accuracy (reward objectivity over confirmation), accountability (members answer for beliefs, with advance notice), and diversity (actively seek dissent). Operationalize Merton's CUDOS: Communism (share all data), Universalism (judge ideas independent of source), Disinterestedness (outcome/belief blindness), Organized Skepticism (civil dissent).

Trade-offs: Requires discipline against the natural drift toward clones and echo chambers; must be freely chosen, never imposed.

Communicate for Feedback (Don't Lead with Your Conclusion)

When to use: Seeking honest input on a decision, inside or outside your group.

How: Describe the situation up to the decision point and omit the outcome and your own opinion ("It doesn't matter how it turned out"). Optionally omit the source too, so the group isn't biased for or against the messenger. Ask specific questions inviting reasons you might be wrong.

Trade-offs: Resisting the urge to reveal "how it ends" is hard, but it prevents infecting listeners with resulting and confirmation.

Truthseek Gently Outside Your Group

When to use: With people (kids, coworkers, friends) who haven't agreed to the charter.

How: (1) Express your own uncertainty first; (2) lead with assent — state specific points of agreement, then add with "and," never "but"; (3) ask permission ("Do you want to vent, or are you looking for advice?"); (4) focus on the future ("What might you do so things turn out better going forward?").

Trade-offs: Slower and less direct, but avoids the defensiveness that shuts down the conversation (see Letterman/Conrad).

Run 10-10-10

When to use: In-the-moment decisions where emotion is running high (tired, on tilt, a bad break).

How: Ask the consequences of each option in 10 minutes, 10 months, and 10 years — or the past-frame ("How would I feel today if I'd decided this 10 minutes / months / years ago?"). Draw on past experiences to engage deliberative mind.

Trade-offs: Won't make you perfectly rational, but keeps momentary events in proportion.

Backcast (Then Premortem)

When to use: Planning toward a goal or committing to a strategy.

How: Backcast — imagine you've already succeeded ("We Achieved Our Goal!") and work backward to list the decisions and events that got you there. Then run a premortem — imagine you've failed ("We Failed to Reach Our Goal") and list every reason why. The positive and negative space must add to 100%.

Trade-offs: The premortem feels pessimistic in the moment, but negative visualization (mental contrasting) makes goals more achievable and shrinks over-optimism to realistic size.

Scenario Planning / Reconnaissance of the Future

When to use: Before any consequential bet; budgeting, sales pipelines, strategy.

How: List the possible futures of a decision, then assign probabilities to each — even wide ranges (20%–80%) beat not guessing. Use expected value (probability × payoff) to prioritize. Memorialize the tree so you don't rewrite it with hindsight.

Trade-offs: People resist guessing probabilities, but you're already guessing whenever you decide; making it explicit reduces resulting and hindsight bias.

Set a Ulysses Contract

When to use: Wherever you can predict a future irrational impulse.

How: Have past-you bind present-you. Raise barriers (throw out junk food, ride-share to the bar, preset settlement floor, home-buying budget) or lower them (carry healthy snacks, automatic retirement allocation). Even a soft, tamper-able version creates a decision-interrupt — a stop-and-think moment.

Trade-offs: Rarely 100% tamper-proof, but the interrupt prompts deliberative thought and reduces reactive decisions.

Keep a Decision Swear Jar

When to use: To catch yourself veering from truthseeking in real time.

How: Predefine words/thoughts that signal irrationality — illusion of certainty ("I know," "always," "0%/100%"), irrational fielding ("so unlucky"), universalism violations ("idiot," "typical ___"), zoom-in language ("worst day ever"), motivated reasoning ("everyone agrees"), and especially the word "wrong." When you catch one, stop and reflect.

Trade-offs: Your list is personal and never complete, but each catch is a decision-interrupt back toward calibration.

Range: Why Generalists Triumph in a Specialized World

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Range — Decision Cheatsheet

Decision Tree: Is this a KIND or WICKED environment?

1. Do the same patterns recur reliably?        no -> WICKED
2. Are the rules stable, complete, and known?  no -> WICKED
3. Is feedback fast (within the decision)?     no -> WICKED
4. Is feedback accurate and unambiguous?       no -> WICKED  <- most decisive
   all four yes -> KIND

Then:

  • KIND → repetition builds real intuition. Specialize, drill, trust the veteran, trust your gut, automate.
  • WICKED → experience builds confidence faster than accuracy. Prefer breadth, outside views, explicit probability, aggressive belief updating. Distrust the confident veteran — including yourself.
  • MIXED / SHIFTING → the common case. Re-score whenever rules change; expertise built under old rules becomes cognitive entrenchment under new ones.

Core Decision Rules

  • When feedback is delayed or ambiguous, do not trust pattern-matching intuition — because the environment never taught you the pattern, only that you had one.
  • When you're early in anything, sample rather than commit — because match quality information is the scarce resource, and head-start advantages fade out.
  • When deciding whether to quit, ask "what have I learned about myself since I chose this?" — because informed switching beats persistence, and grit research was measured on already-selected populations (restriction of range).
  • When practice feels smooth and fast, you are probably learning less — because desirable difficulties depress in-session performance and raise retention.
  • When estimating a project, build a reference class first — because your case's vivid details are exactly what corrupts the estimate.
  • When specialists are stuck, broadcast outward — because winners come from the margins, and the answer may already be published in a literature they don't read.
  • When you can't win on frontier tech, win on application of withered tech — because reach and reliability beat specs in most markets.
  • When the situation stops matching your training, drop the tool, don't grip it harder — because overlearned routines are lethal once conditions change.
  • When a forecaster is famous and certain, discount them — because fame correlates inversely with accuracy (hedgehogs make better television).
  • When your culture feels perfectly aligned, add cross-pressure — because congruence suppresses the dissent that prevents catastrophe.

Specialize vs. Sample

SignalSpecialize nowKeep sampling
EnvironmentKind, stable rulesWicked or shifting
Skill ceilingAge-limited (elite sport, music virtuosity)No hard age ceiling
Self-knowledgeYou've tested the fit against alternativesFit untested or inherited
FeedbackFast and unambiguousDelayed or noisy
Cost of switchingRising steeplyStill low
Your evidence"I tried others; this fits""I never tried anything else"

Breadth vs. Depth

Depth (I-shaped)Breadth (foxes, T/π-shaped)
Wins atRepeating problems, tactics, executionNovel problems, strategy, transfer
Fails atRule changes, novel structureRoutine technical mastery
LearningBlocked practice, fast gainsInterleaving, slow gains, far transfer
Best useKind domains, near-term outputWicked domains, breakthroughs
IdealNot either — breadth plus at least one depth

Thresholds & Defaults Epstein Commits To

  • Default to delayed specialization. Early specialization is the exception, justified only by a kind environment with a hard age ceiling.
  • The sampling period is integral, not a delay. Late specializers catch up fast and match better; they trade a head start for fit.
  • Judge learning on delayed tests and novel problems, never on in-session fluency or current test scores.
  • Use multiple, distant analogies — one near analogy is worse than none.
  • Belief updating frequency is the single best predictor of forecast accuracy — more than intelligence or subject expertise.
  • Plan experiments, not plans. Short-term steps from present interests; revise on results.
  • Breakthroughs are high variance — judge the portfolio and the process, not any single attempt.
  • Don't feel behind. There is no universal timeline; comparison to the Tiger path is the error.

Tells & Smells

A wicked environment is masquerading as kind when: success stories are told retrospectively as if the path were plannable; confident experts disagree with each other; feedback arrives long after the decision, or only via outcomes you can't attribute; "best practice" is defined by what current elites do now.

Specialization is premature when: the choice was made before any alternative was tried; the credential was committed to before the fit was known; interests are described in inherited language ("I've always been a X person"); the main argument for staying is time already invested.

The match is bad when: you're optimizing to survive the role rather than to do it; persistence is motivated by sunk cost, identity, or others' expectations; the "grit" you're exercising is consistency of interests you never chose.
