You're stuck in local search when: everyone consulted shares your training; the problem is stated in terms that presuppose the solution's form; confidentiality reflex blocks asking outsiders; the first familiar approach keeps recurring (Einstellung).

You're gripping a familiar tool when: you demand quantification for a concern that can't be quantified; you defend the process rather than the outcome; dissent went to an offline caucus and came back unanimous; silence is being read as consent.

glossary.md

Range — Glossary

Action at a distance — A force operating without contact; the deep-structure idea Kepler reached only by analogy from light and magnets. (Ch 5)

Active open-mindedness — Jonathan Baron's disposition of treating your own beliefs as hypotheses to be tested rather than treasures to be defended; the strongest correlate of forecasting accuracy. (Ch 10)

Altered gospel — The popularized, truncated version of grit research that drops its caveats and turns "don't quit" into universal advice. (Ch 6)

Ambiguous Sorting Task — A test where problems can be grouped by surface features or by deep structure; people trained across domains sort by deep structure. (Ch 5)

Bansho — Japanese teaching practice of arraying multiple student-generated solutions on the board for comparison, forcing making-connections work. (Ch 4)

Birds and frogs — Freeman Dyson's division: frogs delve into the mud of specific problems; birds survey broadly and connect. Both are needed; ecosystems fail when only frogs are funded. (Ch 9)

Blocked practice — Drilling one skill type repeatedly before moving on. Feels effective, produces fast gains and poor retention. (Ch 4)

Career streams — Viewing a career as a path of experiences and learning rather than a ladder of titles. (Ch 1)

Centaurs — Human-computer teams; in freestyle chess, amateurs with good process beat both grandmasters and standalone engines. (Ch 1)

Chunking — Perceiving meaningful recurring patterns as single units; the mechanism of expertise in kind domains, and useless when patterns don't recur. (Ch 1)

Cognitive entrenchment — Ryan Dane's term for expertise that becomes inflexible: the deeper the specialization, the harder it is to adapt when the environment changes. (Ch 1)

Conceptual Swiss Army knife — Broad, transferable reasoning tools (Fermi-izing, economics, statistics) usable on unfamiliar problems. (Ch 2)

Congruence / Incongruence — Congruence is cultural "fit" among an institution's values, goals, and norms; Epstein argues incongruence (deliberate internal cross-pressure) protects organizations from conformity failures. (Ch 11)

Consistency of interests — The Grit Scale subcomponent measuring how long you stick with the same goals; high scores can indicate a good match or an unexamined one. (Ch 6)

Context principle — Dark Horse Project finding that motivation and performance are situation-specific, not fixed traits. (Ch 7)

Dark Horse Project — Harvard study of unconventionally successful people; nearly all used short-term planning from present interests rather than long-term destination plans. (Ch 7)

Deliberate amateur — Arturo Casadevall's ideal: a trained expert who deliberately works at the edge of their competence, where naivety enables questions insiders won't ask. (Ch 12)

Deliberate practice — Ericsson's narrow construct: effortful repetition with immediate feedback on well-defined tasks. Valid in kind domains; overextended everywhere else. (Intro, Ch 3)

Desirable difficulties — Robert Bjork's term for obstacles that slow learning down and make it stick: spacing, testing, interleaving, generation. (Ch 4)

Dropping your familiar tools — Karl Weick's concept: under pressure, experts cling to overlearned routines even when those routines are killing them; survival requires letting them go. (Ch 11)

Eduction — Raven's term for making meaning out of confusion — solving novel abstract problems without prior instruction. (Ch 2)

Einstellung effect — A fixed mental set: the first familiar approach that comes to mind blocks better alternatives. (Ch 8)

Empowering innovation — Technology that makes an existing capability available to far more people, rather than pushing the frontier for a few. (Ch 9)

End of history illusion — Quoidbach/Gilbert finding that people at every age know they've changed but predict they won't change further. (Ch 7)

Fadeout — The pattern where early head-start advantages evaporate, and sometimes reverse, over time. (Ch 4)

Far transfer — Applying knowledge to a genuinely novel context; the rare, valuable form of transfer that breadth enables. (Ch 4)

Fermi-izing — Decomposing an unanswerable question into estimable parts to get a defensible order-of-magnitude answer. (Ch 2)

Figlie del coro — The all-female musicians of Venice's ospedali, Europe's finest, trained by wide instrument sampling rather than early specialization. (Ch 3)

Flynn effect — The steady rise in abstract-reasoning IQ scores across the 20th century, reflecting modern "scientific spectacles." (Ch 2)

Foxes vs. Hedgehogs — Berlin's distinction, tested by Tetlock: hedgehogs know one big thing and forecast worse the more famous they are; foxes know many small things and forecast better. (Ch 10)

Functional fixedness — Seeing an object or idea only in terms of its conventional use. (Ch 9)

Generation effect — Struggling to produce an answer before being shown it produces far better retention than being given the answer. (Ch 4)

Good Judgment Project — Tetlock's forecasting tournament; superforecasters were broad, numerate, and above all frequent belief-updaters. (Ch 10)

Hypercorrection effect — The more confident you were in a wrong answer, the more durably you remember the correction. (Ch 4)

Interleaving — Mixing problem types within practice so the learner must first identify which strategy applies. Feels worse, transfers far better. (Ch 4)

Kind learning environment — Hogarth's term: patterns repeat, rules are clear, feedback is fast, accurate, and unambiguous. Chess, golf, firefighting. (Ch 1)

Knowledge as a double-edged sword — Expertise that supplies solutions also constrains which solutions get considered. (Ch 8)

Lateral thinking with withered technology — Gunpei Yokoi's doctrine: take cheap, mature, well-understood technology and deploy it in a radically new use, rather than competing on the frontier. (Ch 9)

Local search — Solving a problem by looking only in the domain where it arose; the default that outsider searches beat. (Ch 8)

Match quality — The degree of fit between a person's abilities and interests and the work they do. Epstein's central optimization target — it is found, not planned. (Ch 6, Ch 7)

Moravec's paradox — Machines excel at what humans find hard (calculation) and fail at what humans find easy (perception, judgment in open situations). (Ch 1)

Multi-armed bandit process — The formal explore/exploit trade-off; sampling widely early has informational value that justifies its short-term cost. (Ch 6)

Naturalistic decision making (NDM) — Klein's research program on expert intuition; valid where environments are kind. (Ch 1)

Network of enterprise — Howard Gruber's term for creative people running many loosely connected projects at once. (Ch 9)

Oculostenotic reflex — The cardiologist's impulse to stent a visible blockage because it's visible, regardless of whether it helps. (Ch 11)

Outside view — Kahneman/Tversky: estimating by finding structurally analogous cases (a reference class) rather than reasoning from your case's vivid details. (Ch 5)

Overlearned behavior — A routine practiced to automaticity; efficient in kind conditions, lethal when conditions change. (Ch 11)

Possible selves — The range of future identities you might become; discovered by trying, not introspection. (Ch 7)

Principle of limited sloppiness — Max Delbrück's rule: be sloppy enough that unexpected things can happen, not so sloppy you can't tell what happened. (Ch 12)

Process vs. outcome accountability — Being answerable for following procedure vs. for results; process accountability alone breeds conformity and suppresses dissent. (Ch 11)

Range — Breadth of experience, training, and perspective; the book's title virtue. (Intro)

Restriction of range — The statistical artifact where studying an already-selected population (e.g. West Point cadets) hides how much a trait actually varies. (Ch 6)

Sampling period — The early phase in which future elite performers try many activities, learn their own abilities and interests, then narrow. Integral, not a delay. (Intro, Ch 3)

Scientific spectacles — Luria's finding that modern schooling teaches people to classify abstractly rather than reason from concrete experience. (Ch 2)

Sensemaking — Weick's alternative to decision making: figuring out what situation you are actually in, especially when the familiar frame has broken. (Ch 11)

Serial innovators — Employees who repeatedly create breakthroughs; characteristically broad, high in "systems thinking," and poorly served by narrow hiring rubrics. (Ch 9)

Single-loop learning — Argyris: responding to feedback by refining the existing approach rather than questioning the goal or model. (Ch 1)

Superforecasters — Good Judgment Project's top performers; distinguished by granular probability estimates and aggressive belief updating. (Ch 10)

Surface analogy — A match based on visible similarity rather than causal structure; the failure mode of analogical reasoning. (Ch 5)

T-shaped / I-shaped / π-shaped — Breadth-plus-one-depth, single narrow depth, and breadth-plus-two-depths skill profiles. (Ch 9)

Test-and-learn (vs. plan-and-implement) — Choose a promising next step, try it, learn from the result, revise. The Dark Horse strategy. (Ch 7)

Undiscovered public knowledge — Don Swanson's insight that answers already exist in the literature, unlinked across specialties nobody reads together. (Ch 8)

Whole Candidate Score — West Point's admissions composite; predicted who got in, not who stayed. (Ch 6)

Wicked learning environment — Hogarth's term: rules are unclear or incomplete, patterns don't reliably repeat, feedback is delayed, inaccurate, or absent. Most of the modern world. (Ch 1)

Withered technology — Mature, cheap, thoroughly understood technology — the raw material of lateral innovation. (Ch 9, Ch 12)

patterns.md

Range — Patterns & Techniques

Diagnose the Learning Environment Before Choosing a Strategy

When to use: Before deciding whether to specialize, trust an expert, or trust your own intuition in any domain.

How: Score the domain on Hogarth's four criteria — (1) Do patterns repeat? (2) Are the rules stable and known? (3) Is feedback fast? (4) Is feedback accurate and unambiguous? Four yeses = kind; any no, especially on feedback, = wicked. In kind environments, repetition builds real intuition — specialize, drill, trust the expert. In wicked ones, experience can build confident wrongness — favor breadth, outside views, and explicit belief updating.

Trade-offs: Most real domains are mixed and shift over time. Re-score when the environment changes; expertise built in a formerly kind environment becomes a liability (cognitive entrenchment) when the rules move.

Run a Sampling Period

When to use: Early in any career, skill, or field — and again after any major change in circumstances or interests.

How: Deliberately try several adjacent activities at low commitment. Judge each on two axes: what you're good at, and what you actually want to keep doing. Keep the period lightly structured; the goal is information about yourself, not accumulated hours. Narrow only when a clear match emerges, and expect the eventual specialist phase to be shorter and steeper than a head start would have been.

Trade-offs: You lose early technical head start and will trail the precocious for a while. In genuinely kind domains with fixed early ceilings (elite gymnastics, chess prodigies), that cost is real. Everywhere else, fadeout means the head start wasn't worth much.

Optimize for Match Quality, Not Persistence

When to use: Any decision to stay in or leave a job, field, degree, or project.

How: Treat the choice as a multi-armed bandit — weigh the informational value of switching against the value of continuing. Ask "is this the best fit I know of, given what I have learned about myself since I chose it?" not "am I a quitter?" Enumerate quit conditions in advance, while calm, so the decision isn't made under sunk-cost pressure. Distinguish informed switching (you learned something that changed the calculus) from avoidance (you hit an expected difficulty).

Trade-offs: Switching resets accumulated domain capital and looks like flightiness on a résumé. The cost falls over time as you learn more about yourself, so switch earlier rather than agonizing longer.

Make Practice Deliberately Harder (Desirable Difficulties)

When to use: Any time you want durable learning and transfer rather than a good feeling during the session.

How: Stack four moves. Generation — attempt the answer before seeing it, even wrongly; being confidently wrong then corrected sticks best (hypercorrection). Spacing — leave enough gap that recall is effortful. Testing — retrieve rather than reread. Interleaving — mix problem types so you must first identify which strategy applies, instead of blocking one type at a time.

Trade-offs: Performance during practice drops and learners feel they're learning less — so learners, teachers, and managers all reliably prefer the worse method. Measure on delayed tests and novel problems, never on in-session fluency.

Take the Outside View

When to use: Estimating cost, duration, or success odds for a project — especially one that feels distinctive.

How: Ignore your case's specifics first. Strip it to its structural bones, build a reference class of superficially unrelated situations that share that deep structure, and take the base rate. Only then adjust for genuine particulars. Use multiple, distant analogies rather than one near one — a single surface analogy is worse than none.

Trade-offs: Feels dismissive of hard-won detail, and insiders will object that their case is different. That objection is the inside view talking.

Run an Outsider Search

When to use: A problem has resisted the specialists who own it, or progress has stalled inside a single domain.

How: Write the problem abstractly enough that a non-specialist can grasp it — strip jargon and stated assumptions about the solution's form. Broadcast it outside the field (the InnoCentive model). Expect winners from the margins of the field, whose home domain differs from the problem's. Look for undiscovered public knowledge: answers already published in a literature nobody reads alongside yours.

Trade-offs: Requires disclosing the problem, which cuts against confidentiality reflexes and insider status. Most outside submissions are useless; the value is in the tail.

Lateral Thinking with Withered Technology

When to use: You cannot win a frontier-technology arms race, or you want reach and reliability over specification.

How: Pick technology that is cheap, mature, and thoroughly understood. Invest the creativity in the application, not the components. Ask "what could this well-worn thing do that nobody has tried?" Be a producer who spans domains, not an engineer optimizing one.

Trade-offs: Reads as unambitious, and specialists will mock the specs. The reverse failure is real too — abandoning the doctrine for novel technology you don't fully understand.

Build Incongruence Into a Team or Organization

When to use: Designing a culture where conformity failures would be catastrophic, or diagnosing why dissent isn't surfacing.

How: Deliberately cross-pressure the culture — pair process accountability with outcome accountability, individualist norms with collective ones. Create channels that bypass hierarchy (Monday Notes-style: chain of command is not the chain of communication). Actively prospect for doubts rather than waiting for objections. Never require dissent to be quantified before it counts.

Trade-offs: Uncomfortable, slower, and less "aligned." Strongly congruent cultures are easier to describe and feel better from inside — which is exactly the trap.

Practice Sensemaking Under Pressure

When to use: The situation has stopped matching your training and you feel the pull to execute the familiar routine harder.

How: Name that you are in an unfamiliar situation before choosing an action. Ask what kind of situation this is, not what the procedure says. Identify your overlearned tools — the credential, the model, the standard process — and ask explicitly which to drop. Hold hunches lightly and say them out loud even without data.

Trade-offs: Dropping familiar tools feels like abandoning competence and identity, and is hardest exactly when it matters most.

Protect Deliberate-Amateur Time

When to use: Sustaining creative output over a career; running a research or product group.

How: Reserve recurring unstructured time for work outside your specialty and outside your obligations (Friday night / Saturday morning experiments; dabble time). Deliberately work at the edge of your competence where you can still ask naive questions. Maintain a network of enterprise — several loosely connected projects — and porous boundaries with other fields, importing methods from one to another.

Trade-offs: Unfundable by proposal (you must say what you'll find before you look), invisible on short-term metrics, and mostly unproductive — breakthroughs are high variance, so judge the portfolio, not the session.

Executive Presence: The Missing Link Between Merit and Success

cheatsheet.md

Executive Presence — Cheatsheet

Decision-ready rules from Hewlett. Keep beside you before a high-stakes moment.

The Three Pillars (weight & rule)

Pillar"How you…"Exec weightRule
Gravitasact67% (core)Fix first — without it, no title makes you a leader
Communicationspeak28%It's how not what; content persuades only ~15%
Appearancelook5%The filter — fail it and no one assesses the rest

Rule of thumb: Don't aim for straight A's. Nail ~3 top picks in each pillar to your natural strengths and avoid serious blunders.

Decision Rules

  • When merit isn't translating into advancement → audit all three pillars; the gap is almost always EP, not competence.
  • When in a crisis → own the mistake publicly and fast; handling catastrophe > avoiding it. Never deflect blame.
  • When a decision is being avoided → render a decision (not necessarily the perfect one) when no one else dares — but only after listening and finding the timely opening.
  • When you must show teeth as a woman/minority → frame it around the team/company; take the "I" out.
  • When speaking truth to power → come from a core of values (not grievance); leaven with humor to widen receptivity.
  • When opening a talk → connect in 5 seconds with a short personal story; then lose the props and make eye contact.
  • When you have a point in a meeting → snipe, don't spray: wait for a strong counterpoint or insightful question. But if you're leading, open with a bold agenda-setting statement.
  • When dressing → "appropriate for your environment, authentic to you." Dress for the job you want.
  • When told "you're doing great" → distrust it; ask for specific/timely/prescriptive feedback on a named recent encounter.
  • When given vague criticism ("be more vulnerable") → ask "How is what I'm doing getting in the way of my job?" It's usually the culture, not you.
  • When you hit the fork (conformity costs your identity) → distinguish "playing the game" from "selling out." Only you draw the line; don't put your soul in play.
  • When a culture violates a non-negotiable → walk away. "Nothing is worth that."
  • When you feel slighted → assume ignorance before bigotry; engage rather than withdraw.

Voice & Delivery Thresholds

  • Optimal voice frequency ≈ 125 Hz; lower reads as smart/successful. (−22 Hz ≈ +$187K CEO comp.)
  • Persuasion mix: passion 27% · voice 23% · presence 15% · content 15%.
  • Judgments of competence/likability/trust form in 250 milliseconds.
  • Kill: uptalk, "um/like/you know," shrillness, breathlessness, list-reading, phone-checking.
  • Use: pauses/silence, slowed pace, "phrasing off," narrative over bullet points, succinctness.

The Great Feedback Formula

Timely + Specific + Prescriptive + Business-framed. After it, the receiver knows what the problem is, why it matters, exactly what to do.

  • Give: frequent discrete pointers · never while angry (wait 24h) · good things first · embed correctives · catch people getting it right · "I want you to be successful."
  • Get: request it on a named encounter · thick skin · coach if needed · peer circle · sponsor · don't cry/burn bridges.

Six Gravitas Behaviors (self-audit)

Confidence under fire (79/76%) · Decisiveness (70%) · Integrity/truth-to-power (60%+) · EQ (~60%) · Reputation (56/57%) · Vision (50–54%).

Six Communication Traits

Superior speaking · Command a room · Assertiveness · Read the room · Humor/banter · Body language & posture.

Five Appearance Aspects

Polish & grooming (top) · Fit/wellness (not thinness) · Stylish clothes for your next job · Height (compensable) · Youth/vigor. Golden rule: minimize distractions from your competence.

Blunder Watch (career-enders in bold)

  • Gravitas: lack of integrity, sexual impropriety, bullying, lack of depth.
  • Communication: crying, phone-checking, long-windedness, notes/props, breathlessness.
  • Appearance: provocative dress (women), disheveled/unkempt (men), bling that steals thunder.

The Double Binds (tightrope — recognize, don't internalize)

Bind"Too much""Too little"
Forcebossy / bitch (31%)passive (31%)
Horntooting (29%)self-deprecating (24%)
Warmthtoo niceno empathy
Voiceshrilltentative
Age (women)too oldtoo young (sweet spot 39–42)

Contradictory feedback = hidden bias, not your defect. Widen latitude: team-framed arguments, humor, sniping, a bold brand, credentials, visible care.

glossary.md

Glossary — Executive Presence

250-millisecond judgment — The speed at which colleagues assess your competence, likability, and trustworthiness from appearance alone; these flash judgments stick (Ch 1, Ch 4).

Air cover — Sponsor protection secured before you step out to assert authenticity or take the spotlight; without it, visibility invites attack (Ch 7).

Always on — The principle that every verbal encounter (email, hallway chat, pitch) is a chance to build or erode your EP; you are never not presenting (Ch 3).

Appearance — The third EP pillar ("how you look"); rated least important long-term (5%) but the filter through which the other pillars are evaluated (Ch 1, Ch 4).

Bleached-out professional — Someone who scrubs away ethnic, religious, socioeconomic, or educational identifiers to be seen as "professional"; a lose-lose costing authenticity and visibility (Ch 7).

Command a room — Grabbing and holding an audience's attention; a core communication trait — "never be boring" (Ch 3).

Cracking the EP code — Learning and delivering the (often unwritten) rules of what bosses and coworkers look for (Ch 1).

Diversity dividend — The measurable bottom-line impact when leaders harness gender, ethnicity, culture, and nationality; your difference as a business asset (Ch 7).

Emotional intelligence (EQ) — Reading and acting on others' feelings (self- + situational awareness); a gravitas component and a muscle built by experience, not inborn (Ch 2).

Executive presence (EP) — The amalgam of confidence, poise, and authenticity that telegraphs you're in charge or deserve to be; the missing link between merit and success (Ch 1).

First language / second language — Trevor Phillips's model: your authentic identity (first) vs. the conventions of the dominant world you learn to survive (second) (Ch 7).

Fork in the road — The career rung where suppressing your difference no longer feels worth it (Ch 7).

Goldilocks syndrome — Being perpetually "too this, too that," never "just right" — the signature of hidden bias against those who don't fit the leader stereotype (Ch 6).

Grace under fire — Composure and confidence at the center of a crisis; the #1 gravitas behavior (79% women / 76% men) (Ch 2).

Gravitas — The first and core EP pillar ("how you act"); the "heft that marks you as worth following into the fire" (Ch 1, Ch 2).

Great Feedback Formula — Feedback that is timely + specific + prescriptive + framed in business outcome (Ch 5).

Invisible knapsack — The kit of inborn privileges the dominant group can't perceive it carries (Ch 6).

Iron core — The deep self-confidence you reach for to "lean into the wind" in a crisis (Ch 2).

Likability vs. competence trade-off — The most tenacious double bind: successful women (unlike men) suffer social rejection and lost trust (Ch 6).

Marzipan layer — The rich, sticky talent layer just below top management where qualified women and minorities stall for lack of EP feedback (Ch 5).

Narrow band of acceptability — The constrained range of behavior/appearance women (and minorities) are allowed before being penalized in one direction or the other (Ch 5, Ch 6).

Non-negotiables — The values or cultures that don't deserve your compliance; know them and walk away (Ch 7).

Personal brand / right-sizing your reputation — Proactively managing how you're perceived before others do it for you; a gravitas component (Ch 2).

Playing the game vs. selling out — Distinguishing benign conformity from a compromise of your soul; only you can draw the line (Ch 7).

Props — Notes, slides, lists, glasses, podiums — anything that blocks eye contact and signals you don't command your material (Ch 3).

Reading a room — Sensing mood and cultural cues and course-correcting on the spot; EQ applied to communication (Ch 3).

Shrillness — A high-pitched, emotion-raised voice; the most-cited destroyer of a woman's EP — the "hint of hysteria" (Ch 3).

Showing teeth — Being (and appearing) decisive; imposing direction and owning it — but do it discriminately (Ch 2).

Signature look — A consciously built, personalized appearance/brand that telegraphs you embrace the code yet channel individuality (Ch 4).

Speaking truth to power — Voicing convictions upward from a core of unshakable values; a gravitas component (Ch 2).

Sponsor — A powerful leader vested in your success who advocates, steers assignments, protects you, and gives the blunt EP feedback mentors won't (distinct from a mentor) (Ch 5, Ch 7).

Telegraph — To signal (vs. perform); EP is a measure of image you telegraph, not of performance (Ch 1).

The three pillars — Gravitas (act), communication (speak), appearance (look); the universal structure of EP (Ch 1).

Uptalk — Ending declarative statements on a rising note as if questioning; denies closure and undermines the message (Ch 3).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Executive Presence

Concrete, repeatable moves drawn from the book. Grouped by situation.

Deepening Gravitas

When to use: You're not yet perceived as leadership material despite the credentials.

How: Surround yourself with people better than you; be generous with credit; stick to what you know (back claims with firsthand examples); show humility (admit failings); smile more; empower others' presence to build your own; drive change rather than be changed.

Trade-offs: Humility disarms detractors but requires security; over-deference reads as weakness.

Grace Under Fire (Crisis Composure)

When to use: A crisis, a mistake (yours or others'), a hostile grilling.

How: Reach for your "iron core"; own mistakes publicly and fast; lay out concrete steps; never break eye contact; speak with empathy. Handling catastrophe > avoiding it.

Trade-offs: Deflecting blame to look clean (Hayward) is catastrophic; owning it (Dimon) bolsters gravitas.

Show Teeth Discriminately

When to use: A decision everyone is avoiding.

How: Listen, gather info, weigh options, wait for the opening (when others writhe in indecision), then demand action. Hide your teeth more often than you bare them; pair every hard call with EQ.

Trade-offs: For women, decisiveness risks the "bitch"/"not a team player" penalty — frame around the team.

Establish Connection in 5 Seconds

When to use: Opening any talk or presentation.

How: Unveil just enough of your inner core (a personal story) that the audience starts pulling for you — without oversharing. Give the impression you don't need to be liked.

Trade-offs: Over-revelation reads as neediness; too withheld reads as cold (especially penalizing for women).

Deliver Words as a Musician Delivers Notes

When to use: High-stakes speaking; when you want a point to land.

How: Vary phrasing, inflection, pace. "Phrase off" the ends of sentences for closure (kills uptalk). Slow down. Surround key words with silence — "a musician's impact lies in the rests."

Trade-offs: None if practiced; silence feels risky but reads as confidence.

Lose the Props → Make Eye Contact

When to use: Any presentation or important meeting.

How: Know your material cold so you can ditch notes, slides, and glasses. Prepare until the arc is "muscle memory." Move the podium; use a lavaliere mic to roam.

Trade-offs: Requires heavy prep; but reliance on props signals a lack of command.

Be a Sniper, Not a Machine Gun

When to use: A meeting where you want your voice to carry weight.

How: Don't speak unless you have a strong point; wait to make a counterpoint or ask an insightful question. When leading, invert: open immediately with a bold, agenda-setting statement.

Trade-offs: Silence early can be mistaken for having nothing to say — so land a strong first contribution.

Assert with the Company's Interest (Take Out the "I")

When to use: Pushing back, negotiating, or disagreeing upward.

How: Frame the demand around what's best for the company/team, not what you want. Mind tone and body language. Ask, "How will this be heard by those in power?" Follow a confrontation privately to reframe intent.

Trade-offs: Slower than blunt assertion, but avoids the "not a team player" brand.

Achieve Polish (Golden Rule: Minimize Distractions)

When to use: Always; especially first impressions and client meetings.

How: Regular nails/hair; well-cut attire for your body type; accessorize without billboarding; never let clothing advertise your body; look "appropriate for your environment, authentic to you."

Trade-offs: Provocative dressing distracts and costs credibility; disheveled reads as poor judgment.

Dress for the Job You Want

When to use: Angling for a promotion or stretch role.

How: Study the leaders above you; upgrade to their register; build a signature look with one distinctive style piece. Get "over the bar" first, then earn latitude to set your own code.

Trade-offs: Inauthentic clothing saps confidence — the look must still be you.

Great Feedback (Give)

When to use: Developing talent; a core leadership competency.

How: Timely (right before/after the blunder) + specific (one behavior) + prescriptive (what to do) + framed in business outcome. Frequent discrete pointers, not semi-annual downloads. Never while angry (wait 24h). Good things first. Embed correctives. Catch people getting it right. Preface: "I'm telling you this because I want you to be successful." For appearance, route through personal brand. Enlist a third party if litigation is a risk.

Trade-offs: Uncomfortable, but withholding stalls the marzipan layer and questions your own leadership.

Get the Feedback You Need (Receive)

When to use: You suspect an EP gap but keep hearing "you're doing great."

How: Recognize you need it; develop a thick skin; request specific, timely, prescriptive feedback on a recent high-EP encounter; if superiors won't, hire a coach (even on your own dime); build a peer feedback circle; cultivate a sponsor; listen for the "ring of truth"; demonstrate you'll act; don't cry or burn bridges.

Trade-offs: Vulnerable and painful — but far less painful than learning your blunders too late.

Widen Your Latitude (Tightrope Strategies)

When to use: You face the narrow band of acceptability (women/minorities).

How: Show teeth for the team; speak truth with humor; snipe don't spray; build a latitude-granting personal brand (Branson); wield credentials consciously ("Dr."); show you care (public good works).

Trade-offs: Doesn't erase the bias — navigates it while preserving authenticity.

Own Your Authenticity (Resolve the Tension)

When to use: At the "fork in the road" where conformity costs your identity.

How: Know your non-negotiables and walk away from cultures that don't deserve compliance; never fake a style that isn't you; play the long game (traditional role, untraditional execution); read slights as ignorance not bigotry; leverage and differentiate by your difference; secure air cover (a sponsor) before stepping out.

Trade-offs: Asserting difference invites bias — but bleaching out costs you personally and professionally, and difference is now a diversity dividend.

Indistractable — Cheatsheet

The 4-Part Model (apply IN ORDER — don't skip)

#StepCore moveChapter
1Master internal triggersDeal with discomfort (the root cause)Ch 2
2Make time for tractionTimebox values into a calendarCh 3
3Hack back external triggersRemove cues that don't serve youCh 4
4Prevent distraction with pactsPrecommit to stop yourself slidingCh 5

Two decision rules that resolve most cases

  • Traction or distraction? → "Did this move me toward or away from what I planned?" (You can't call it distraction unless you know what it distracts you from.)
  • The Critical Question (external triggers) → "Is this trigger serving me, or am I serving it?" Serving me = keep. I'm serving it = hack back.

When an urge hits (internal trigger)

1. Name the discomfort preceding it. 2. Curiosity, not contempt. 3. 10-minute rule — allow it, but wait 10 min. 4. Surf the urge; it passes. → Never suppress (white-bear rebound). After a slip: self-compassion, not shame.

Which pact for which job?

SituationUseBecause
Can add physical frictionEffort pactMakes the bad behavior harder
Short task, removable triggerPrice pactLoss aversion; moves pain to now
Long-term change of selfIdentity pact"I don't" > "I can't"

Price-pact pitfalls: skip if trigger is inescapable, task is long, or you beat yourself up.

Email (TNT = n × t)

  • Reduce n: office hours · delay-send · unsubscribe/black-hole.
  • Reduce t: batch · touch twice · tag by reply-time ("Today"/"This Week"), not topic · answer in blocks.

Smartphone in <1 hour — the 4 R's

Remove unused → Replace (social/YouTube → desktop; wear a watch) → Rearrange (home screen = Primary Tools + Aspirations only) → Reclaim (sound/sight notifications per app; Do Not Disturb).

Meetings & chat tells

  • No agenda + proposed solution → no meeting. Meetings = consensus, not thinking out loud. One laptop per room.
  • Group chat: in/out at scheduled times; only necessary people; not a place to think aloud.

Workplace diagnosis

Chronic distraction/tech-overuse = symptom. Disease = low psychological safety + high job strain (high expectations × low control). Fix: leaders model focus → pilot one small change with one team → open a safe forum.

Kids — the smell test

  • Overuse = symptom of unmet Autonomy / Competence / Relatedness (feed these offline first).
  • Set limits with them, not for them (imposed limits → resentment + cheating).
  • Tech-readiness test: can they use the device's own settings (Do Not Disturb, notifications) to turn off triggers? If not, not ready.
  • Don't be the interrupting external trigger yourself.

Relationships

  • Phubbing → ask sincerely: "I see you're on your phone. Is everything OK?"
  • Protect intimacy with all 4 steps: manage the urge → device-free bedtime (traction) → phones out of bedroom → router/timer shut-off (effort pact).

Identity default

Call yourself "indistractable." It's a strived-for identity, not perfection — "strive" means struggle. You'll still slip; get back on track.

glossary.md

Indistractable — Glossary

Attention residue — The lingering focus on a prior task that makes refocusing after a switch harder (Sophie Leroy) (Ch 4).

Autonomy — One of three psychological nutrients: volition and freedom of control over one's choices (Ch 7).

B = MAT (Fogg Behavior Model) — A behavior occurs only when Motivation, Ability, and a Trigger converge simultaneously (Ch 4).

Burn or burn — A price pact: a $100 bill + lighter beside the calendar; exercise or burn the bill (Ch 5).

Competence — Psychological nutrient: the feeling of mastery, progress, and growth (Ch 7).

Cycle of responsiveness — Off-hours responsiveness trains others to expect it, escalating demands into an always-on norm (Leslie Perlow) (Ch 6).

Distraction — Any action that draws you away from what you planned to do (Ch 1).

Effort pact — A precommitment that makes an unwanted behavior harder to do (kSafe, Forest, Focusmate) (Ch 5).

Effort-reward imbalance — Work condition where little pay/recognition returns for hard effort; predicts depression (Ch 6).

Ego depletion — The largely debunked belief that willpower is a finite fuel that runs out (Ch 2).

External trigger — An environmental cue (ping, ding, person, object) that prompts action (Ch 1).

Hedonic adaptation — The tendency to return to a baseline of satisfaction no matter what happens; one of four factors making satisfaction temporary (Ch 2).

"I don't" vs. "I can't" — Identity framing; "I don't eat meat" resists temptation better than "I can't" (Ch 5).

Identity pact — A precommitment to a self-image ("I'm indistractable") so behavior follows identity (Ch 5).

Indistractable — Striving to do what you say you will do; the defining skill of the 21st century (Ch 1).

Internal trigger — A cue from within (boredom, anxiety, loneliness) that prompts action (Ch 1).

Ironic process theory — Suppressing a thought makes it rebound more strongly ("don't think of a white bear," Wegner) (Ch 2).

Job strain — High expectations combined with low control; predicts workplace depression and distraction (Ch 6).

Liminal moments — Transitions between activities where "just a second" balloons into lost time (Ch 2).

Loss aversion — We're more motivated to avoid losses than to seek equal gains; the engine of price pacts (Ch 5).

Multichannel multitasking (cross-modal) — Pairing one attention-heavy channel with a low-demand one (audiobook + walking) (Ch 4).

Need density hypothesis — The more needs go unmet in real life, the more they're sought in virtual realities (Ryan) (Ch 7).

Negativity bias — Bad events demand attention more powerfully than good; one of four dissatisfaction factors (Ch 2).

Phubbing — Phone + snubbing: ignoring a person by attending to a device (Ch 8).

Precommitment — A choice made in advance that binds your future self (Ulysses pact) (Ch 5).

Price pact — A precommitment putting money on the line, forfeited if you get distracted (Ch 5).

Proximate vs. root cause — Devices are the proximate cause we blame; escaping discomfort is the root cause (Ch 2).

Pseudowork — Tasks that look like work but aren't aligned with top priorities (Ch 3).

Psychological safety — Belief that one won't be punished or humiliated for speaking up (Amy Edmondson) (Ch 6).

Relatedness — Psychological nutrient: feeling important to others and that others matter to you (Ch 7).

Reflect & Refine — Weekly 15-minute review of what worked in your schedule and what to change (Ch 3).

Residual beneficiary — The one who gets only leftover time; don't let loved ones become this (Ch 3).

Rumination — Repeatedly dwelling on bad experiences; one of four dissatisfaction factors (Ch 2).

Self-compassion — Talking to yourself like a friend after a slip; predicts resilience and well-being (Ch 2).

Self-determination theory — Ryan & Deci: the psyche needs autonomy, competence, and relatedness to thrive (Ch 7).

Social antibody — A group norm that blocks the spread of a harmful behavior (Paul Graham) (Ch 8).

Social contagion — The spread of behaviors (device use, overeating) through a social group (Ch 8).

Surf the urge — Riding a craving like a wave — observing, neither suppressing nor acting — until it subsides (Ch 2).

Sterile cockpit rule — Aviation rule banning non-essential activity below 10,000 ft; model for interruption-free zones (Ch 4).

Temptation bundling — Only allowing a tempting activity alongside one you should do (audiobooks only at the gym; Milkman) (Ch 4).

Ten-minute rule — When an urge hits, allow it — but wait ten minutes first (Ch 2).

Three life domains — You, Relationships, Work — the framework for allocating time (Ch 3).

Timeboxing — Deciding what to do and when; eliminating white space via implementation intentions (Ch 3).

TNT (T = n × t) — Total email time = number of messages × time per message; reduce both (Ch 4).

Traction — Any action that draws you toward what you planned to do (Ch 1).

Ulysses pact — A freely made decision designed to bind oneself in the future (Ch 5).

4 R's (smartphone) — Remove, Replace, Rearrange, Reclaim (Ch 4).

patterns.md

Indistractable — Patterns & Techniques

Reimagine the Internal Trigger (4 steps)

When to use: A recurring urge to distract (googling instead of writing, phone-checking).

How: (1) Look for the discomfort preceding it; (2) Write down the trigger — time, activity, feeling; (3) Explore the sensation with curiosity ("leaves on a stream"); (4) Beware liminal moments (transitions).

Trade-offs: Requires honest self-observation; takes trials to notice internal (vs. external) triggers.

The 10-Minute Rule / Surf the Urge

When to use: An in-the-moment craving for a pacifying distraction.

How: Tell yourself you can give in — but not for ten minutes. Ride the urge like a wave without suppressing or obeying it. Reassess after ten minutes (the urge usually passes).

Trade-offs: Not a hard "no," so it relies on the urge genuinely subsiding — works because most do.

Timeboxing the Three Life Domains

When to use: Whenever your days feel reactive or your calendar doesn't reflect your values.

How: Decide hours per week for You / Relationships / Work; build a "perfect week" template with zero white space; judge success by adherence, not output.

Trade-offs: Feels rigid at first, but constraints reduce decision fatigue and make distraction visible.

Reflect & Refine (weekly review)

When to use: Every week, ~15 minutes.

How: Reflect ("when did I do what I said vs. get distracted?"), then Refine ("what calendar change would help me live my values?"). Treat the week as an experiment.

Trade-offs: Only works if you commit to the schedule between reviews.

Schedule Syncing with Stakeholders

When to use: Any shared-time relationship — manager, partner, multiple bosses.

How: Share your timeboxed schedule; agree on it in regular increments (usually weekly; daily if it changes daily).

Trade-offs: Requires vulnerability/transparency; pays back in fewer imposed distractions.

The Critical Question

When to use: On any external trigger.

How: Ask "Is this trigger serving me, or am I serving it?" Keep triggers that lead to traction; hack back the rest.

Email TNT (T = n × t)

When to use: Email overload.

How: Cut n — office hours, delay-send, unsubscribe/black-hole. Cut t — batch; touch each email twice, tagging by when it needs a reply ("Today"/"This Week"), answer in scheduled blocks.

Trade-offs: Slower replies; usually a feature, not a bug (many issues self-resolve).

Smartphone 4 R's

When to use: Phone feels distracting (one-time, <1 hr).

How: Remove unused apps → Replace where/when you use tempting ones (desktop, wristwatch) → Rearrange home screen to Primary Tools + Aspirations → Reclaim notifications (sound/sight per app; Do Not Disturb).

Temptation Bundling + Multichannel Multitasking

When to use: To make a "should" (exercise) attractive or reclaim commute/chore time.

How: Only allow a tempting reward (audiobooks, saved articles) alongside the should. Pair one attention-heavy channel with a low-demand one (audio + walking).

Trade-offs: Only works across modalities — never two complex tasks at once.

Effort Pact

When to use: A distraction you can add friction to.

How: Make it physically harder — app blockers (Forest, SelfControl, Freedom), kSafe, co-working/Focusmate, iOS Downtime.

Trade-offs: Determined self can override; friction just has to exceed the impulse.

Price Pact

When to use: Short, well-defined task where you can remove the external trigger.

How: Put money on the line ("burn or burn"; forfeit to a friend). Exploits loss aversion.

Trade-offs: Four pitfalls — no escapable trigger, short tasks only, scary to start, not for the self-critical.

Identity Pact

When to use: Long-term behavior change.

How: Adopt a noun ("I'm indistractable"); say "I don't," not "I can't"; tell others to solidify it.

Trade-offs: Slower to take hold, but self-reinforcing once it does.

Create Psychological Safety (Edmondson's 3 steps)

When to use: Leading a team that overuses tech / can't raise concerns.

How: (1) Frame work as a learning problem; (2) Acknowledge your own fallibility; (3) Model curiosity, ask questions. Pilot small (one predictable night off, one team) and open a regular forum.

Social Antibody Against Phubbing

When to use: Someone uses a device in a social setting.

How: Sincerely ask, "I see you're on your phone. Is everything OK?" — offering a graceful exit or a return to the group.

Factfulness — Cheatsheet

The 10 Instincts → Warning Sign → Control Rule

#InstinctWarning sign (the "tell")Control rule
1Gap"the gap," two opposed groups, us/them, developed/developingLook for the majority
2Negativity"things are getting worse," bad news, nostalgiaExpect bad news
3Straight linea trend assumed to continue straightLines might bend (5 shapes)
4Fearfrightening images, "in times like these"Calculate the risk = danger × exposure
5Sizea lonely big number, one vivid victimCompare & divide (+ 80/20)
6Generalization"they," one example → whole group, "their culture"Question your categories
7Destiny"it will never change," "it's their culture"Slow change is still change
8Single perspectiveone cause/solution for everythingToolbox, not a hammer
9Blamea clear villain (or hero)Causes, not villains; systems, not heroes
10Urgency"now or never," "act today"Take small steps

The Four Income Levels (memorize this first)

LevelIncome/dayPeopleLife looks like
1~$1~1bnbarefoot, walk for dirty water, ~5 kids, extreme poverty
2~$4~3bnbike, sandals, gas stove, kids in school, unstable power
3~$16~2bncold tap, fridge, motorcycle, multiple jobs, high school
4>$64~1bncar, 12+ yrs education, hot water, air travel (you)

Each step up ≈ 4× income. PIN code of the world: 1-1-1-4 (Americas-Europe-Africa-Asia) → 1-1-4-5 by 2100.

Decision rules

  • See a lonely number? → Never trust it alone. Compare (vs. last year / a comparable place) AND divide (per person). Then judge.
  • See a doubling/tripling number? → Look closer (Ebola, terrorism), but get a 3rd data point before extrapolating.
  • Scared by a news event? → Ask: what's the actual death toll / proportion? Is this frightening or dangerous? Get calm before acting.
  • Tempted to extrapolate a line? → Which curve shape? Need 3 points. Does my Level-4 view apply to Levels 1–3?
  • Hear "majority"? → Ask 51% or 99%?
  • Hear "it's their culture / they'll never change"? → Feeling disguised as fact. Find a counterexample; talk across generations.
  • Offered one cause/solution for everything? → Get a toolbox. Test it against someone who disagrees.
  • Reaching for a villain? → You've stopped thinking. Find the system. Look in the mirror.
  • Told "act NOW or never"? → Almost always manipulation. Ask for time + data. Demand a range of scenarios, not one.
  • Forecasting? → Show mid + best + worst; round to your own disadvantage to protect credibility.

The "safe bet" heuristic

On Rosling's fact questions, the most positive answer is usually correct. When unsure about a global trend, guess that things are better than your instinct says.

Proportions people get wrong (reality is ~80–90%, guessed ~20%)

Vaccinated 1-yr-olds 88% · electricity access 80% · girls in primary school 90% · world life expectancy ~72 · extreme poverty (last 20 yrs) halved (29%→9%).

Thresholds & rules of thumb

  • 80/20: ~20% of a list's items = ~80% of the total — handle those first.
  • Rule of 70: years to double ≈ 70 ÷ growth%. (1%→70yr, 2%→35yr, 3%→24yr.)
  • Statistics caution: ignore differences smaller than ~10% — likely noise.
  • Forecast accuracy tracks system simplicity: demographics (decades) ≫ economics ≫ weather (a week).

The 5 global risks worth real urgency

Global pandemic · financial collapse · World War III · climate change · extreme poverty (+ the unknown risk). Approach all with cool heads, robust independent data, baby steps — never cry wolf.

Two foundational values

Humility (it's hard to get facts right; say "I don't know"; change your mind) + Curiosity (seek disconfirming facts; "how interesting that I was wrong"). Be a possibilist, not an optimist or pessimist.

glossary.md

Factfulness — Glossary

80/20 rule — Find the few largest items in any list; usually ~20% of items make up ~80% of the total. Deal with those first. (Ch 5)

Attention filter — A mental shield with ten instinct-shaped holes; only drama-fitting information passes, so we believe the unusual is usual. (Ch 4)

Bad and better — Holding two thoughts at once: a level can be bad while its direction is improving. (Ch 2)

Blame instinct — The urge to find a simple, guilty individual or group for a bad event; it stops thought and blocks systemic understanding. Control: look for causes, not villains. (Ch 9)

Chimpanzee benchmark — Random guessing scores 33% per 3-option question (~4/12); humans average ~2/12, i.e., worse than random. (Intro)

Chemophobia — Exaggerated fear of invisible chemical contamination, generalized from a few vivid examples; blocks data-driven argument. (Ch 4, Ch 6)

Compare and divide — The two "magic tools" for proportion: never trust a lonely number — compare it (over time/place) and divide it into a rate (per person). (Ch 5)

Cool chains — Refrigerated logistics keeping vaccines cold from factory to child; require the same infrastructure as new factories. (Ch 6)

Curve shapes — Trends come in five shapes: straight line, S-bend, slide, hump, doubling line. Three points are needed to tell them apart. (Ch 3)

Destiny instinct — Belief that innate traits fix the unchanging destiny of people/cultures/nations. Control: remember slow change is still change. (Ch 7)

Dollar Street — Project photographing ~300 families across 50+ countries by income, showing that income (not culture/religion/country) is the main factor in how people live. (Ch 1, Ch 6)

Dramatic instincts — The ten evolved mental shortcuts (gap, negativity, straight line, fear, size, generalization, destiny, single perspective, blame, urgency) that crave drama and distort the worldview. (Intro)

Doubling income scale — Comparing income by doublings ($1→$2→…→$64) because each extra dollar matters far more at low levels; six doublings span the four levels. (Ch 3)

Fear instinct — Attention to frightening things, which aren't necessarily the most dangerous (harm, captivity, contamination). Control: calculate the risks. (Ch 4)

Fill-up effect — Population grows ~3 billion more not from more births but from already-born children growing into adults over three generations, then stops. (Ch 3)

Four Income Levels — The book's master framework replacing developed/developing: Level 1 (~$1/day, ~1bn), Level 2 (~$4, ~3bn), Level 3 (~$16, ~2bn), Level 4 (>$64/day, ~1bn). Each step ≈ 4× income. (Ch 1)

Frightening vs. dangerous — Frightening = perceived risk; dangerous = real risk. Direct fear at the dangerous. (Ch 4)

Gap instinct — The urge to split things into two conflicting groups with a gap between; reality is usually a continuum with the majority in the middle. Control: look for the majority. (Ch 1)

Generalization instinct — Lumping together different things/people, or judging a category from one example. Control: question your categories. (Ch 6)

Hammer and nails — Overusing your favorite tool/expertise where it doesn't fit. Get a toolbox, not a hammer. (Ch 8)

Konzo — Incurable paralytic disease from improperly processed cassava that Rosling researched; central to the Nacala and Makanga stories. (Ch 10, Ch 11)

Mega misconception — A wrong belief so basic it distorts all global proportions. The three: world divided in two (Ch 1), world getting worse (Ch 2), population just increasing (Ch 3).

Negativity instinct — Noticing the bad more than the good, from misremembered pasts + selective reporting + feeling. Control: expect bad news. (Ch 2)

Overdramatic worldview — The instinctive, too-negative picture: world divided, worsening, gap widening. Opposite of the fact-based worldview. (Intro)

Peak child — The point (now reached) where the number of children worldwide stops increasing. (Ch 3)

PIN code of the world (1-1-1-4) — Population in billions: Americas 1, Europe 1, Africa 1, Asia 4. By 2100 → 1-1-4-5. (Ch 5)

Possibilist — Someone who "neither hopes without reason, nor fears without reason," resisting both optimism and pessimism. (Ch 2)

Recovery position — Laying an unconscious person prone so vomit drains; correct for soldiers but wrongly generalized to sleeping babies. (Ch 6)

Risk = danger × exposure — Real risk equals how dangerous a thing is times how exposed you are — not how scared it makes you feel. (Ch 4)

Single perspective instinct — Attraction to one cause/solution that explains everything; blinds you to disconfirming information. Control: get a toolbox, not a hammer. (Ch 8)

Size instinct — Misjudging importance: a lonely number looks big, a visible victim outweighs statistics. Control: get things in proportion. (Ch 5)

Slow change is not no change — 1%/yr doubles in 70 years; small annual changes compound into transformation. (Ch 7)

Statistics as therapy — Plain official data, shown to people with a too-negative worldview, makes them feel better ("a new kind of happy pill"). (Ch 2)

Straight line instinct — Assuming a trend continues straight; most trends don't. Control: remember curves come in different shapes. (Ch 3)

Urgency instinct — A decision feeling "now or never" when it rarely is; drives drastic, untested action. Control: take small steps. (Ch 10)

View from up here — From Level 4, Levels 1–3 all look equally poor — like looking down from a tall building. (Ch 1)

patterns.md

Factfulness — Techniques & Patterns

The ten instinct-control techniques, each with how to apply it. Use these whenever you read news, evaluate a claim, make a forecast, or prioritize resources.

1. Look for the Majority (Gap Instinct)

When to use: A claim splits the world into two opposed groups (rich/poor, us/them, developed/developing), or cites "the gap."

How:

  • Replace the binary with the Four Income Levels.
  • Beware comparisons of averages (check the spreads — they usually overlap).
  • Beware comparisons of extremes (the majority is in the middle).
  • Beware the view from up here (from the top, everything below looks equally small).

Trade-off: Real gaps occasionally exist (apartheid South Africa) — verify before dismissing.

2. Expect Bad News (Negativity Instinct)

When to use: You feel the world is getting worse, or a story implies decline.

How: Separate level (bad) from direction (better). Ask: "If an equally large improvement had happened, would I have heard about it?" Distrust rosy memories of the past.

Trade-off: Don't over-correct into rosy positivity — aim for accuracy, not a feel-good counterweight.

3. Don't Assume Straight Lines (Straight Line Instinct)

When to use: Extrapolating any trend into the future.

How: Ask which of five shapes it is — straight, S-bend, slide, hump, doubling. Get a third data point (1,2,3 is linear; 1,2,4 is doubling). Remember the part of a curve you see on Level 4 may not apply on Levels 1–3.

Trade-off: Some lines really are straight (income↔health) — identify, don't assume.

4. Calculate the Risks (Fear Instinct)

When to use: Fear is driving attention or a decision.

How: Compute Risk = danger × exposure, not the feeling. Distinguish frightening (perceived) from dangerous (real). When afraid, get calm before deciding — make as few decisions as possible until panic subsides.

Trade-off: Fear is useful when aimed at real risks; don't suppress it entirely.

5. Get Things in Proportion (Size Instinct)

When to use: A single number looks impressive, or one victim dominates attention.

How: Compare (vs. last year, vs. a comparable region) and Divide (into a per-person rate). Use the 80/20 rule on lists/budgets — handle the biggest items first.

Trade-off: Numbers, but not only numbers — keep the human reality in view.

6. Question Your Categories (Generalization Instinct)

When to use: A claim treats a group (nation, religion, "Africa") as uniform, or generalizes from one example.

How:

  • Look for differences within groups and similarities across groups.
  • Beware "the majority" (51% or 99%? ask for the number).
  • Beware vivid/exceptional examples; ask for more, or flip the example.
  • Assume you are not "normal" and others are not idiots ("In what way is this smart?").
  • Don't generalize from one group to another (soldiers ≠ babies).

Trade-off: We must categorize to function — aim for better categories (the Four Levels), not none.

7. Remember Slow Change Is Still Change (Destiny Instinct)

When to use: Someone says a culture/country/religion "will never change" or "it's their culture."

How: Track gradual improvements (1%/yr doubles in 70 yrs). Update your knowledge (social facts expire). Talk to Grandpa (compare generations). Collect counterexamples of cultural change.

Trade-off: Slow ≠ instant — change is real but takes decades; stay patient and possibilistic.

8. Get a Toolbox, Not a Hammer (Single Perspective Instinct)

When to use: One idea (free market, equality, one metric, one technology) is offered as the answer to everything.

How: Test your ideas against people who disagree. Respect limited expertise (experts only within their field). Watch hammers and nails (tool overuse). Use numbers but not only numbers. Beware simple solutions — answer is usually "both, case-by-case."

Trade-off: Simple ideas are seductive and time-saving; trade speed for accuracy when it matters.

9. Resist Finding a Scapegoat (Blame Instinct)

When to use: Something went wrong (or right) and you're reaching for a villain (or hero).

How: Look for causes, not villains — understand the interacting system. Look for systems, not heroes — ask whether the good outcome would have happened anyway. Look in the mirror. Credit institutions and technology.

Trade-off: Accountability still matters; the point is to find the system, not to excuse everyone.

10. Take Small Steps (Urgency Instinct)

When to use: A decision feels "now or never," or you're being pushed to act immediately.

How: Take a breath (ask for time and information). Insist on the data (relevant and accurate). Beware fortune-tellers (demand a range of scenarios; round to your disadvantage). Be wary of drastic action (ask the side effects; prefer step-by-step + evaluation).

Trade-off: A few risks are genuinely urgent — the five global risks — but even those need cool heads, not panic.

---

Meta-pattern: Test for ignorance

When to use: In your own organization, field, or community.

How: Ask "What are the most important facts here, and how many people know them?" Pose a few multiple-choice fact questions humbly. Expect worse-than-random results — and an avalanche of curiosity once revealed.

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The 4-Hour Work Week

Decision rules (if X, do Y, because Z)

  • If you're avoiding a decision "until the timing is right" → run fear-setting now, because the only real answer is fear and inaction is the bigger risk.
  • If a task feels important but isn't moving you toward a goal → eliminate it, because efficiency at the wrong task is worthless (effectiveness > efficiency).
  • If a task keeps expanding → give it a hard, short deadline, because work fills the time allotted (Parkinson).
  • If a recurring task interrupts you → batch it on a schedule, because setup/switching cost is fixed (~45 min to resume).
  • If someone needs your OK for something small → give a written if-then rule + spending limit, because that's an empowerment failure, not real management.
  • If you want a permanent change accepted → propose a small reversible trial (Puppy Dog Close), because people resist permanence but accept "just once."
  • If you're about to delegate → check you can't eliminate or automate it first, because you'd be paying to preserve waste.
  • If you have a product idea → find the market first, then micro-test before manufacturing, because filling demand beats creating it and behavior beats opinion.
  • If cash flow already funds your dreams → stop chasing more customers, because that's W4W.
  • If you feel overwhelmed → take a break and 80/20 both business and life, because lack of time is lack of priorities.

Core formulas & thresholds

ThingRule / number
Relative income$/hr = annual pay ÷ (weeks × hrs/week); this, not $/yr, is wealth
Target Monthly IncomeTMI = (4 dream costs + monthly expenses) × 1.3
Target Daily IncomeTDI = TMI ÷ 30
80/20 review cadenceevery 2–4 weeks, business + personal
Muse product price$50–200 (premium end)
Muse manufacture time≤ 3–4 weeks
Muse market sizemagazine full-page ad < $5,000; ≥ 15,000 readers
Micro-test~$500, ~5 days; 100 narrow terms @ $0.10 > 10 broad @ $1.00
Outsourcer autonomyfix anything under ~$400 without asking
Email frequency1–3×/day → weekly as problems allow
Perfection thresholdgreat for a few things, good enough for the rest (95% = 6 mo; 98% = 20–30 yr)
VA test2–4 weeks, $100–400, ROI in ~10–14 days

DEAL — the sequence (and DELA for employees)

StepWhatKey tools
Definitionrewrite the rules, set the targetNew Rich rules, fear-setting, dreamlining/TMI
Eliminationbuy timeeffectiveness, 80/20, Parkinson, low-info diet, batching
Automationbuy incomeeliminate→automate→delegate, VAs, muse, MBA architecture
Liberationbuy mobilityhourglass remote escape, mini-retirements

Employees implement as DELA: secure location freedom before cutting hours.

The 10 New Rich Rules (fast recall)

1 Retirement = worst-case insurance · 2 Energy is cyclical (mini-retirements) · 3 Less ≠ laziness · 4 Timing is never right · 5 Ask forgiveness, not permission · 6 Emphasize strengths, don't fix weaknesses · 7 Excess → its opposite · 8 Money alone isn't the fix · 9 Relative > absolute income · 10 Kill distress, seek eustress.

Tells & smells (you're in trouble if…)

  • You check email first thing / last thing / constantly → resets the whole day.
  • You're the tollbooth every decision passes through → build rules and route around yourself.
  • You're solving the same problem twice → write an if-then rule.
  • You're making non-urgent things urgent, or blowing up minutiae → W4W relapse.
  • You feel busy but can't name the 20% that matters → skipped your 80/20 review.
  • You're "researching" with no decision pending → just-in-case information; stop.
  • You work where you live/sleep/relax → separate environments.

The Not-to-Do List (9)

1 Don't answer calls from unknown numbers · 2 Don't email first/last thing · 3 No meetings/calls without a clear agenda + end time · 4 Don't let people ramble ("how can I help you?") · 5 Don't check email constantly — batch · 6 Don't over-serve low-profit, high-maintenance customers · 7 Don't work more to fix overwhelm — prioritize · 8 Don't carry a phone 24/7 · 9 Don't expect work to fill a void relationships/activities should.

Refusal scripts

  • Invader at your desk: "I'm right in the middle of something. How can I help you?" (unclear in 30s → "send me a quick email to remind me.")
  • Time limit: "OK, I've got two minutes before a call — what's the situation and how can I help?"
  • Replace "How are you?" with "How can I help you?" — get specific, no stories.

glossary.md

Glossary — The 4-Hour Work Week

80/20 Principle (Pareto's Law) — 80% of outputs come from 20% of inputs; often 90/10 or 95/5. Apply via two questions: which 20% causes 80% of problems (cut) and which produces 80% of results (multiply). (Ch 5)

Absentee management — see Management by Absence. (Ch 11)

Absolute income — income measured in raw dollars per year, ignoring hours worked. Contrast with relative income. (Ch 2)

Batching — grouping similar recurring tasks (email, calls, errands) and doing them on a set schedule to avoid repeated setup/switching cost (up to 45 min to resume interrupted work). (Ch 7)

Bracketing — asking for more than you need in a negotiation so your fallback position is still your real target. (Ch 12)

Comfort challenge — deliberate practice at social discomfort to build the action habit and dissolve fear. (Ch 3)

Cost of inaction — the financial, emotional, and physical price of not acting, measured over 1/5/10 years; usually far larger than the risk of acting. (Ch 3)

Dealmaker — one who treats rules outside science and law as negotiable; "Reality is negotiable" without being unethical. (Ch 1)

DEAL — Definition → Elimination → Automation → Liberation; the New Rich process and the book's structure. (Ch 1)

DELA — the employee's implementation order: read in DEAL order but win Liberation (location freedom) before cutting hours. (Ch 1)

Deferred-life plan — sacrificing your most capable years for freedom "someday"; the book's central target. (Ch 1)

Distress — harmful stress that weakens you (abusive bosses, destructive criticism); to be removed. (Ch 2)

Dreamlining — applying 6- and 12-month timelines to dreams (Have/Be/Do), then pricing them into a Target Monthly Income. (Ch 4)

Drop-shipping — the manufacturer ships directly to your customer, so you hold no inventory and pay a fraction of retail on delayed terms. (Ch 10)

Effectiveness — doing the things that move you toward your goals. Beats efficiency. (Ch 5)

Efficiency — doing a task (important or not) economically; useless unless applied to the right things. (Ch 5)

Eliminate before you delegate — never automate what can be eliminated; never delegate what can be automated. (Ch 8)

Empowerment failure — an interruption caused by someone needing your approval for something small; fixed with written if-then rules. (Ch 7)

Eustress — healthy, growth-producing stress (role models, training, comfort-expanding risk); to be sought. (Ch 2)

Fear-setting — a written exercise defining the worst case, its repairability, and the cost of inaction, to escape paralysis. (Ch 3)

Freedom multiplier — money's practical value multiplied by control of the four W's (what/when/where/whom). (Ch 1)

Geoarbitrage — exploiting global price/wage differences: earn strong currency, spend or hire in weak. (Ch 8, 13)

Hourglass approach — long proof-of-concept → short remote trial → negotiate back up to full-time remote. (Ch 12)

Information product — how-to content (book, DVD, course); the ideal muse: fast to make, high markup, FAQ-able. (Ch 9)

Interruption — anything preventing start-to-finish completion of a critical task; three types: time consumers, empowerment failures, self-generated. (Ch 7)

Just-in-time vs. just-in-case information — pull information only when a task needs it; never hoard "in case." (Ch 6)

License (licensee/licensor) — pay an inventor a royalty (~3–10% wholesale) to sell their product, or invent and let others sell yours. (Ch 9)

Lifestyle Design (LD) — deliberately engineering how and where you spend time rather than accepting the default track. (Ch 1)

Low-information diet — consuming only immediately actionable information; begins with a one-week media fast. (Ch 6)

Management by Absence (MBA) — a self-correcting business architecture that runs without you; be the roadside cop, not the tollbooth. (Ch 11)

Media fast — an abrupt one-week total cutoff of news and non-essential information. (Ch 6)

Mini-retirement — a recurring 1–6+ month relocation/sabbatical distributed throughout life instead of one end-of-life retirement. (Ch 2, 13)

Minimum effective load — doing the least necessary for maximum effect. (Ch 1)

Muse — an automated, low-maintenance business built solely to fund your dreamlines with minimal time. (Ch 9)

New Rich (NR) — those who design a free lifestyle now using time and mobility as currency. (Ch 1)

Nonfinishing (art of) — the skill of quitting boring/unproductive books, tasks, or media mid-stream. (Ch 6)

Parkinson's Law — a task swells in perceived importance/complexity to fill the time allotted; short deadlines force focus. (Ch 5)

Premium positioning — pricing above competitors ($50–200 range) to raise margin, perceived value, and customer quality. (Ch 9)

Puppy Dog Close — winning permanent change by proposing a small, reversible "just try it once" trial. (Ch 7)

Relative income — income per hour of life ($/hr); the true New Rich measure of wealth once absolute income clears your dream threshold. (Ch 2)

Reselling — buying wholesale and reselling; easiest to start, least profitable, fastest to die to price competition. (Ch 9)

Selective ignorance — the trained ability to ignore or redirect irrelevant information and interruptions. (Ch 6)

Target Daily Income (TDI) — TMI ÷ 30; a daily income target. (Ch 4)

Target Monthly Income (TMI) — (four dream costs + monthly expenses) × 1.3; the cash-flow goal your muse must hit. (Ch 4)

Virtual architecture — the interchangeable chain of outsourcers (fulfillment, call center, processor) that runs the muse. (Ch 11)

Virtual assistant (VA) — a remote assistant used as low-risk management training and life outsourcing. (Ch 8)

W4W (work for work's sake) — staying busy to feel productive or avoid hard questions; the book's most-hated acronym. (Ch 1, 5, 13)

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — The 4-Hour Work Week

Fear-Setting (the 7 questions)

When to use: any big, scary decision you keep postponing.

How: in writing — (1) Define the nightmare in detail; rate permanence/probability 1–10. (2) Steps to repair the damage. (3) Benefits of more-probable outcomes (rate 1–10). (4) If fired today, how to regain financial control. (5) What you're putting off out of fear. (6) Cost of inaction over 1/5/10 years. (7) What are you waiting for?

Trade-offs: takes an hour and forces honesty; defuses fear but won't remove real (rare) irreversible risks — those you keep.

Dreamlining → TMI/TDI

When to use: to convert "I want freedom" into a concrete income target.

How: 6- and 12-month timelines × (Have / Be / Do), 5 each; convert "Be" → "Do"; star top 4; TMI = (4 dream costs + monthly expenses) × 1.3; TDI = TMI ÷ 30.

Trade-offs: monthly cash-flow framing makes dreams look affordable, but requires honest expense accounting.

The 80/20 Two-Question Audit

When to use: every 2–4 weeks, on business and personal life.

How: (1) Which 20% of sources cause 80% of problems/unhappiness? → eliminate/fire. (2) Which 20% produce 80% of results/happiness? → double down.

Trade-offs: firing the draining 20% can feel risky; usually the revenue/energy math strongly favors it.

Parkinson's Law (short deadlines)

When to use: any task that expands to fill available time.

How: assign an aggressively short deadline; force execution of essentials only. Pair with 80/20 (limit tasks and shorten time).

Trade-offs: quality is usually equal or better; occasionally too tight — recalibrate, don't abandon.

The Low-Information Diet

When to use: overwhelm, news anxiety, chronic "researching."

How: one-week total media fast (cold turkey) → rebuild only just-in-time sources → ask "will I use this immediately and importantly?" → practice nonfinishing.

Trade-offs: you'll miss some conversations; you lose almost nothing actionable.

Batching + the Batch Cost/Benefit Test

When to use: recurring time-consumer tasks (email, calls, mail, reports).

How: pick a frequency; compute (hours saved × your $/hr) − (cost of problems caused by the delay). If net positive, batch further apart; if negative, step back one frequency (weekly → twice-weekly, not daily).

Trade-offs: slower responses; large gains in deep-work time; risk capped (Ferriss: nothing cost >$300 to fix).

Empowerment via If-Then Rules

When to use: to stop being a decision bottleneck.

How: give outsourcers/co-workers written rules + a spending limit (e.g., "fix anything under $400 without asking"); review monthly and add new rules from their best decisions.

Trade-offs: occasional small losses; huge time freedom and a self-improving system.

The Puppy Dog Close

When to use: overcoming resistance to a permanent change (remote work, no-meeting policy, autonomy).

How: propose a small, reversible "let's just try it once" trial; the return rarely happens.

Trade-offs: slower than demanding the change; far higher success rate.

Eliminate → Automate → Delegate

When to use: before assigning any task to a VA or system.

How: cut the task; if it survives, systematize it; only then delegate what remains. Assign VAs one task at a time (two max), each with a clear deliverable.

Trade-offs: more upfront thinking; prevents paying to preserve worthless work.

Muse Design (product + market)

When to use: building automated income to hit your TMI.

How: (1) niche market first (magazine full-page ad <$5,000; ≥15,000 readers); (2) product meeting 4 criteria — one-sentence benefit, $50–200, ≤3–4 wk to make, FAQ-able; (3) source via resell < license < create (info products ideal); control distribution, hold premium pricing.

Trade-offs: narrow markets cap size but cut competition and cost, and command premium prices.

Micro-Testing (validate before manufacturing)

When to use: before spending on inventory.

How: 1–3 page test site → Google AdWords PPC (~$500, ~5 days, many narrow keywords > few broad) → "temporarily out of stock" page captures purchase intent without charging → read conversion. Or probe on eBay first. Manufacture only if it converts.

Trade-offs: costs ~$500 and a few days; saves months and inventory risk.

Virtual Architecture (Management by Absence)

When to use: after a validated muse, to remove yourself from operations.

How: 3-phase rollout — DIY (build FAQ from real questions) → local fulfillment (net-30) → end-to-end fulfillment + call center + processor that talk to each other. Use replaceable contract companies, not freelancers; check reports weekly/monthly, banks 1st & 15th.

Trade-offs: setup fees and coordination; buys near-total absence and scalability.

The Hourglass Remote-Work Escape (5 steps)

When to use: employees wanting location freedom (DELA).

How: (1) raise your value + get invested-in; (2) prove remote productivity covertly with records; (3) build a business-case bullet list; (4) propose a small revocable trial (bracket: ask 2, accept 1); (5) expand stepwise to full-time; keep a funded willingness to quit as leverage.

Trade-offs: takes ~2 months and nerve; if refused, the job is "beyond repair" — leave.

Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals
