cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Four Thousand Weeks

Burkeman's judgment distilled into decision rules. The throughline: you can't do everything; choose your neglect consciously and the rest gets better.

The One Rule Behind Everything

When you feel overwhelmed, the answer is never "do more / get more efficient." It's "confront the limit and choose what to drop." Efficiency surfaces more demands; acceptance ends the spiral.

Decision Rules

When you…Don'tDo (because…)
feel "too much to do"try to fit it all inaccept you can't, then pick what to consciously neglect (the to-do list is infinite by design)
clear your inbox / deckscelebrate being "on top of it"expect more to flow in — efficiency speeds the conveyor belt
evaluate a productivity tipask "does it fit more in?"ask "what does it let me neglect?" — that's the only real help
face a tempting opportunityqueue it for "later"run Buffett 25/5: top-5 → yes; bottom-20 → actively avoid (it's a trap, not a backlog)
have a high-value goalwait for spare timepay yourself first — do it today, first; spare time never comes
juggle many projectskeep all irons in the firecap WIP at ~3; finish or drop before adding
want "work-life balance"chase it (nobody achieves it)decide in advance what to fail at; choose deliberate imbalance
get distracted from hard workblame the appnotice you're fleeing the task's discomfort (the intimate interrupter) — stay with it
feel a project is derivativejump to a new directionstay on the bus — routes diverge into originality only past the shared stretch
rush a problem / personforce the pacelet it take its time; tolerate not-knowing (impatience backfires)
feel guilty about leisurejustify rest as recovery for more worktreat rest as an end in itself (atelic) — that's the point of the time
feel insignificant / behinddespairuse cosmic insignificance therapy — lower the bar to human scale; relief, not pressure
crave certainty before actingwait for the guaranteeact wholeheartedly without it — "I don't mind what happens"
have a generous impulsedefer to do it perfectlyact now, imperfectly — the gift you make beats the one you don't

Thresholds & Defaults

  • Lifespan budget: ~4,000 weeks (80 yrs). The number is the reframe, not a countdown to optimize.
  • Closed list cap: ~10 items; add only by completing.
  • WIP limit: ≈3 active projects (≤1 work + ≤1 non-work for big serialized projects).
  • Buffett split: top 5 of 25 ambitions; avoid the other 20.
  • Daily creative stint (radical incrementalism): small and fixed; never more than ~4 hrs; stop on time even with energy left; weekends off.
  • Work boundaries: set start/stop hours in advance; let the container do the deciding.
  • "Do nothing" practice: 5–10 min.

Tells & Smells (you're avoiding finitude when…)

  • You're "keeping your options open" → really avoiding the commitment that would make life meaningful.
  • You feel you must do more than you can → logically impossible; the inner taskmaster is simply wrong.
  • You're busy but nothing important advances → you're using busyness to numb the discomfort of choosing.
  • You live in "when I finally…" → instrumentalizing the present; the future is a place you never arrive.
  • You can't sit still / must act → you'll make bad choices just to feel in control (practice doing nothing).
  • Every cause feels equally urgent → the attention economy talking; consolidate your caring.

Good vs Bad Procrastination

  • Bad: avoiding a project to dodge the fear of doing it imperfectly / facing your limits (the architect who never builds).
  • Good (creative neglect): consciously choosing what to not do so you can finish what matters. Procrastinate on the right things, on purpose.

The Liberating Reframes (use when stuck)

  • "I'll never get on top of everything" → good news: stop berating yourself; start choosing.
  • "Missing out is guaranteed" → that's exactly what makes a choice mean something.
  • "I have far less control than I want" → and confronting that is the most effective time-management move there is.

glossary.md

Glossary — Four Thousand Weeks

Active patience — Patience reframed not as passive resignation but as an "almost muscular state of alert presence." (Ch 11)

Art of creative neglect — The decision discipline of deliberately, calmly choosing what not to do; treating neglect as a skill, not a failure. (Ch 4)

Atelic activity — An activity with no end point or external goal, valuable in itself (a walk, listening to music). Contrast telic. (Ch 9, via Kieran Setiya)

Attention economy — The system in which companies profit by capturing your finite attention, incentivized to show you enraging or distracting material. (Ch 5)

Being-toward-death — Heidegger's idea that authentic living means facing mortality rather than fleeing it; finitude defines human existence. (Ch 3)

Buffett's 25/5 rule — List 25 ambitions, keep the top 5, and actively avoid the other 20 as traps. (Ch 4, Appendix tool 3)

Causal catastrophe — Valuing present activities only for what they cause/lead to, never for themselves — so the present is endlessly sacrificed to a future that never arrives. (Ch 8)

Clock time — Treating time as an abstract, measurable resource separate from life, to be spent efficiently; the modern default. Contrast deep time. (Ch 1)

Closed / open lists — A two-list system: an unbounded "open" list of everything, and a "closed" list capped (~10) you can only add to by completing an item. (Appendix tool 1)

Consolidate your caring — Deliberately narrowing the causes/worries you engage so your finite capacity for care makes a real difference. (Appendix tool 5)

Conveyor belt of time — Edward Hall's image: time as a belt delivering containers (hours/weeks) we must fill; becoming "productive" just speeds the belt up. (Ch 0–1)

Cosmic insignificance therapy — The relief of recognizing your life matters far less on a cosmic scale than your ego demands, freeing you to live a meaningful human-scale life. (Ch 13)

Creative neglect — See art of creative neglect. (Ch 4)

Deep time — The expansive, timeless absorption in reality that comes from forgetting the abstract yardstick of the clock ("living in deep time," Richard Rohr). (Ch 1)

Decide what to fail at — Strategic underachievement: pre-selecting domains where you'll deliberately not seek excellence. (Appendix tool 3)

Done list — A list that starts empty each day and fills with what you accomplished, countering "productivity debt." (Appendix tool 4)

Efficiency trap — The pattern where becoming more efficient surfaces more demands rather than freeing time. (Ch 2)

Eigenzeit — German for "the time inherent to a process itself"; letting things take the time they take. (Ch 1)

Fixed-volume approach — Designing your work around hard, predetermined limits (work hours, list caps) instead of trying to expand capacity. (Appendix tool 1)

FOMO / JOMO — Fear of missing out vs. joy of missing out; since missing out is guaranteed, it's what makes choices meaningful. (Ch 3–4)

Helsinki Bus Station Theory — Arno Minkkinen's parable: early work resembles others' until you "stay on the bus" long enough for your route to diverge into originality. (Ch 11)

Human disease, the — The compulsion to demand certainty and cosmic reassurance about the future. (Ch 14)

Impatience spiral — The self-reinforcing loop where demanding speed erodes our tolerance for slowness, making everything feel more frustrating. (Ch 10)

Instantaneous generosity — Acting on a generous impulse immediately rather than deferring it (the only donation that counts is the one you make). (Appendix tool 9)

Instrumentalizing time — Treating each moment merely as a means to a future end. (Ch 8)

Intimate interrupter, the — The inner source of distraction: we flee toward distraction to escape the discomfort of a finite, difficult task. (Ch 6)

Joyless urgency — Marilynne Robinson's phrase for the modern compulsion to always be getting more done. (Ch 0–1)

Limit-embracing life — Organizing your days knowing you definitely can't do everything, and making hard choices consciously. (Ch 1)

Paradox of limitation — The more you chase total control over time, the worse life gets; the more you confront finitude, the better it gets. (Ch 1, the book's thesis)

Pay yourself first (with time) — Do your most-valued activity today, first, instead of hoping for leftover time. (Ch 4, Appendix tool 1)

Practice doing nothing — Training the capacity to not-act, so you stop making poor choices just to feel like you're acting. (Appendix tool 10)

Radical incrementalism — Robert Boice's finding: sustained creative output comes from short, fixed daily sessions, stopping on time. (Ch 11)

Researcher in relationships — Adopting curiosity (not a desired outcome) toward other people and the future. (Appendix tool 8)

Rocks-in-the-jar lie — Covey's "big rocks first" parable is rigged: reality has more big rocks than any jar can hold. (Ch 4)

Serialize — Work one big project at a time, finishing before starting the next. (Appendix tool 2)

Sisyphus's inbox — The endlessly refilling task list; the work is never done by design. (Ch 2)

Strategic underachievement — See decide what to fail at. (Appendix tool 3)

Task orientation — Pre-clock way of living where rhythms emerge from tasks themselves, not an abstract timeline. (Ch 1)

Telic activity — An activity aimed at a goal/end point, valued for its completion. Contrast atelic. (Ch 9)

Work in progress (WIP) limit — Capping active projects (≈3) so new work waits until a slot frees. (Ch 4, Personal Kanban)

You are time — We don't have time as a possession; our existence is time, so "managing" it as a resource is a category error. (Ch 3)

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Four Thousand Weeks

The book's concrete, repeatable practices. Most come from Chapter 4, Chapter 11, and the Appendix. These are practices, not insights — pick one or two and run them this week.

The Two-List System (fixed-volume productivity)

When to use: your to-do list is bottomless and you never feel "on top of it."

How: Keep an open list (everything, however long) and a closed list capped at ~10. You may only move a task from open→closed when you complete one already on the closed list. Optionally add an "on hold" list for items awaiting others.

Trade-offs: forces conscious prioritization and a felt sense of completion; requires accepting the open list will never empty.

Predetermined Time Boundaries

When to use: work expands to fill all available hours.

How: Decide in advance your start and stop times (e.g., start by 8:30, hard stop 5:30). Let the fixed container force wiser choices. (Newport: "you could fill any arbitrary number of hours with what feels to be productive work.")

Trade-offs: the constraint is the whole point; resist the urge to extend "just this once."

Pay Yourself First (with time)

When to use: a high-value pursuit keeps getting deferred to "leftover" time.

How: Do an hour of your most-valued work first, before email/meetings. Block recurring calendar "meetings" with yourself. Claim time; don't try to find it — spare time never arrives.

Trade-offs: something else gets less of you, on purpose.

Limit Work in Progress (WIP ≈ 3)

When to use: you keep starting things and bouncing between them when one gets hard.

How: Cap active projects at ~3. New demands wait in a queue until a slot frees by completion or deliberate abandonment. Name slots as next achievable steps ("draft ch4 outline"), not giants ("write book").

Trade-offs: from Personal Kanban; converts the false comfort of many open projects into real completion.

Buffett's 25/5

When to use: too many moderately attractive options compete for your finite life.

How: List your top 25 ambitions, rank them, circle the top 5. The other 20 are avoid-at-all-costs, not a someday list — they're appealing enough to distract, not important enough to build a life on.

Trade-offs: the hardest "no" is to things you genuinely want.

Serialize

When to use: anxiety tempts you to start everything at once.

How: One big project at a time (at most one work + one non-work). Consciously postpone everything else and tolerate the resulting anxiety. Only truly essential maintenance (bills, school run) is exempt.

Trade-offs: feels worse short-term, finishes more long-term.

Decide in Advance What to Fail At (strategic underachievement)

When to use: "work-life balance" feels impossible because everything demands excellence.

How: Pre-select domains to deliberately neglect (lawn, tidy kitchen) with zero shame. In essential domains, fail cyclically — bare minimum at work for two months while you focus on kids, then switch.

Trade-offs: replaces impossible balance with deliberate, confident imbalance.

Keep a "Done List"

When to use: you can never feel good because work is never finished ("productivity debt").

How: Start each day with an empty list; log what you actually accomplish. In a rut, lower the bar ("made coffee" counts). Leverages the motivating power of "small wins."

Trade-offs: a reframe, not more output — but small wins compound.

Radical Incrementalism (Boice's method)

When to use: long-horizon creative/knowledge work prone to bingeing and burnout.

How: A fixed, modest daily block (Boice's academics: sometimes 10 min, never >4 hrs). Show up every day; stop when the block ends, even mid-flow, to preserve the appetite to return. Take weekends off.

Trade-offs: slower on any single day, far more sustainable over a career; beats all-day binges.

Stay on the Bus (Helsinki Bus Station)

When to use: your work looks derivative and you're tempted to start over in a new direction.

How: Assume you simply haven't ridden far enough; keep committing to your route. Routes diverge into originality only past the shared early stretch of imitation and skill-building.

Trade-offs: requires enduring a long unoriginal phase; restarting resets you to the station.

Consolidate Your Caring

When to use: social media makes you feel you must care about every crisis at once.

How: Pick your battles — devote spare capacity to a couple of causes for a couple of years. Not because others don't matter, but because real impact needs focus.

Trade-offs: deliberately ignoring worthy causes; the attention economy pressures every cause to claim uniqueness.

Make Technology Boring

When to use: focused work keeps losing to one-swipe-away distraction.

How: Remove social apps; set the phone to grayscale (Settings > Accessibility > Color Filters); use single-purpose devices (Kindle). Strip the seductive escape from limitation out of your tools.

Trade-offs: less convenience, more reclaimed attention.

Seek Novelty in the Mundane

When to use: years feel like they're accelerating and collapsing.

How: Don't cram in exotic experiences — pay deeper attention to ordinary life. New route to work, unplanned walks, photography, journaling, "I Spy" with a kid. Novel attention lays down memory.

Trade-offs: subtle; works through presence, not novelty-chasing.

Be a Researcher in Relationships

When to use: you're trying to control how time with others (or the future) unfolds.

How: In a hard or boring moment, switch to curiosity — "who is this person?" Curiosity is satisfied whether they please you or not; a demand for outcomes is frustrated each time. Choose curiosity over worry about the future too.

Trade-offs: relinquishes control of outcomes.

Instantaneous Generosity

When to use: a generous impulse arises (give, praise, check in).

How: Act now, imperfectly. The donation/message you actually send beats the perfect one you never do. We defer not from meanness but from control-seeking.

Trade-offs: none worth mentioning — it also makes you happier immediately.

"Do Nothing" Meditation

When to use: you can't tolerate not-acting, so you make poor choices just to feel active.

How: Set a 5–10 min timer; sit; stop trying to do anything. Each time you notice you're "doing" something (even thinking, or focusing on the breath), stop doing it. Keep stopping until the timer ends.

Trade-offs: rebuilds autonomy from the urge to evade how reality feels right now.

What Got You Here Won't Get You There: How Successful People Become Even More Successful

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Decision Rules & Diagnostics

Decision Rules

  • When you're about to correct someone's idea, do nothing, because you'll improve the idea 5% and cut their commitment 50% (fallacy of added value, #2).
  • When you're about to speak, run the four gates first — will this help our customers / our company / the person I'm talking to / the person I'm talking about? — because if it fails all four, being right is worthless.
  • When the question is "is it true?", switch to "is it worth it?", because roughly half of what you were going to say is accurate and still not worth the damage.
  • When you're diagnosing a problem in yourself, don't — get feedback, because self-diagnosers see cancer where a professional sees a muscle pull.
  • When a behavior seems tied to your success, ask "because of or in spite of?", because the superstition trap is what keeps successful people from changing.
  • When you want to change more than one thing, pick one, because one gun, one bullet; multiple simultaneous changes is a personality makeover, not improvement.
  • When you can't decide whether to be nicer or stop being a jerk, stop being a jerk, because omission is cheap and commission requires filling an entire box.
  • When you apologize, stop talking, because every added word converts the apology into a defense.
  • When you've improved but no one has noticed, advertise harder, because you must get 100% better to earn 10% credit; you're in the dumb phase.
  • When someone gives you feedback or a suggestion, say only "thank you", because it's the one response that cannot be argued with or escalated.
  • When you want ideas without defensiveness, ask for two future suggestions (feedforward), not a critique, because people accept ideas about the future and reject verdicts on the past.
  • When you're deciding whether to keep coaching someone, stop if they don't think they have a problem, they're in the wrong job, or they think everyone else is the problem. Test: "if we shut down today — surprised, sad, or relieved?"
  • When you're 70 and being corrected for the ten-thousandth time, let it go — and grant the same to others.

Diagnostic: Symptom → Habit → Fix

What you observeLikely habitFix
Debates trivia; must be right about restaurant choice#1 Winning too muchAsk "is winning this worth it?" Concede on the trivial.
"Great idea, but here's how to make it better"#2 Adding too much valueSay "thank you" and stop. Let them own it.
Rates every contribution good/bad#3 Passing judgmentReceive input with a neutral "thank you."
Sarcasm that "makes you sound sharp"#4 Destructive commentsMonetize it: $10 a shot.
Sentences opening "No…" "But…" "However…"#5 No/But/HoweverFine yourself per instance; substitute a pause.
Name-drops, corrects others' facts, fakes prior knowledge#6 Telling the world how smart we areSay "I didn't know that. Thank you."
Uses temper as a lever#7 Speaking when angrySilence is the only reliable strategy; "no one is in the other boat."
Unrequested "let me explain why that won't work"#8 NegativityWait to be asked.
Hoards data; people learn things last#9 Withholding informationDefault to over-sharing; audit who wasn't copied.
Never praises; "I expected great work"#10 Failing to give recognitionTwice-weekly name-list review; recognize or do nothing.
Retells shared wins in the first person#11 Claiming creditList a win's contributors; publicly reassign credit.
"That's just how I am" / "I'm impatient"#12 Making excusesBan the phrase; treat the trait as behavior, not fate.
Blames upbringing, prior boss, history#13 Clinging to the pastRedirect every past sentence to a future one.
Rewards flattery; has an inner circle#14 Playing favoritesRank reports by contribution vs. by adoration; compare.
Never says sorry#15 Refusing to express regret"I'm sorry. I'll try to do better." Then nothing.
Checks phone, finishes sentences, interrupts#16 Not listeningCount to fifty; make them the most important person in the room.
Treats help as expected#17 Failing to express gratitudeThe 25-names note-writing drill.
Snaps at whoever brings bad news#18 Punishing the messengerThank the messenger before responding to the message.
"Marketing dropped the ball"#19 Passing the buckOwn it first, publicly, then fix it.
"That's just who I am" as a virtue#20 Excessive need to be "me"Ask whether the trait is a value or a habit wearing a value's costume.
Hits every target while the team burns out or bends rules#21 Goal obsessionAsk what the goal was for. Check for time pressure, hurry, "it's important," dependents.

Thresholds & Defaults Goldsmith Commits To

ItemDefault
Behaviors to change at once1
Feedback raters~8–15 (avg 15), all passing the Four Commitments
Follow-up cadenceevery month or so
Total change horizon12–18 months
Feedforward askexactly 2 suggestions, future only
Fine per offense when monetizing$10–$20
Expected non-actors among sincere intenders~30%
Credit earned for improvement100% better → ~10% credit

Trade-offs

ChoiceTake the left whenTake the right when
Feedback vs. FeedforwardYou need to know what is wrongYou need ideas for how to fix it
Being right vs. being effectiveFacts materially change the outcomeIt's a preference, a detail, or someone's idea
Coaching vs. letting them goThey own the problem and want to changeThey deny it, are in the wrong job, or blame everyone else
Skill training vs. behavioral changeThe gap is competenceThe gap is how people experience you
Doing something vs. doing nothingThe act helps someone besides youThe act mainly proves you're smart

Tells & Smells (a habit is firing)

  • You start a sentence with "No," "But," or "However" — you've already said "I'm right, you're wrong."
  • "Great idea — and you could also…" — #2 in progress.
  • "I already knew that." — #6.
  • "That's just the way I am." — #12/#20.
  • "I don't suffer fools gladly." — the classic defense for #16.
  • You're re-explaining an apology — you've undone it.
  • You feel you're "too busy" to follow up — you're in the 30%.
  • You're winning an argument with your own direct report — it isn't a fair fight.
  • You hit the number and the team is quietly leaving — #21.

glossary.md

Glossary — What Got You Here Won't Get You There

The Twenty Habits (Ch 4) — by name

1. Winning too much — The need to win at all costs and in all situations; the root habit behind most of the others (Ch 4).

2. Adding too much value — The overwhelming desire to add our two cents to every discussion (Ch 4).

3. Passing judgment — The need to rate others and impose our standards on them (Ch 4).

4. Making destructive comments — Needless sarcasm and cutting remarks we think make us sound sharp and witty (Ch 4).

5. Starting with "No," "But," or "However" — Overuse of negative qualifiers that secretly say "I'm right. You're wrong." (Ch 4).

6. Telling the world how smart we are — The need to show people we're smarter than they think we are (Ch 4).

7. Speaking when angry — Using emotional volatility as a management tool (Ch 4).

8. Negativity, or "Let me explain why that won't work" — The need to share our negative thoughts even when we weren't asked (Ch 4).

9. Withholding information — Refusing to share information in order to maintain an advantage over others (Ch 4).

10. Failing to give proper recognition — The inability to praise and reward (Ch 4).

11. Claiming credit that we don't deserve — The most annoying way to overestimate our contribution to any success (Ch 4).

12. Making excuses — Repositioning our annoying behavior as a permanent fixture so people excuse us for it (Ch 4).

13. Clinging to the past — Deflecting blame onto events and people from our past; a subset of blaming everyone else (Ch 4).

14. Playing favorites — Failing to see that we are treating someone unfairly (Ch 4).

15. Refusing to express regret — Inability to take responsibility, admit we're wrong, or recognize how our actions affect others (Ch 4).

16. Not listening — The most passive-aggressive form of disrespect for colleagues (Ch 4).

17. Failing to express gratitude — The most basic form of bad manners (Ch 4).

18. Punishing the messenger — The misguided need to attack the innocent who are usually only trying to help us (Ch 4).

19. Passing the buck — The need to blame everyone but ourselves (Ch 4).

20. An excessive need to be "me" — Exalting our faults as virtues simply because they're who we are (Ch 4).

21. Goal obsession — The twenty-first habit; not a flaw but a creator of flaws — pursuing a goal so hard you forget what it was for (Ch 5).

Terms A–Z

Advertising — Deliberately telling colleagues what you are changing, repeatedly, because perception lags behavior (Ch 8).

Apology formula — "I'm sorry. I'll try to do better in the future." Then say nothing (Ch 7).

Because of vs. in spite of — The test that breaks the superstition trap: are you successful because of this behavior or in spite of it? (Ch 3).

Blindside event — Unsolicited feedback that reveals something everyone else already knew (Ch 6).

Dumb phase — The period (borrowed from wine) when improvement is real but invisible to others; keep advertising through it (Ch 8).

Feedback — Past-tense information about what happened; tells you what to change, not how (Ch 6).

Feedforward — Feedback going in the opposite direction: asking for two suggestions for the future, listening, saying thank you. "If feedback is past tense, feedforward is future perfect." (Ch 12).

Four Commitments — What you must ask of raters/helpers: (1) let go of the past, (2) tell the truth, (3) be supportive, not a cynic/critic/judge, (4) pick one thing to improve in themselves (Ch 6).

Four Gate Questions — Before speaking, ask: will this comment help our customers? our company? the person I'm talking to? the person I'm talking about? (Ch 4).

Fallacy of added value — Improving someone's idea by 5% while cutting their commitment to it by 50% by stealing ownership (Ch 4).

Global Leadership Inventory — The Appendix's 72-item, 15-dimension 360 instrument on a 5-point satisfaction scale (Appendix).

Goal obsession — See habit 21. Arises from misunderstanding what we want, or what others want us to do (Ch 5).

Golden Rule Fallacy — Managing people the way you want to be managed; "you are not managing you" (Ch 14).

Great Western Disease — "I will be happy when…" — deferring meaning to a future milestone (Coda).

"How'm I doing?" — Ed Koch's model for follow-up: ask constantly and publicly (Ch 11).

"How to Handle Me" memo — A leader's honest, accurate, and relevant self-description shared with the team (Ch 14).

Is it worth it? — The listening/speaking filter: not "is it true?" but "will saying this help?" (Ch 4, Ch 9).

"Let it go" — Knowing when to stop trying to change someone (or yourself); appears verbatim in Ch 14's "Stop Trying to Coach People Who Shouldn't Be Coached" (Ch 14).

Mission neutral — Behavior that is neither good nor bad; the target state for a bad habit is often simply nothing (Ch 4, Ch 13).

Monetizing the habit — Charging yourself a fixed sum ($10–$20) per offense to make an invisible habit visible and costly (Ch 4, Ch 13).

Natural law — People change only if it's demonstrably in their own best interests as defined by their own values (Ch 3).

One gun, one bullet — Pick exactly one behavior to change at a time (Ch 13).

Program of the month — The cynical read colleagues apply to any change effort that isn't followed up (Ch 11).

Shifting into neutral / the empty box — Becoming nicer means filling a box with positive acts; ceasing to be a jerk just means leaving it empty (Ch 4).

Solicited feedback — Asking "How can I do better?" — the only feedback question that reliably works (Ch 6).

Stengel's thirds — Any team splits into those who love you, hate you, and are undecided; manage the undecided (Ch 14).

Success delusion — The four beliefs (I have succeeded / I can succeed / I will succeed / I choose to succeed) that make successful people resist change (Ch 3).

Superstition trap — "I behave this way, and I am successful, therefore I must be successful because I behave this way." (Ch 3).

Thanking — The one response to feedback that cannot be argued with, escalated, or trumped (Ch 10).

"There is never anyone in the other boat" — Your anger is at a projection; the empty boat has no one to blame (Ch 4).

To Stop list — The counterpart to a To Do list; Drucker: leaders need to learn what to stop (Ch 4).

Transactional flaws — Interpersonal behaviors between people — not flaws of skill, intelligence, or fixed personality (Ch 4).

95-Year-Old Exercise — Imagine you're 95 and dying; advise your present self, write it down, then do it (Coda).

70/30 split — Of people who intend to change, ~70% act and ~30% do nothing, consistently across companies and cultures (Ch 11).

patterns.md

Patterns — Goldsmith's Change Techniques

The seven steps run in order. Skipping any one is the usual reason change fails.

1. Feedback — Get the Truth

When to use: First. Before you can change, you must know which behavior actually costs you, in others' eyes, not yours.

How:

1. Pick 8–15 people who see your interpersonal behavior daily — peers, reports, customers, your best friend at work.

2. Qualify each against the Four Commitments: will they (1) let go of the past, (2) tell the truth, (3) be supportive rather than a cynic, critic, or judge, (4) pick one thing to improve in themselves? If a name fails any of the four, drop it.

3. Collect confidentially and in aggregate so the data can't be attributed — or denied.

4. Ask the only question that works: "How can I do better?" Never argue with the answer.

5. Self-administered substitutes: list your remarks for a week; watch yourself with the sound off; complete "It would make my life easier if my colleagues stopped ___"; audit your self-aggrandizing remarks; ask at home.

Trade-offs: Feedback tells you what to change, never how. It also forces people to relive the past, which is why it stalls — hence feedforward later. Anonymity is what buys you honesty; sacrifice it and you get flattery.

2. Apologizing — Clear the Ledger

When to use: Immediately after feedback, before announcing any change. Nothing else works until the emotional debt is cleared.

How: Say "I'm sorry." Add "I'll try to do better in the future." Then say nothing. Get in and get out fast.

Trade-offs: The entire power comes from the silence after. Every word of explanation, context, or qualification dilutes it into a defense. Winking, joking, or "I'm sorry if you felt…" converts an apology into a fresh offense.

3. Advertising — Tell the World

When to use: After apologizing. Because you have to get 100% better before colleagues will grant you 10% credit — their perception is filtered through the old stereotype.

How:

1. Announce specifically what behavior you are changing.

2. Repeat it, week after week, metronome-steady — not a "one day sale."

3. Ask everyone for ideas, which makes them invested in your success.

4. Be your own press secretary: treat every day as a message opportunity and stay on message with near-shameless discipline.

Trade-offs: Feels immodest and repetitive to you long before it registers with them. Expect a dumb phase where you are genuinely better and nobody notices. Advertise anyway.

4. Listening — Earn the Right

When to use: Continuously; it is the habit most often cited and the cheapest to fix.

How: Three things all good listeners do — think before you speak, listen with respect, and ask "Is it worth it?" Tactically: don't interrupt, don't finish sentences, don't say "I already knew that," never open with "no," "but," or "however," say "thank you," and ask questions that make the other person talk. Drill: count silently to fifty before responding.

Trade-offs: Roughly half of what you were about to say may be correct — and still not worth saying. You trade being right for being effective. The paradox: the more you subsume your desire to shine, the more you shine.

5. Thanking — Close the Loop

When to use: As the response to every piece of feedback or suggestion, and as a standing practice.

How: Say "thank you" and stop. It is the one reply that cannot be argued with, escalated, or trumped — the only counter is "you're welcome." Drill: list the 25 people most responsible for your success, ask whether you ever actually told them, and write each a note.

Trade-offs: Some read gratitude as submissive; it isn't, but expect the flinch. Overuse as a conversational full-stop can shut down dialogue you actually wanted.

6. Following Up — Make It Stick

When to use: Every month or so, for 12 to 18 months. This is the step that converts intention into perceived change.

How: Go back to all the coworkers who gave you feedback and ask: "Last month I said I'd work on X. Do you think I've put your ideas into practice?" Then thank them and repeat. Ed Koch's "How'm I doing?" is the model — it advertises, involves, imprints, and forces you to walk the talk.

Trade-offs: This is a grind, not an event — no nitroglycerin tablet. But the evidence is blunt: across ~86,000 respondents, leaders who did no follow-up showed no perceived improvement regardless of effort; consistent follow-up produced dramatic gains. Note: about 30% of people who fully intend to change do nothing, almost always pleading "too busy."

7. Feedforward — Replace Criticism with Ideas

When to use: Whenever you want improvement ideas without triggering defensiveness — yours or anyone else's. It never has to stop.

How (four steps):

1. Pick one behavior you want to change.

2. Describe it one-on-one to anyone — expertise is irrelevant; strangers can be ideal partners.

3. Ask for two suggestions for the future. No discussion of the past is permitted.

4. Listen, take notes, and say only "Thank you." No judging, rating, or critiquing — not even "that's a good idea." Then repeat with someone else.

Trade-offs: You give up the right to debate or defend, which is the point. It works because successful people accept future ideas while rejecting past criticism, because you can change the future but not the past, and because it costs the giver nothing — no need to be right, no career risk in "criticizing the boss." Weakness: it generates volume, not validation; you still need feedback and follow-up to know whether anything landed.

Supporting Pattern: Monetizing the Habit

When to use: When a habit is invisible to you in the moment (starting with "no/but/however," destructive comments).

How: Appoint a witness and pay a fixed fine — $10 or $20 — per offense, on the spot, to charity.

Trade-offs: Crude and public, which is exactly why it works fast. It builds awareness, not judgment; retire it once the behavior is neutral.

Until the End of Time: Mind, Matter, and Our Search for Meaning in an Evolving Universe

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Until the End of Time

The Cosmic-Era Timeline (Empire State Building: floor n = 10^n years after the bang)

FloorYearsWhat ends / what happens
1–910–10⁹Particles, atoms, stars, planets, life, mind. We are on floor ~10.
1010¹⁰Present epoch. Sun dies ~5 Gyr; Milky Way + Andromeda → Milkomeda
1110¹¹Distant galaxies pass the cosmic horizon; the observable sky empties
12–1410¹²–10¹⁴Era of red dwarfs; last star formation ends; traditional life/mind window closes
15–2010¹⁵–10²⁰Burnt-out stars and wandering planets; solar systems unbind via gravitational waves
~34+>10³⁴Proton decay (if grand unification holds) dissolves complex matter
38–6810³⁸–10⁶⁸Black hole era; stellar-mass holes evaporate by floor 68
10210¹⁰²Largest supermassive holes finish evaporating — top of the building
102–359—Estimated window for Higgs vacuum decay
10^6810^(10⁶⁸)Boltzmann brains become likely (unwritable exponent)

Rule: predict this timeline in broad strokes only. Structure, not specifics.

Entropy vs. Local Order — Decision Rules

If you see…Then…Because
Order appearing spontaneouslyFind the energy flow and the waste sinkEntropic two-step: local decrease requires larger export
No identifiable sinkYour accounting is wrong, not the second lawTotal entropy never decreases
Entropy apparently vanishingLook for the hidden ledger entryBekenstein: it went into horizon area
A low-entropy configurationSuspect an organizing influence, not luckLow entropy = rare = special
An entropy-raising change that isn't happeningLook for a missing catalystEntropic hurdles block accessible states
A system that must keep runningAsk how it purges waste heatYou are a steam engine; erasure, not thought, costs entropy
Gravity involvedExpect self-sustaining orderNegative heat capacity: losing heat makes it hotter
A far-future structure proposedCheck the sink still exists at that eraExpanding, cooling space eventually offers none

Threshold: entropy = number of configurations that "pretty much look the same." Long/short, likely/unlikely have no absolute meaning — always state the comparison scale.

Which Level of Explanation Applies Here?

The question is about…Answer at this levelDo NOT
What will happen next, physicallyParticles and fieldsInvoke purpose or will
Why this structure is possible at allEntropy + energy flowClaim it explains which structure
Why this variant persistedSelection (incl. molecular Darwinism)Assume adaptation before ruling out byproduct
What a person is doing and whyInstinct, memory, perception, social expectationSay "it's just particles" — the insight isn't there
What a work of art meansStory, myth, artistic truthDemand propositional verification
Whether something mattersCreated meaning, inside mindsLook for it in the laws — it isn't there

Test: layers must be consistent with those below, never replaceable by them. If your explanation dismisses a level, you've lost information; if it exempts a level from physics, you've lost the constraint.

Fast Tells

  • "It's all just particles" → eliminativism smuggled in as reductionism.
  • "This trait evolved because it does X" → run the byproduct check first.
  • "It feels wonderful" → proximate explanation only; the ultimate one is still owed.
  • "That's too unlikely to matter" → over an open horizon, compute waiting time instead.
  • "The theory implies I can't trust my evidence" → the model is incomplete (Boltzmann brains).
  • "Coincidence, therefore significance" → pattern-detection outrunning analysis (the tarantula).
  • "My legacy will endure" → symbolic immortality is real but bounded by the era of minds.
  • "Do you believe X?" → reframe as calibrated confidence; then name literal vs. metaphorical register.
  • Existential dread about the far future dismissed as silly → no principled basis for the dismissal (Scheffler, Wolf); the timescale intuition is parochial, not the worry.

Meaning — the closing rules

1. The universe does not exist as an arena for life and mind; it will not hug you.

2. Value and meaning are created inside subjective worlds, not found in the laws.

3. Invented ≠ arbitrary: evolved predispositions + group feedback loops constrain what emerges.

4. Finitude generates the calculus of value. Unlimited do-overs would drain choices of consequence.

5. Species continuity, not personal continuity, is what secures the sense that things matter.

6. Equations have no intrinsic worth — "their worth derives from the minds they inhabit." Same for every artifact.

7. Look inward. "That is the noble direction to look."

glossary.md

Glossary — Until the End of Time

Adaptation vs. byproduct (spandrel) — Whether a trait was selected for its own effects or came bundled free with something else that was selected for (Ch 6, 7, 8).

Aperiodic crystal — Schrödinger's prescient term for the information-bearing molecule of heredity (Ch 4).

ATP — The strained-spring molecule synthesized by membrane turbines that ferries energy through the cell (Ch 4).

Attention schema — Graziano's proposal that consciousness is the brain's radically simplified model of its own attention (Ch 5).

Belief calculus — The mixed reasoning-plus-emotion-plus-authority process by which beliefs actually form, mostly below awareness (Ch 7).

Big bounce / cyclic cosmology — Steinhardt–Turok–Ijjas alternative in which expansion dilutes entropy enough for cycles of hundreds of billions of years to repeat (Ch 10).

Big crunch — Collapse following a tunneling of dark energy to a negative value (Ch 10).

Big rip — Scenario where dark energy strengthens until repulsive gravity tears apart galaxies, stars, molecules, and atoms (Ch 9).

Black hole evaporation — Slow shrinkage via Hawking radiation, once a hole's temperature exceeds the ambient temperature of space (Ch 10).

Boltzmann brain — A free-floating mind assembled by a rare spontaneous entropy drop, complete with false memories (Ch 10).

"Cheesecake for the mind" — Pinker's claim that the arts are adaptively useless confections pressing pleasure buttons evolved for other purposes (Ch 8).

CMB (afterglow of creation) — The big bang's residual heat, now 2.7 K, with hot/cold spots differing by ~1 part in 100,000 (Ch 3).

Cosmic horizon — Boundary beyond which objects recede faster than light; it glows at a tiny constant temperature (Ch 9, 10).

Costly signaling — Extravagant, hard-to-fake investment that certifies commitment or quality (Ch 7, 8).

Dark energy — Uniformly spread energy whose gravity is repulsive, driving accelerated expansion (Ch 9).

Denial of death — Becker's thesis that mortality awareness drives literal and symbolic immortality systems (Ch 1, 7, 8).

Dissipative adaptation — England's proposal that driven particle collections spontaneously reconfigure to absorb and dissipate energy more efficiently (Ch 4).

Dissipative structures — Prigogine's configurations that spontaneously order under sustained energy flow (Ch 4).

Eliminativism — The position that consciousness is an illusion; idealism is its mirror (Ch 5).

Emergence — The appearance of genuinely new descriptive levels — entropy, life, mind — from coordinated simple constituents (Ch 5).

Empire State Building timeline — Cosmic time mapped onto floors, where floor n = 10^n years since the big bang (Ch 9, 10, 11).

Entropic two-step — Any process in which a system's entropy decreases because it exports a more than compensating increase to its environment (Ch 2, 3, 4, 9).

Entropy — A count of how many microscopic rearrangements yield the same macroscopic configuration; high = common, low = special (Ch 2, 3).

Erasure cost — Computation can be heat-free, but erasing memory necessarily produces waste heat — new thoughts, not thoughts per se, cost entropy (Ch 9).

Event horizon — A black hole's boundary of no return, radius proportional to mass (Ch 10).

Fitness indicator — A display whose expense certifies the quality it advertises (Ch 8).

FOXP2 — Gene implicated in speech and grammar; identical in Neanderthals (Ch 6).

Free will vs. human freedom — Volitional intercession in physical law (rejected) vs. an emancipated range of response (affirmed) (Ch 5, 11).

Hard problem of consciousness — Chalmers' question of why physical processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all (Ch 5).

Hawking radiation — Particles emitted at a horizon when quantum-fluctuation pairs are split, causing the hole to lose mass (Ch 10).

Higgs field — Space-filling field (value 246) giving particles mass; possibly metastable (Ch 10).

Hyperactive agency detection — Evolved bias toward over-attributing agency; cheap false positives beat costly false negatives (Ch 6, 7).

Inflaton field — The "cosmic fuel" whose uniform energy produces repulsive gravity (Ch 3).

Integrated information theory (IIT) — Tononi and Koch's proposal that consciousness is highly integrated, highly differentiated information, quantified by ф (Ch 5).

Macrostate — The set of microscopic configurations sharing the same macroscopic properties; entropy counts its members (Ch 2).

Meaning as created, not found — Greene's conclusion that value and purpose are invented inside subjective worlds, constrained but not dictated by evolved predispositions (Ch 11).

Milkomeda — The merged Milky Way–Andromeda galaxy (Ch 9).

Minimally counterintuitive concept — An idea violating one or two intuitive expectations, making it memorable and transmissible (Ch 6, 7).

Molecular Darwinism — Natural selection operating on replicating molecules before life exists (Ch 1, 4).

Monomyth — Campbell's template: call, perilous adventure, return transformed (Ch 6).

Multiverse — If space is infinite, a patchwork of ~90-billion-light-year regions in which every history recurs infinitely often (Ch 10).

Negative entropy — Schrödinger's term for the low-entropy structure organisms ingest to hold their own entropy down (Ch 4).

Nested stories (reductionism without eliminativism) — Multiple level-specific accounts of one reality; consistency across levels is required, replacement is not possible (Ch 1, 4, 5).

Past hypothesis — The postulate that the universe began in an extraordinarily low-entropy state (Ch 2, 3).

Panpsychism / proto-consciousness — Chalmers' revival of an irreducible primitive subjective quality in matter (Ch 5).

Physicalism — The view that conscious experience will be fully explained by physical properties and existing physical law (Ch 5).

Proton decay — Predicted disintegration of protons; not yet observed, lower bound ~10^34 years (Ch 9).

Proximate vs. ultimate explanation — "It feels wonderful" answers the immediate impetus only, not the evolutionary origin (Ch 8).

Qualia — The subjective felt characters of experience (Ch 5).

Redox reaction — Electron transfer; life's universal slow burn, staged in small steps (Ch 4).

Repulsive gravity — Outward-pushing gravity arising when energy is spread uniformly rather than clumped (Ch 3, 9).

RNA world — Hypothesis exploiting RNA's dual role as software and hardware to bypass the origin-of-life chicken-and-egg (Ch 4).

Sacred, the — The status conferred on certain stories and rules that elevates them above all others (Ch 7).

Scheffler's afterlife scenario — Thought experiment removing descendants rather than yourself, isolating what anchors value (Ch 11).

Second law of thermodynamics — Total entropy of a system plus its environment overwhelmingly likely to increase (Ch 2, 3).

SPONCH — Sulfur, phosphorus, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon, hydrogen — the atoms dominating all known life (Ch 4).

Story as flight simulator — Oatley's refinement of Pinker: fiction as safe, cheap rehearsal that refines intuition (Ch 6).

Sublime, the — Experience so enveloping it feels like stepping beyond time (Ch 8).

Substrate independence of mind — Treating life and mind as processes rather than as cells and brains (Ch 9).

Symbolic immortality — Rank's displacement of the urge for eternity onto self-authored works (Ch 1, 8).

Terror management theory — Mortality salience covertly amplifies defense of one's cultural worldview (Ch 7).

Theory of mind — Attribution of beliefs, desires, and intentions to other agents and to oneself (Ch 5, 6, 7).

Universal grammar — Chomsky's innate neurobiological language primer (Ch 6).

Vacuum decay — Higgs tunneling to a new value, spreading near light speed and rewriting physics inside the bubble (Ch 10).

Worm at the core — James's term for tamped-down awareness of one's own ending underlying ordinary delight (Ch 1).

patterns.md

Patterns — Reasoning Moves from Until the End of Time

Greene offers explanatory methods, not procedures. Each pattern below is a reasoning move: a way of setting up a question so the physics, biology, or philosophy can answer it.

Entropic Two-Step Reasoning

When to use: Any time order appears where the second law seems to forbid it — a star forming, a cell metabolizing, a brain thinking, a civilization building.

How: (1) Identify the local entropy decrease (the structure that got built). (2) Find the energy flow that paid for it. (3) Locate the waste sink — where the more-than-compensating entropy was dumped (heat, radiation, excreta, expanding space). (4) Confirm the total went up. If you cannot name the sink, your accounting is wrong, not the second law.

Trade-offs: Powerful and universal, but it explains permission, not cause — knowing a structure is entropically affordable does not tell you why this structure rather than another. Pair it with a selection argument. Also: it only works if a sink actually exists; in the far future (Ch 9) or inside a black hole (Ch 10) the sink is the binding constraint.

Choosing a Level of Description (Nested Stories)

When to use: When someone claims one level of explanation is the real one — "it's all just particles," or conversely "you can't reduce this."

How: (1) Identify which layer the question actually lives on (particle, chemical, biological, neural, mental, cultural). (2) Answer in that layer's own vocabulary and grammar. (3) Check the answer is consistent with the layers beneath, not replaceable by them. (4) Keep the linkages explicit — Cervantes's neurons and Don Quixote's yearning are connected but not interchangeable.

Trade-offs: This is reductionism without eliminativism, and it costs you a unified theory of everything-that-matters. The discipline is refusing both moves: no dismissing a higher story as "just" lower-level activity, and no exempting a higher story from physical constraint.

Evaluating an Adaptationist vs. Byproduct Claim

When to use: Any assertion that a human behavior — storytelling, art, music, religion — "evolved because it does X."

How: (1) State the proposed adaptive benefit precisely. (2) Ask the byproduct question first: could this be a package-deal consequence of something else already selected for (theory of mind, agency detection, pattern sensitivity, pleasure circuits)? (3) Apply the "just so" story test — does the account make any prediction that could fail? (4) Separate proximate from ultimate explanation: "we do it because it feels wonderful" answers only the immediate impetus. (5) Accept that the debate may stay open, and check whether your downstream conclusion actually depends on which side wins.

Trade-offs: Byproduct explanations are cheap to generate and hard to falsify, so the test cuts both ways. Greene's own practice in Ch 11 is instructive: he leaves the origin question unresolved and rests his conclusion on the observed function — a longing to be part of something larger — which holds under either account.

Reasoning About Far-Future Timescales

When to use: Any claim about the fate of stars, life, mind, or civilization beyond a few million years.

How: (1) Convert everything to the Empire State timeline — floor n = 10^n years. (2) Predict in broad strokes, not fine detail: commit to structural claims (stars burn out, protons may decay, black holes evaporate), refuse detail-level extrapolation of technology or civilization. (3) Replace "likely vs. unlikely" with waiting time vs. horizon — over unbounded time, probability × duration is what matters, so no nonzero-probability process may be discarded. (4) Ask the thinker question for any proposed future mind: can it still expel the waste heat that new thought requires?

Trade-offs: The method's honesty is its limitation — it yields a skeleton, not a scenario. It also resurrects self-undermining conclusions (Boltzmann brains); treat self-undermining as evidence the model is incomplete rather than as a result to accept.

Testing What Anchors Value (The Doomsday Move)

When to use: When you need to know whether a commitment rests on personal continuation or on humanity's continuation.

How: (1) Imagine a terminal prognosis for yourself; note the reaction (typically: heightened intensity, significance conferred on ordinary moments). (2) Now use Scheffler's variant — thirty days after your natural death, everyone remaining is obliterated — which excises your own premature mortality. (3) Re-ask activity by activity: would I still do the research, finish the book, send the kids to school? (4) Whatever survives step 3 is intrinsically motivated; whatever collapses was resting on descendants.

Trade-offs: Responses genuinely differ (Frankfurt thinks art and science survive; Greene thinks they don't), so the exercise reveals your own structure of value rather than a universal fact. Use imminence only as artificial urgency to catalyze an authentic response — the intuition then transfers to the far future, since long and short have no absolute meaning.

Calibrating Belief Instead of Declaring It

When to use: Contested claims where "do you believe X?" invites tribal rather than evidential answers.

How: Replace the yes/no with "what is my calibrated confidence, given the evidence, and what would update it?" Then check the register: a claim read literally and contradicting established science is simply false; the same claim read as poetry, symbol, archive, or community practice remains inside rational discourse — a belief in the value of the content rather than its veridicality.

Trade-offs: The register move can be used dishonestly, to retreat from a falsified literal claim while keeping its rhetorical force. Name which register you are in before arguing.

Diagnosing Low Entropy as Evidence

When to use: On encountering any strikingly ordered configuration — biological, cosmological, or social.

How: Treat low entropy as evidence of an organizing influence, not of luck; then find the influence (gravity, selection, an engineer, an energy gradient). Where entropy appears simply to vanish, look for the ledger entry (Bekenstein's answer to Wheeler: it went into horizon area).

Trade-offs: A statistical fluke is possible and, given enough time or enough regions, eventually mandatory — see the past hypothesis and the multiverse. The pattern tells you where to look first, not what you will find.

Keep Sharp: Build a Better Brain at Any Age

cheatsheet.md

Keep Sharp — Cheatsheet

The one-line thesis

Cognitive decline is NOT inevitable. Lifestyle > genes (>90% of longevity is in your hands). Build the brain with 5 pillars; motivate by running toward a sharp brain, not away from fear.

The 5 Pillars (memorize)

Move · Discover · Relax · Nourish · Connect

If you do only ONE thing: Move. Exercise is the only behavioral activity scientifically proven to help the brain.

Decision rules

When…Do…Because…
You can do only one brain-health thingExercise (break a sweat daily)Only proven behavioral intervention; boosts BDNF
Motivating behavior changeFrame as running toward a goalFear activates amygdala → intense but transient
Choosing a "brain game"Pick complex + novel + social learning you enjoyCrosswords flex only word-finding; games are over-hyped
Memory "fails" on namesFix attention (stop multitasking) or retrievalUsually not systemic failure — both are trainable
Deciding whether to napCap at 30 min, early afternoonLonger/later naps wreck night sleep
Tempted by a supplementBuy walking shoes or a pillow insteadNo supplement reliably prevents dementia; industry unregulated
Someone offers "gluten-free will help your brain"Ignore unless celiac/sensitivityNo evidence; low-gluten-low-whole-grain can raise heart risk
A relative gets a dementia diagnosisRule out mimics (NPH, meds, depression) firstMany "dementias" are treatable
Talking to someone with dementiaNever correct them; redirectForces impossible recall, causes distress
You're a caregiverPut yourself on your to-do listCaregivers are the "invisible second patient" (up to 6x risk)

Numbers & thresholds worth committing

MetricTarget
Exercise, minimum150 min/week; 30 min cardio × 5 days
Exercise, optimal longevity~450 min/week (~64 min/day, mostly walking)
Sitting break≥2 min every hour
Sleep7–8 hrs nightly (need is constant with age)
Caffeine cutoff2:00 p.m.
Last meal before bed~3 hours
Bedroom temp60–67°F
Warm light2700–3000K
Alcohol moderation≤2 drinks/day (men), ≤1 (women); prefer red wine
Colored foods/day7 different real-food colors
Purpose (ikigai) effect~20% lower future dementia risk
MIND diet adherence (top third)53% lower Alzheimer's risk (~7.5 yrs of aging)
Alzheimer's preclinical windowstarts 20–30 yrs before symptoms

S.H.A.R.P. eating (fast recall)

Slash sugar · Hydrate smartly (drink instead of eat) · Add omega-3s (from food) · Reduce portions · Plan ahead

Food ABCs

  • A (regularly): greens, berries, fish, healthy fats (EVOO/avocado/eggs), nuts/seeds
  • B (include): beans, whole fruits, low-fat dairy, poultry, whole grains
  • C (limit): fried, sweets, processed, red meat, high-fat dairy, salt

Tells & smells (recognize the situation)

  • "Sitting is the new smoking" → prolonged sitting (>8 hr) harms metabolically even if you're lean.
  • Sleep as a badge of honor → red flag; no data links success to less sleep; you can't "game" the body clock.
  • Excessive daytime napping → possible early Alzheimer's sign (tau in wakefulness centers).
  • Long-term anticholinergics (Benadryl, "PM" meds) → 54% higher dementia risk at 3+ years.
  • Amyloid-riddled brain, no symptoms → cognitive reserve at work; goal = "asymptomatic Alzheimer's."
  • Loneliness → treat as a vital sign; social pain = physical pain in the brain.

Daily productivity/rest toolkit (from Ch6)

  • Pomodoro: 25 min focus / 5 min break.
  • Don't multitask — single-task "like a surgeon"; guard mornings for creative work; no email first thing.
  • Marbles before sand: schedule big commitments first.
  • Gratitude journal + 15 min/day for yourself + daydream (neural reset).
  • Analytical meditation / deep breathing (exhale to count of 20) to lower cortisol.

12-week program in one line

Add one habit per pillar per week; never restart — accumulate. Get a baseline checkup, re-check at week 12. Set nonnegotiables. "Progress is better than perfection."

glossary.md

Glossary — Keep Sharp

ABCs of food — GCBH framework: A-list (eat regularly), B-list (include), C-list (limit) foods (Ch7).

ABCs of prevention (Isaacson) — Anthropometrics, Biomarkers, Cognitive performance; reassessed every 6 months (Ch7, Ch10).

Advance directive — Legal document stating treatment/end-of-life wishes; includes living will and durable power of attorney for health care (Ch11).

Alzheimer's disease — Most common dementia (>half of cases); hallmarks are amyloid plaques and tau tangles (Ch2, Ch10).

Amyloid (beta-amyloid) — Sticky protein plaques that accumulate between neurons; healthy in normal form, harmful when misfolded (Ch2).

Amyloid Cascade Hypothesis (ACH) — Theory that plaque accumulation causes Alzheimer's; repeatedly failed in drug trials (Ch2).

Analytical meditation — Placing a problem in a mental "bubble" to isolate it from emotion and find clarity; taught by the Dalai Lama (Ch6).

Anticholinergics — Drugs blocking acetylcholine (Benadryl, some antidepressants); 3+ years' use linked to 54% higher dementia risk (Ch6, Ch10).

APOE gene — Risk gene with alleles E2 (protective), E3 (neutral), E4 (raises risk); not deterministic (Ch2, Ch10).

BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) — "Miracle-Gro for the brain"; boosted by exercise, sleep, stress reduction, sunlight, fasting (Ch3, Ch7).

Blood-brain barrier — Semipermeable wall protecting the brain; when leaky, toxins enter and worsen decline (Ch2).

Blue Zone — Region with unusually long-lived people (e.g., Okinawa) (Ch8).

Chrono eating — Eating aligned to daylight/circadian rhythm; frontloading calories (Ch7, Ch9).

Circadian rhythm — ~24-hr cycle governing sleep-wake, hormones, temperature (Ch6).

Cognitive reserve (brain resiliency) — The brain's ability to improvise around damage via built-up networks; from education, work, lifelong learning (Ch2, Ch5).

Conservatorship / guardianship — Court-appointed control when families can't agree; costly and abuse-prone (Ch11).

Cortisol — Stress hormone; chronic excess shrinks the hippocampus (Ch4, Ch6).

CTE (chronic traumatic encephalopathy) — Degenerative disease from repeated head blows; linked to tau (Ch2).

Dementia — Group of symptoms (memory loss, poor judgment), not one disease; spectrum from mild to severe; some causes reversible (Ch0, Ch10).

Dendrite — Branched extension of a neuron that receives signals; grows with novelty, entrenches with repetition (Ch1).

Dirty Dozen (myths) — The 12 destructive myths about the aging brain (Ch3).

Encoding — First memory phase: perception → hippocampus; requires attention (Ch1).

Entourage effect — Nutrients work best within whole food, not isolated supplements (Ch7).

Flow — State of total, energized immersion in an activity; requires purpose (Csikszentmihalyi) (Ch5).

Ghrelin / leptin — Appetite hormones (hunger / satiety); disrupted by poor sleep (Ch6).

Glymphatic system — The brain's self-cleaning drainage; runs in overdrive during sleep, clears amyloid (Ch6).

Hippocampus — Seahorse-shaped memory center; integrates sensory input; shrinks with stress/decline (Ch1).

Hogeweyk — Dutch "dementia village"; person-centered care model (Ch11).

Ikigai — Japanese "reason for being"; sense of purpose (Ch5).

Inflammation — Common thread across all brain-decline theories and most illness (Ch2).

Intermittent fasting — Limiting eating windows (12–16 hr); boosts BDNF and insulin sensitivity (Ch7, Ch9).

Invisible second patient — The caregiver, up to 6x more likely to develop dementia (Ch11).

KAER process — Gerontological Society four-step tool for detecting cognitive impairment (Ch10).

MCI (mild cognitive impairment) — Often a precursor to dementia; sometimes reversible (Ch4, Ch10).

MIND diet — Mediterranean–DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay; up to 53% lower Alzheimer's risk (Ch7).

Moai — Okinawan lifelong social support group (Ch8).

Neurogenesis — Birth of new neurons throughout life (proven 1998) (Ch1, Ch3).

Neuroplasticity — The brain's ability to rewire and reorganize connections; a two-way street (Ch1).

Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) — Treatable dementia mimic; CSF buildup fixed with a shunt (Ch10).

Omega-3 fatty acids — Brain-nourishing fats (DHA, EPA, ALA); get from food, not supplements (Ch7).

Pomodoro technique — 25 min focused work + 5 min break; dopamine-reward productivity method (Ch6).

Preclinical time — 20–30 year window between brain changes and symptoms; prime intervention period (Ch10).

Prions — Proteins that trigger others (amyloid, tau) to misfold; universally fatal diseases (Ch2).

Pseudodementia — Dementia-like symptoms from severe depression; reversible when treated (Ch10).

Retrieval — Final memory phase: pulling info into conscious awareness (Ch1).

S.H.A.R.P. — Slash sugar, Hydrate smartly, Add omega-3s, Reduce portions, Plan ahead (Ch7).

Sleep spindles — Deep-sleep activity bursts moving memories from hippocampus to neocortex (Ch6).

Sundowning — Late-day confusion/agitation in ~20% of dementia patients (Ch11).

SuperAgers — 80+ people with memories as sharp as those decades younger (Ch3).

Synapse — Gap where neurons connect via neurotransmitters; strengthens with use (Ch1).

Tau / neurofibrillary tangles — Protein "railroad tracks" inside cells; knot up when damaged ("the bullet") (Ch2).

Triple threat (Gary Small) — Walk + friend + honest conversation (Ch8).

Type 3 diabetes — Nickname for Alzheimer's as an insulin-resistance disease of the brain (Ch2, Ch7).

VO2 max — Aerobic-fitness measure; higher fitness → healthier white matter → better cognition (Ch4).

White matter — Nerve-fiber bundles connecting gray-matter regions; health signals inter-region communication (Ch4).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Keep Sharp

The 5 Pillars (master framework)

When to use: any brain-health plan; the backbone of the whole book.

How: Move · Discover · Relax · Nourish · Connect. One chapter each (Ch4–8), assembled in the 12-week program (Ch9).

Trade-offs: Move has the strongest evidence; the others are synergistic and reinforce each other.

Exercise Prescription (Pillar: Move)

When to use: building or upgrading a fitness routine.

How: ≥150 min/week; 30 min cardio × 5 days (heart rate ≥50% above resting for ≥20 min); add interval + strength training; optimal-longevity dose ~450 min/week (much can be brisk walking). Sedentary start: 5–10 min burst (30 sec effort / 90 sec recovery) → 20 min × 3/week.

Trade-offs: weightlifting alone is insufficient — you must go aerobic. Break up sitting every hour (2-min moves).

S.H.A.R.P. Eating (Pillar: Nourish)

When to use: designing brain-healthy meals.

How: Slash sugar (+ ABCs of food) · Hydrate smartly (drink instead of eat) · Add omega-3s from food · Reduce portions (cook at home, smaller plates) · Plan ahead (avoid starving → junk).

Trade-offs: a style, not a rigid diet; moderation beats elimination of whole food groups.

The ABCs of Food

When to use: quick food triage at the store or on a menu.

How: A-list (regularly): leafy greens, berries, fish, healthy fats, nuts/seeds. B-list (include): beans, whole fruits, low-fat dairy, poultry, whole grains. C-list (limit): fried food, sweets, processed food, red meat, high-fat dairy, salt.

Memory Diagnosis: Encode → Store → Retrieve

When to use: figuring out why memory fails and where to fix it.

How: Encoding needs attention (stop multitasking); storage needs sleep + no alcohol for short→long transfer; retrieval is trainable. "Bad memory" for names is usually attention or retrieval, not systemic failure.

Analytical Meditation (Pillar: Relax)

When to use: solving a nagging problem; building focus; daily rest.

How: eyes closed, place the problem in a large clear bubble in front of you; rotate/flip it; let it disentangle from emotion until the answer illuminates. First 2 min are hardest, then flow.

Trade-offs: different from single-point meditation; better for problem-solvers/skeptics.

Deep Breathing / Relaxation Response

When to use: fast stress relief anywhere.

How: sit relaxed, inhale through nose filling the diaphragm, take in a bit more at the top, exhale slowly to a count of 20; ≥5 rounds. Triggers parasympathetic response, lowers cortisol.

Pomodoro Technique (productivity)

When to use: focused work, beating procrastination.

How: pick your most important task, 25 min no-distraction work, 5 min break (dopamine reward), repeat.

Don't Multitask — "Tackle Your Day Like a Surgeon"

When to use: any cognitively demanding work.

How: the brain only switches attention, it doesn't parallel-process. Single-task in focused sequences; guard mornings ("golden time") for creative work; avoid email first thing.

Marbles-and-Sand Planning

When to use: weekly/daily prioritization.

How: put the marbles (big commitments — exercise, sleep, key tasks) in the jar first; let sand (email, nonurgent items) fill gaps. Sunday-night check-in: "What must I accomplish this week to call it a success?"

The Triple Threat (Pillar: Connect)

When to use: combining social + physical + emotional benefit in one act.

How: take a walk + with a friend/neighbor + talk through what worries you. Add appropriate touch (hand-holding lowers cortisol).

Social Engagement + Challenge

When to use: maximizing the brain benefit of socializing.

How: socialize around a challenging shared activity (class, quilting, photography), not passive chit-chat; keep a large, cross-age network and ≥1 reliable confidante.

Cognitive Reserve Building (Pillar: Discover)

When to use: choosing genuinely brain-building activities.

How: pick complex + novel + effortful + ideally social learning you enjoy (language, instrument, real class). Avoid crosswords-only and hyped "brain games." Define your ikigai; seek flow.

Intermittent Fasting / Chrono Eating

When to use: reducing calories, boosting BDNF and insulin sensitivity (with doctor's OK).

How: gentle 12-hr overnight fast (stop 7–8 p.m., resume 9–10 a.m.); 16-hr version skips breakfast. Frontload calories: "breakfast like a king, dinner like a peasant."

Trade-offs: not for everyone (esp. diabetics — consult doctor).

Sleep Hygiene (Top 10 Secrets, Pillar: Relax)

When to use: fixing poor sleep.

How: fixed wake time; sleep before midnight; morning light; no caffeine after 2 p.m.; no food 3 hrs pre-bed; cool/dark/quiet (60–67°F); no screens/blue light; 30–60 min calming ritual; know the warning signs → sleep study.

Rule out Dementia Mimics

When to use: before accepting a dementia diagnosis.

How: evaluate NPH (treatable with shunt), medications (anticholinergics, opioids, benzos, steroids), and depression (pseudodementia). Tell the doctor every drug/supplement.

Post-Diagnosis Planning Checklist (caregivers)

When to use: immediately after a dementia diagnosis.

How: line up support/education programs, early-stage engagement, clinical trials, home safety, legal plan (will/trust/POA/advance directive), financial plan, and a care team. Communicate with family early to avoid conservatorship.

The Cardinal Caregiving Rule

When to use: interacting with someone who has dementia.

How: never correct them. Early phase: gently guide with questions. Later: don't deny their reality; redirect. Use music (longest-surviving faculty) and touch; break repetition with an activity. Put yourself on your own to-do list.

HBR's 10 Must Reads on Communication
