cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Decision Rules

First branch: what kind of communication problem is this?

  • You need one person to say yes → Ch 1 (classify their decision style) + Ch 4 (audit your credibility first)
  • You need many people to change behavior → Ch 2 (six principles) + Ch 7 (springboard story)
  • People are not saying what they think → Ch 5 (spiral of silence) + Ch 3 (linguistic style, not competence)
  • You have to stand up and deliver → Ch 6 (rehearse intent) + Ch 9 (the five messages)
  • The conversation itself is the hard part → Ch 10 (three stressful types)
  • You are selling a creative idea → Ch 8 (pitcher types)

Decision styles: how to argue (Ch 1)

Style% of execsLead withNeverLatency
Follower36%Precedent, proven-elsewhere casesNovelty framed as untestedDays
Charismatic25%The exciting result, then risks you name yourselfOversellingFast, then verifies
Skeptic19%Credibility borrowed from someone they trustContradicting them publiclyDays or on the spot
Thinker11%Methodology and alternatives consideredJumping to conclusionsWeeks–months, 2 meetings
Controller9%Structured linear memos, problem dataRequesting the meeting yourselfMonths; wait for a trigger
  • If you cannot classify them, they are a follower — the other four announce themselves.
  • ~80% of presentations are pitched at skeptics and controllers, who are 28% of executives. Assume your default is wrong.
  • Sequence to a thinker is roughly the reverse of the sequence to a charismatic.

Cialdini: which principle fits (Ch 2)

SituationPrincipleMove
New relationship, no historyLikingSurface a genuine similarity; give real praise
You want future helpReciprocityGive first, visibly and without a ledger
Peers resist a changeSocial proofLet a respected peer speak, not the boss
Behavior must persist unsupervisedConsistencyActive + public + voluntary written commitment
Audience does not know youAuthorityMake real credentials visible before influencing
Information favors acting nowScarcityExclusive and loss-framed, only if true
  • Never on a false premise. Detection kills the offer and reciprocity returns the dishonesty.
  • Combine principles in one interaction; do not deploy them serially.

Conger: order of operations (Ch 4)

1. Credibility — if absent, stop and buy it. Steps 2–4 are futile without it.

2. Common ground — if no shared advantage exists, change the position, not the framing.

3. Vivid evidence — data alone does not move people; supplement with story, metaphor, analogy.

4. Emotional connection — match their state, not yours. End on hope, not doom.

Four ways not to persuade: hard sell up front; refuse to compromise; rely on argument alone; treat it as an event rather than a process. Enter with concessions already prepared.

Story selection (Ch 7)

GoalDetailToneForm
Spark actionMinimal — secondsPositive + evidencedSpringboard
Communicate who you areRichEitherFull narrative, told in person
Transmit valuesRich, believableEitherOnly works if you live it
Foster collaborationMoving, sharedEitherThen open the floor
Tame the grapevineEnough to expose incongruityHumorOnly if the rumor is false
Share knowledgeDetailed on the fixNegativeProblem/fix, no hero
Lead into the futureVague on specificsPositiveNever predict particulars
  • Goal is action → subtract detail. Goal is trust → add detail.
  • Rumor true or plausible? Do not ridicule — admit, reframe, move on. Denying gives it credibility.

Pitching: is your type working for you? (Ch 8)

  • Categorization happens in under 150 ms; character judgment inside 30 minutes.
  • ~1% of ideas survive the initial pitch; ~25% of pitchers avoid fast elimination.
  • Negative cues outweigh positive ones → eliminate pushover / robot / used-car salesman / charity case before optimizing anything else.
  • Have a track record? Lead with it and skip type-play entirely. Do not fake the artist — genuineness is the credibility.
  • Catcher's rule: if you feel swept away by a positive type match, start testing — showrunners are the favorite and the most dangerous.

Silence: speak or stay quiet? (Ch 5)

Invert the default. Ask "is this one of the rare times to stay quiet?" Stay quiet only if:

  • the issue is forgettable within a week or a month, or
  • the relationship is short-lived and unimportant.

Defer (with a stated time) when emotions are hot or a deadline is imminent — indefinite postponement guarantees the difference returns. Never resolve conflict by dividing the work. Tell: chronic gossip about someone you have never confronted means you are already in a spiral.

Stressful conversations (Ch 10)

TypeGambitOpening line shape
"I have bad news for you"Honor thy partnerAcknowledge your own share, then state the news plainly
"What's going on here?"Disarm by restating intentions"I can see how you took it that way. That wasn't what I meant."
"You are attacking me!"Fight tactics, not peopleName the behavior's effect, not their character
  • The opening determines the conversation. Never ease into bad news with small talk.
  • Clarity is not brutality: content is not brutal, delivery is. Default tone is neutral.
  • If it is not an emergency, split it — raise in meeting one, discuss in meeting two.
  • Improvement is unilateral: prepare against your predictable vulnerability, not their unpredictable behavior.

Leader's defaults (Ch 9)

  • Announce reorgs whole and fast; never preview (HP's preview cost ~a full quarter).
  • Cap each direct report at 3 initiatives per quarter. The enemy is starting the 85th thing.
  • Withhold your own theory in problem-solving meetings — the boss's answer stifles the room.
  • Define winning numerically, not adjectivally.
  • Treat missed results as a diagnostic, never as a blame trigger.

Cross-cutting tells

  • "Poor communication" → assume differing linguistic styles until shown otherwise (Ch 3).
  • Confidence judged from speech is unreliable — public claims diverge from private ones (Ch 3).
  • Rehearsed gestures lagging the words is what audiences read as fake (Ch 6).
  • There is no one best way to communicate — outcome depends on situation, culture, relative rank, and the interaction of two styles.

glossary.md

Glossary

84 Great Things — 7 direct reports x 3 doable initiatives per quarter x 4 quarters; the yearly output cap that keeps a team from over-starting (Ch 9)

Answer man trap — a leader whose identity rests on having the answer, which suppresses everyone else's thinking (Ch 9)

Antistory — the cynical counter-narrative an audience invents when a story sounds implausibly rosy (Ch 7)

Artist — pitcher type who inverts the power differential by commanding the catcher's imagination with thought experiments (Ch 8)

Authority — Cialdini principle: people defer to visible, genuine expertise as a shortcut through complexity (Ch 2)

Buffered feedback — praise-then-criticism ritual; literal listeners hear only the praise (Ch 3)

Buzzwords — style-specific vocabulary that holds a particular decision maker's attention (Ch 1)

Catcher — the executive who judges a pitch; judges the pitcher's creativity, not only the idea (Ch 8)

Charismatic — decision style: exuberant, visual, risk-seeking, short attention span; decides on balanced information (Ch 1)

Clarification technique — grant the other person's perception, own the words/intent mismatch, resume the substance (Ch 10)

Coalition-building — testing a concern with one savvy peer before voicing it upward (Ch 5)

Commitment (active, public, voluntary) — the three-part test a commitment must pass to bind future behavior (Ch 2)

Common ground framing — stating a position in terms of tangible benefit to the audience; if none exists, change the position (Ch 4)

Consistency — Cialdini principle: people align with commitments they have gone on record for (Ch 2)

Controller — decision style: abhors ambiguity, implements only his own ideas, avoids accountability (Ch 1)

Conversational rituals — conventionalized exchanges (ritual apology, ritual opposition, compliment exchange) that break when taken literally (Ch 3)

Creative collaborator — the catcher recast as co-author of the idea, which sharply lowers rejection odds (Ch 8)

Credibility (expertise + relationships) — Conger's two sources; the prerequisite to any persuasion attempt (Ch 4)

Credibility transfer — borrowing trust by having someone the audience already trusts deliver the message (Ch 1, Ch 4)

Danger zone — a conversation or counterpart you already know you handle badly (Ch 10)

Default mode of decision making — the style a person reverts to under complexity and consequence (Ch 1)

Definitional control — claiming a loaded term's meaning before rumor supplies one (Ch 9)

Deviant act — deliberately violating a silencing norm, e.g. asking the hard question nobody asks (Ch 5)

Emotional matchmaking — tuning emotional intensity to the audience's current state, not your own (Ch 4)

Five Messages Leaders Must Manage — hierarchy, financial results, the leader's job, time management, culture (Ch 9)

Follower — decision style: largest group, risk-averse, decides by precedent; wants innovative-yet-proven (Ch 1)

Four Aims / intents — Morgan's rehearsal targets: be open, connect, be passionate, listen (Ch 6)

Four Essential Steps of Persuasion — establish credibility, frame on common ground, reinforce with vivid evidence, connect emotionally (Ch 4)

Grapevine — the informal river of organizational communication; steer it rather than dam it (Ch 7)

Hip-pocket phrases — pre-rehearsed lines you can recall under pressure (Ch 10)

Honor thy partner — opening a bad-news conversation by acknowledging your own share of the problem (Ch 10)

Indirectness — meaning without spelling it out; used by the powerful as softened orders as much as by subordinates (Ch 3)

Knowledge duet — the showrunner's give-and-take of shared references before landing the idea (Ch 8)

Knowledge-sharing narrative — plotless, heroless, negative-toned problem/fix account; the workhorse story (Ch 7)

Liking — Cialdini principle: people comply with those similar to them and who like them (Ch 2)

Linguistic style — a person's characteristic speaking pattern: directness, pacing, pausing, jokes, questions, apologies (Ch 3)

Loss language — framing around what is forfeited by inaction rather than gained by action (Ch 2)

Maximalist account — the fully rendered story; engrossing but action-suppressing (Ch 7)

Mental opt-out — comply while contributing nothing; the terminal state of a silence spiral (Ch 5)

Neophyte — pitcher type who exploits the power differential by asking boldly for help (Ch 8)

Person prototypes — stereotype sets used to categorize a stranger in under a second (Ch 8)

Persuasion as learning and negotiating — an iterative move toward a shared solution, not a one-shot convincing (Ch 4)

Practical intelligence — feel for which ideas will actually work commercially; the showrunner's edge (Ch 8)

Reciprocity — Cialdini principle: people repay in kind; give first what you want to receive (Ch 2)

Red zone — a thwarting tactic paired with your own known vulnerability (Ch 10)

Results as diagnostic — treating a missed number as a root-cause investigation, not a punishment trigger (Ch 9)

Ritual apology — "I'm sorry" as expressed concern rather than admitted fault (Ch 3)

Ritual opposition — testing ideas through verbal combat; over when it's over (Ch 3)

Scarcity — Cialdini principle: people want more of what is less available; exclusive information outperforms common information (Ch 2)

Second conversation — the nonverbal channel, which fires before words and wins whenever the two conflict (Ch 6)

Showrunner — pitcher type who levels the power differential with a knowledge duet; the catcher's favorite and most dangerous type (Ch 8)

Silencing — declining to confront a difference, in yourself or in others (Ch 5)

Skeptic — decision style: combative, suspicious of anything challenging his worldview; decides fast on gut (Ch 1)

Social proof — Cialdini principle: people follow similar others, not distant strangers (Ch 2)

Speed trap — deadline pressure produces silencing, which produces worse decisions and more pressure (Ch 5)

Spiral of silence — silence, resentment, disconnection, self-protection, more fear, more silence (Ch 5)

Splitting the conversation — raising an issue in one meeting and discussing it in a later one (Ch 10)

Springboard story — minimal-detail, true, recent story with one protagonist that makes listeners leap to "why not here?" (Ch 7)

Status/rapport dynamic — every utterance both conveys ideas and negotiates relative position (Ch 3)

Substitute credibility — credibility borrowed from consultants, independent research, pilots, or allies (Ch 4)

Thinker — decision style: cerebral, risk-averse, data-hungry; slowest and toughest to persuade (Ch 1)

Thought experiment — the artist's invitation into an imagined world (Ch 6, Ch 8)

Thwarting tactics — shouting, accusation, distortion, digression, manipulation used to derail a conversation (Ch 10)

Vivid evidence — stories, metaphors, and analogies that make data land emotionally (Ch 4)

patterns.md

Patterns

Concrete techniques from across the ten articles.

Style-Matched Persuasion (Ch 1)

When to use: You have one identifiable chief decision maker and a proposal that has already failed on merit alone.

How: Classify the person (charismatic, thinker, skeptic, follower, controller). Keep the content constant; change sequence, format, pacing, and vocabulary. Charismatic: lead with the exciting result, then undersell by naming each risk yourself. Thinker: lead with methodology and alternatives considered, reserve two meetings. Skeptic: establish credibility before you open your mouth. Follower: show precedent and a proven track record. Controller: send structured linear memos, never request the meeting.

Trade-offs: Misclassification costs you the proposal. If a person resists classification, treat them as a follower.

Credibility Audit (Ch 4)

When to use: Before beginning any persuasion effort, especially with a new audience.

How: Ask two expertise questions (do I have a track record here, does the audience know it) and two relationship questions (do they see me as helpful and trustworthy, will they listen). Validate the answers with a colleague who will be honest. Where either is thin, buy it: hire an outside expert, cite independent research, run a visible pilot, or recruit a trusted sponsor.

Trade-offs: Slow and ego-bruising. Most managers considerably overestimate both scores.

Listening Tour Before Framing (Ch 4)

When to use: You need a position that carries real shared advantage, not a rationalized version of your own.

How: One-on-one conversations with key stakeholders to gather perspective, explicitly not to pitch. Then frame the position in terms of the benefit they named. If no shared advantage exists, change the position.

Trade-offs: Months of calendar time. Frequently reveals that your original proposal was wrong.

Active, Public, Voluntary Commitment (Ch 2)

When to use: You need behavior to persist without supervision.

How: Have the person summarize the agreement in their own words in writing, circulate it, and connect it to a value they already hold. Applied pressure voids the effect.

Trade-offs: Worthless if coerced. Coerced agreement is a burden, not a commitment.

Peer Testimony Over Boss Speech (Ch 2)

When to use: Veterans resist a new initiative and your positional authority is the wrong lever.

How: Find a respected long-tenured colleague who genuinely supports the change and have them raise it at the team meeting.

Trade-offs: You surrender control of the framing.

Structure the Meeting, Not the Person (Ch 3)

When to use: Capable people are consistently silent in mixed or hierarchical groups.

How: Control turn-taking, recognize speakers explicitly, do not reward whoever needs the shortest pause. Track who originated each adopted idea separately from who spoke longest.

Trade-offs: Less spontaneous, slower. But telling individuals to change their style asks them to change who they are.

Ritual Test Before Attribution (Ch 3)

When to use: Someone's behavior seems inexplicable — a fight that evaporates, an apology with no fault attached.

How: Ask "is this literal or is this a form?" and interpret it in the speaker's system before assigning motive.

Trade-offs: Risks over-excusing genuinely bad behavior.

Leader-Goes-First Debrief (Ch 5)

When to use: After a visible failure, to break a spiral of silence.

How: The authority figure names their own specific contribution to the failure before asking anyone else. Then redirect what surfaces from individual blame to systemic cause.

Trade-offs: Requires real vulnerability from the person with power; hollow versions backfire badly.

Rehearse Intent, Never Gestures (Ch 6)

When to use: Preparing any high-stakes talk.

How: Four separate rehearsal passes, one per intent — be open (imagine speaking to a close friend), connect (imagine a distracted child, then a teenager), be passionate (ask what is at stake and what result you want), listen (predict the audience's emotional state, then adapt live).

Trade-offs: Rehearsed gestures lag the words, and audiences read that lag as fake. Live adaptation requires knowing the material cold.

Springboard Story (Ch 7)

When to use: Driving adoption of a change after data and slides have failed.

How: A true, recent event with one identifiable protagonist and an authentically happy ending. Strip detail aggressively — seconds, not minutes. Close with "imagine if we did this everywhere."

Trade-offs: Less memorable than a fully told story. Without evidence of the positive outcome, jaded audiences generate an antistory.

Negative-Polarity Knowledge Story (Ch 7)

When to use: Transferring hard-won know-how.

How: Lead with the mistake, explain in detail why the fix worked, invite better alternatives. Often has to be teased out by first asking about successes.

Trade-offs: Boring, narrow audience, and cannot be compelled.

Engineered Yield Point (Ch 8)

When to use: Any pitch to a decision maker.

How: Pre-identify one element you will genuinely concede, surface it as early as possible, and invite the catcher's suggestions so they become a creative collaborator.

Trade-offs: Yield readily on everything and you become the pushover stereotype.

Compressed Reorg Announcement (Ch 9)

When to use: Restructuring.

How: Announce whole and fast, never preview. Frame as business necessity, show the chart on the spot, state the scope of change, give a bounded window to react and a stated time when work resumes.

Trade-offs: No consultation period, so the framing must be right the first time. Previewing cost HP roughly a full quarter.

Clarification Technique (Ch 10)

When to use: You are blindsided by a charged reaction you cannot explain.

How: Grant their perception, own the mismatch between your words and your intent, then return to the substance. Concede nothing about the facts.

Trade-offs: Unsatisfying if what you wanted was vindication.

Fight Tactics, Not People (Ch 10)

When to use: Facing shouting, accusation, distortion, or digression.

How: Name the behavior without attacking character — describe the difficulty the tactic creates for you rather than labeling the person.

Trade-offs: Makes the tactic the topic, delaying the substantive issue.

Rehearse With a Neutral Friend (Ch 10)

When to use: Before any conversation in a known danger zone.

How: Dump the content raw, restate it as if unloaded, fine-tune phrasing into temperate substitutes, check body language, write down hip-pocket phrases.

Trade-offs: Time cost; over-memorized scripts sound stiff.

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Decision Rules

Should you speak at all?

  • No compelling central idea → decline the invitation. Delivery can be coached out; the story cannot be coached in (Ch 1).
  • Idea indicts the audience's intelligence, judgment, or morality → expect to lose regardless of technique. Proceed only if it matters enough to your company and your identity (Ch 7).
  • You can't or won't change behavior → don't apologize. It will sound hollow (Ch 8).

Choosing your delivery mode (Ch 1)

SituationDo this
High stakes + weeks of rehearsal timeMemorize verbatim — but only if you can get past the valley of awkwardness
Limited prep timeBullet points on note cards; focus on the transitions
Any amount of prepNever read from script or teleprompter
Forced to readAt minimum, look up and make eye contact

Which persuasion frame? (Ch 7)

FrameVerdict
Business benefitsSafest and strongest — quantify, and find a second department that benefits
Opportunity ("don't miss this")Strong — gives audience control, inspires optimism
Threat ("here's what we lose")Coin flip — may produce fight or flight
Moral ("this is wrong")Weakest — reads as judgment of character

Which motivating language, how much? (Ch 6)

  • Unfamiliar task or unknown opponent → direction giving dominant.
  • Underdog, high stakes, or shaken confidence → empathy + meaning making dominant.
  • Veterans mid-operation → mostly direction; they're all business.
  • Purpose self-evident (e.g. staff who lost loved ones to the disease you treat) → dial meaning making down; it's already there.
  • Default sequence: direction → meaning → empathy → recap.

Warmth/competence diagnosis (Ch 4)

Emotion you elicitYour positionFix
Envy (respect + resentment)Competent, coldLead with warmth; validate feelings; share something personal
Pity (compassion + neglect)Warm, incompetentFull-height posture, deliberate movement, stillness; demonstrate track record
ContemptNeitherRebuild both, warmth first
TrustHappy warriorMaintain; stay a member of the group, not "them"
  • Threshold: a strongly disliked manager's odds of being rated a good leader ≈ 1 in 2,000.
  • Rule: stand up straight and smile — the only move that raises strength without costing warmth.

Should you apologize, and how hard? (Ch 8)

1. Violation real or perceived? → perception counts; decide before the investigation finishes.

2. Core (strikes the mission) → maximum apology on every dimension. Noncore → flexibility.

3. Large/high-status org harming a low-power person → assume public outrage.

4. Committed to change? → if no, don't apologize; if yes, name the specific change.

DimensionCore violation setting
WhoCEO or most senior leader available
WhatCandor + remorse + concrete change
WhereHigh profile; consider the site itself
WhenImmediately; placeholder if facts pending
HowSpoken, plain, self-implicating

Which visualization work am I doing? (Ch 10)

ConceptualData-driven
DeclarativeIdea illustration → editing + designEveryday dataviz → design + storytelling
ExploratoryIdea generation → facilitation, rapid sketchingVisual discovery → BI, programming
  • If it takes >3 seconds to read → it's a handout, not a slide.
  • If discussion is about the chart rather than the idea → the chart failed.
  • Exploring → iterate fast, ignore aesthetics. Declaring → aesthetics are the job.

Thresholds & defaults

  • Prep ratio: ~1 hour practice per minute of performance; ≥3 full trial runs (Ch 1).
  • Speech rate: reading ~300 wpm vs. listening ~150–160 wpm; 10 minutes ≈ 1,300 words (Ch 2).
  • Pauses: aim for 2–3 seconds at key moments; average speaker manages only ~3.5 pauses/minute (Ch 1).
  • Video clips: under 60 seconds or you lose the room (Ch 1).
  • Eye contact: pick 5–6 friendly faces spread across the room (Ch 1).
  • Power pose: 2 minutes before the encounter (Ch 4).
  • Finalize content: one month before the event (Ch 1).
  • Issue selling: all seven tactics combined ≈ 40% of the success/failure difference (Ch 7).
  • Warmth + competence: >90% of the variance in impressions (Ch 4).

Tells & smells

  • Audience calls a polished talk "calculated," "phoned in," or "not real" → you rehearsed gestures instead of intents (Ch 2).
  • You're describing your organization's achievements → you've lost them; switch to the problem you're solving (Ch 1, Ch 3).
  • Your draft has no antagonists → nobody will believe it; rosy pictures foment distrust (Ch 3).
  • You're arguing headquarters' logic to a skeptical field → reframe around their profit (Ch 5).
  • People comply but don't adopt → you led with strength, not warmth (Ch 4).
  • Your networking pitch is chronological → you're a fact teller; lead with where you're going (Ch 9).
  • Your presentation ends with a to-do list → add the new bliss (Ch 11).
  • Your chart shows two decades when the point is three years → subtract (Ch 10).
  • You feel defensive and unfairly blamed → that's the apology-delay reflex, not analysis (Ch 8).

Timing rules for selling upward (Ch 7)

  • Deadline far off, decision makers exploring → open-ended inquiry beats a specific proposal.
  • Imminent launch or release → propose now.
  • Priorities shifting, new players arriving, boss's preoccupations changing → window open.
  • Informal first to gauge interest → then formal to create pressure to respond.
  • Boss lacks power or interest → ask to accompany whoever pitches; if going direct, keep the boss in the loop.

glossary.md

Glossary

Accumulation of antagonists — Stacking successive obstacles in a story so the audience genuinely doubts a happy ending (Ch 3)

Apology Formula — The who/what/where/when/how framework for executing an organizational apology (Ch 8)

Apology rehearsal — Role-playing likely apology scenarios before they occur (Ch 8)

Battle exhortation — Precombat oratory; Keith Yellin identified 23 recurring "common topics" across history (Ch 6)

Board of advisers — A small designated circle who repeatedly hear and react to your evolving transition story (Ch 9)

Bundling — Attaching a small idea to a larger initiative to raise its prominence (Ch 7)

Catching the wave — Timing an issue to a trend more people are starting to care about (Ch 7)

Click and viz — Converting spreadsheet cells straight to a chart without thinking about purpose (Ch 10)

Coach out vs. coach in — Delivery flaws can be coached away; a missing central idea cannot be coached in (Ch 1)

Coherence — The quality of a life story in which past, present, and future link causally; the main generator of listener trust (Ch 9)

Companyspeak — PowerPoint, dry memos, and hyperbolic corporate communications that draw cynicism (Ch 3)

Core vs. noncore violation — Whether a failure strikes at the organization's central mission or a peripheral function (Ch 8)

Crutch words — Verbal fillers ("um," "ah," "like," "you know") that erode credibility; replace with pauses (Ch 1)

Declarative vs. exploratory — Communicating information vs. figuring something out; the second dataviz question (Ch 10)

Desire — The protagonist's core need, "the blood of a story"; not a shopping list (Ch 3)

Detective-story structure — Present a problem, describe the search, deliver an "aha" that shifts perspective (Ch 1)

Direction giving — Uncertainty-reducing language: exactly how to do the task and how performance will be judged (Ch 6)

Dread — Knowing what will happen and being unable to stop it; distinct from fear, which is not knowing (Ch 3)

Education plot — A transition story driven by growing insight and self-understanding (Ch 9)

Empathetic language — Praise, encouragement, gratitude, and acknowledgment of difficulty (Ch 6)

Everyday dataviz — Declarative + data-driven: simple charts for formal presentations (Ch 10)

Expertise — One of the two sources of credibility: track record and demonstrated knowledge (Ch 5)

Fact tellers — People who recite chronological credentials instead of telling a story; hard to help (Ch 9)

Four Aims (Intents) — Be open, connect, be passionate, listen; rehearse these instead of gestures (Ch 2)

Framing for common ground — Describing a position in terms of the listener's tangible benefits (Ch 5)

Happy Warrior — A leader combining high warmth with high strength; faces troubles without being troubled (Ch 4)

Idea generation — Exploratory + conceptual: whiteboard sketching to work through ambiguity (Ch 10)

Idea illustration — Declarative + conceptual: org charts, process diagrams, frameworks (Ch 10)

Inciting incident — The event that throws life out of balance and starts a story (Ch 3)

Inside-out vs. outside-in — Preparing by setting your emotional state vs. executing prescribed nonverbal cues (Ch 4)

Issue selling — Winning attention and resources from senior decision makers for an idea from below (Ch 7)

John Wayne approach — Stating a strong position up front and pushing to a close; gives opponents a target (Ch 5)

Lion tamer — Engaging the other party obliquely rather than presenting a clear target (Ch 5)

Mask — The persona individuals and institutions present; compelling stories live beneath it (Ch 3)

Maturation plot — A transition story about becoming your own person (Ch 9)

Meaning making — Language explaining why a task matters, linking mission to listeners' goals; the hardest MLT element (Ch 6)

Motivating Language Theory (MLT) — Mayfield framework: direction giving + empathy + meaning making (Ch 6)

New bliss — The closing depiction of how much better the audience's world becomes (Ch 11)

Persuasive story pattern — What is / what could be oscillation across beginning, middle, and end (Ch 11)

Placeholder apology — A fast interim apology issued while facts are still being gathered (Ch 8)

Poise — Stillness plus full-height posture; telegraphs equilibrium and stability (Ch 4)

Power poses — Open, expansive postures held two minutes; raise testosterone, lower cortisol (Ch 4)

Private conformity vs. outward compliance — Trust changes beliefs; fear changes only behavior (Ch 4)

Profluence of development — John Gardner's term for a story's felt sense of going somewhere (Ch 9)

Psychological contract — Stakeholders' unwritten expectations of an organization's responsibilities (Ch 8)

Pyramid search — Finding experts via adjacent-field experts who refer you onward (Ch 10)

Relationships — The second source of credibility: a history of listening and acting in others' interest (Ch 5)

Report–story continuum — Every presentation sits between data-rich report and engaging story (Ch 1)

Second conversation — Nick Morgan's term for the nonverbal channel, which fires before words (Ch 2)

Self-knowledge — The root of great storytelling; building characters by asking what you would do (Ch 3)

Seven issue-selling tactics — Tailor, frame, manage emotions, time, involve others, adhere to norms, suggest solutions (Ch 7)

Signposting — Explicit verbal markers ("to begin," "finally") essential in speech though inelegant in writing (Ch 2)

Skepticism — Believing nothing at face value; distinguishing text from subtext (Ch 3)

Spontaneous trait inferences — Snap judgments from brief exposure; warmth registers faster than competence (Ch 4)

Strategic unapologeticness — Deliberately refusing to apologize in order to affirm a value (Ch 8)

Talk as a journey — Framing a presentation by choosing where to start and where to end (Ch 1)

Turning point — The point of no return closing act two; usually made significant by the telling, not by the event (Ch 9)

Valley of awkwardness — The half-memorized stage where a talk sounds recited; rehearse past it or use notes (Ch 1)

Visual confirmation — Rapid prototyping of charts to test a hypothesis (Ch 10)

Visual discovery — Exploratory + data-driven: mining large data sets visually (Ch 10)

Visual exploration — Open-ended, inclusive plotting when you don't know what you're looking for (Ch 10)

Vivid evidence — Stories, metaphors, and analogies that make data emotionally memorable (Ch 5)

Warmth–competence matrix — The two dimensions of social judgment accounting for >90% of impressions (Ch 4)

What is / what could be — The two poles whose contrast generates presentation tension (Ch 11)

patterns.md

Patterns

Frame the Talk as a Journey

When to use: At the very first outline, before any slide exists (Ch 1).

How: Decide where to start (calibrated to what the audience already knows and cares about) and where to end (a changed view of the world). Limit scope to what you can explain and illustrate with examples in the available time. Go deeper, not broader — your unique contribution, not your whole field.

Trade-offs: Narrow framing means abandoning material you're proud of; overcorrecting into overexplanation insults an intelligent audience.

Detective-Story Structure

When to use: When the content is an insight or discovery (Ch 1, Ch 3).

How: Present a problem → describe the search for a solution → deliver the "aha" that shifts perspective.

Trade-offs: Requires you to genuinely have a problem worth solving; without one it becomes contrived suspense.

Rehearse the Four Intents

When to use: Any talk where credibility and buy-in matter more than information transfer (Ch 2).

How: Practice the speech four times, once per intent. Open: imagine speaking to someone you're totally relaxed with. Connect: imagine capturing an inattentive child's attention, then a distractible teenager's. Passionate: identify what's at stake and let the underlying emotion into every word. Listen: imagine what the audience will be feeling and watch for their signals.

Trade-offs: Slower than gesture drills and feels indirect, but rehearsed gestures fire late and read as fake.

Replace Fillers with Pauses

When to use: Whenever "um," "ah," "like," or "you know" recur (Ch 1).

How: Watch video or read a transcript of your last talk to identify your crutch words. Pair each with a physical action (tap your leg) or have a friend clap when you use one. Record yourself narrating your day using pauses instead of fillers. Prepare thoroughly — nervousness drives filler.

Trade-offs: Pauses feel far longer to the speaker than to the audience; great speakers pause two to three seconds.

The 1:60 Preparation Ratio

When to use: Sizing rehearsal for an important talk (Ch 1).

How: Roughly one hour of practice per minute of performance; minimum three full trial runs. Finalize content a month before the event; rehearse alone and in front of an audience. Be choosy about feedback givers — prefer experienced presenters.

Trade-offs: Not every presentation is worth that investment; if you can't get past the valley of awkwardness, use bullet points on note cards instead of memorizing.

Warmth Before Strength

When to use: First impressions, new teams, any stalled influence attempt (Ch 4).

How: Lower pitch and volume as if comforting a friend; validate what the room actually feels ("I know everybody's feeling a lot of uncertainty right now"); smile genuinely (eyes engaged, not just mouth); share one appropriately personal story. Then add strength: full-height posture, deliberate movement, stillness when finished.

Trade-offs: Amped-up enthusiasm reads as fawning; raised eyebrows while smiling signal anxiety and cost more strength than they gain warmth.

Power Pose Warm-Up

When to use: Two minutes before a high-stakes pitch or speech (Ch 1, Ch 4).

How: Adopt an open, expansive, space-occupying posture — standing tall, hands on hips, feet apart. Add deep breathing before going onstage.

Trade-offs: Builds personal agency and self-regulation, not dominance over others; it's an inside-out preparation, not a performance move.

Credibility Audit and Repair

When to use: Before beginning any persuasion campaign (Ch 5).

How: Score yourself separately on expertise (track record others know and respect) and relationships (seen as helpful, trustworthy, in sync). Test your self-assessment with trusted colleagues. Repair expertise by learning, hiring an outside expert, enlisting internal experts, citing independent research, or running a pilot. Repair relationships with one-on-one meetings that gather perspectives rather than pitch, and by involving allies who already have standing.

Trade-offs: Borrowed credibility works but takes time and can dilute your ownership of the idea.

Vivid Analogy Substitution

When to use: When your case rests on abstract projections the audience can't feel (Ch 5).

How: Find a comparable situation the audience already understands and map your idea onto it (software as supermarket vs. restaurant; weekly sales meetings as early Christian gatherings). Lead or close a point with one relevant statistic; never recite strings of numbers.

Trade-offs: A strained analogy is worse than none; test it on someone outside the project.

Emotional Matchmaking

When to use: Before any high-stakes internal presentation (Ch 5).

How: Canvass key individuals who have a pulse on the room's mood; ask how your proposal will land emotionally. Match your fervor to their receptivity. If they need recognition first, give it in a separate session before delivering bad news. End with hope rather than doom.

Trade-offs: Splitting recognition and warning across two meetings costs time and momentum, but combining them can produce open resentment.

The Seven-Tactic Issue-Selling Campaign

When to use: Selling any idea upward over weeks or months (Ch 7).

How: Tailor the pitch to each decision maker's goals; frame in business benefits and opportunity; regulate your emotions and protect the boss's standing; time it to a trend or decision window; build a coalition including people the target trusts; follow house norms; always bring a solution or a process for finding one. Start informal to gauge interest, then go formal.

Trade-offs: All seven combined explain ~40% of the difference between success and failure, but campaigns cost social capital — choose battles by asking how important the issue is to the company and to you.

Motivating Language Mix

When to use: Any pre-performance moment, one-on-one or to a crowd (Ch 6).

How: Include direction giving, empathy, and meaning making, then weight by need. Unknown challenge → more direction. Underdog or high stakes → more empathy and meaning. Obvious purpose → less meaning making. Sequence that works (McChrystal): direction → meaning → empathy → recap. Continue all three one-on-one after the speech.

Trade-offs: Veterans mid-operation want the plan, not reassurance; over-emphasized empathy reads as doubt in their capability.

Organizational Apology Execution

When to use: After the four diagnostic questions indicate an apology is warranted (Ch 8).

How: Match apologizer seniority to violation severity; address the actual victims; include candor, remorse, and a concrete commitment to change; choose a setting proportional to the harm; move fast, with a placeholder if facts are pending; use plain, self-implicating language, preferably spoken.

Trade-offs: On-site, in-person apologies maximize sincerity signals but are uncontrolled — rejection becomes a public confrontation.

Coherent Transition Story

When to use: Career change, interviews, networking, internal moves (Ch 9).

How: Ground the reasons in character ("I discovered I'm good at that"), cite multiple complementary reasons, extend the goal back in time and explain what blocked it, reframe past experience to surface the connecting pieces, and choose a familiar plot (maturation or education). Acknowledge the size of the jump explicitly.

Trade-offs: External causes ("I got fired") must be incorporated but never carry the justification; downplaying discontinuity to seem safe makes you dull and untrustworthy at once.

Multiple Stories for Multiple Selves

When to use: Early transition, when several paths are live (Ch 9).

How: Develop a distinct coherent story per possible self and test each with the audience that relates to it. Let responses tell you which to pursue hardest.

Trade-offs: Not deception, but requires discipline — airing all options with one audience destroys coherence.

The Story-Shaped Résumé

When to use: Whenever your target role differs from your last one (Ch 9).

How: Three parts, all pointing at one goal — (1) the position you want, (2) bulleted experience highlights proving you can do it, drawn from all experience including volunteer work, (3) a reverse-chronological professional summary phrased in the same terms, so every highlight claim is supported below. Build a separate version per target.

Trade-offs: A CV is exhaustive and neutral; a résumé is interpretive and must be rebuilt for each direction.

The Dataviz Two Questions

When to use: Before opening any charting tool (Ch 10).

How: Ask whether the information is conceptual or data-driven, and whether you're declaring or exploring. The quadrant tells you which skills to bring: editing and design (idea illustration), facilitation (idea generation), BI and programming (visual discovery), design and storytelling (everyday dataviz).

Trade-offs: Slower than clicking a chart type, but convenience produces charts that visualize a spreadsheet rather than an idea.

Subtractive Chart Design

When to use: Any chart destined for a live presentation (Ch 10).

How: One message, few variables. Cut historical context the decision doesn't need. If it takes more than a few seconds to digest, move it to paper or a personal screen instead of a slide.

Trade-offs: Requires courage — busy charts advertise your effort, clean ones advertise only the idea.

What Is / What Could Be Oscillation

When to use: Structuring any presentation intended to change behavior (Ch 11).

How: Open by describing the audience's reality until they nod, then introduce the alternative. Alternate the two poles through the middle, pairing every obstacle with its answer. Close with a call to action, then new bliss — concrete future rewards.

Trade-offs: Requires naming problems out loud; hiding them collapses the tension the pattern runs on.

Cheatsheet — Decision Rules

Core if/then rules

SituationDo thisBecause
A capable leader is failingAsk: rudderless, clueless, or blindsided?Each maps to a different missing focus and a different fix (Ch 2)
Conversation is overheatingSwitch from emotional to cognitive empathyUnderstanding the perspective intellectually keeps you calm enough to help (Ch 2)
Current behavior contradicts the value you wantAmplify existing good behavior; do NOT announce the idealWhen norms and ideals clash, people follow what others do (Ch 3)
Someone resists needed learningDiagnose the attribute first, then swap the self-talk"No time / not relevant" is an aspiration symptom, not an argument (Ch 4)
You need helpAsk one person directly, name the impact, follow upGroup emails diffuse responsibility; help rates run ~48% above expectation (Ch 5)
Pitching your bossOne frame only, in private, tied to their stated goalsMixed opportunity+threat framing gets the least support of any option (Ch 6)
About to give unsolicited feedbackAsk for feedback on your own work firstAdvising confers power; asking first hands it back (Ch 7)
Feedback recipient is from a more indirect culturePraise the good specifically; omit the badThe omission communicates the criticism clearly enough (Ch 7)
Conflict has gone personalWork the third entity, not the personConverts an adversary into a co-owner of a shared problem (Ch 9)
Someone needs to change a behaviorStart from their dreams, not their deficitsCompliance coaching triggers guilt and self-consciousness; vision coaching activates learning circuits (Ch 10)
Writing feels flatFind the missing SDiagnosis beats "make it better" (Ch 11)
Under time pressure on a moral callSleep on itRushing strongly predicts unethical action (Ch 13)

Which frame for which boss (Ch 6)

Boss tellsFocusPitch
Obeys rules and SOPs, meticulous, careful planner, hates mistakesPreventionThe problem or loss this avoids
Starts more than she finishes, talks about the future, delegates details, lets small errors slidePromotionThe new opportunity and its upside
UnclearWatch one meeting for which language dominates; never hedge by using both—

Which empathy, which listening, which voice

If you need to…Empathy (Ch 2)Listening (Ch 8)Voice (Ch 12)
Explain yourself so it landsCognitiveCo-createContext
Mentor or read the roomEmotionalCo-createConnection
Decide what someone needs from youEmpathic concernCo-createCuriosity
Refocus a scattered team——Clarity
Enter a likely conflictCognitiveCo-createCharacter

Feedback loop by team maturity (Ch 7)

  • Never exchanged feedback → one-to-one chats, private
  • Some trust established → speed-dating, 3 min each way, rotate, each names one action
  • Mature, strong relationships → live 360 circle over a meal; recipient listens and says thank you

Thresholds & numbers the authors commit to

NumberMeaning
0.07 secTime to form a trust judgment in conversation (Ch 8)
200 msEmotional connotation processed — before meaning (Ch 11)
80%Minimum share of talking the coachee should do (Ch 10)
48%How much more willing helpers are than askers predict; also the persistence gain from "together" (Ch 5)
30%Reduction in a manager's felt threat when you pitch privately (Ch 6)
15–18%Endorsement gain from matching the boss's regulatory focus (Ch 6)
57%Influence gain from speaking up on behalf of others vs. yourself (Ch 6)
5×How much more often men give women unrequested advice than the reverse (Ch 7)

18–254 daysRange for forming a new habit — plan for the long end (Ch 10)

Tells & smells

  • You're being clueless: you're technically strong, people avoid you, and when told, you blame back (Ch 2)
  • You've hit a phantom norm: the attitude you think is dominant belongs to the loudest one or two people (Ch 3)
  • It's an aspiration problem, not a time problem: the objections are "too long," "old way works," "flash in the pan" (Ch 4)
  • Your ask will fail: you opened with "May I ask you a favor?", apologized profusely, offered reciprocity, or minimized the need (Ch 5)
  • Your pitch will fail: it names both the upside of acting and the risk of not acting (Ch 6)
  • Your feedback will land as dominance: majority member → underrepresented colleague, unasked (Ch 7)
  • You're listening to protect: you're rehearsing your reply and guarding your position (Ch 8)
  • Confirmation bias has set in: a colleague's occasional missteps have hardened into "X is difficult" (Ch 9)
  • You're coaching for compliance: you're doing most of the talking and naming gaps (Ch 10)
  • You're rationalizing: "everyone does this," "just following orders," "not like I'm robbing a bank" (Ch 13)
  • Your environment is eroding self-control: high uncertainty, cognitive overload, late nights, back-to-back stretch goals (Ch 13)

Defaults

  • Assume your view is a view; ask the challenge questions anyway (Ch 9)
  • Assume the quiet majority is already empathic; your job is volume (Ch 3)
  • Assume people will help; the constraint is how you ask (Ch 5)
  • Assume delivery, not content, decides whether feedback lands (Ch 7)
  • Assume your future self is less virtuous than you think (Ch 13)
  • Set your relationship goals low if needed — "functional" is a legitimate target (Ch 9)

glossary.md

Glossary

Affinity bias — Unconscious tendency to align with people similar to you in appearance, beliefs, and background (Ch 9)

Anticipatory utility — The pleasure of expectation itself; readers' reward circuits peak before a passage's high point (Ch 11)

Aspiration — The wanting-to-learn attribute; raisable by shifting focus from challenges to future benefits (Ch 4)

Attentional blink — Momentary lapse causing missed words in a list; emotionally significant words produce none (Ch 11)

Automated social hierarchy detection — Inferring org standing from response latency; slower repliers hold more power (Ch 2)

Coachable moment — An opening for development: an evident challenge, a wake-up call, or a vague unease (Ch 10)

Coaching for compliance — Drilling into problems and targets; works for predetermined goals, fails for behavioral change (Ch 10)

Coaching with compassion — Coaching from the person's dreams and vision; activates brain regions for openness and learning (Ch 10)

Cognitive control — Putting attention where you want it and holding it against temptation; colloquially, willpower (Ch 2)

Cognitive empathy — Understanding another's perspective by thinking about feelings rather than feeling them (Ch 2)

Confirmation bias — Reading new evidence as proof of existing beliefs, making it harder for others to disprove you (Ch 9)

Connectors — The most-connected people in a group, through whom information, ideas, and values flow (Ch 3)

Developmental network — The extended circle supporting someone's change; a personal board of advisers (Ch 10)

Downgraders — Words that soften criticism ("kind of," "a little," "maybe") plus deliberate understatement (Ch 7)

Effectiveness (reinforcement) — Making clear what you need and what impact the help will have (Ch 5)

Emotional empathy — Feeling what another feels; used for mentoring, clients, and reading group dynamics (Ch 2)

Empathic concern — Sensing what another person needs from you; requires managing distress without numbing (Ch 2)

Ethical mirage — Overestimating the virtuousness of your future self (Ch 13)

Eulogy virtues — What people praise after you've died: character and what you did for others (Ch 13)

Fair witness — An inner voice that reports the facts of a situation in balance, neither defensive nor punishing (Ch 4)

Fundamental attribution error — Attributing others' behavior to personality and your own to circumstances (Ch 9)

Humble inquiry — Setting aside your own assumptions and letting the other person do 80% of the talking (Ch 10)

Identity segmentation — Compartmentalizing personal and professional life under different moral codes (Ch 13)

Ideals vs. norms — What a group says people ought to do vs. what most members actually do; norms win (Ch 3)

Implementation intentions — "If X happens, then I will do Y," specified in advance and voiced aloud (Ch 13)

In-group (reinforcement) — Assuring a potential helper you're on the same team and the team matters (Ch 5)

Intentional Change Theory — Ideal self → real self → learning agenda → experimenting and practicing (Ch 10)

Job crafting — Proactively reshaping your tasks, relationships, and view of your job to make it meaningful (Ch 13)

Know-it-all vs. learn-it-all — Status-seeking expertise display vs. humility to hear criticism and diverse views (Ch 7)

Learning agenda — A road map from strengths and passions toward the ideal self; not a performance improvement plan (Ch 10)

Listening to co-create — Listening to connect and explore, with psychological safety (Ch 8)

Listening to protect — Defensive listening that guards your identity; the speaker feels ignored (Ch 8)

Manvising — Men giving women advice they neither asked for nor want (Ch 7)

Mirror test — Would you like the person in the mirror after this decision? (Ch 13)

Moral humility — Recognizing that anyone can transgress without vigilance (Ch 13)

Naive realism — Believing you see an issue objectively, so dissenters must be uninformed or biased (Ch 9)

Open awareness — Noticing broadly without judging, censoring, or getting swept up in any one thing (Ch 2)

Personal balance sheet — Strengths, weaknesses, and enduring distinctive qualities, weighed against a long-term vision (Ch 10)

Personal vision statement — A short written statement of the ideal self, kept present as a daily reminder (Ch 10)

Phantom norms — Behaviors that seem dominant only because a few loud or prominent people display them (Ch 3)

Positive identity (reinforcement) — Framing the helper as a helpful person uniquely placed to assist (Ch 5)

Prevention focus — Orientation toward vigilance, downside management, and playing not to lose (Ch 6)

Processing fluency — How little brainpower a reader spends extracting your meaning (Ch 11)

Promotion focus — Orientation toward aspirations, ideals, the future, and playing to win (Ch 6)

Psychic attrition — Erosion of attention to others that accompanies rising rank and power (Ch 2)

Publicity test — Would you be comfortable with this choice on the newspaper's front page? (Ch 13)

Radical candor — Kim Scott's argument that blunt feedback beats withholding it ("ruinous empathy") (Ch 7)

Readiness to change — Whether someone is open to the reflection and experimentation coaching requires (Ch 10)

Resonant relationship — The caring, trusting bond that makes coaching effective (Ch 10)

Résumé virtues — Listable skills, abilities, and accomplishments; largely what you've done for yourself (Ch 13)

Reward circuit — Midbrain neurons that light up in response to pleasurable stimuli, including good prose (Ch 11)

Self-talk — Internal narration about yourself; the lever for aspiration, self-awareness, curiosity, and vulnerability (Ch 4)

Social skills (C-suite sense) — Self-awareness, listening/communication, cross-group facility, and theory of mind (Ch 1)

Somatic markers — Gut sensations from the insula and amygdala signaling that something feels right or wrong (Ch 2)

Status incongruence — When your role's societal status doesn't match the role you play in context (Ch 7)

Systems effect — One weak team member degrading the whole group's performance (Ch 1)

The Eight S's — Simplicity, specificity, surprise, stirring language, seductiveness, smart thinking, social content, storytelling (Ch 11)

The Third Entity — You, your colleague, and the dynamic between you; work on the third thing (Ch 9)

Theory of mind — Inferring how others think and feel; the hardest-to-fake social skill (Ch 1)

Three A's of feedback — Assist, actionable, asked for (Ch 7)

Triad of Awareness — Focus on yourself, on others, and on the wider world (Ch 2)

True North groups — Small trusted groups where self-knowledge begins with self-revelation (Ch 2)

Upgraders — Words that intensify criticism ("absolutely," "totally," "completely") (Ch 7)

Vulnerability (learning attribute) — Tolerating your own beginner mistakes on the way up the curve (Ch 4)

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques

Decompose "Soft Skills" Before Assessing (Ch 1)

When to use: Hiring, promoting, or developing anyone where "good with people" is the criterion.

How: Score separately on self-awareness, listening/communication, cross-group facility, and theory of mind. Place high-potentials in roles that force contact with varied constituencies and monitor performance there.

Trade-offs: Slower than a résumé screen; no established tool exists at the executive level, so you must build one.

The Triad Diagnostic (Ch 2)

When to use: A capable leader is failing and you can't name why.

How: Map symptom to missing focus — rudderless (inward), clueless (others), blindsided (outward).

Trade-offs: Diagnostic only; each focus is trained differently, and strength in one doesn't transfer.

Pick the Right Empathy (Ch 2)

When to use: Any high-stakes interpersonal moment.

How: Cognitive empathy to explain yourself and to de-escalate an overheated conversation; emotional empathy to mentor and read a room; empathic concern to judge what someone needs from you.

Trade-offs: Too much emotional empathy causes compassion fatigue; too little numbs you.

Attention Reps (Ch 2)

When to use: Building focus as a trainable capacity.

How: Notice the mind has wandered, return it to the chosen object, hold. Protect uninterrupted reflection time to enable exploration.

Trade-offs: Sleep loss, stress, and overload disable the switch from exploitation to exploration.

Amplify Existing Norms Instead of Announcing Ideals (Ch 3)

When to use: Any culture change, especially when current behavior contradicts the target.

How: Measure the actual norm; find where the desired behavior already happens; make it visible via recognition and incentives; identify connectors and co-create the initiative with them.

Trade-offs: Slower and less visible than a values launch — but a values launch that outruns the norm produces cynicism.

Self-Talk Substitution (Ch 4)

When to use: You or someone you coach is resisting required learning.

How: Diagnose which attribute is blocked, then swap the phrase. "I don't need to learn this" → "What would my future look like if I did?" "I'm already fine" → "Am I really? How do I compare with peers?" "This is boring" → "I wonder why others find it interesting." "I'm terrible at this" → "I'm making beginner mistakes, but I'll get better."

Trade-offs: Requires catching the thought in flight; not a substitute for real capability gaps.

Import Curious Language (Ch 4)

When to use: A required topic bores you.

How: Notice the How…? Why…? I wonder…? phrasing you use about a genuine interest; aim it at the boring topic; take exactly one action to answer one question.

Trade-offs: You only need one spark, but arguing someone into interest never works.

The Three Reinforcements (Ch 5)

When to use: Asking anyone for help, and in day-to-day priming.

How: In-group (shared experience over shared trait); positive identity (identity nouns, tailored, plus pre-emptive gratitude); effectiveness (state the need and the impact, follow up afterward, allow alternative forms of help).

Trade-offs: Reciprocity framing, apology, and minimizing all backfire; ask individually, never by group email.

Single-Frame Pitching (Ch 6)

When to use: Proposing anything upward.

How: Read the boss's tells for promotion vs. prevention focus, then pitch opportunity or threat — never both. Pitch in private, tie it to their stated goals, and pre-answer resources, coalition difficulty, and political cost.

Trade-offs: Raises endorsement 15–18%; mixed frames get the least support of any framing.

Recruit Allies Before Pitching (Ch 6)

When to use: Before raising anything contentious.

How: Socialize with colleagues first; ask to cite their support or have them co-present; ideally let a well-positioned colleague who won't benefit make the case.

Trade-offs: Speaking on behalf of others is 57% more influential — but takes time and cedes some ownership.

The Three A's Filter (Ch 7)

When to use: Before any unsolicited feedback, mandatorily across power or identity lines.

How: Is it meant to assist? Is it actionable? Was it asked for — and if not, ask for feedback on your own work first.

Trade-offs: The third A costs a step but neutralizes the power transfer that makes advice read as dominance.

Match Upgraders and Downgraders (Ch 7)

When to use: Cross-cultural feedback.

How: Listen for the intensity words your counterpart uses and mirror them. In indirect cultures, praise the good specifically and omit the bad; the silence carries the message.

Trade-offs: Feels evasive to direct-culture speakers and blunt to indirect ones — calibrate to the recipient, not your comfort.

Feedback Loops by Team Maturity (Ch 7)

When to use: Building a candid culture on a diverse team.

How: One-to-one chats (new teams) → speed-dating rounds, three minutes each way (closer teams) → live 360 circles over a meal (mature teams). Structure content as one strength + one improvement, or start/stop/continue.

Trade-offs: Public formats require courage but prevent backchannel gossip and normalize feedback.

Choose Your Listening Attitude (Ch 8)

When to use: Any conversation where the relationship matters.

How: Name whether you're listening to protect, to judge, or to co-create. In co-create mode hold four questions: What are they trying to say? What are they thinking? What do they expect to explore with me? How can I connect to their world?

Trade-offs: Costs attention up front; the alternative is a threat response you then have to repair.

The Third Entity Reframe (Ch 9)

When to use: A conflict has become personal and polarized.

How: Imagine three parties — you, them, and the dynamic. Make progress on the dynamic (a decision, an assignment, the tension itself) rather than trying to change the person.

Trade-offs: Doesn't fix genuinely abusive behavior; sometimes you must cut losses.

Conflict Experiments (Ch 9)

When to use: A difficult relationship you haven't been able to shift.

How: Pick two or three tactics, define what you'll do differently, set a time period, observe. Keep, tweak, or abandon. Do something the other person doesn't expect to interrupt the pattern.

Trade-offs: Treat failures as information; repeating a dead tactic is the real error.

Compassionate Coaching Sequence (Ch 10)

When to use: Helping someone through a real behavioral or career change.

How: Check readiness → ask ideal-self questions and let them talk 80% → write a short personal vision statement → build a personal balance sheet including enduring qualities → set a learning agenda from strengths → experiment, review regularly, and surround them with a developmental network.

Trade-offs: Slower than advice-giving; advice is faster but triggers stress and blocks learning for broad goals.

The Eight S's Revision Pass (Ch 11)

When to use: Revising any business writing.

How: Ask which S is missing. Simplicity (cut, activate, drop tangents); specificity (concrete nouns, memorable shorthand); surprise (novelty, wordplay); stirring (emotional verbs, metaphor); seductiveness (open with a question or mystery); smart (fresh distinction, universal truth); social (people, your own voice, second person); story.

Trade-offs: Passive voice can cut comprehension accuracy 10%; nested clauses slow reading and add errors.

Five Voices Selection (Ch 12)

When to use: Choosing how to show up in a given moment.

How: Character before hard conversations; context before details and when presenting up; clarity when the team is scattered (including empowering them to say no); curiosity when work is interdependent, when coaching, or when emotions run high; connection to stay visible as your span grows.

Trade-offs: Requires the self-awareness to notice which voice the moment wants.

The Newspaper Headline Question (Ch 12)

When to use: Annual or quarterly prioritization with a direct report.

How: Ask, "If we were to publish this in a newspaper, what would you want the big headlines to be for you and your team at the end of the year?" Then use the answer as the reference point for later re-prioritization.

Trade-offs: Forces hard trade-offs some people would rather defer.

Ethical Pre-Commitment (Ch 13)

When to use: Before you face a moral challenge — which is the only time it works.

How: Write eulogy-virtue goals; make specific if-then plans aloud; recruit ethical mentors inside and outside; screen employers for moral fit and ask about it in interviews; signal your standards subtly.

Trade-offs: Feels theoretical until needed; that's precisely the ethical mirage it counters.

The Three Rationalization Tests (Ch 13)

When to use: Any decision where you notice yourself constructing a justification.

How: Publicity (front page?), generalizability (precedent for everyone?), mirror (would you like that person?). Also run rules / consequences / virtues. If any answer is no, stop.

Trade-offs: Requires slowing down — and rushing is itself a strong predictor of unethical action.

Cheatsheet — How Great Ideas Happen (Newman)

Which stage am I in? (diagnose, then act)

TellStageDo thisMode
No idea where to look; scanning randomlySurveyingExpand influences; low-res survey many domains; find the problemDeep → surface
Have a direction, no mapGriddingWrite the guiding question; build the What/Why GridDeep
Have a mapped cell, few ideasDiggingVolume; evaluation-free; double your targetSurface
Too many ideas, can't chooseSiftingDistance + subtraction; others pickDeep

Decision rules

  • When your idea feels strikingly original, cut the novelty — audiences penalize excess originality; hits cluster at ~90–95% conventional / 5–10% novel.
  • When you feel tapped out mid-session, run another round — the creative cliff is an illusion; late ideas rate higher.
  • When you must judge your own ideas, don't — the creative endowment effect is immune to warnings and examples; only elapsed time or another person's eyes fix it.
  • When the brief feels impossibly constrained, stop negotiating the constraints — the most-constrained groups produce the highest-rated work.
  • When an idea makes you uncomfortable, develop it 10–15 min before discarding — discomfort marks an information gap, which is where curiosity (and value) peaks.
  • When editing, ask what to remove first — people default to adding; subtraction has to be prompted explicitly.
  • When the work underperforms, tweak and ship again — don't restart — Wright's law: ~10–15% improvement per doubling of cumulative output.
  • When everyone around you agrees, go to weak ties — strong ties know what you already know.
  • When you notice a cross-domain analogy, don't stop at Recognition — map Relevance element-by-element, or it's decoration.
  • When you're stuck and working harder, change inputs instead of effort — read others' work, adjacent fields, new places.
  • Never say "be creative" — the instruction itself cuts idea productivity ~20%. Say "as many ideas as possible."

Guiding question — four-criteria gate

Keep it only if it is specific · open-ended · motivating · measurable.

Template: "What is a [project type] that [unique value/meaning] for [audience] in [context], despite [obstacle]?"

  • Bored delivering your own one-minute pitch? → the idea is wrong, not the pitch.
  • Starting from what you want to say? → flip inside-out → outside-in: what will they think about on the drive home?

Three Roadblocks (Conclusion) — pick the diagnosis

  • Stuck with nothing → not enough work up front. Missing why/guiding question or grid. Go back to Gridding.
  • Stuck with a mediocre idea → settled too early. "Ideas are cheap" is false; breakthrough ideas are rare. Go back to Digging.
  • Stuck defending an idea → in love with the idea, not the process. Also applies to being attached to finishing. Go to Sifting-with-others.

Transplanting: the Three R's — where it fails

RQuestionFailure mode
RecognitionWhat in another domain resembles this?Stopping here (most common)
RelevanceWhich elements map, exactly?Metaphor mistaken for mapping
RefinementDoes it survive prototyping here?Skipping domain experts

Different people are good at different R's — staff each stage separately.

Tower vs. Raft (Sifting posture)

Building a TowerFloating a Raft
StanceCram everything in, defendAudience hunts for holes
MoveAddSubtract
Test"Look what I made""What does this element contribute to my guiding question?"

Default is Tower. Force the Raft frame deliberately.

Feedback triage

  • Weight the tails, not the agreeable middle — outlier comments carry the signal.
  • Then apply the frequency rule to the middle: many people tripping on the same thing is real, however badly they explain it.
  • Ask "What specific aspects are strong / could be improved?" and "Does this remind you of things you've seen?" — never "Do you like it?"
  • State your guiding question as context first, and pre-declare what you will not change.

glossary.md

Glossary — How Great Ideas Happen (George Newman)

5% Novelty Rule — Hit ideas sit at roughly 90–95% conventional and 5–10% novel; make a small, sharp departure from an established concept rather than a wholesale one (Ch 2).

Adjacent possible — The set of moves reachable from where you currently stand; ideas arrive only when their neighboring components already exist (Ch 6).

Analogical reasoning — Using a familiar concrete case to unlock the abstract relational structure of a new problem; Hofstadter's "engine of cognition" (Ch 6).

Attending to negative space — Deliberately examining what is absent or unmarked in a scene, rather than the labeled objects (Ch 3).

Bottom-up processing — Building a representation from the sensory data actually present, rather than from expectation (Ch 3).

Brick-counting fallacy — Mistaking accumulation of facts for progress toward an idea; volume of detail is not directed thinking (Ch 11).

Brilliance-focused culture — An environment that prizes innate genius; signals belonging to a narrow group and drives talent out (Ch 11).

Broker — A person who connects otherwise disconnected clusters of a network, and therefore sees combinations no one inside either cluster can (Ch 6, Burt).

Building a Tower — The creator's default posture: cram in every element you built, defending the whole (Ch 10). Contrast Floating a Raft.

Close looking — Sustained 30–60 minute examination of a single object or scene, past the point where the inner explainer stops you (Ch 3).

Collective intelligence — A team's general problem-solving capacity; driven by emotional intelligence and turn-taking, not average member IQ (Ch 8).

Creative Cliff Illusion — The false belief that idea quality collapses after the first couple of minutes; in fact late-session ideas rate higher (Ch 7, Lucas & Nordgren).

Creative Endowment Effect — Overvaluing an idea because you authored it, which wrecks your ability to sift your own list (Ch 10).

Creative explorer — Newman's replacement for the genius myth: someone who searches for ideas that already exist in the landscape (Introduction).

Curation — Selecting with intent from a large generated set; the human half of working with AI (Ch 9).

Digging — Stage 3: generating many candidate ideas within the region you have gridded (Part III).

Directed thinking — Reasoning aimed by a structural question rather than by accumulating facts (Ch 11, Wertheimer on Einstein).

Early diversification — Sampling widely across styles/domains early in a career; predicts later hits via skill portfolio, transferable expertise, and better talent-matching (Ch 8, Berg).

Evaluation-free zone — A declared period in which no idea may be judged, protecting the Digging stage from premature Sifting (Ch 7, Ch 8).

Floating a Raft — Reframing your idea as something an audience will inspect for holes, which puts you in subtraction mode (Ch 10).

Gridding — Stage 2: sectioning the conceptual space so every combination gets examined, and you know where you haven't looked (Part II).

Guiding Question — The compass question fusing what you are making with why it matters; must be specific, open-ended, motivating, and measurable (Ch 4).

Identity trap — Refusing a needed change because the current version feels like you; blocks tweaks (Ch 12).

Information-gap theory of curiosity — Curiosity peaks for questions you sort of already know the answer to; discomfort marks the gap worth digging into (Ch 11, Loewenstein).

Inner explainer — The internal voice that labels a scene and thereby ends observation (Ch 3).

Inside-out method — Starting a project from your own goals and interests; Newman's own failure mode. Contrast outside-in method (Ch 4).

Kernel idea / the spark — The seed that cues something specific and complex — core idea, satellites, mood, energy, flow — and is therefore worth elaborating (Ch 9).

King of the Mountain — Tournament-style group selection: each person brings their top two ideas, and rounds narrow to a top three (Ch 8, Ex. 25).

Knowledge funnel — Deep expertise in one or two domains, shallow familiarity with many, plus skill at translating between them (Ch 3).

Low-resolution surveying — Knowing a little about a lot, deliberately; the input side of transplanting (Ch 2).

Mid-Stakes Event — A scheduled, dated exposure of work to a real but non-gatekeeping audience, used to force selection and test predictions (Ch 10, Ex. 32).

Multiple discovery — The same idea reached independently by several parties, often simultaneously; evidence that ideas are found, not conjured (Ch 1).

Narrative Reversal — Listing your assumptions and asking "what if the opposite were true?" (Ch 7, Knight).

Originality Ostrich — A creator who assumes originality only helps, blind to the fact that audiences penalize excess novelty (Ch 2).

Outside-in method — Starting from the audience's anticipated end experience and working backward (Ch 4).

Problem finding — Letting the problem emerge from close observation instead of importing a predefined one (Ch 3, Csikszentmihalyi & Getzels).

Psychological distance — Separation from your own work via elapsed time or other people's eyes; the prerequisite for subtraction (Ch 10).

Refinement — Third R: prototyping and iterating a transplanted concept in its new context, usually with other experts (Ch 6).

Recognition — First R: spotting a candidate cross-domain connection (Ch 6).

Relevance — Second R: mapping element-by-element what actually overlaps between the two domains (Ch 6).

Second-mover advantage — The tweak, not the original, is usually what breaks through (Ch 2).

Set of ideas — What to hunt for instead of "the right idea": a localized cluster of near-variants to compare (Ch 7).

Sifting — Stage 4: choosing which ideas to pursue, mostly by subtraction (Part IV).

Sleeping Beauty — A dormant idea that lies unused for years until a new domain awakens it (Ch 6).

Structural hole — The gap between disconnected network clusters that a broker spans (Ch 6, Burt).

Subtraction neglect — The robust human tendency to improve things only by adding, never by removing (Ch 10, Adams).

Surveying — Stage 1: reading the conceptual terrain to decide where to search (Part I).

The Three R's of Transplanting — Recognition, Relevance, and Refinement; skipping past Recognition is the standard failure (Ch 6).

The Unconscious Grid — The implicit constraint structure that produces the sensation that "the story writes itself" (Ch 5).

The What and Why Grid — A two-axis grid (what you make × why it matters) whose cells you fill to find unoccupied combinations (Ch 5).

Top-down processing — Perception driven by prior expectation; the source of seeing what you expected rather than what is there (Ch 3).

Transplanting — Taking an existing concept from one domain and applying it somewhere new and unexpected (Ch 6).

Turtling-up — Retreating into your existing strong-tie network when threatened, which starves you of new information (Ch 8).

Wright's law — Cost/effort per unit falls a predictable ~10–15% with each doubling of cumulative output; the most successful entrepreneurs are identifiable by adherence to it (Ch 12).

"Yes, and" — The improv rule adopted as a group Digging protocol: build on contributions rather than evaluating them (Ch 8).

patterns.md

Patterns — techniques from How Great Ideas Happen

The 5% Workshop

When to use: You have a domain and want a viable idea fast, without the originality penalty.

How: Copy a celebrated existing work verbatim (score it, rebuild it, retype it). Brainstorm ≥10 distinct modifications that alter roughly 5% of it. Implement one at a time and compare.

Trade-offs: Feels like cheating and produces no origin story. But it targets the 90–95% conventional / 5–10% novel band where hits actually cluster; pure originality reliably underperforms with audiences.

Close Looking

When to use: You need a problem worth solving and don't have one — or your read of a situation is running on assumption.

How: Pick one mundane scene from your actual work (people reacting to an idea, customers browsing, your own routine). Observe 10–60 minutes without labeling. When the inner explainer names the thing, keep going. Record what is absent, not just what's present.

Trade-offs: Slow and feels unproductive; there is no deliverable. It's the only reliable route from top-down assumption to bottom-up data.

The Guiding Question Template

When to use: Start of any project, and again whenever you feel directionless mid-project.

How: Fill in — "What is a [type of project] that [provides a unique form of value or meaning] for [a particular audience] in [a specific context/environment], despite [potential obstacles]?" Test it against four criteria: specific, open-ended, motivating, measurable. If you bore yourself delivering it as a one-minute elevator pitch, the idea needs work, not the pitch.

Trade-offs: A too-specific question forecloses search; too broad and it fails as a compass. Expect to sharpen it with data as you go — it's meant to be dynamic.

The Outside-In Flip

When to use: Your work is well-crafted but isn't landing.

How: Replace "What do I want to say?" with "What does my audience need to hear?" and "What will they be thinking about on the drive home?" Design backward from that end experience.

Trade-offs: Can slide into pandering if you skip the why. Pair with the guiding question so audience-fit doesn't erase point of view.

The What and Why Grid

When to use: You have a guiding question and need to map the search space before generating.

How: (1) Gather data — list existing successes in the space. (2) Derive what categories and why categories from that list. (3) Build the grid: what = columns, why = rows. (4) Fill every cell, weighting toward your expertise; delete barren rows/columns. (5) Pick the cell with the most branching options and narrow in.

Trade-offs: Overhead before any ideation, and the axes you choose bound what you can find. Its payoff is knowing where you didn't look — free brainstorming can't tell you that.

Constraints into Opportunities

When to use: The brief feels impossibly restrictive (budget, format, tech, time).

How: List every constraint. Invent one named audience persona with a history and goals. Convert each constraint into an advantage for that person. Repeat with a different persona.

Trade-offs: Requires taking the constraints as fixed, which is wrong sometimes. But the more rigid the box, the better people think inside it — the most-constrained groups produce the highest-rated work.

The Three R's of Transplanting

When to use: You've noticed a concept in another domain that might apply to yours.

How: Recognition — name the candidate connection. Relevance — map element to element what actually overlaps; be explicit, not metaphorical. Refinement — prototype in the new context with domain experts. Different people are often good at different R's; staff each stage separately.

Trade-offs: Stopping after Recognition is the default failure — a pleasing analogy that never gets tested. Relevance is where most transplants die, and should.

Push Past the Creative Cliff

When to use: Any Digging session, at the exact moment you feel tapped out.

How: Set a target and then double or triple it. Run a deliberate second and third round after the point where you'd normally stop. Sort output into at least 3 categories to expose thin regions.

Trade-offs: Uncomfortable and feels wasteful. The felt cliff is an illusion — later ideas rate higher in quality, and the first idea suppresses creativity while the ninety-seventh may enhance it.

Narrative Reversal Sweep

When to use: The idea set is competent but predictable.

How: List the assumptions your idea rests on. For each, ask "what if the opposite were true?" Keep the ones that are still coherent.

Trade-offs: Generates a lot of nonsense per usable reversal. Cheap enough that the ratio doesn't matter.

Group Digging Protocol

When to use: Ideation with more than one person.

How: Declare an evaluation-free zone. Separate Digging from Sifting into different sessions. Formalize turn-taking (randomize with cards or an RNG). Accept anonymous submissions. Purposely generate bad ideas. Let someone other than the senior person lead. Enforce "yes, and."

Trade-offs: Feels bureaucratic. Without it, the highest-status voice sets the frame and collective intelligence collapses.

Engaging Your Weak Ties

When to use: Your idea set is converging and everyone around you agrees with you.

How: Consult acquaintances outside your cluster — unprimed, without pre-explaining what you want to hear. Reach for people whose domain doesn't overlap yours.

Trade-offs: Weak ties give less committed help. But strong ties mostly know what you already know; turtling-up under pressure is the anti-pattern.

Sifting with Others

When to use: You must select from your own list — i.e., always, because the creative endowment effect makes self-selection unreliable.
