How: Hand your list to someone else and compare their picks with yours. Or shelve the list for weeks-to-months and re-select with time-created distance. Warning yourself about the bias does not work; only distance does.

Trade-offs: Costs calendar time or social capital. Being told about the bias, or shown examples, demonstrably fails to correct it.

Floating a Raft (not Building a Tower)

When to use: Cutting an over-built piece of work.

How: Write out your guiding question. Go element by element and state what each contributes to it. Cut anything that doesn't serve it — including material you love. Ask what an audience inspecting this for holes would find.

Trade-offs: Painful; the tangent material is often the prettiest. People almost never edit by subtraction unless explicitly prompted to.

The Mid-Stakes Event

When to use: The work could drift indefinitely, and low-stakes feedback isn't forcing decisions.

How: Schedule a dated exposure to a real but non-gatekeeping audience. Before it, write down predicted reactions. After, audit your predictions against what happened.

Trade-offs: Manufactured deadlines can force premature closure. The prediction audit — not the feedback — is the durable payoff: it calibrates your taste.

Develop the Uncomfortable Idea

When to use: Sifting a list where one idea keeps making you uneasy.

How: Rank ideas most to least comfortable. Take the most uncomfortable and develop it for 10–15 minutes before discarding. Treat discomfort as an information gap, not a verdict.

Trade-offs: Most uncomfortable ideas are just bad. Cheap to test, and the ones that survive are disproportionately the interesting ones.

Planning for Feedback

When to use: Before every feedback conversation.

How: Decide the purpose of the feedback. Provide context — state your guiding question first. Ask better questions: replace "Do you like this?" with "What specific aspects are strong / could be improved?" and "Does this remind you of other things you've seen?" Pre-declare what you will not change.

Trade-offs: Framing the ask constrains what you'll hear. Unframed feedback is mostly noise about taste.

The Bell Curve of Feedback

When to use: Triaging a pile of responses.

How: Weight the tails — the outlier comments — over the agreeable middle. Then triage the middle by frequency: if many people trip on the same thing, it's real regardless of how they explain it.

Trade-offs: Tails include cranks. Frequency alone would have you optimize for the median and sand off everything distinctive.

Tweak, Don't Restart (Wright's law)

When to use: The work is underperforming and starting over feels attractive.

How: Pivot adjacent and ship again. Volume of iterations, not restarts, drives the improvement curve — roughly 10–15% better per doubling of cumulative output.

Trade-offs: Locks you into the current region of the space, so it only works after Surveying and Gridding were done honestly. Watch for the identity trap: refusing a tweak because the current version feels like you.

AI as Excavator

When to use: Digging within a region you have already mapped.

How: Guide it to the specific gridded region, solicit many candidates, then curate with intent. Keep the human on Surveying, Gridding, and Sifting.

Trade-offs: Powerful for volume, but produces a homogenization effect across users. Use it for surface work (Digging); keep deep work — deciding where to search and what to keep — yours.

In the Line of Fire: How to Handle Tough Questions...When It Counts

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — In the Line of Fire

The one rule above all

Question → Buffer → Answer (head-on, ≤60s, with evidence) → Topspin. Skip the answer = evasive (politician's sin). Skip the Topspin = no influence (businessperson's sin). And: every answer must be true.

Decision tree: a question just landed

  • Do I understand it 100%? No → Return to Sender ("I'm sorry, I didn't follow; would you mind restating?"). Never interpret/speculate.
  • Is it factually inaccurate / an accusation? → Skip the Buffer; refute immediately ("No."), then support, then restate rebuttal.
  • Is the charge actually true? → Guilty-as-Charged: Buffer → Agree → "But…" → Evidence → Call to action+benefit.
  • Multiple unrelated questions? → Pick ONE; answer; then "You had another question."
  • Otherwise → Buffer (paraphrase or key word) → wait for head nod → answer → Topspin.

Buffer: pick your form

FormWhenCost
Paraphrase ("Why this price point?")hostile question; need thinking timeoveruse = stilted
"You" + paraphrase ("Your question is…")want Eye Connect + read the nodsounds like a "hoot owl" if every time
Key Words ("Our pricing rationale is…")Roman Column already crystal clearzero thinking time — must be sure

Cool-zone rule (positioning the Roman Column)

  • Repeat the charged question → land in "Guilty!" (left danger zone).
  • Reverse/invalidate it → land in "Contentious!" (right danger zone).
  • Neutral paraphrase of the bare key word → cool zone. ✅

Find the Roman Column — don't grab the wrapper

Hostile question ends with…Wrapper (wrong)Roman Column (right)
"…charging so much!"overpricing/expensiveprice
"…think you can survive?"survivecompete
"…you, a woman…old boy network?"sexismcapability
"…throw in your lot / get acquired?"mergeindependence

Tells & smells (read the room)

  • Involuntary head nod after your Buffer = you nailed the Roman Column → answer now. Frown / head-shake = wrong → Return to Sender.
  • Questioner's voice rises on "really" / "saying" ("What I'm really asking…") = "You're not listening!" alarm.
  • Your own slouch / hands-in-pockets / glance at watch = audience reads "bored, doesn't care" within ~5 seconds.
  • On camera, involuntary disdain (Scowl/Sigh) is fatal — assume you're always on a split screen.

Three ways to lose (diagnose fast)

Defensive (squirm/stammer) · Evasive (answer a different question) · Contentious (attack — the worst; = visible loss of control). All are Fight-or-Flight. Antidote: firm, calm resolve + the sequence.

Delete from your vocabulary

"Let me see if I have this right…" · "Could you repeat the question?" · "Does that answer your question?" · "Is what you're asking…?" · "The question is…" · "What you're really asking…" · "If I understand your question…" · "The issue/concern is…" · "As I said…" · "Why do you ask?"

Special questions — fast rules

  • Unknown → admit, promise follow-up, ask for a card (unless central — then answer).
  • Confidential → give a positive reason (policy/security/legality); never "I can't reveal that." Then Topspin.
  • Speculative/forecast → "It's impossible to say how long it'll take, but…" → Topspin to Point B + WIIFY.
  • Irrelevant → there's no such thing; Buffer the snicker away, then answer or take offline.

Topspin targets

Point B = what you want them to DO (call to action). WIIFY = WHY they should (their benefit). End on one or both — never on a negative. Earn it by answering first.

Prep checklist (before the session)

☐ List the questions you don't want to hear ☐ Position statement (press-release style) for each red-flag issue (Mgmt, Competition, Growth, Price, Contingencies, Timing, Problems, IP) ☐ Gather evidence ☐ Verbalize aloud Buffers + answers + a Topspin on each, with colleagues firing questions ☐ Set time expectations; plan the countdown.

Open-the-floor mechanics

Open hand, never point (one-plus-three). All names or no names — never selective. Raise your hand to invite hands — but not with investors/board.

glossary.md

Glossary — In the Line of Fire

Active Listening — Concentrating fully on the questioner to extract the Roman Column; the martial art of Concentration (Ch 4).

Agility counters Force — Core principle: beat a stronger/larger opponent (one-against-many) with skill and leverage, not brute force (Intro, Ch 9).

Anticipate — Pre-compile the worst questions you might face (questions only, not canned answers) (Ch 6, 8).

Back reference ("As I said…") — Citing earlier material; banned in Q&A as condescending. Use forward references only (Ch 5).

Buffer — A neutral restatement of a question that deflects negativity and tees up the answer; first line of self-defense. Three forms: paraphrase, "you"+paraphrase, Key Words (Ch 5).

Contentious — Combative reaction to a question (e.g., Perot's "You're lying!"); most damaging negative behavior (Ch 1, 9).

Control — The one-word thesis of the book; managing the question, answer, questioner, audience, time, and yourself (Intro).

Cool Zone — The neutral center where the Roman Column belongs; left zone = "Guilty!" (repeat), right zone = "Contentious!" (reverse) (Ch 5).

Defensive — Self-protective reaction (squirming, stammering) under a tough question (Ch 1).

Double Buffer — A buffer in front of the Buffer ("The question is…", "Glad you asked"); mostly useless fillers — fix by inserting "you" (Ch 5).

Effective Management (Perceived) — The positive subliminal impression created by well-handled questions; the goal of all techniques (Intro).

Empty your cup — Zen lesson: clear your own thoughts to receive the questioner's (Ch 4).

Evasive — Answering a different question than the one asked (Lott; Pedro Martinez) (Ch 1).

Eye Connect — Locking eyes with the questioner until they look back ("the click of engagement"); stronger than "eye contact" (Ch 4, 5).

Fight or Flight — The instinctive stress reaction underlying defensive/evasive (flight) and contentious (fight) behavior (Ch 1, 7).

Forward reference — Answering presented material fresh, without "as I said"; the only reference allowed in Q&A (Ch 5).

Guilty as Charged — A question whose charge is true; handled by the 5-step sequence: Buffer → Agree → "But…" → Evidence → Call to action + benefit (Ch 6).

Head nod (involuntary) — The questioner's automatic assent to a correct Buffer; your accuracy meter (a frown = wrong) (Ch 5).

Key Words (Buffer) — The most advanced Buffer: embed the key word and roll straight into the answer; zero thinking time, maximum sharpness (Ch 5).

Manage the Answer — Meet the issue only head-on; no tangents; ~60-second max (Ch 6).

Paraphrase — Restating the question "alongside" (para) in neutral form — NOT re-phrasing (re = again, carries the negative). Interrogative + Roman Column, voice drops at end (Ch 5).

Point A → Point B — A = audience uninformed/unconvinced; B = convinced and ready to act. Point B is your call to action (Ch 6).

Quid Pro Quo — "If they ask it, you must answer it"; address the Roman Column directly (Ch 6).

Red Flag Issues (Universal) — The handful of recurring concern areas: Management, Competition, Growth, Price/Cost, Contingencies, Timing, Problems, Intellectual Property (Ch 6).

Return to Sender — When you don't understand 100%, hand the floor back: "I'm sorry, I didn't follow; would you mind restating the question?" (Ch 4, 5).

Roman Column — The one or two words at the heart of a question (named for orators' memory-trigger columns); find it before answering. Questions can have a double Roman Column (Ch 4).

Sub-vocalization — Silently naming the key issue under your breath to crystallize the Roman Column (Ch 4).

Topspin — Ending an answer with Point B/WIIFY for a strong, offensive close (tennis metaphor); must be earned by answering first (Ch 6, 7).

Triple Fail-Safe — Three checkpoints before answering: ① grasp the Roman Column (else Return to Sender) ② Buffer + wait for head nod ③ frown → Return to Sender (Ch 5).

Verbalize — Rehearse answers aloud (Buffers, answers, Topspin) like a tennis volley (Ch 5, 8).

Visual Listening — Physical signals of attentiveness: balanced stance, Eye Connect, head nods, voice assent, steady fingers (Ch 4).

WIIFY — "What's In It For You" (pronounced "whiffy"); the audience's reason to act — why they should move to Point B (Ch 6).

Winning Sequence — Question → Buffer → Answer (with evidence) → Topspin (Ch 10).

Worst-Case Scenario — Prep assumption: every question maximally hostile, every group large (Ch 2).

"Wrong Q&A" — Weissman's rename of "Rude Q&A": pre-canning answers before understanding the question (Ch 3).

"You're not listening!" — The fatal audience perception (cousins: "That's not what I asked," "What I'm really asking…") (Ch 3).

"Ready, Fire, Aim!" — Answering before the target (key issue) is in your sights (Ch 3).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — In the Line of Fire

The Winning Sequence (master pattern)

When to use: every challenging question.

How: Question → Buffer (neutralize) → Answer the Roman Column head-on, with evidence → Topspin (Point B / WIIFY).

Trade-offs: Politicians skip the answer (jump to Topspin) → look evasive. Businesspeople skip the Topspin → exert zero influence. Do all four.

Find the Roman Column

When: before answering anything.

How: "Empty your cup"; listen for the 1–2 nouns/verbs that are the essence; sub-vocalize them ("She's worried about cost"). Strip away emotion, misinformation, ramble. Watch for a double column.

Trade-offs: Mistaking the emotional wrapper (e.g., "sexism," "survive") for the column lands you in a danger zone.

Paraphrase Buffer

When: hostile/charged questions; buys thinking time.

How: Interrogative (What/Why/How/Does/Can/Is) + Roman Column, voice drops at end. Strip charged words; fewest words possible. Keep it in the cool zone (don't repeat = guilty; don't reverse = contentious).

Trade-offs: Overuse sounds stilted ("hoot owl"), especially "you"-phrased.

Key Word Buffer (advanced)

When: you already have 100% clarity; non-challenging direct questions; when you want to look razor-sharp.

How: embed the key word and roll straight into the answer ("Our pricing rationale is…").

Trade-offs: zero thinking time — only safe when the Roman Column is crystal clear. (Powell, Schwarzkopf.)

The Power of "You"

When: building a Double Buffer you'd otherwise delete.

How: "Your question is…" not "The question is…"; keeps Eye Connect, reads the head nod, most persuasive word in English.

Triple Fail-Safe

When: every answer, as a guard against rushing.

How: ① Don't retake the floor without the Roman Column → Return to Sender. ② Buffer with the key word; hold Eye Connect until the involuntary head nod. ③ Frown instead of nod → Return to Sender.

Return to Sender

When: you don't understand 100% (not 99.999%), or you get a frown.

How: take responsibility — "I'm sorry, I didn't follow; would you mind restating the question?" Never interpret, speculate, or use the deafness ruse.

Guilty-as-Charged Sequence (5 steps)

When: the charge is true.

How: Buffer → Agree (their words) → "But…" (loud; don't agree too long) → Evidence → Call to action + benefit (Point B + WIIFY).

Trade-offs: In media exchanges, do NOT agree (sound-bite risk) — counter immediately or bury the admission in a subordinate clause before Topspin.

Refute the Inaccurate Question

When: a question contains/implies a falsehood ("When did you stop beating your wife?").

How: skip the Buffer; immediate complete refutation — "No." Then support, then restate the rebuttal. (Powell: "No, of course not… But there is no list.")

Handle Special Question Types

  • Multiple disparate: pick ONE (easiest/hardest/last/surprising), Buffer + answer it, then "You had another question."
  • Statement (non-question): turn into a question via paraphrase.
  • Irrelevant/Tangential: no such thing as irrelevant — Buffer to suppress the snicker, then answer or take offline.
  • Unknown: admit it, promise follow-up, ask for a card (unless central — then you must answer).
  • Confidential/Speculative: give a positive reason (policy/security/legality); don't forecast; still pivot to Topspin.
  • Presented material: answer fresh, forward references only, never "As I said…"; be succinct.

Topspin

When: after a real answer, to close strong.

How: end with Point B (what you want them to do) and/or WIIFY (why they should). Add multiple upward swirls. Counters any "too-anything" charge (Yang to Yin).

Trade-offs: Topspin before answering = evasive (G.W. Bush / Lisa Kee). Never end on a negative (Dukakis).

Manage the Time

When: opening any Q&A.

How: set expectations up front ("time for only a few questions"); count down at the end ("two more… last question"). (Schwarzkopf: 10 questions in 2:48.)

Q&A Cycle Control Moves

Open floor (control time + traffic; open hand, never point; all-names-or-no-names) → Recognize → Yield (mind your body language — no slouch) → Retake (Buffer) → Answer (+Topspin). Repeats per questioner.

Prepare & Verbalize

When: before any mission-critical session.

How: list worst questions → position statement (press-release style) per red-flag issue → enlist colleagues to fire questions → verbalize aloud your Buffers, answers, and a Topspin on each, repeatedly. Treat every Q&A like an IPO road show.

Thinking, Fast and Slow

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Thinking, Fast and Slow

Decision rules and tells you'd want beside you while judging, forecasting, or choosing.

Bias → Tell → Countermove

If you notice…You're probably in…Do this
A story feels complete and obviousWYSIATI / illusion of validityAsk "what's missing?"; check evidence quality, not just coherence
A vivid case drives your risk estimateAvailability heuristicLook up the actual base rate / frequency
A number was mentioned before you estimatedAnchoringEstimate independently first; argue the anchor is wrong
A description matches a stereotypeRepresentativeness / base-rate neglectStart from the base rate, adjust by evidence's real validity
Extreme result → confident causal storyRegression fallacyExpect regression to the mean; no cause needed
"This time/we are different"Planning fallacy / competition neglectTake the outside view (reference class)
Confident expert in a noisy fieldIllusion of skillApply the two-condition test (below)
One good trait colors the whole judgmentHalo effectScore independent traits separately
You're holding a loser to avoid selling at a lossSunk cost / disposition effectAsk "would I buy this today?"
Choice flips when rewordedFraming effectRestate in the opposite frame + common units

Should I trust this intuition? (Expert-intuition test)

1. Is the environment regular/predictable (valid cues exist)? → if No, don't trust it.

2. Was there prolonged practice with rapid, clear feedback? → if No, don't trust it.

3. Both Yes → trust the intuition. (High validity: anesthesiology, chess, firefighting. Low: stock picking, long-term political forecasting.)

Subjective confidence ≠ accuracy. Certainty is a feeling, not evidence.

Prospect theory in one screen

  • Value is over changes from a reference point, not final wealth.
  • Loss aversion: losses hurt ~1.5–2.5× more than equal gains delight.
  • Diminishing sensitivity: $0→$100 feels bigger than $900→$1000.
  • Decision weights ≠ probabilities: rare events overweighted; near-certain events underweighted.

Fourfold pattern (risk attitudes)

GainsLosses
High probability (certainty effect)Risk-averse — take the sure thing (accept unfavorable settlement)Risk-seeking — gamble to avoid sure loss (reject favorable settlement, "go to court")
Low probability (possibility effect)Risk-seeking — buy lottery ticketsRisk-averse — buy insurance

Forecasting rules of thumb

  • Regress predictions to the mean by (1 − correlation): weak evidence → stay near baseline.
  • Equal-weight formulas beat holistic judgment in low-validity settings; consistency > cleverness.
  • Reference-class base rate first, case details second.
  • Run a premortem before locking a big decision.

Two selves — decision defaults

  • Experiencing self feels moments; remembering self keeps score via peak-end + duration neglect.
  • Memory over-rewards good endings and ignores duration → don't confuse a good story with a good life.
  • Focusing illusion: "Nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it." Discount how much any single change (income, climate, new car) will shift lasting well-being.

System 1 vs System 2 (fast reference)

System 1System 2
SpeedFast, automaticSlow, effortful
FeelEffortless, always onCostly, lazy, depletable
JobImpressions, intuitions, patternsChecking, computing, self-control
Failure modeBiases, WYSIATIEndorses System 1 without checking

System 2 is the lazy controller: it usually ratifies System 1. Deliberate friction (slow down, ask for base rates, reframe) is the only reliable fix.

glossary.md

Glossary — Thinking, Fast and Slow

Affect heuristic — Letting likes and dislikes determine beliefs about risks and benefits; emotion substitutes for analysis (Ch 9, Ch 13).

Affective forecasting — Predicting how future events will make you feel; usually distorted by the focusing illusion (Ch 38).

Anchoring effect — A number you consider before estimating pulls your estimate toward it, even when arbitrary (Ch 11).

Anchoring index — The ratio measuring how much an anchor moves estimates; ~55% is common (Ch 11).

Associative activation — One idea automatically triggering a cascade of linked ideas, emotions, and bodily responses (Ch 4).

Availability cascade — A self-sustaining chain where media coverage of a minor risk breeds public fear that breeds more coverage (Ch 13).

Availability heuristic — Judging frequency or probability by how easily examples come to mind (Ch 12, Ch 13).

Base rate — The prior probability of an outcome in the population, before individuating evidence (Ch 14, Ch 16).

Base-rate neglect — Ignoring statistical base rates in favor of a representative description (Ch 14, Ch 16).

Bernoulli's error — Modeling utility as a function of wealth states rather than changes relative to a reference point (Ch 25, Ch 26).

Broad framing — Evaluating decisions as part of a portfolio of many similar choices rather than one at a time (Ch 31, Ch 34).

Certainty effect — Overweighting outcomes that move from very likely to certain; drives the fourfold pattern (Ch 29).

Cognitive ease — A pleasant state of low mental strain signaling that things are familiar, true, and safe; opposite of cognitive strain (Ch 5).

Competition neglect — Ignoring rivals' plans when forecasting your own success ("this town is big enough only for us") (Ch 24).

Conjunction fallacy — Judging a specific conjunction (Linda is a feminist bank teller) as more probable than one of its parts (Ch 15).

Decision weights — The psychological weights the mind assigns to outcomes, differing from their objective probabilities (Ch 29, Ch 30).

Denominator neglect — Focusing on the numerator (13 winning marbles) and ignoring the denominator, so vivid frequencies beat probabilities (Ch 30).

Diminishing sensitivity — Each additional unit of gain or loss feels smaller as you move away from the reference point (Ch 26).

Disposition effect — Selling winners and holding losers to avoid closing a mental account at a loss (Ch 32).

Duration neglect — When evaluating an experience, ignoring how long it lasted (Ch 35).

Ego depletion — Reduced self-control and effort after prior mental exertion (Ch 3).

Endowment effect — Valuing something more merely because you own it; selling price exceeds buying price (Ch 27).

Experiencing self — The self that lives in the present moment and feels each experience as it happens (Ch 35, Ch 37).

Expert intuition — Reliable pattern recognition, valid only in high-validity, regular environments with prolonged practice and rapid feedback (Ch 22).

Focusing illusion — "Nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it"; attention inflates the felt weight of any factor (Ch 38).

Fourfold pattern — The signature pattern of risk attitudes across gains/losses × high/low probability (Ch 29).

Framing effect — Logically equivalent descriptions (survival vs. mortality, 90% fat-free vs. 10% fat) producing different choices (Ch 34).

Halo effect — Letting one salient trait (or first impression) color your evaluation of everything else about a person (Ch 7, Ch 19).

Hindsight bias — After an event, believing you knew it would happen; the "I-knew-it-all-along" effect (Ch 19).

Illusion of validity — Unjustified confidence in a judgment that fits a coherent story, despite poor predictive accuracy (Ch 20).

Intensity matching — Translating a value on one scale (crime severity) onto another (loudness, dollars) automatically (Ch 8, Ch 9).

Law of small numbers — Overtrusting small samples and seeing patterns in what is really sampling noise (Ch 10).

Loss aversion — Losses loom larger than equivalent gains, by a factor of roughly 1.5–2.5 (Ch 26, Ch 28).

Mental accounting — Keeping money and outcomes in separate psychological accounts that shouldn't be treated separately (Ch 32).

Mere exposure effect — Repeated exposure to a stimulus increasing liking for it (Ch 5).

Mood/coherence (WYSIATI) — "What You See Is All There Is": building confident stories from available evidence while ignoring what's missing (Ch 7, Ch 19–20).

Narrative fallacy — Constructing simple, coherent stories of the past that overweight skill and intention and hide the role of luck (Ch 19).

Norm theory — System 1 maintains a model of what's normal; deviations trigger surprise and a search for causes (Ch 6).

Outside view — Forecasting by using the statistics of a reference class of similar cases, instead of the details of your own case (Ch 23).

Peak-end rule — Retrospective evaluation of an episode is dominated by its most intense moment and its ending (Ch 35).

Planning fallacy — Plans and forecasts that are unrealistically close to best-case scenarios (Ch 23).

Possibility effect — Overweighting a change from impossible to merely possible (0% → 5%) far more than a proportional change in the middle (Ch 29, Ch 30).

Priming — Exposure to one idea unconsciously influencing thoughts and actions related to it (Ch 4).

Prospect theory — Kahneman & Tversky's descriptive theory of choice: value defined over gains/losses from a reference point, with loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity, and nonlinear decision weights (Ch 26).

Regression to the mean — Extreme observations tend to be followed by more average ones, purely statistically (Ch 17).

Regression fallacy — Inventing a causal story for what is only regression to the mean (praise/punishment "working") (Ch 17).

Remembering self — The self that keeps score, tells the story, and makes decisions based on memories, not moments (Ch 35, Ch 36).

Representativeness — Judging probability by similarity to a stereotype or prototype, ignoring base rates and sample size (Ch 14, Ch 15).

Reference point — The status quo or expectation against which outcomes are coded as gains or losses (Ch 26).

Risk policy — A standing rule to treat repeated small risks broadly ("always take the favorable gamble"), reducing narrow-framing errors (Ch 31).

Substitution — Answering an easier heuristic question in place of the hard target question, without noticing (Ch 9).

Sunk-cost fallacy — Continuing a failing endeavor because of resources already invested (Ch 32).

System 1 — Fast, automatic, effortless, associative, intuitive thinking; always on (Ch 1).

System 2 — Slow, effortful, deliberate, rule-governed thinking; lazy and capacity-limited (Ch 1, Ch 3).

Theory-induced blindness — Once you accept a theory, its flaws become nearly impossible to see (Ch 25, Ch 26).

U-index — The fraction of time a person spends in an unpleasant emotional state (Ch 37).

Utility (experienced vs. decision) — Experienced utility is the pleasure/pain actually felt; decision utility is the weight given to an outcome when choosing (Ch 25, Ch 37).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Thinking, Fast and Slow

Concrete, reusable methods Kahneman endorses for making better judgments and decisions.

Take the Outside View (Reference-Class Forecasting)

When to use: Any plan, estimate, or forecast (project timelines, budgets, success odds).

How:

1. Identify a reference class of past, similar cases.

2. Get the distribution of actual outcomes for that class (the base rate).

3. Use that base rate as your anchor.

4. Adjust for your specific case only with information that has proven predictive value.

Trade-offs: Feels impersonal and can be resisted ("we're different"); requires real reference data. Counters the planning fallacy and optimism bias.

Run a Premortem

When to use: Before committing to a major decision the group is converging on.

How: Assemble the people who know about the decision. Say: "Imagine it's a year from now and this plan has failed disastrously. Write the history of that failure." Legitimizing dissent surfaces risks that groupthink and the illusion of validity suppress.

Trade-offs: Doesn't stop bad decisions outright; it widens the search for problems and tempers overconfidence.

Decompose an Intuitive Prediction (Regress Toward the Mean)

When to use: Predicting an outcome (GPA, sales, performance) from an impression or single indicator.

How:

1. Start from the baseline (the average outcome / base rate).

2. Make your intuitive prediction from the evidence.

3. Estimate the correlation between your evidence and the outcome.

4. Move from baseline toward your intuitive prediction by that fraction (e.g. correlation 0.3 → move 30% of the way).

Trade-offs: Deliberately sacrifices vivid, extreme predictions for calibrated moderate ones; feels less satisfying but is more accurate.

Adopt Broad Framing & Risk Policies

When to use: Repeated, small, independent risky decisions (investments, insurance, deadlines).

How: Decide a standing rule you'll apply to the whole class ("never buy extended warranties"; "always take the favorable gamble if I can afford the loss") rather than agonizing over each instance in isolation.

Trade-offs: Reduces loss-averse, narrow-framing errors and emotional churn; requires discipline to hold the policy when a single loss stings.

Use Algorithms / Simple Formulas Over Clinical Judgment

When to use: Repeated predictions in low-validity, noisy environments (hiring, admissions, loan approval, medical triage).

How: Select 2–6 predictive, independent attributes; score each on a standard scale; sum with equal weights. Trust the total over a holistic gut feel. (Apgar score is the archetype.)

Trade-offs: Experts resist ceding judgment; formulas beat them mainly because they're consistent, not smarter.

Structure Interviews to Beat the Halo Effect

When to use: Evaluating candidates or options where a first impression contaminates the rest.

How: Predefine 4–6 independent traits. Score each trait separately, one at a time, across all candidates before forming an overall view. Sum the scores; give the formula its due weight.

Trade-offs: Slower and less "intuitive"; sharply improves validity.

Reframe to Neutralize Framing Effects

When to use: Any consequential choice stated in one frame (losses vs gains, survival vs mortality, monthly vs annual cost).

How: Restate the same facts in the opposite frame and in a common unit; decide only if your choice survives both framings. Adopt "Econ" defaults where possible.

Trade-offs: Effortful System 2 work; most people won't do it unaided — so design defaults for others (nudges).

Trust Expert Intuition Only Under Two Conditions

When to use: Deciding whether to believe a confident expert (or yourself).

How: Ask (1) Is the environment regular and predictable enough to contain valid cues? (2) Did the expert have prolonged practice with rapid, unambiguous feedback? Both yes → trust it. Otherwise treat the confidence as an illusion of validity.

Trade-offs: Confidence and subjective certainty are not evidence of skill; long experience in an irregular world (e.g. stock picking) breeds skill-less confidence.

Guard Against WYSIATI

When to use: Whenever a story feels coherent and conclusion feels obvious.

How: Ask "What would I need to know that I don't?" and "What's the quality and quantity of the evidence?" Deliberately seek disconfirming data and the base rate.

Trade-offs: Coherence is seductive; this friction is the price of calibration.

Design for the Peak-End & Duration Neglect

When to use: Designing experiences (service, care, events) or reasoning about your own well-being.

How: Improve the most intense moment and, especially, the ending; don't assume adding pleasant-but-milder time at the end helps memory. For your own choices, ask whether you're optimizing the experiencing self or the remembering self.

Trade-offs: What memory rewards (a good ending) and what the experiencing self lives through can diverge.

The Personal MBA: Master the Art of Business

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Personal MBA decision rules

One page of Kaufman's judgment: when to do what, and why.

The master diagnostic — Five Parts of Every Business

A struggling business is failing at one of these. Diagnose in order:

1. Value Creation — does it make something people want? (If no market wants it, nothing else matters — Iron Law.)

2. Marketing — does the right audience pay Attention?

3. Sales — do they trust you enough to buy at a price you can support?

4. Value Delivery — do they get what they expected, repeatably?

5. Finance — is there enough profit to keep going?

If you can't clearly describe all five for an idea, you don't have a business yet.

Decision rules

When…Do…Because…
Evaluating any ideaScore the market on the Ten Ways firstThe Iron Law: market beats offer every time
You "feel sure" about an ideaList CIAs and Shadow Test themConviction isn't evidence; a preorder is
Gathering feedbackIgnore friends/family; seek paying strangersOnly money is honest feedback
Setting a priceCompute 4 methods, price on Value ComparisonValue-to-buyer is almost always the highest support
A price feels "too high to charge"Raise it and support itAll prices are arbitrary (Pricing Uncertainty Principle)
Prospect hesitatesAdd Risk Reversal + a Damaging AdmissionShifting risk and admitting flaws both build Trust
Want more revenuePull one of the Four Methods; start with ReactivationLapsed customers are the cheapest to sell
Deciding marketing spendCap it at AAC (marketing slice of LTV)Spend more and each customer loses money
Improving anythingRun WIGWAM, maximize Iteration VelocityMore at-bats beats one big bet
A system underperformsFind the one Constraint, fix only thatOptimizing non-constraints yields nothing
OptimizingAttack the Critical Few (20%); stop at the 85% SolutionDiminishing Returns make the last 15% costly
Tempted to act when unsureConsider Cessation (do nothing)Absence Blindness makes "do nothing" feel wrong when it's right
Designing a new complex systemStart simple, evolve itGall's Law: complex-from-scratch never works
Behavior won't changeChange the Environment, not the willpowerGuiding Structure beats discipline
DelegatingGive Commander's Intent, not step-by-stepPeople adapt to Change only if they know why

Numbers & thresholds Kaufman commits to

  • Team size: 3–8 people (Communication Overhead grows fast past that).
  • Dunbar's number: ~150 — beyond it, minds treat people as statistics (Cognitive Scope Limitation).
  • Decide at 40–70% of available information; less is reckless, more is paralysis.
  • Loss Aversion ≈ 2×: losses feel about twice as strong as equal gains.
  • Pareto: ~20% of inputs → ~80% of outputs (often more extreme).
  • 85% Solution: stop optimizing where added effort exceeds returns.
  • Personal R&D: reinvest ~5% of monthly income in your own learning.
  • Attention span: ~30 min before even motivated minds need Novelty.
  • MITs: 2–3 per day, chosen before the day starts.

Quality & value formulas

  • Quality = Performance − Expectations (manage both; never over-promise).
  • Perceived Value = better End Result + less customer effort.
  • Profit Margin = (revenue − cost) ÷ cost; Value Capture too high → customers flee.
  • Sufficiency = the profit point where continuing is worth it ("ramen profitable").

Tells & smells (recognize the trap fast)

  • Measuring an easy proxy (lines of code, hours logged) → you'll reward the wrong behavior.
  • A correlation cited as a reason to act → demand the full cause-effect chain first.
  • "We'll just add more automation" → recall the Paradox of Automation: you need better humans, not fewer.
  • Optimizing a metric while the system gets fragile → you're trading Resilience for Throughput.
  • Defending a choice by past investment → that's a Sunk Cost; ignore it.
  • Blaming a person's character for a failure → likely Attribution Error; check circumstances.
  • Tightly coupled system "running fine" → Normal Accidents: failure is when, not if. Build a Fail-safe now.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Personal MBA

Key terms with one-line definitions and the chapter that introduces them.

Absence Blindness — We can't perceive what isn't there, so prevention and "doing nothing" go unrewarded; beat it with checklists (Ch 7).

Accumulation — Small helpful or harmful inputs compound over time into huge results (Ch 5).

Addressability — How easily you can reach people who might want your offer (Ch 3).

Akrasia / Conflict — Two control systems fighting over the same perception (work vs. rest = procrastination) (Ch 7, Ch 8).

Allowable Acquisition Cost (AAC) — The maximum you can spend to acquire a new customer; the marketing slice of Lifetime Value (Ch 6).

Amortization — Spreading the cost of a large resource investment across its useful life (Ch 6).

Amplification — A small change to a scalable system produces a huge result (Ch 5).

Analytical Honesty — Measuring data dispassionately, resisting the pull to make things look better (Ch 11).

Association — The mind links co-occurring things even when illogical (Coke = happiness) (Ch 7).

Attention — The scarce, rationed resource every offer competes for (Ch 3).

Attribution Error — When others fail we blame their character; when we fail we blame circumstances (Ch 9).

Authority — People comply with authority figures even against their own judgment (Milgram) (Ch 9).

Autocatalysis — A self-reinforcing loop whose output feeds the next cycle (network effects) (Ch 10).

Barrier to Competition — Every Value Stream improvement makes you harder to replicate (Ch 5).

Barriers to Purchase — The five standard objections blocking a sale: too expensive, won't work, won't work for me, can wait, too hard (Ch 4).

Breakeven — The point where cumulative revenue exceeds cumulative expenses (Ch 6).

Buffer — A third party (agent, broker) empowered to negotiate for you (Ch 4).

Bundling / Unbundling — Combine offers to raise perceived value, or split one into many to open new sales (Ch 2).

Bystander Apathy — More people who could act means fewer who actually act (Ch 9).

Call-to-Action (CTA) — Directing a prospect to one single, obvious next action (Ch 3).

Caveman Syndrome — We run demanding modern life on survival-tuned biology (Ch 7).

Cessation — Intentionally stopping something counterproductive; often the better move (Ch 12).

Checklist — An externalized, predefined SOP for a specific task (Ch 12).

Clanning — Humans automatically form in-groups and out-groups (Ch 9).

Cognitive Scope Limitation — Past ~150 people (Dunbar's number) we treat people as statistics (Ch 7).

Cognitive Switching Penalty — Every attention shift forces the brain to reload context — a Friction cost (Ch 8).

Commander's Intent — Tell people why a task matters, not just how, so they adapt when circumstances change (Ch 9).

Common Ground — The overlap between your options and the prospect's; a precondition for a deal (Ch 4).

Communication Overhead — Time spent communicating instead of producing; grows with team size — keep teams 3–8 (Ch 9).

Comparative Advantage — Capitalize on your strengths; specialize and trade rather than do everything (Ch 8, Ch 9).

Constraint (Theory of Constraints) — One critical input limits the whole system; fix it and Throughput rises (Ch 10).

Context — Related measurements used to interpret data; numbers in isolation say little (Ch 11).

Contrast — We judge by comparison to what's present, not what's absent (pricing camouflage) (Ch 7).

Convergence and Divergence — Group members grow alike; rival groups grow apart (Ch 9).

Core Human Drives — Five drives shaping buying: Acquire, Bond, Learn, Defend, Feel (Ch 2).

Correlation and Causation — Moving together (correlation) is not a repeatable cause-effect chain (causation) (Ch 11).

Counterparty Risk — The risk that a partner won't deliver, damaging your Reputation (Ch 5, Ch 10).

Critical Few (Pareto / 80-20) — ~20% of inputs produce ~80% of outputs (Ch 12).

Critically Important Assumptions (CIAs) — Facts that must be true for the offer to succeed (Ch 2).

Damaging Admission — Volunteering a real drawback, which counterintuitively raises Trust (Ch 4).

Deconstruction — Break a system into the smallest subsystems, understand each, rebuild (Ch 11).

Decision — Committing to one path by cutting off others; decide at 40–70% of information (Ch 8).

Desire — The visceral wanting marketing connects to; you can't manufacture it, only tap it (Ch 3).

Diminishing Returns — Past a point, more of a good thing is detrimental (the "85% Solution") (Ch 12).

Distribution Channel — How value reaches the user: direct (control, capped) or intermediary (reach, less control) (Ch 5).

Duplication — Reliably reproducing something of value; near-free for information (Ch 5).

Economically Valuable Skills — Only skills tied to the Five Parts get paid (Ch 2).

Education-Based Selling — Make prospects better-informed customers; builds Trust and willingness to pay (Ch 4).

End Result — The experience/emotion the prospect wants ("holes, not drills") (Ch 3).

Energy Cycles — Circadian and ~90-min ultradian rhythms; maximize peaks, rest on downswings (Ch 8).

Environment / Guiding Structure — The structure around you is the biggest determinant of behavior (Ch 7, Ch 10).

Expectation Effect — Quality = Performance − Expectations (Ch 5).

Experimental Mindset — Constant experimentation as the only reliable way to learn (Ch 12).

Externalization — Converting internal thoughts into written/spoken form to reprocess them (Ch 8).

Fail-safe — A backup built before it's needed, kept separate from the system it protects (Ch 12).

Feedback — Real-prospect signal sought via open questions; a preorder is the strongest (Ch 2).

Feedback Loop — When a system's output becomes the next cycle's input (Ch 10).

Five Parts of Every Business — Value Creation → Marketing → Sales → Value Delivery → Finance (Ch 1, Ch 2).

Five-Fold Why / How — Repeated "why" to find what you truly want; repeated "how" to reach action (Ch 8).

Fixed vs Variable Costs — Fixed are incurred regardless of output; variable scale with output (Ch 6).

Flow / Stock / Slack — Movements of resources (flows), pools that accumulate (stocks), and how much sits there (slack) (Ch 10).

Force Multiplier — A tool that multiplies force, thought, or attention; the only good use of debt (Ch 5).

Four Methods to Increase Revenue — More customers, bigger transactions, more frequency, higher prices (Ch 6).

Four Pricing Methods — Replacement Cost, Market Comparison, Discounted Cash Flow/NPV, Value Comparison (Ch 4).

Framing — Emphasizing some details, de-emphasizing others; inevitable, not lying (Ch 3).

Free — Giving genuine value away to win Attention fast (Ch 3).

Friction — Any force that removes energy from a system over time (Ch 12).

Gall's Law — Every working complex system evolved from a working simple one (Ch 10).

Garbage In, Garbage Out — Bad input always yields useless output (Ch 11).

Golden Trifecta — Treat everyone with appreciation, courtesy, and respect (Ch 9).

Habits — Regular supportive actions; install one at a time via triggers (Ch 8).

Hierarchy of Funding — Financing ladder from cheapest/most-control to costliest/least-control (Ch 6).

Hook — A single phrase conveying the offer's primary benefit ("1,000 songs in your pocket") (Ch 3).

Humanization — Using data to tell a real person's story, often via personas (Ch 11).

Importance — Everyone craves feeling Important; listening makes it happen (Ch 9).

Inhibition — The forebrain's ability to override instinct ("free won't"); fueled by Willpower (Ch 7).

Internal Controls — Standard procedures keeping finances accurate and protected (Ch 6).

Interdependence — Reliance of one system on others; tightly vs. loosely coupled (Ch 10).

Iron Law of the Market — Market size and quality cap every business (Ch 2).

Iteration Cycle (WIGWAM) — Watch, Ideate, Guess, Which?, Act, Measure (Ch 2).

Iteration Velocity — Speed through cycles; more at-bats beats one big bet (Ch 2).

Key Performance Indicator (KPI) — The few measurements of a system's critical parts (Ch 11).

Leverage — Borrowed money that magnifies gains and losses alike (Ch 6).

Lifetime Value — Total value of a customer over the whole relationship (Ch 6).

Locus of Control — Separate what you can control/influence from what you can't (Ch 8).

Loss Aversion — Losses feel ~2× as strong as equivalent gains (Ch 7).

Management — Coordinating a group toward a Goal amid Change and Uncertainty (Ch 9).

Mean / Median / Mode / Midrange — Four measures of typicality (Ch 11).

Mental Simulation — Imagining an action's result before acting; needs a "point B" Goal (Ch 7).

Middle Path — The shifting balance between too little and too much (Ch 12).

Minimum Economically Viable Offer (MEVO) — The smallest offer that produces an actual sale (Ch 2).

Monoidealism — The flow state of focusing all attention on one thing (Ch 8).

Most Important Tasks (MITs) — The 2–3 critical tasks that drive your results (Ch 8).

Motivation — An emotion linking feeling to action; "move away" beats "move toward" by default (Ch 7).

Narrative — A story (often Hero's Journey) that makes the customer the hero (Ch 3).

Next Action — The next concrete physical step to move a project forward (Ch 8).

Next Best Alternative — What each party does with no deal; power lies with who can walk away (Ch 4).

Normal Accidents — In tightly coupled systems, failure is "when," not "if" (Ch 10).

Norms — Historical measurements used as Context for current ones (Ch 11).

Novelty — New sensory data is required to hold Attention (Ch 7).

Onion Brain — Hindbrain (survival) → midbrain (emotion) → forebrain (logic) (Ch 7).

Option Orientation — When something goes wrong, focus on options, not the problem (Ch 9).

Overhead — Minimum ongoing resources to keep operating regardless of sales (Ch 6).

Paradox of Automation — The more efficient the automation, the more crucial its human operators (Ch 12).

Pattern Matching — The brain auto-learns cause-effect patterns; experts hold better ones (Ch 7).

Perceived Value — Better End Result + less user effort = higher value and price (Ch 2).

Perceptual Control — People act like thermostats: act only when a perception drifts out of range (Ch 7).

Permission — Asking to follow up after giving Free value; a reusable asset (Ch 3).

Personal R&D — Earmark ~5% of income for your own learning and tools (Ch 8).

Planning Fallacy — People underestimate completion times; plan anyway for the Mental Simulation (Ch 9).

Point of Market Entry — The moment someone crosses the interest threshold (Ch 3).

Power — The ability to influence others' actions: influence or compulsion (Ch 9).

Predictability — Customers want to know what to expect; deliver it the same way every time (Ch 5).

Pricing Power — Ability to raise prices over time without losing too many customers (Ch 6).

Pricing Uncertainty Principle — All prices are arbitrary but must be supported (Ch 4).

Priming — Programming your Pattern Matching to flag relevant information (Ch 8).

Probable Purchaser — The specific person perfectly suited to your offer (Ch 3).

Profit / Profit Margin — Bringing in more than you spend; the gap as a percentage (Ch 6).

Prototype — An early tangible representation made to gather feedback (Ch 2).

Proxy — Measuring a closely correlated stand-in for what you care about (Ch 11).

Purchasing Power — Sum of all liquid assets you can deploy (Ch 6).

Qualification — Deciding if a prospect is a good customer before they buy (Ch 3).

Ratio — Comparing two measurements by dividing one by the other (Ch 11).

Reactivation — Getting lapsed customers to buy again — cheapest revenue source (Ch 4).

Receptivity — How open someone is to your message (what + when) (Ch 3).

Reference Level — The set point/range that defines "under control" (Ch 7).

Refactoring — Improving a system's efficiency without changing its output (Ch 12).

Referrals — Transferring "known and liked" trust to a stranger (Ch 9).

Reinterpretation — Rewriting the meaning of past events to change future simulations (Ch 7).

Remarkability — Designing an offer literally worth remarking on (Purple Cow) (Ch 3).

Reorganization — Random trial-and-error when a Reference Level is violated but the fix is unknown (Ch 7).

Reputation — What people generally think of your offer; "branding" demystified (Ch 3).

Resilience — Toughness/flexibility to handle an uncertain world (Ch 12).

Risk Reversal — Shifting transaction risk from buyer to seller via a guarantee (Ch 4).

Return on Investment (ROI) — Value created per unit of time/resources invested (Ch 6).

Safety — Communication requires both parties feel safe; threatened people stonewall (Ch 9).

Sampling — Using a small random share of output as a proxy for the whole (Ch 11).

Scale — Ability to reliably Duplicate/Multiply as volume rises (Ch 5).

Scarcity — Limited quantity/time triggers Loss Aversion; fake scarcity backfires (Ch 7).

Scenario Planning — Constructing hypotheticals and simulating your response (Ch 12).

Second-Order Effects — Consequences have consequences, sometimes opposite to intent (Ch 10).

Segmentation — Splitting data into subgroups to reveal hidden relationships (Ch 11).

Selection Test — The environmental constraint deciding which systems survive (Ch 10).

Shadow Testing — Selling an offer before it exists (transparently) to test CIAs (Ch 2).

Social Proof — Learning how to act by watching others, especially when ambiguous (Ch 9).

Social Signals — Tangible indicators of an intangible quality (a Rolex's message) (Ch 9).

Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) — A predefined process for a recurring task (Ch 12).

States of Being — Present-experience qualities used as decision criteria, not goals (Ch 8).

Stress and Recovery — Run near, not at, 100%, with guilt-free rest (Ch 8).

Stress Testing — Simulating extremes to find a system's breaking point (Ch 12).

Sufficiency — The profit point that makes continuing worthwhile ("ramen profitable") (Ch 6).

Sunk Cost — Unrecoverable past investment that should not drive forward decisions (Ch 6).

Systemization — Making a process explicit, repeatable, and externalized (Ch 5).

Ten Ways to Evaluate a Market — Score a market 0–10 on ten dimensions before entering (Ch 2).

Threat Lockdown — Perceived threat triggers fight/flee/freeze, killing productive work (Ch 7).

Three Dimensions of Negotiation — Setup, Structure, Discussion (two happen before you sit down) (Ch 4).

Three Universal Currencies — Negotiations trade in resources, time, and flexibility (Ch 4).

Throughput — The rate at which a system reaches its goal (Ch 5, Ch 10).

Transaction — An exchange of value; the defining moment of every business (Ch 4).

Trust — Belief you'll deliver what you promise; no Trust, no Transaction (Ch 4).

Twelve Standard Forms of Value — Product, Service, Shared Resource, Subscription, Resale, Lease, Agency, Audience Aggregation, Loan, Option, Insurance, Capital (Ch 2).

Uncertainty — Unknown unknowns (black swans); distinct from plannable Risk (Ch 10).

Value Capture — Retaining a share of value created per transaction; too much and customers flee (Ch 6).

Value Stream — Every step from Value Creation through delivery to the customer (Ch 5).

Value-Based Selling — Reinforcing the Reasons Why the offer is valuable to this buyer (Ch 4).

Visualization — Helping prospects imagine life after accepting your offer (Ch 3).

Willpower Depletion — Willpower runs on glucose and depletes with use (Ch 7).

patterns.md

Patterns — Techniques & Procedures from The Personal MBA

Concrete, repeatable methods you can run. Each: when to use, how, trade-offs.

Test an Idea Before Building It (Shadow Testing + MEVO)

When to use: You have a business idea and want evidence of real demand before investing.

How:

1. List your Critically Important Assumptions (CIAs) — the facts that must be true for it to work.

2. Build a Prototype / Minimum Economically Viable Offer (MEVO): the smallest thing that can produce an actual sale (landing page, one-pager, mockup).

3. Shadow Test: transparently offer it for sale (or take preorders) before it fully exists.

4. Treat a preorder/payment as the only feedback that counts; refund if you can't deliver.

Trade-offs: Must stay transparent (don't take money you can't honor). Friends/family feedback is noise — only paying strangers validate.

Evaluate a Market Before Entering (Ten Ways + Iron Law)

When to use: Choosing among business or product ideas.

How: Score the market 0–10 on each: Urgency, Market Size, Pricing Potential, Cost of Customer Acquisition, Cost of Value Delivery, Uniqueness of Offer, Speed to Market, Up-Front Investment, Upsell Potential, Evergreen Potential. Sum and compare. Remember the Iron Law of the Market: a great offer to a market that doesn't want it still fails.

Trade-offs: Scores are estimates, not facts — use to compare options, not to predict revenue. A low total is a strong stop signal; a high total is not a guarantee.

Run an Improvement Loop (The Iteration Cycle — WIGWAM)

When to use: Improving any offer, process, or skill.

How: Watch what's happening → Ideate options → Guess which will help most → Which? (choose) → Act → Measure → repeat. Optimize for Iteration Velocity (cycles per unit of time/money).

Trade-offs: Favors many small bets over one big bet; needs honest measurement or it degenerates into noise.

Support a Price (Four Pricing Methods)

When to use: Setting or defending a price.

How: Compute all four as inputs — Replacement Cost (what to rebuild it), Market Comparison (what similar things sell for), Discounted Cash Flow/NPV (value of future cash it produces), Value Comparison (worth to this buyer). Use the first three as a floor/baseline; price on Value Comparison because it's almost always highest.

Trade-offs: Value pricing requires understanding the buyer's Reasons Why; without that you fall back to commodity (market) pricing.

Close More Sales (Trust + Risk Reversal + Damaging Admission)

When to use: Prospects hesitate at the buying moment.

How: Dissolve the five Barriers to Purchase (too expensive, won't work, won't work for me, can wait, too hard). Build Trust via Education-Based Selling; volunteer a real drawback (Damaging Admission) to raise credibility; apply Risk Reversal (strong guarantee) so the buyer, not the seller, is protected.

Trade-offs: Risk Reversal can attract abusers; price in the refund/return rate. Works only when you can actually deliver.

Grow Revenue (Four Methods)

When to use: You want more money from an existing business.

How: There are only four levers — (1) increase the number of customers, (2) increase average transaction size, (3) increase transaction frequency per customer, (4) raise prices. Pick the lever with least Friction first; Reactivation of lapsed customers is usually cheapest.

Trade-offs: Discounting to add customers can shrink margin; raising prices tests Pricing Power and may lose price-sensitive buyers.

Size Customer Acquisition Spend (Lifetime Value vs AAC)

When to use: Deciding how much to spend on marketing/acquisition.

How: Estimate Lifetime Value (total profit per customer over the relationship). Your Allowable Acquisition Cost (AAC) is the marketing share of that — spend up to AAC to win a customer and still profit.

Trade-offs: Overestimating LTV (ignoring churn) leads to overspending; revisit as real retention data arrives.

Find What You Actually Want (Five-Fold Why / Five-Fold How)

When to use: Goal-setting, or stuck on motivation.

How: Ask "why do I want this?" ~5 times to reach the core desire (a State of Being). Then ask "how can I get this?" ~5 times to descend to a concrete Next Action you can take now.

Trade-offs: Surfacing a deeper want can reveal your stated goal is the wrong one — useful but unsettling.

Protect Focus (Monoidealism + Kill the Switching Penalty)

When to use: Important cognitive work.

How: Eliminate Conflict and interruptions; do one thing (Monoidealism). Batch similar tasks to avoid the Cognitive Switching Penalty. Pre-commit your 2–3 MITs before the day starts; spend Willpower on Environment design, not moment-to-moment resistance.

Trade-offs: Requires saying no and protecting blocks of time; multitasking feels productive but isn't.

Change Behavior by Changing Structure (Guiding Structure + Habits)

When to use: You want a behavior to stick (yours or a team's).

How: Don't rely on willpower — change the Environment so the desired action is the path of least resistance. Install Habits one at a time with explicit triggers.

Trade-offs: Slower than forcing it, but durable; one habit at a time respects Willpower Depletion.

Delegate With Autonomy (Commander's Intent + Reason Why)

When to use: Assigning work to others.

How: State the Reason Why and Commander's Intent (the purpose and end-state) so people respond intelligently when reality shifts. Treat them with the Golden Trifecta (appreciation, courtesy, respect). Keep teams to 3–8 to limit Communication Overhead.

Trade-offs: Requires trusting judgment over compliance; pays off only with capable people.

Find and Fix the Bottleneck (Theory of Constraints)

When to use: A system underperforms and you want max leverage.

How: Identify the single Constraint limiting Throughput. Alleviate or eliminate it; the next constraint "gets a promotion." Re-measure and repeat.

Trade-offs: Optimizing anything other than the constraint produces no system-level gain — and can add cost.

Choose the Right Metric (KPI + Avoid Correlation/Causation Traps)

When to use: Measuring and improving a system.

How: Pick a few KPIs on the system's critical parts; supply Context (Norms, Ratios). Before acting on a pattern, demand a complete repeatable cause-effect chain — correlation ≠ causation. Use Sampling and Segmentation to keep it cheap and revealing.

Trade-offs: Bad inputs = Garbage In, Garbage Out; vanity metrics (e.g. lines of code) reward the wrong behavior.

Improve a System Safely (Critical Few + SOP + Fail-safe)

When to use: Optimizing an existing, working system.

How: Apply the Critical Few (find the ~20% of inputs driving ~80% of results) and optimize those. Reduce Friction. Codify recurring work as SOPs/Checklists. Build Fail-safes before they're needed; Stress Test in "demon mode." Stop at Diminishing Returns (the "85% Solution"). Sometimes the right move is Cessation — stop doing something.

Trade-offs: Over-optimizing Throughput sacrifices Resilience; remember the Paradox of Automation — efficient automation makes human operators more critical, not less.

The Essential Psycho-Cybernetics: The Science of Success

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Which mechanism am I running, and what do I do now?

The one diagnostic question

Am I feeding this machine a goal, or feeding it my inferiority? Same servo-mechanism either way. It is impersonal and it executes whatever picture it gets.

Which mechanism am I running?

TellMechanismDo this now
I'm rehearsing how it goes wrongFailure (worry = rehearsal reversed)Same technique, flip the content. The Method, 10 min.
I'm straining, pushing, grippingFailure (trying too hard)Stop. Ask "what am I actually accomplishing at this pace?" Accept the limit.
I keep replaying the injuryFailure (Resentment)Ask what the condemnation is buying you. Then cancel the debt.
I'm waiting for tomorrow / better conditionsFailure (Mañana Inc.)Do the constructive thing today. Postpone only the resentment.
I have no goal for todayFailure (Emptiness)Write one goal, however small. That is the whole intervention.
I did well and now feel uneasyComfort-zone tensionNormal. You left the effectiveness range. Raise the picture, don't retreat.
I'm calm and aimed at somethingSuccessContinue; stoke the winning feeling.

F-A-I-L-U-R-E → what each needs

Fear → a goal (converts fear to growth) · Anger → count to 12 · Inferiority → self-image work, not skill training · Loneliness → compassion; reach out · Uncertainty → a goal bends it · Resentment → audit the anxiety underneath · Emptiness → direction

S-U-C-C-E-S-S → the build order

Sense of direction · Understanding · Courage · Compassion · Esteem · Self-acceptance · Self-confidence

Decision rules

  • If effort isn't producing results → stop adding effort. Change the self-image first. Behavior is always consistent with the picture; work outside the effectiveness range produces tension and reversion, not growth.
  • If affirmations feel like lying → they will not work. "When it is incompatible with the self-image, it absolutely will not work." Do The Method before the recitation.
  • If you made a mistake → it's a course correction, never a stop sign. Aware → evaluate the outcome as unwanted → correct at once. The "at once" is what makes it a reflex; a review period makes it rumination.
  • If the decision is made → stop the worrying. Anxiety is creative while choosing among options and is dead weight after. Call on past successes instead.
  • *If you can't solve it → sleep on it, not with it.*
  • If you're doing three things → you're doing none. One thing, one thought, one goal at a time.
  • If you can't relax → check two roadblocks only. (1) Are you refusing your limitations? (2) Are you holding a grudge? "Compassion and love are parents of relaxation." You cannot have peace of mind while you hate.
  • If you're nervous before a performance → don't fix the nerves. Fix the expectation of failure. Accept the fear explicitly, then recall triumphs.
  • If you're inhibited around people → you're over-monitoring. Stop trying to impress; stop calculating effect; stop thinking about what they think.
  • If a limit has stopped you for years → check whether the glass is still there. The pike starves beside minnows; the elephant stays at a stake it could uproot.
  • If you can't forgive → find your payoff first. "As long as we condemn another, we can feel superior to him." Name the benefit, then cancel with no reservations.
  • If you're punishing yourself for a mistake → ask what you gain. There is no answer. Be kind to yourself instead.
  • If you're comparing yourself to someone → wrong comparison class. Keep up with yourself.

Thresholds & defaults

QuantityValue
Minimum before judging any self-image change21 consecutive days
Daily mental rehearsal10 minutes
Goal Builder cadence1 per week — 6 days on, 1 off
Micro-drill cadence (Mirror Magic)6 days
Anger delaycount to 12
Quiet-place entryat least once daily
Vacation frequencydaily, not annual
Goals per dayat least one, however small
Deadlineson written plans — never on affirmations ("time limits are deadly; they create tension")

Tells & smells

  • "I'll start tomorrow" → Mañana Inc. You are a member and you will get no dividends.
  • "I read the book" → passive reading. Positive doing is the method.
  • "I don't feel better" after the external problem is fixed → the scar was never the physical one.
  • Envy inside your admiration of someone → your self-respect is low; Rule 1 first.
  • *Hurt by what you think they think* → a feedback loop with no external input.
  • "I'm just being realistic about myself" → check whether you are sampling only failures. Truth about yourself is usually false, and biased downward.
  • Calm on the surface, no rest inside → concealment, not relaxation.
  • A grudge older than a few days → past the cleansing window; now it's the disease.
  • Someone who dropped the script and didn't flinch → their self-image held. That's the only variable under load.

The four principles of relaxation (memorize)

1. Forgive others. 2. Forgive yourself. 3. See yourself at your best. 4. Keep up with yourself.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Essential Psycho-Cybernetics

Active Forgiveness — Forgiveness as an all-out daily operation rather than a word; includes forgiving wrongs you only imagine were done to you (Ch 7).

Affirmation — A written present-tense statement used to feed the subconscious; governed by nine rules (personal, positive, present, non-progressive, non-comparative, no "can," balanced, realistic, no time limits) (Ch 14).

As if — Acting in imagination the way you intend to be. "Act the way you want to be (in your imagination), and you'll be the way you act" (Ch 14, Ch 17).

Automatic Success Mechanism — The goal-striving servo-mechanism when fed success goals; impersonal, automatic, supplies the how once you supply the objective (Ch 17).

Comfort zone / effectiveness range — The performance band around your self-image. Performance outside it produces tension and reverts (Ch 12).

Compassion — The pivot quality; the second C of S-U-C-C-E-S-S. "With compassion, you are somebody; without compassion, you are nobody" (Ch 1, Ch 24).

Creative Mirror Watching — Looking past your face to the person you intend to become; distinguished from narcissism and self-prosecution (Ch 8).

Daily Dozen (12 Ways to a New Self-Image) — Book Four's twelve instruments: Truth, Imagination, Relaxation, That Winning Feeling, Good Habits, The Aim of Happiness, Unmasking, Compassion, Accepting Your Weakness, Living with Your Mistakes, Being Yourself, Never Retiring (Ch 23).

Daily Dozen for Tranquility — Twelve forces to fight, spelling TRANQUILITY: Tension, Resistance, Arrogant aggressiveness, Negation, Quandary, Unbelief, Inferiority, Life of loneliness, Laissez-faire, Irritation, Trepidation, Yesterday Incorporated (Ch 9).

Daily vacation — A flight into the quiet room of your mind taken every day, not annually (Ch 22).

Decompression chamber — A designated room in the mind for regrouping under frustration (Ch 3).

Delay Your Response — Count slowly to 12 at the moment you know anger can no longer be checked; aim is control of action, not absence of feeling (Ch 22).

Descriptive Statement — The detailed written "why" of a goal, written before the short affirmation (Ch 14).

Divine Discontent — Negative feedback signalling you are off your ultimate heading (Ch 11).

Emotional scars — Invisible injuries, deeper and harder to remove than physical scars, which generate new injury until you resolve to heal them (Ch 17, Ch 19).

Failure Mechanism / F-A-I-L-U-R-E — Fear, Anger, Inferiority, Loneliness, Uncertainty, Resentment, Emptiness. The same machine as the success mechanism, fed negative aims (Ch 3, Ch 24).

Five Rules for Winning Friends — Be a friend to yourself; reach out; imagine you're the other person; accept their individuality; meet their needs (Ch 21).

Five Roadblocks of Frustration — Worrying after the decision; worrying about yesterday and tomorrow; too many things at once; wrestling problems around the clock; refusing to relax (Ch 24).

Four Principles of Relaxation — Forgive others; forgive yourself; see yourself at your best; keep up with yourself (Ch 4).

Goal Builders — Fourteen weekly exercises (six days on, one off) converting Book Two's chapters into physical practice (Ch 5–10).

Happiness Habit — Happiness as a cultivable thinking habit and a by-product of goals, never a target aimed at directly (Ch 3, Ch 16).

Keep up with yourself — Compare only against your own past, never another person's present (Ch 4).

Kybernetes — Greek for "helmsman"; the root of cybernetics and the source of the steering metaphor (Ch 11).

Mañana Incorporated — The membership of people who defer everything to a tomorrow nobody has experienced. Members never get dividends (Ch 2, Ch 6).

The Method — Ten minutes daily, eyes closed, body still, imagining yourself successful in vivid multi-sensory detail as a participant; 21 consecutive days (Ch 14).

Mirror Magic Practice — Six-day drills attached to existing daily events: morning breathing and the friend question, garbage disposal, closing the door on the past, the red traffic light (Ch 16).

Miracle drugs (four) — For emotional scars: accept your limitations; forget your mistakes; forgive others; see yourself at your best (Ch 19).

Negative feedback — A signal that you are off course. "Never a STOP sign"; its purpose is to adjust direction, not halt action (Ch 15).

Peace of mind — The port Psycho-Cybernetics steers toward — not achievement (Ch 11).

Positive doing — Maltz's correction to positive thinking; the method is a practice, not a reading (Ch 3).

Psycho-Cybernetics — Steering your mind to a productive, useful, worthwhile, predetermined goal (Ch 11).

Quiet Place — A retreat constructed in imagination, furnished to your taste, entirely private, entered at least once a day (Ch 13).

Retirement Mechanism — Ten components of withdrawal from life, each paired with an alternative: Retreat→Return, Eviction→Conviction, Withdrawal→Courage to Act, →Imaginative Power, →Reaffirmation, →Responsibility, Mañana→Today, Ennui→Emancipation, No direction→Goal Orientation, Traitor→Friend (Ch 9).

Self-image — The master framework: the picture you have of yourself; the ceiling on the effectiveness with which you can use your true potential. Behavior, feelings and abilities are always consistent with it (Ch 12).

Servo-mechanism — The subconscious understood not as a mind but as an automatic goal-striving machine directed by consciousness (Ch 17).

Seven Rules for Happy Living — Get the happiness habit; declare war on negative feelings; strengthen your self-image; learn how to laugh; dig out your buried treasures; help others; seek activities that make you happy (Ch 19).

Success Cycle — Success leading to success leading to more success; the constructive counterpart of the failure cycle (Ch 4).

S-U-C-C-E-S-S — Sense of direction, Understanding, Courage, Compassion, Esteem, Self-acceptance, Self-confidence (Ch 4, Ch 24).

Synthetic experience — Manufactured success experience, valid because the nervous system cannot distinguish a vividly imagined event from a real one. Requires Desire, Information, Repetition (Ch 14).

Theater of the mind — The staging device for all mental rehearsal: you are producer, director, writer, actor, technician and audience (Ch 17).

Therapeutic forgiveness — Cancelling the debt with no reservations, because you come to see the debt itself was never valid (Ch 24).

Think Sheets — Written self-interrogation exercises for surfacing goals and assumptions (Ch 14).

Tomorrow Illusion — Deferring your life to a day that never arrives; frustration as the thief of time (Ch 2).

Twelve Faces of Frustration — Book One's diagnostic list of frustration's forms (Ch 1); mirrored by the Twelve Faces of Success (Ch 4).

Winning feeling — The maintained sense of being someone who deserves success; feeds the automatic success mechanism (Ch 23).

Wonderful computer — Maltz's name for the goal-striving mechanism in the mid-brain (Ch 3).

Yesterday Tomorrow Complex — Living roughly 60% in yesterday and 20% in tomorrow, leaving almost nothing for today (Ch 9, Ch 24).

21-day rule — "For a person to experience a noticeable change in a mental picture, a minimum of twenty-one consecutive days must elapse" (Ch 11).

patterns.md

Patterns — Maltz's Runnable Techniques

The techniques are the point of this book. Each is stated so it can be run today.

---

The Method (mental rehearsal in the theater of the mind)

When to use: To change any behavior, capability or reaction that has resisted effort. The core practice of the whole system.

How:

1. Ten minutes daily, alone, no distractions, eyes closed. Make the body still — "the greater energies of the mind are available only when the body is still and the door to the senses is closed."

2. Pick one situation you handle badly.

3. Build it in full sensory detail — the room, light, sounds, what you're wearing, who is present. Environmental detail is what makes the nervous system accept it.

4. Be inside it as a participant, not an onlooker. Think from the goal, not about it. A goal you think of is a possibility; a goal you think from is "overpoweringly real."

5. See yourself handling it as you intend. Past performance is explicitly irrelevant during these ten minutes.

6. Shift to the feeling of already being that person. "Begin by knowing you have arrived."

7. Mark off the day. 21 consecutive days, then judge.

Trade-offs: Requires a real daily slot and a strong desire for the goal — the mechanism needs a defined objective, and a lukewarm one won't drive it. Watching yourself from outside produces a pleasant picture and no change. It also works in reverse: worry is this exact technique pointed at the failure.

---

The daily relaxation practice (Quiet Place + daily vacation)

When to use: Every day as maintenance; immediately on agitation.

How:

1. One-time build. Sit undisturbed, close your eyes, and construct a private retreat in imagination — plan, paint, furnish and decorate it to your own taste until you genuinely feel at home. Beach house on an uncharted island, a cloud, deep in the earth, a distant planet; the constraint is comfort, not realism.

2. Set two rules: completely isolated from the outside world, and nobody knows where it is.

3. Daily entry. Close your eyes and go. It takes an instant — the same instant it takes to picture the Golden Gate Bridge.

4. Rest the nervous system there. Also work there: accept your insecurities, re-picture past successes, set today's goals.

5. Return and use the carry-over — the tranquility transfers into whatever action follows.

Trade-offs: Useless if built for the first time mid-crisis; build it in calm. Sharing its location converts it from a refuge into a topic. Maltz pre-empts the "escapism" objection and tells you to ignore it.

---

The "act as if" drill

When to use: When you need a capability you don't believe you have — an interview, a difficult conversation, a performance.

How:

1. Take the method actor's stance: a man playing a king "tries to think as if he were that king," and projects it into living reality.

2. Decide who you are being for this specific occasion — not a fantasy self, the self you'd be on your best day.

3. Rehearse it in imagination first (The Method above).

4. Then act it in reality. "Act the way you want to be (in your imagination), and you'll be the way you act." Emerson's version: "Do the thing, and you will have the power."

Trade-offs: This is not the mask. The mask conceals a self-image you consider indefensible; "as if" rehearses one you intend to inhabit. If it's producing strain rather than release, you're wearing the mask.

---

The forgiveness exercise (therapeutic forgiveness)

When to use: On any grudge held more than a few days — against another person or yourself.

How:

1. Name the specific item. Not "everything," not "the relationship" — one act.

2. Run the honesty check: Is this an inconsiderate act that I, in my own imperfection, might have committed?

3. Run the motive check: what am I getting from the condemnation? Maltz's answer — "As long as we condemn another, we can feel superior to him," and there is "a perverse sense of satisfaction in feeling sorry for yourself." Until you see the payoff you're taking, you won't release it.

4. Cancel the debt with no reservations. The surgical standard: "no partial, tentative, or halfway measures. The scar tissue is cut out completely."

5. The endpoint: recognizing "there is and was nothing for us to forgive" — the debt itself was not valid.

6. Then the self-directed pass. Mirror, write FORGIVENESS, say aloud: "I will try to forgive myself. I will try to forgive others. We are all human and imperfect."

Trade-offs: Maltz permits a few days of bitterness after real injury — "better to cleanse your system than to let inner hate eat away at you." What is forbidden is permanent residence. Verbal forgiveness ("I forgive him," then a catnap) does nothing.

---

The Goal Builder protocol (generalized)

When to use: To convert any idea from the book into behavior.

How: One goal per week — six days of application, one day of rest. Each day: (1) a seeing component (an imagined scene, a walk, a sound); (2) a mirror component — write the goal word on the glass in erasable pencil or lipstick; (3) a spoken component — a first-person sentence said to your reflection; (4) erase the word, keep the feeling.

Trade-offs: Deliberately serialized — running all fourteen at once is the failure mode. The physicality (writing, speaking aloud) is not decoration; an internal resolution is not the same act.

---

The anxiety audit

When to use: Chronic worry, or resentment you can't locate a cause for.

How: Write down today's worries. Then last week's. Then last month's. Then a year ago's, if you can recall them. Study the list and check each one: was it realistic? Did it make sense? Observe your own hit rate.

Trade-offs: The evidence is the argument — don't substitute reassurance for the written list. Maltz's prediction: most were unrealistic. Use the discovered overreaction rate on today's fears.

---

The negative-feedback reflex

When to use: The instant you make an error or get rejected.

How: (1) Be aware of the negative — it's a warning light, and nobody gets upset at a warning light; (2) evaluate the outcome as unwanted and unacceptable — the outcome, not yourself; (3) correct at once. Then return attention to the objective: glance at the negatives, concentrate on the positives. Repeat until automatic.

Trade-offs: The "at once" is what installs the reflex; a period of review installs rumination instead. Excess attention to the indicator is the malfunction.

---

Delay Your Response (the 12-count)

When to use: At the moment you recognize anger can no longer be checked — not at first irritation.

How: Identify your over-reaction domains in advance (money, status, criticism). When the flood arrives, count slowly to twelve. Then act.

Trade-offs: You will still be irritated at twelve. The success criterion is control of action, not absence of feeling.

---

The daily recitation

When to use: As the standing 21-day practice; pairs with The Method.

How: Read Maltz's daily statement each morning ("This is the beginning of a new day… My thinking and my attitudes are calm and cheerful… I respond in a calm and intelligent manner, without alarm, no matter what the situation"). Mark off 21 consecutive days.

Trade-offs: Will not work if incompatible with your current self-image — "when it is incompatible with the self-image, it absolutely will not work." If it feels like lying, do The Method first.

---

Mirror Magic (six-day micro-drills)

When to use: To attach practice to events that already happen daily.

How: pick one for six days. (a) Morning: breathing exercises, then the mirror question — "Am I a friend to myself?" (b) Garbage: as you throw out the household's accumulation, discard the mental accumulation too. (c) Front door: closing it symbolically closes the door on yesterday's mistake. (d) Red light: the red is your fear of failure holding you back; when it turns green, move forward as toward a useful goal, with the confidence of past successes.

Trade-offs: Deliberately small. They work by attachment to an existing trigger — don't try to schedule them as new appointments.

---

The crisis protocol

When to use: Stage fright, high-stakes performance, pressure.
