How: Set your goal → believe in the goal → bring back your triumphs (recall past successes in sensory detail) → permit the nervousness ("I will accept my fear. And my nervousness. And my panic.") → stop expecting yourself to fail → do your best.

Trade-offs: Intervene on the expectation, never on the symptom. Recalled successes serve double duty: they displace nervousness now, and if you do fail they make the failure easier to accept.

The Myth of Normal: Trauma, Illness, and Healing in a Toxic Culture

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Myth of Normal

Diagnostic questions and decision rules, not a symptom checklist. Not medical, psychiatric, or therapeutic advice.

---

The four questions that reframe almost anything

Instead of askingAskBecause
What's wrong with you?What happened to you?Trauma is not what happens to you, it's what happens inside you — the wound, not the event
Why the addiction?Why the pain?Addiction is an adaptation to pain, not a disease of choice or a moral failure
What does she have?What process is unfolding, and what sustains it?Disease is a process in a life, not a thing that invades a separate self
How do I get rid of this?What is this for? Why is this here?Everything within us exists for a purpose; it was once protective

---

Decision rules

  • When a diagnosis explains the symptoms but not the person → ask what was happening in that life in the 2–5 years before onset. The answer is data.
  • When someone is described admiringly as "never angry," "no ego," "always thinking of others," "so easy to care for" → treat that as a coping style, not a virtue. Maté's position: habitual self-suppression and repressed anger are physiologically consequential.
  • When a behavior looks irrational → assume it was once an adaptation. Ask what it solved, and when.
  • When a child's behavior is the problem → look first at the state of the attachment relationship and the adults' capacity to attune, not at the child's will.
  • When "normal" is offered as reassurance → ask normal for whom, and by what standard? Widely shared does not mean healthy. That is the myth.
  • When a cause is attributed to genes → genes load possibilities; environment and experience largely decide expression. Ask what turned it on.
  • When a symptom is being treated and the context is untouched → the intervention is incomplete, however correct the treatment.
  • When self-compassion is absent → do not command it. Notice the absence and get curious about it. Compassion brooks no "should."
  • When healing is discussed → separate it from cure. Healing is a direction, a movement toward wholeness; cure is absence of disease. You can have either without the other. Never promise the second by way of the first.

---

Tells & smells

If you seeSuspect
"I never get angry" / conflict avoidance as identityRepressed anger, authenticity traded for attachment
Illness onset shortly after a loss, betrayal, or role collapseChronic process made acute by interpersonal stress
"Idiopathic" on the chartNo one asked about the life
A patient apologizing for taking up your timeSelf-suppression pattern, likely lifelong
Compulsive niceness, inability to say noThe childhood adaptation still running
Strong self-condemnation in familiar bodily sensationsThe critic is old and was once protective
A parent describing a toddler's needs as manipulationCulture's toughening script; attunement is being withheld
"You must have brought this on yourself"Victim-blaming — the distortion Maté explicitly rejects

---

The critical distinctions (get these wrong and you get Maté wrong)

Not thisBut this
You caused your illnessIllness is multifactorial and contextual; responsibility is not blame
Personality causes cancerMaté's position is that emotional repression is a significant contributing factor — a contested claim, not consensus
Blame the parentsParents are themselves shaped by their own trauma and by a culture that undermines parenting
Trauma = the terrible eventTrauma = the internal wound and the adaptation it forced
Big-T Trauma is the only real traumasmall-t trauma — chronic unmet need, absence of attunement — is pervasive and consequential
Acceptance = resignationAcceptance = allowing what is, which is what makes change possible
Healthy anger = ventingHealthy anger flares, defends the boundary, and subsides
Healing = self-improvementHealing = self-retrieval
Disillusionment = lossDisillusionment = gain; the cost of refusing is higher

---

The authenticity/attachment audit — fast version

Signal appears (tension, anxiety, irritability, regret, depression, fatigue) → ask:

1. What inner guidance am I defying or avoiding?

2. What truth am I withholding, and what am I afraid of losing by saying it?

3. Where, recently, did I abandon myself?

4. What story made that feel necessary — and where did I learn it?

The chronic pattern matters, not the isolated lapse. Deliberate, chosen sacrifice is not the target; habitual, unwilled selflessness is.

---

Safety rails

  • Anything that lands as "you did this to yourself" has done harm. Say so plainly and correct it.
  • Never frame Maté's work as a reason to decline, delay, or discontinue medical or psychiatric treatment. His own cases pair conventional treatment with inner work.
  • Contested claims (personality→cancer, ADHD as a stress/attunement phenomenon, psychedelics) are Maté's position and emerging research, not settled science. Attribute them.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Myth of Normal

Acceptance — Allowing that reality is as it is right now; the precondition for change, not resignation or approval. One of the four A's. (Ch 26)

ACEs (Adverse Childhood Experiences) — The ten categories of childhood adversity from the Fellitti/Anda study; dose-dependently associated with adult physical and mental illness. Maté treats them as a floor, not a ceiling — they capture overt harm and miss the absence of attunement. (Ch 1, 9)

Activism / Advocacy — The two additional A's for collective healing: organizing for change, and using privilege to amplify silenced voices. Cannot be individual pursuits. (Ch 33)

Agency — Free, responsible authorship of one's own responses and life. Not control over outcomes, and not blame for what was done to you. (Ch 26)

Anger, healthy — Boundary-defending energy of the moment: it flares, fends off the threat, and subsides. Distinct from rage, resentment, spite, or venting. Both suppressed and amplified anger are toxic. (Ch 26)

Attachment — The drive for proximity and connection with a caregiver; in a child, a survival need that outranks everything else. (Ch 7, 9)

Attachment vs. authenticity — The central developmental trade-off: when a child cannot have both, attachment wins, authenticity is suppressed, and that adaptation becomes the adult pathology. (Ch 7)

Attunement — The caregiver's accurate reading of and resonance with a child's inner state. Its chronic absence is itself traumatic, even where nothing overtly bad happens. (Ch 9)

Authenticity — Fidelity to one's own felt sense, needs, and values; lived rather than conceptual. Cannot be pursued, only embodied. (Ch 7, 26)

Big-T Trauma — Trauma from overt, identifiable catastrophic events: abuse, violence, war, disaster. (Ch 1)

Biopsychosocial — Medicine that treats biological, psychological, and social factors as one inseparable system rather than separate domains. (Ch 2, 3)

Cartesian split — The mind/body separation Maté rejects; the philosophical error underwriting modern medicine's blindness to context. (Ch 2)

Compassionate Inquiry (CI) — Maté's own methodology: open-ended, non-judgmental exploration of the beliefs and behaviors that don't serve us, tracking bodily sensation and familiarity to reach origins. Both a therapist training and a self-reflection practice. (Ch 28, 30)

Compassions, the five — Ordinary human compassion; the compassion of curiosity and understanding (context); of recognition; of truth; of possibility. Non-hierarchical and mutually reinforcing. (Ch 26)

Coping style — Habitual emotional patterns — self-suppression, compulsive niceness, repressed anger, chronic role-taking — that Maté's position links to autoimmune illness and cancer risk. A contested empirical claim, not settled consensus. (Ch 2, 5, 6)

Cure — The absence of disease. Distinct from healing; either can occur without the other. (Ch 25)

Developmental trauma — Trauma arising from the conditions of early development itself — unmet needs, absent attunement, stressed caregivers — rather than from discrete events. (Ch 1, 9)

Disillusionment — Shedding an illusion. Maté treats it as a healing gain rather than a loss, and as the confrontation with denial that makes social change thinkable. (Ch 33)

Epigenetics — The mechanism by which environment and experience switch gene expression on or off; Maté's counter to genetic determinism. (Ch 4, 10)

Foes to friends — The move of turning a distressing inner pattern from enemy into ally by asking what purpose it originally served. (Ch 30)

Healing — A natural movement toward wholeness. A direction, not a destination; closer to self-retrieval than to self-improvement. (Ch 25)

Idiopathic — Medicine's term for a condition of unknown cause; in Maté's reading, often a confession that no one asked about the life. (Ch 6)

Inner critic — The internalized self-accusing voice. Approached not by defeat but by inquiry into what it was once protecting. (Ch 30)

Interpersonal biology — The finding that human physiology is regulated by relationship: nervous systems, immune systems, and hormones are shaped by the people around us. (Ch 3)

Interpersonal neurobiology — Siegel's field describing how relationships physically shape the developing brain. (Ch 3, 9)

Mind-body unity — The premise that emotional, psychological, and social life are inseparable from physiology; therefore the social is always also biological. (Ch 2)

Myth of normal, the — The book's title claim: a toxic culture normalizes conditions that are in fact pathogenic, so widespread does not mean healthy and "normal" is not a standard of health. (Introduction, Ch 19–24)

"Not why the addiction, but why the pain" — Maté's reframe of addiction: the substance or behavior is an adaptation that solved something, so the question is what pain it relieved. (Ch 15, 16)

Peer orientation — Children turning to peers rather than adults for attachment cues, undermining the parenting relationship. (Ch 12, after Gordon Neufeld)

Responsibility vs. blame — Maté's key distinction: responsibility is the capacity to respond now; blame is fault for what happened. He explicitly rejects the "you caused your cancer" reading of his work. (Ch 6, 25, 27)

Rupture and repair — Standard attachment-theory terminology for the cycle of relational break and reconnection: repair, not the absence of rupture, builds security, and unrepaired rupture is where damage accumulates. Maté does not use this exact phrase in this book; Ch 9 makes the same argument as unconditional acceptance holding through correction and momentary anger. He uses rupture separately, in his definition of trauma as a lasting rupture or split within the self. (Ch 9; cf. Ch 1)

Self-compassion — The attitude of non-judgment toward one's own suffering; says simply "I am hurting." Distinct from self-pity, which wraps pain in narrative, and from self-improvement. (Ch 26, 28)

Self-suppression — The habitual, unwilled subordination of one's own needs and feelings to others'. Maté's central pathogenic coping style. (Ch 2, 5, 28)

small-t trauma — Trauma from chronic unmet need and absent attunement rather than overt catastrophe. Pervasive, easily missed, and consequential. (Ch 1)

Sociopathy as strategy — Maté's argument that institutional and corporate structures reward and require the traits that would be pathologized in an individual. (Ch 21)

Toxic culture — The social, economic, and material conditions that systematically frustrate human needs while presenting themselves as normal. (Ch 19–24)

Trauma — Not what happens to you, but what happens inside you as a result — the wound and the adaptations built around it, not the event. (Ch 1)

Wholeness — The state toward which healing moves: recovering the parts of self that were exiled to preserve attachment. (Ch 25, 32)

patterns.md

Patterns & Practices — The Myth of Normal

Maté's actual working methods. These are inquiries, not instructions. None of them is a substitute for medical, psychiatric, or therapeutic care, and none is a self-improvement program — the aim is self-retrieval, not self-betterment.

---

Compassionate Inquiry (CI)

When to use: whenever a symptom, behavior, or self-judgment resists being argued away — chronic illness, addiction, self-loathing, compulsive people-pleasing. Also as an ongoing self-reflection practice.

How:

1. Suspend what you already know about yourself. The personality is an expert on itself and that is precisely the problem. Aim to know yourself, not to know about yourself.

2. Inquire, don't interrogate. An inquiry is open-ended; it starts from the possibility that you haven't yet found the right question.

3. Bring compassion as an attitude, not a feeling. Feelings come and go; an attitude can be invited in any emotional state. The attitude is inexhaustible non-judgment toward whatever surfaces.

4. Never issue a "should." Compassion brooks no should, and walled-off parts don't respond to demands. If self-compassion is absent, don't manufacture it — get curious about its absence. Once seen, it softens.

5. Track the body. Ask where the belief lives as sensation (throat, chest, belly), then ask: is this sensation new, or deeply familiar? The answer is almost always "familiar" — which relocates the material from the present grievance to its origin.

6. When self-judgment arises, stay curious about its origin without believing its content.

Trade-offs: slow, and it surfaces pain before relief. Done without safety or without genuine non-judgment it becomes another form of self-attack. Maté insists CI participants spend months on their own material before using it with anyone else.

---

The Self-Inquiry Exercise ("Before the Body Says No")

When to use: as a weekly written practice, especially where chronic self-suppression is suspected. Handwritten, undistracted.

How — six questions, in order:

1. In my life's important areas, what am I not saying no to? (Where did a "no" want out and a "yes" or a silence came instead?)

2. How does my inability to say no impact my life?

3. What bodily signals have I been overlooking? What symptoms have I ignored that could be warning signs?

4. What is the hidden story behind my inability to say no? (The belief that makes the "no" feel impossible.)

5. Where did I learn these stories?

6. Where have I ignored or denied the "yes" that wanted to be said?

Trade-offs: Maté is explicit that this is not about stigmatizing genuine altruism. Deliberate, chosen self-sacrifice — a parent up at night with a sick child — is not the target. The target is habitual, unwilled selflessness that operates without consent. Get current, stay specific, look for chronic patterns rather than lapses. Notice reluctance to do the exercise at all, without judgment — that reluctance is itself data.

---

The Authenticity Audit

When to use: when tension, anxiety, irritability, regret, depression, or fatigue surfaces. Maté treats these as the signal that authenticity is missing, not as the problem itself.

How — ask:

  • Is there an inner guidance I am defying, resisting, ignoring, or avoiding?
  • Are there truths I'm withholding from expression or even contemplation, out of fear of losing security or belonging?
  • In a recent encounter, is there some way I abandoned myself, my needs, my values?
  • What fears, rationalizations, or familiar narratives kept me from being myself?
  • Do I even know what my own values are?

Trade-offs: authenticity can't be pursued, only embodied — striving toward an idealized authentic self is itself inauthentic. The most direct route is noticing where authenticity isn't, then applying curiosity and gentle skepticism to the limiting beliefs standing in its place. And the cost is real: choosing authenticity may not preserve every attachment. That grief is the adult reversal of the childhood trade, and Maté does not minimize it.

---

Foes to Friends — Working with the Inner Critic

When to use: self-accusation, self-condemnation, guilt, self-loathing — anything you have been trying to get rid of.

How:

1. Start from the first principle of compassionate self-inquiry: everything within us exists for a purpose; nothing is there that shouldn't be. However debilitating, it was once functional.

2. Shift the question from "How do I get rid of this?" to "What is this for? Why is this here?"

3. Externalize the accusation to make it examinable. Maté's courtroom move: If this were a trial and you were the defendant, what would the prosecution say about you? Then: What's the verdict — because you did those things, that makes you what? This exposes that the person is simultaneously plaintiff, prosecutor, accused, and hanging judge.

4. Locate the verdict in the body, then ask how familiar the sensation and the self-concept are. Familiarity dates the belief to childhood, where it was protective.

5. Do not judge yourself for judging — that keeps the wheel of shame turning.

Trade-offs: turning a foe into a friend is not the same as agreeing with it. The aim is that the critic relax and stop hounding, not that it be defeated.

---

The Five Compassions

When to use: as a diagnostic on the quality of your own regard — for a patient, a person you judge, or yourself. Non-hierarchical; they reinforce one another.

1. Ordinary human compassion — the ability to be with suffering and to be moved by it. Distinct from pity, which requires unequal roles. Self-compassion says "I am hurting"; self-pity wraps the pain in narrative.

2. The compassion of curiosity and understanding (the compassion of context) — everything exists for a reason and the reason matters. Seek the why before leaping to the how.

3. The compassion of recognition — we are all in the same boat. When intense judgment arises, check your own body state; inquire into the judging mind rather than obeying or condemning it.

4. The compassion of truth — pain is not the enemy; it is information. Shielding people from inevitable hurt is neither kind nor effective. But truth without safety does no healing work, and "I'm just being honest" is not compassion.

5. The compassion of possibility — there is more to a person than their conditioned personality and their behavior. A present quality, not a someday hope.

---

The A's of Healing

When to use: as guideposts for the territory, explicitly not as how-to steps. Maté: no one can plot another's course of healing.

AWhat it isWhat it is not
AuthenticityFidelity to one's own felt sense and values; lived, not conceptualPerformed "realness"; an idealized self to strive toward
AgencyFree, responsible authorship of one's own life and responsesControl over outcomes; blame for what happened to you
Healthy AngerBoundary-defending energy of the moment — flares, does its job of fending off threat, subsidesRage, bluster, resentment, spite, venting, or a grievance kept and fed. Both suppressed and amplified anger are toxic
AcceptanceAllowing that reality is as it is right now — the precondition for changeResignation, approval, or ceasing to work for change

Plus two, for collective healing (Ch 33): Activism and Advocacy — socially meaningful syntheses of the first four, adding solidarity and collective thinking. These cannot be individual pursuits.

Trade-offs: each A corresponds to a human need that was likely driven underground early. Welcoming it back is slow and often frightening. Treating the four as a checklist to complete inverts their purpose.

---

Disillusionment as a Healing Step

When to use: whenever an illusion is protecting you from a truth about your history, your relationships, or your society.

How: treat losing an illusion as a gain, not a loss. Ask which you would rather be — deluded or disillusioned. Expect the ache of loss and the sense of being unmoored first; what follows is the relief of no longer having to hold impossible contradictions together. Disillusionment also confronts denial, which is the main buttress of an unhealthy status quo.

Trade-offs: it does carry a real cost — you may have to relinquish something you valued or a perspective you took refuge in. Maté's point is that the cost of refusing is higher and less visible.

Never Split the Difference: Negotiating As If Your Life Depended On It

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Never Split the Difference

Decision rules (if → then → because)

  • If you're about to compromise → don't; hold out or walk → "No deal is better than a bad deal"; splitting = one black + one brown shoe.
  • If you want a "Yes" fast → ask a "No"-oriented question instead → pushing for "Yes" makes people defensive.
  • If you hear "You're right" / "I'll try" → keep going with calibrated "How" questions → no buy-in; nothing will get implemented.
  • If you hear "That's right" → you've reached a breakthrough; advance → they've embraced your framing as their own.
  • If they drop "Fair" on you ("We just want what's fair") → don't concede; say "I apologize — show me where I treated you unfairly" or mirror "Fair?" → it's a destabilizing move.
  • If you're attacked/insulted → pause, bite your tongue, ask a calibrated question → counterattacking triggers a showdown.
  • If you don't know market value → let them anchor first → their opening may beat your target.
  • If pushed to name a price first → cite a high number "someone else" charges, or a bolstering range → avoids over-anchoring yourself low.
  • If the deal seems done but only with the people on the call → ask "How does this affect the rest of your team?" → behind-the-table players kill more deals than table players make.
  • If the counterpart seems "crazy" → assume ill-informed, constrained, or hidden interest → and dig for the Black Swan.
  • If a deadline is pressuring you → remember it's usually imaginary and cuts both ways → revealing yours often gets a better deal.

Voice selection

ToneWhenEffect
Positive/playful (smile)defaultmental agility, collaboration
Late-night FM DJ (downward)selectively, to make a pointcalm authority, "I've got it covered"
Direct/assertiverarelytriggers pushback — avoid

The core verbal toolkit

ToolOpenerGoal
Mirror(repeat last 1–3 words)?elaborate, build rapport
Label"It seems like…"defuse/reinforce emotion
Calibrated Q"How…/What…"illusion of control, info
Summarylabel + paraphrasetrigger "That's right"
Accusation audit"You'll probably think I'm…"pre-empt negatives

"No" without the word (in order)

1. "How am I supposed to do that?"

2. "Your offer is very generous, I'm sorry, that just doesn't work for me."

3. "I'm sorry, I just can't do that."

4. "I'm sorry, no." → 5. "No."

Ackerman numbers (memorize)

65 → 85 → 95 → 100% of target · decreasing raises · non-round final number · + a token non-cash item at the limit.

Three leverage types

  • Positive — give/withhold what they want ("I want…").
  • Negative — make them suffer (use sparingly; label, don't shove).
  • Normative — use their own norms/beliefs; expose hypocrisy.

Negotiator types & their silence

TypeTime meansSilence meansApproach
Analystpreparationthinkingdata, warn early, give time
Accommodatorrelationshipangersociable + calibrated questions for action
Assertivemoney"talk more"let them be heard; mirrors, "that's right"

→ Black Swan rule: treat them as they need, not as you'd want.

Tells & smells

  • Lots of "I/me/my" → low decision power; "we/they/them" → the real decider.
  • More words + third-person pronouns → likely lying (Pinocchio Effect).
  • Tone/body ≠ words (7-38-55) → label the incongruence.
  • "You're right" / "I'll try" → not bought in.
  • Specific, escalating threats → real consequences approaching; vague threats → early stage.
  • Any response that isn't outright rejection → you have the edge.

Go-to calibrated questions

  • "What is the biggest challenge you face?"
  • "What are we trying to accomplish here?"
  • "How am I supposed to do that?"
  • "How will we know we're on track?" / "…if we're off track?"
  • "How on board are the people not on this call?"

One Sheet (prepare every time — ~7:1 ROI)

I high-end Goal · II Summary (→"That's right") · III 3–5 labels/accusation audit · IV 3–5 calibrated questions · V non-cash offers.

glossary.md

Glossary — Never Split the Difference

Accommodator — negotiator type who prizes the relationship and free-flowing exchange; friendly, win-win seeking; for them silence = anger (Ch 9).

Accusation Audit — listing every negative thing the counterpart could say about you, then voicing it first to "take the sting out" (Ch 3, Ch 6).

Ackerman Model — offer-counteroffer haggling system: target → 65% / 85% / 95% / 100%, non-round final number + a token non-cash item (Ch 9).

Active Listening — the foundation skill set: pauses, minimal encouragers, mirroring, labeling, paraphrasing, summarizing (Ch 2, Ch 5).

Amygdala — brain's fear center; labeling a fear shifts activity to rational areas and defuses it (Ch 3).

Analyst — methodical, data-driven negotiator type that hates surprises; silence = thinking (Ch 9).

Anchor (emotional) — setting low expectations via an accusation audit before an offer, to trigger loss aversion (Ch 6).

Anchor (extreme/price) — an aggressive first number that bends the counterpart's reference point (Ch 6, Ch 9).

Anchor-and-adjustment effect — tendency to extrapolate from the first number heard (Ch 6).

Assertive — direct, time-is-money negotiator type that must be heard first; silence = a chance to talk more; mirrors work well (Ch 9).

BATNA — Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement; critiqued for tricking negotiators into aiming low (Ch 1, Appendix).

Behavioral Change Stairway Model (BCSM) — five stages: active listening → empathy → rapport → influence → behavioral change (Ch 5).

Behind-the-table (Level II) players — parties not at the table who can kill or implement a deal (Ch 8, Appendix).

Black Swan — a hidden, game-changing piece of information (unknown unknown); ~3–5 exist per negotiation (Ch 10).

Bolstering range — citing a range whose low end is what you actually want (Ch 6).

Calibrated Question — open-ended "What"/"How" question with no fixed answer that directs the conversation while giving the illusion of control (Ch 1, Ch 7).

Certainty Effect — preferring sure things to better-odds gambles (Ch 6).

Chris Discount — using your own name to humanize yourself and gain concessions ("What's the Chris discount?") (Ch 8).

Cognitive Bias — unconscious, irrational mental processes distorting perception (Ch 1).

Counterfeit Yes — a "yes" meant to stall or escape, with no commitment (Ch 4, Ch 8).

Forced Empathy — asking for help (e.g. "How am I supposed to…?") so the counterpart engages with your problem via reciprocity (Ch 7, Ch 8).

FM DJ Voice — late-night, deep, slow, downward-inflecting voice conveying calm authority (Ch 2).

Fairness ("the F-word") — emotionally loaded term; used defensively, distractingly, or positively ("stop me if I'm being unfair") (Ch 6).

Illusion of Control — making the counterpart feel in charge while you frame the conversation (Ch 7).

Known knowns / known unknowns / unknown unknowns — info you have / gaps you're aware of / Black Swans (Ch 10).

Labeling — naming an emotion aloud ("It seems like…") to validate and defuse/reinforce it (Ch 3).

Leverage (Positive / Negative / Normative) — ability to give what they want / make them suffer / use their own norms against them (Ch 10).

Loss Aversion — acting more strongly to avoid a loss than to gain an equal amount (Ch 1, Ch 6, Ch 10).

Minimal Encouragers — short cues ("uh-huh," "I see") signaling full attention (Ch 5).

Mirroring (isopraxism) — repeating the last 1–3 words to prompt elaboration and build rapport (Ch 2).

Multi-step "No" — four soft ways to say no before the word, to get the counterpart bidding against themselves (Ch 8).

Neural resonance — brains aligning during good listening, enabling anticipation (Ch 3).

"No"-oriented question — a question inviting a "No" ("Is now a bad time?") to give safety/control (Ch 4).

Pinocchio Effect — liars use more words and more third-person pronouns (Ch 8).

Pivot to nonmonetary terms — offering items cheap to you but valuable to them (Ch 6, Ch 9).

Prospect Theory — Kahneman/Tversky theory of choice under risk (Ch 6).

Religion (knowing their) — the worldview/values that hold authority over the counterpart; where Black Swans live (Ch 10).

Rule of Three — getting agreement to the same thing three times to test genuine commitment (Ch 8).

Similarity Principle — we trust those we see as similar/in-group (Ch 10).

Strategic Umbrage — well-timed, controlled offense-taking to wake the counterpart to a problem (Ch 9).

Summary — paraphrasing + labeling; reflecting "the world according to them" to trigger "That's right" (Ch 5).

System 1 / System 2 — fast emotional mind / slow logical mind; System 1 steers System 2 (Ch 1).

Tactical Empathy — recognizing and vocalizing the counterpart's perspective and what's behind it, to influence (Ch 1, Ch 3).

"That's right" — the breakthrough phrase signaling genuine understanding and buy-in (better than "Yes") (Ch 5).

"You're right" — a brush-off signaling no buy-in; nothing changes (Ch 5, Ch 8).

Wants vs. Needs — aspirations vs. the bare minimum/survival floor (Ch 2).

Wimp-win — settling low to protect self-esteem, dressed up as "win-win" (Ch 9, Appendix).

7-38-55 Rule — 7% words, 38% tone, 55% body language (Mehrabian) (Ch 8).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Never Split the Difference

Mirroring

When to use: build rapport, keep them talking, buy time, disagree without being disagreeable.

How: repeat the last 1–3 (or critical) words with an inquisitive upward inflection → then stay silent. Sequence: FM DJ voice → "I'm sorry…" → mirror → silence (≥4s) → repeat.

Trade-offs: feels awkward at first; stepping on it with a follow-up question kills its power.

Labeling

When to use: defuse a negative emotion or reinforce a positive one; whenever the counterpart is tense.

How: detect the emotion, then "It seems like… / It sounds like… / It looks like…" (never "I…"), then go silent. If they reject it: "I didn't say that's what it was. I just said it seems like that."

Trade-offs: must be neutral; "I"-framing raises guard.

Accusation Audit

When to use: before a confrontation likely to surface accusations against you.

How: list the worst things they could say → convert to anticipatory labels → role-play pacing/pauses → voice them first in the meeting.

Trade-offs: feels self-loathing; said aloud, accusations sound exaggerated and the counterpart often denies them.

Triggering "No"

When to use: openings, stalls, unresponsive counterparts.

How: "Is now a bad time to talk?"; ask what they don't want; mislabel to provoke correction ("It seems like you want this project to fail"); the "No"-oriented email "Have you given up on this project?"

Trade-offs: counterintuitive; goes against the "be nice / get to yes" instinct.

Summary → "That's right"

When to use: break deadlock; confirm genuine buy-in.

How: paraphrase + label = summary. Reflect "the world according to them" fully enough that the only reply is "That's right." (If you get "You're right," you've failed — no buy-in.)

Trade-offs: requires real listening; slow but durable.

Calibrated "How"/"What" Questions

When to use: nudge without pushiness, gather info, defuse confrontation, force empathy, guarantee execution.

How: avoid closed verbs (can/is/are/do/does). Start with What/How (rarely Why). Go-tos: "What's the biggest challenge you face?", "How am I supposed to do that?", "What are we trying to accomplish here?", "How will we know we're on track?"

Trade-offs: useless without emotional self-control; "Why" is accusatory unless aimed to serve you.

Multi-step "No" (bidding against themselves)

When to use: bargaining, getting concessions without counteroffering.

How: (1) "How am I supposed to do that?" → (2) "Your offer is very generous, I'm sorry, that just doesn't work for me" → (3) "I'm sorry, I just can't do that" → (4) "I'm sorry, no" → (5) "No."

Trade-offs: best when the counterpart has no other buyer.

Emotional Anchoring + Loss Aversion

When to use: before delivering a lowball or unwelcome offer.

How: accusation audit to anchor expectations low ("you're going to think I'm a lousy businessman…"), then frame the offer as something they'll lose to someone else.

Trade-offs: manipulative if misused; pairs with empathy.

Anchoring, Ranges & Odd Numbers

When to use: price discussions.

How: usually let them anchor first (you lack market info). When you must speak, use a bolstering range (low end = your goal). Use precise non-round numbers ($37,263) for credibility. Surprise with an unrelated gift to trigger reciprocity.

Trade-offs: brace for an extreme anchor from a pro; never open if you don't know market value.

Ackerman Bargaining

When to use: brass-tacks haggling toward a target price.

How: target → first offer 65% → raises to 85%, 95%, 100% (decreasing increments) → empathy + many "No"s to make them counter before each raise → non-round final number → toss in a token non-cash item at the limit.

Trade-offs: mechanical but powerful; the diminishing raises make them feel they squeezed you dry.

Reading People (verify & detect)

When to use: testing commitment and honesty.

How: Rule of Three (agree 3× via varied tactics); 7-38-55 (watch tone/body vs. words, label incongruence); pronoun analysis (lots of "I" = low power; "we/they" = real decider); Pinocchio Effect (liars use more words / third-person).

Trade-offs: heuristics, not proof; confirm with follow-up.

Black Swan Hunting

When to use: high-stakes or stuck negotiations; whenever the counterpart seems "crazy."

How: get face time; mine unguarded moments (start/end of meetings, interruptions); understand their "religion"/worldview; use the similarity principle; diagnose "crazy" as ill-informed / constrained / hidden interests; deploy positive, negative (sparingly), and normative leverage.

Trade-offs: hard to find over email; threats (negative leverage) leave toxic residue.

Three Negotiator Types (the Black Swan rule: treat them as they need)

Analyst — prepared data, warn early, give silence/time; apologies have little value.

Accommodator — be sociable but use calibrated questions to convert talk into action; uncover hidden objections.

Assertive — let them be heard first; mirrors, labels, summaries; aim for "that's right."

The Negotiation One Sheet (preparation)

When to use: before any significant negotiation (≈7:1 return on time).

How: 5 sections — (I) optimistic high-end Goal; (II) Summary the counterpart will answer "That's right" to; (III) 3–5 labels / accusation audit; (IV) 3–5 calibrated questions (incl. behind-the-table & deal-killer questions); (V) non-cash offers.

Trade-offs: don't over-script; stay agile.

Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Deep Work — Cheatsheet (decisions, defaults, tells)

The one formula

High-Quality Work Produced = (Time Spent) × (Intensity of Focus) → to produce more, raise intensity, not just hours.

Pick your depth philosophy (decision tree)

  • Can you shed almost all shallow duties? → Monastic
  • Can you clear whole days/seasons but need open time too? → Bimodal (min unit ≈ 1 day)
  • Regular job, need a reliable daily habit? → Rhythmic (same time daily, keep the streak) ← default for most
  • Already have trained, on-demand focus and an unpredictable schedule? → Journalistic (not for beginners)

Is this task deep or shallow?

Ask: "How many months to train a smart recent college grad (no field training) to do it?"

  • Few months → shallow → batch it, minimize it, fit it in the budget
  • Years of expertise → deep → protect a dedicated block for it

Keep or kill a tool? (craftsman test)

1. List the few goals that define success (work + life).

2. Does the tool substantially help the key activities behind them?

- Yes → keep · "some benefit" / "might miss out" → kill (that's any-benefit reasoning)

3. Unsure? Run the 30-day quit: gone 30 days — would it have been notably better? Did anyone care? Both must be a clear yes to readopt.

Willpower rule

Willpower is finite → never rely on resolve; rely on rituals, fixed times, and pre-decisions. If starting deep work requires a burst of willpower, your system is wrong.

4DX for depth (run all four)

DisciplineIndividual version
Wildly Important1–2 ambitious goals; say yes to the compelling goal, not no to distractions
Lead MeasureTrack deep-work hours (not papers/revenue — those are lag)
Compelling ScoreboardVisible tally; circle the hour that produced a result
Cadence of AccountabilityWeekly review confronting the scoreboard

Defaults & thresholds

  • Shallow-work budget: aim ~30–50% max; anything over → decline with the budget as reason.
  • Fixed endpoint: set when you stop (e.g., 5:30, no nights/weekends), then prune backward.
  • Internet blocks: schedule allowed windows; offline between them; need it early → move the next block a few min out, never jump online on impulse.
  • Schedule every minute: ~30-min blocks; rebuild the remaining day when derailed (thoughtfulness > obedience).

Email: become hard to reach

  • Sender filter → put the burden on them ("reply only if it's a good match").
  • Process-centric reply → answer the whole project in one message; kill the back-and-forth.
  • Don't respond → ambiguous / uninteresting / disproportionately costly = professionally ignorable.

Tells & smells (you're in trouble if…)

  • You "just quickly check" your inbox mid-task → attention residue is taxing every hour.
  • Your calendar is full but you can't name what you produced → busyness as proxy for value.
  • You reach for your phone at every micro-boredom (line, elevator) → training distraction addiction; your focus muscle is atrophying.
  • You justify a tool with "it has some benefit" → any-benefit trap.
  • Work thoughts loop at night → no shutdown ritual (Zeigarnik effect).
  • You default to the easiest task available → Principle of Least Resistance running your day.

End-of-day shutdown (algorithm)

inbox check → capture loose tasks → skim all lists + next few days' calendar → rough plan for tomorrow → say "Shutdown complete."

glossary.md

Glossary — Deep Work (Cal Newport)

Any-Benefit Approach — The flawed rule that a network tool is justified if it offers any possible benefit or you might miss anything by not using it; approves everything because every tool has some benefit (Ch 7).

Attention Residue — Sophie Leroy's finding that after switching from Task A to Task B, part of your attention stays stuck on A, degrading performance on B; worse when A is left unfinished (Ch 2).

Attention Restoration Theory (ART) — Directed attention is a finite resource that depletes; time in nature (or restful downtime) replenishes it, aiding subsequent deep work (Ch 5).

Bimodal Philosophy — Divide time into clearly defined deep stretches (days or a season) and open shallow periods; minimum deep unit usually a full day (e.g., Jung, Adam Grant) (Ch 5).

Busyness as a Proxy for Productivity — Doing lots of visible stuff as a stand-in for value, used when knowledge work lacks clear productivity metrics (Ch 3).

Cadence of Accountability — 4DX Discipline #4: a regular (weekly) review confronting your scoreboard and committing to next actions (Ch 5).

Compelling Scoreboard — 4DX Discipline #3: a physical, visible tally of your lead measure (deep-work hours); "people play differently when they're keeping score" (Ch 5).

Craftsman Approach to Tool Selection — Adopt a tool only if its positive impact on your core success/happiness factors substantially outweighs its negatives (Ch 7).

Cult of the Internet — Treating any new technology as inherently good/necessary, branding skeptics Luddites, so tools spread unchecked (Ch 3).

Deep Work — "Professional activities performed in a state of distraction-free concentration that push your cognitive capabilities to their limit. These efforts create new value, improve your skill, and are hard to replicate" (Intro).

Deep Work Hypothesis — The ability to do deep work is becoming rarer and more valuable; the few who cultivate it and center their work on it will thrive (Intro).

Deliberate Practice — Ericsson's mechanism of skill acquisition: focused, feedback-driven strain on a specific ability just beyond current reach; incompatible with divided attention (Ch 2).

Depth Philosophy — Your chosen pattern for integrating deep work: Monastic, Bimodal, Rhythmic, or Journalistic (Ch 5).

Eudaimonia Machine — David Dewane's conceptual building whose architecture channels occupants from social space into progressively deeper chambers ending in isolated deep-work rooms; a metaphor for engineering depth (Ch 5).

Fixed-Schedule Productivity — Fix a firm workday endpoint, then work backward, ruthlessly pruning shallow obligations to fit deep work into the constrained hours (Ch 8).

Flow — Csikszentmihalyi's state of full absorption when mind/body is stretched to its limits on a worthwhile task; the reliable source of satisfaction (Ch 4).

Grand Gesture — A radical change to environment or investment that raises a task's perceived importance and mobilizes focus (e.g., Rowling's hotel suite) (Ch 5).

Hub-and-Spoke — Architecture of collaboration: expose yourself to "hub" spaces for serendipitous idea exchange, then retreat to isolated "spoke" spaces for deep execution (Ch 5).

Journalistic Philosophy — Fit deep work into any open gap on demand; requires trained concentration and confidence (e.g., Walter Isaacson); hard for beginners (Ch 5).

Lag Measure — A metric describing the outcome you ultimately want (papers published, revenue); arrives too late to steer daily behavior (Ch 5).

Law of Productivity — High-Quality Work Produced = (Time Spent) × (Intensity of Focus); raise intensity to produce more per hour (Ch 2).

Law of the Vital Few — ~80% of a desired effect comes from ~20% of possible causes; concentrate effort on the high-impact minority (Ch 7).

Lead Measure — A metric for the controllable behavior that drives the lag measure (for depth: hours spent in deep work); movable day-to-day (Ch 5).

Metric Black Hole — The impact of distraction/depth on productivity is real but hard to measure, so it goes unmanaged (Ch 3).

Monastic Philosophy — Maximize depth by radically eliminating or minimizing shallow obligations (e.g., Knuth, Stephenson) (Ch 5).

Myelination — Growth of insulating myelin around repeatedly-fired neural circuits; the physical basis of skill, triggered by isolated intense focus (Ch 2).

Principle of Least Resistance — Without clear feedback on bottom-line impact, we default to whatever behavior is easiest in the moment (Ch 3).

Process-Centric Email — A reply that resolves the whole underlying project/loop in one message to minimize future back-and-forth (Ch 8).

Productive Meditation — Focusing attention on a single well-defined professional problem during physical-but-not-mental activity (walking, driving); redirect from distraction and looping (Ch 6).

Rhythmic Philosophy — Make deep work a daily habit at a fixed time, sustained via a streak/chain ("don't break the chain") (e.g., Brian Chappell) (Ch 5).

Ritual (Deep Work Ritual) — A preset answer to where/how long you'll work, how you'll work (rules/metrics), and how you'll support the work — to minimize willpower cost of starting (Ch 5).

Roosevelt Dash — A burst of maximal-intensity focus on one task under a deadline far shorter than normal, used to stretch your concentration ceiling (Ch 6).

Sender Filter — Published expectations shifting the burden of contact to the sender, reducing inbound email you must handle (Ch 8).

Shallow Work — "Noncognitively demanding, logistical-style tasks, often performed while distracted... tend not to create much new value and are easy to replicate" (Intro / Ch 8).

Shallow Work Budget — An explicit agreed percentage of time (often 30–50%) allowed for shallow work, defended against overrun (Ch 8).

Shutdown Ritual — An end-of-day algorithm confirming every incomplete task has a trusted plan or is captured, ending in a set phrase ("Shutdown complete") (Ch 5).

The Great Restructuring — Economic split by intelligent machines/connectivity into those who work with depth (winners) and those who don't (Intro).

Willpower Depletion — Willpower is finite and drains with use; hence rely on rituals, not resolve, to sustain deep work (Ch 5).

Zeigarnik Effect — Incomplete tasks dominate our attention; the shutdown ritual neutralizes it by capturing/planning open loops (Ch 5).

4DX (Four Disciplines of Execution) — Framework applied to individual depth: focus on the wildly important → act on lead measures → keep a compelling scoreboard → create a cadence of accountability (Ch 5).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Deep Work (Cal Newport)

Choose a Depth Philosophy

When to use: Setting up how deep work fits your life; do this before any scheduling tactic.

How: Pick the one matching your constraints — Monastic (eliminate shallow entirely), Bimodal (deep in day/season blocks), Rhythmic (same time daily, keep a streak), Journalistic (any open gap, on demand).

Trade-offs: Monastic needs a job that tolerates it; Journalistic needs pre-trained focus. Rhythmic is the safe default for most jobs. A mismatch derails the habit.

Deep Work Ritual

When to use: Every deep session, to spend minimal willpower starting.

How: Pre-decide (1) where and for how long; (2) how you'll work (rules — no internet; metrics — words/20min); (3) how you'll support it (coffee, food, walk, tidy space).

Trade-offs: Feels mechanical, but that's the point — remove in-the-moment decisions that leak willpower.

4DX for Individual Depth

When to use: To translate "work more deeply" into a driven, tracked habit.

How: (1) Set a small number of wildly important goals; (2) track the lead measure — deep-work hours — not lag outcomes; (3) keep a compelling scoreboard (visible tally, circle hours that produced results); (4) run a weekly cadence of accountability review.

Trade-offs: Requires honest daily tracking; the scoreboard only motivates if you actually confront it.

Shutdown Ritual

When to use: End of every workday.

How: Algorithm — check inbox for anything urgent → capture loose tasks into master lists → skim every list + next few days' calendar → make a rough plan for tomorrow → say a closing phrase ("Shutdown complete").

Trade-offs: Takes 10–15 min; defeats the Zeigarnik effect so evenings truly restore attention.

Grand Gesture

When to use: A high-stakes project that deserves a jolt of importance.

How: Make a conspicuous investment/change of environment (a hotel room, a trip, a paid retreat) that raises the psychological stakes and mobilizes focus.

Trade-offs: Costs money/effort; overuse dilutes the effect. Reserve for projects that warrant it.

Hub-and-Spoke Collaboration

When to use: When ideas benefit from exchange but execution needs isolation.

How: Spend time in shared "hub" spaces for serendipitous encounters, then retreat to isolated "spoke" spaces to work deeply on what surfaced. The whiteboard effect: working with someone on a hard problem can push depth further.

Trade-offs: Pure isolation misses cross-pollination; pure openness kills focus. Alternate deliberately.

Scheduled Internet Blocks (Embrace Boredom)

When to use: Default operating mode to rebuild concentration.

How: Schedule the blocks when internet use is allowed; stay fully offline between them. If you need it sooner, reschedule the next block a few minutes out — never jump online impulsively.

Trade-offs: Uncomfortable at first; the discomfort is the training. Works at home too, not just at work.

Roosevelt Dash

When to use: To stretch your focus ceiling, or to blast through an important task.

How: Estimate the time a task needs, set a deadline well under it, work at total intensity (no email, no drift) to make it.

Trade-offs: Exhausting; use occasionally as interval training, not constantly.

Productive Meditation

When to use: During walks, commutes, showers — physical-but-not-mental time.

How: Hold one well-defined work problem in mind; when you notice distraction (drift to easier thoughts) or looping (rehashing knowns), gently redirect. Structure it: identify variables → determine next-step question → consolidate the gain.

Trade-offs: Frustrating early; builds both focus and problem-solving output over time.

Craftsman Tool Selection + Law of the Vital Few

When to use: Deciding whether to keep any network/social tool.

How: (1) Name the few high-level goals defining professional and personal success. (2) List the 2–3 key activities supporting each. (3) Keep a tool only if it substantially helps those (not "any benefit"). Concentrate on the ~20% of activities driving ~80% of results.

Trade-offs: Requires honesty about what actually matters; you'll drop tools that feel socially expected.

30-Day Quit (Packing-Party Test)

When to use: To measure a tool's real value.

How: Quit it quietly for 30 days. Then ask: (1) Would these 30 days have been notably better with it? (2) Did anyone care I wasn't using it? Readopt only on a clear yes to both.

Trade-offs: Mild FOMO; usually reveals the tool was justified only by the any-benefit standard.

Schedule Every Minute

When to use: Every workday, to prevent shallow drift.

How: Block the day in ~30-min chunks with an assigned task each; keep an overflow column; when reality derails a block, rebuild the remaining schedule rather than abandoning it.

Trade-offs: Not about rigid obedience — about staying thoughtful. Expect frequent revision.

Quantify Depth (College-Grad Heuristic)

When to use: To classify any ambiguous task as deep or shallow.

How: Ask "How many months to train a smart recent college grad with no field training to do this?" Few months → shallow; years → deep.

Trade-offs: A heuristic, not a law; but surprisingly clarifying for borderline tasks.

Shallow Work Budget + Fixed-Schedule Productivity

When to use: To cap shallow work and force prioritization.

How: Ask your boss what % of time should be shallow (often 30–50%); defend the budget. Separately, fix a hard workday endpoint and prune obligations backward to fit deep work into fewer hours.

Trade-offs: Requires saying no often; the constraint is the mechanism, not a limitation.

Become Hard to Reach

When to use: To reclaim attention from email.

How: (1) Sender filters — publish expectations that put the burden on the sender; (2) do more work per email — send process-centric replies that close the whole loop; (3) don't respond to ambiguous/uninteresting/disproportionately costly messages.

Trade-offs: Some senders bristle; net attention reclaimed is large. Not for messages where non-response has real cost.

The Media Training Bible: 101 Things You Absolutely, Positively Need to Know Before Your Next Interview

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Media Training Bible (Brad Phillips)

Decision rules

  • Should I do the interview? If the story is about you and runs with or without you → yes (1-for-3 beats 0-for-3). Decline only if irrelevant, off-brand, or zero upside.
  • Reporter calls now? Don't interview on the spot. Get the topic, promise a fast call-back, prep, then call before they've written — not just by deadline.
  • Can't answer this? Never "no comment." Explain why you can't, then give what you can.
  • Tempted to say "off the record"? Don't. Assume everything is on the record, always.
  • Asked a negative/loaded question? Never repeat the loaded word. Reframe positively, then transition to a message.
  • Open-ended "what" question? Use Why + What (lead with why it matters).
  • Any other answer? Lead with the conclusion (start at the end), keep to ≤30 seconds, make each sentence stand alone and on-message.
  • Don't know the answer? Peter Jennings Rule — say what you do know.
  • Print/edited interview? Pause ~3 seconds before answering. Live/hostile? Don't pause long — just let the question finish.

The ATMs (tough-question formula)

Answer (1 word) → Transition → Message (+ supports) → sell (optional)

Time split: 10–20% A+T, 80–90% M+s. Don't use on every answer. Drop the "A" for false-premise and guarantee questions.

Trap-question quick reference

TrapMove
False premiseReject at once: "I don't agree with the premise…" then M
False choice (this/that)"That's like choosing between air and water."
Yes/No (damaging)Reframe with context; don't concede the bad word
Demands a guarantee"Here's what I can guarantee…"
Speculation / hypothetical"I can't speculate, but here's what I can tell you…"
About a competitor"I'll let them speak for themselves, but here's why ours is a hit…"
Indirect attribution ("people say")Dismiss the anonymous claim; return to message
Left fieldPledge to learn more / talk about what you know / zoom out
Don't knowPeter Jennings Rule
ParaphraseReject unless 100% accurate; don't repeat their word

Message thresholds & defaults

  • 3 messages, one sentence each. ≥2 stories + ≥2 statistics + ≥2 sound bites per message (~21 answers).
  • Message ≤ 30 words, ≤ 2 commas, concrete images, spoken aloud to test.
  • Audiences need 7–15 exposures to act. Avg TV quote = 7.3 sec / ~18 words; print quote = 8–20 words.
  • Answers ≤ 30 seconds. Speak 10–15% louder than feels natural.

CUBE A (message checklist)

Consistent · Unburdened (no jargon/abstraction) · Brief (1 sentence) · Ear-worthy (speak it aloud) · Audience-focused (their needs/values)

Statistics: make numbers land

Give context ("122 Fenway Parks") · make it personal ($1,250/family, not $100B) · use ratios ("1 in 3") · avoid bare percentages · give relative distance ("Maine to Miami").

Body language & voice tells

  • Energy: you feel an 8, the room sees a 4 → go bigger. Eye contact: aim ~100% (not the conversational 40–60%).
  • Posture: lean slightly forward, off the chair-back; no crossed legs/arms, no swivel chairs.
  • Voice levers: volume, pace (slow for complex/key points), pitch (avoid upticks), tone, silences, diaphragmatic breathing.
  • Smell test for "off message": if you say "Oh, by the way…" / "Incidentally…" you've strayed.

Attire defaults

Solids in gray/blue/earth tones · high contrast · both sexes wear makeup · shined shoes, long dark socks · avoid stripes/checks, pastels (hard fields), lapel pins, gloss/shimmer, day-of haircut. HD → subtle, smooth, spotless.

The 10 Truths of a Crisis (if you see X, do Y)

1. You'll suffer first — contain it, don't let it "jump the fire line."

2. Cast as good/bad guy — show you "get it."

3. Communicate within the hour — be present in your own coverage.

4. Media side with victims — right facts + wrong tone = clueless.

5. Spokesperson choice signals scale — err high, don't always lead with the CEO.

6. Train receptionists, guards, even spouses — anyone can be the confirming source.

7. Don't bury bad facts — tear the Band-Aid off; no drip-drip.

8. Social media first — correct misinformation within ~30 min.

9. Apologize fully the first time — no "if/then" half-apology; pledge action.

10. Lawyers can deepen the crisis — weigh reputation against legal payout.

Format fast rules

  • Phone: stand, headset, landline, gesture, listen for typing (slow down/repeat).
  • Radio: prepare for abrupt start, match/exceed host energy, make your own plug.
  • TV: phone off, monitor away, you're always "on" (split screen), stay seated till clear; in a crisis no logos in your background.
  • Edited: never say "as I mentioned earlier," "in conclusion," a date, or the reporter's name.
  • Skype: the one format where you limit gestures (jumpy on low bandwidth).
  • Social media: treat as a nonstop, permanent, on-the-record press conference.

Prep ritual (7 steps)

Worksheets → file cards (trigger words) → interview the reporter → research both sides → small Q&A (≤12) → recorded practice → pick 3 improvement areas. Remember less to perform better.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Media Training Bible

Ambush interview — A reporter showing up unannounced or blindsiding you with an off-topic question mid-interview; win by denying them a defensive "money shot" (Ch 4).

ATMs — Phillips' core system for tough questions: Answer, Transition, Message, sell. Spend 10–20% on A+T, 80–90% on M+s (Ch 4).

Audience focused — The "A" in CUBE A: a message must incorporate the audience's needs and values, not just your points (Ch 2).

Bites interview — The most common TV format; producers use only a few sound bites. Look at the interviewer, not the camera (Ch 5, Ch 6).

Brief — The "B" in CUBE A: one sentence per message; the average TV quote is 7.3 seconds / ~18 words (Ch 2).

Comment without commenting — Declining to answer by explaining why you can't, instead of saying "no comment" (Ch 1).

Consistent — The "C" in CUBE A: repeat the same themes across all platforms; 7–15 exposures move an audience to action (Ch 2).

Crisis — An event, precipitated by a specific incident, that draws critical media attention for a definite period (Ch 7).

CUBE A — The five elements of an effective message: Consistent, Unburdened, Brief, Ear-worthy, Audience focused (Ch 2).

Deskside briefing — A casual one-on-one briefing at a journalist's office; treat everything as quotable (Ch 6).

Diaphragmatic breathing — Breathing from the stomach (not chest) for a fuller, less nasal voice and better breath control (Ch 5).

Ear-worthy — The "E" in CUBE A: write for the ear, not the eye — short, everyday words, contractions; speak it aloud (Ch 2).

Edited interview — Any interview aired/printed in clips; you can restart answers, but avoid "as I mentioned earlier," "in conclusion," dates, and the reporter's name (Ch 6).

Effective frequency — The number of exposures before a message drives action; Phillips' rule is 7–15+ (Ch 2).

File cards — Index cards distilling each message + supports to trigger phrases, so you sound extemporaneous on air (Ch 8).

Head/heart principle — Jordan-Meier's test for crisis spokespersons: deliver the right words in the right (believably caring) way (Ch 7).

IFB (interruptible feedback) — The TV earpiece through which you hear the studio; test it before air (Ch 6).

Jump the fire line — When a specific, limited crisis becomes a referendum on your whole brand's competence (Toyota) (Ch 7).

Live-to-tape — Prerecorded but aired unedited; treat as live, but ask if you can restart on a mistake (Ch 6).

Message — A one-sentence statement marrying one of your key points to one of your audience's needs/values; aim for three (Ch 2).

Message disconnect — When your words and body language contradict; the audience believes the body (Ch 5).

Message support — A story, statistic, or sound bite that reinforces a message (the "three-legged stool"); build ≥2 of each per message (Ch 2).

Money shot — The dramatic, guilty-looking visual a reporter wants in an ambush; deny it by staying calm (Ch 4).

"No comment" — The most damaging phrase in a spokesperson's lexicon; reads as guilt. Never use it or its equivalents (Ch 1).

Off the record — Info that can't be used in any form — but the term is defined inconsistently by journalists; unreliable, so banish it (Ch 1).

On background — Info usable but the source can't be named or quoted (Ch 1).

On the record — The default state of all communication with reporters (Ch 1).

Peter Jennings Rule — When you don't know the answer, tell the public what you do know ("That's unclear, but here's what we know…") (Ch 4).

Phoner — A print or radio interview conducted by phone; stand, use a headset and landline, gesture (Ch 6).

Present in your own coverage — Showing up and speaking so reporters use you as the primary source in a crisis (Ch 7).

Rule of Thirds — A story has three voices (you, opponent, reporter); refusing to comment makes you go "0-for-3." Don't make your opponent's case (Ch 1).

Seven-second stray — A brief off-message moment that becomes the only quote that airs — repeatedly; your message is your "lifeboat" (Ch 4).

Sound bite — A short, memorable/witty phrase expressing a message; usually planned in advance, delivered as if improvised (Ch 2).

Split screen / reaction shot — TV formats where you appear while not speaking; act as if you're always "on" (Ch 6).

Strong language — Declarative words ("here's what we know") replacing hedges ("we think," "we hope") (Ch 3).

Target person — One specific individual you visualize and speak to, representing the whole audience (Ch 3).

Ten Truths of a Crisis — Phillips' crisis framework (Ch 7), e.g. communicate immediately, side with victims, apologize the right way.

Twelve-Year-Old-Nephew Rule — Strip jargon by explaining as you would to a bright 12-year-old (simplify, don't "dumb down") (Ch 3).

Unburdened — The "U" in CUBE A: free of wordiness, jargon, abstractions (≤2 commas, ≤30 words, concrete images) (Ch 2).

Uptick — Rising pitch at the end of statements, making them sound like questions and eroding credibility (Ch 5).

Verbal filler — "Uhhh," "ummm," "like," "you know"; kill with pre-answer pauses and the 30-second-object drill (Ch 5).

Walk and talk — An interview conducted while walking; visually interesting but distracting — slow down or stop to make a key point (Ch 6).

Why + What — Answer open-ended "what" questions by leading with why your work matters, then what you do (Ch 3).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — The Media Training Bible

The ATMs (answering any tough question)

When to use: Off-topic, hostile, or trap questions where you must answer and stay on message.

How: Answer (often one word) → Transition (bridge phrase) → Message (+ supports) → sell (optional call to action). Spend 10–20% on A+T, 80–90% on M+s. Drop the "A" when the transition can serve as the answer (false premise, guarantee).

Trade-offs: Don't use on every answer — overuse reads as canned/evasive.

CUBE A (building a message)

When to use: Drafting or stress-testing your three core messages.

How: Make each message Consistent (repeatable theme), Unburdened (≤2 commas, ≤30 words, no jargon), Brief (one sentence), Ear-worthy (speak it aloud), Audience-focused (their needs/values).

Trade-offs: Frustrating self-editing; the discipline is the point.

The Message-Support Stool (staying on message without repeating)

When to use: Every interview — to answer many questions on-message without sounding repetitive.

How: For each of 3 messages, prepare ≥2 stories, ≥2 statistics, ≥2 sound bites (~21 answers). Pair a support with a message or use it alone.

Trade-offs: Front-loaded prep work; pays off in flexibility.

Why + What

When to use: Open-ended questions ("What does your company do?").

How: Lead with why your work matters (a striking context/stat), then what you do.

Trade-offs: Slightly less direct than a normal lead — reserved for open-enders only.

Start at the End (don't bury the lead)

When to use: Most answers, especially live interviews.

How: Open with your conclusion/most important point → add context → restate the lead.

Trade-offs: Cuts against the chronological storytelling instinct; requires practice.

The Three-Second Pause

When to use: Print and most edited interviews.

How: After a question, stay quiet a few seconds, form the answer, then speak. Kills filler, sharpens focus.

Trade-offs: Skip in live/hostile interviews (long silence reads as evasive) — instead just let the question finish before speaking.

The Peter Jennings Rule (unknown answers)

When to use: Asked something you don't know or shouldn't guess.

How: "That's unclear, but here's what we know…" — give value from what you do know.

Trade-offs: If pressed for the specific fact afterward, it's fine to say you don't know.

Rewrite the Hostile Question

When to use: Aggressive, loaded, or insulting questions.

How: Silently restate the question in neutral terms; answer that. "I disagree with the premise, and am happy to share our accomplishments…"

Trade-offs: Don't repeat the loaded language while doing it.

Trap-Question Playbook

When to use: The ten recurring trap types.

How: False premise → reject immediately, drop the "A." False choice → "that's like choosing between air and water." Yes/No → reframe with context, don't concede the damaging word. Guarantee → "Here's what I can guarantee…" Speculation → "I can't speculate, but here's what I can tell you…" Competition → "I'll let them speak for themselves, but here's why ours is a hit…" Indirect attribution → dismiss the anonymous claim, return to message.

Trade-offs: Zoom-out/general answers can invite more probing follow-ups — practice in advance.

Comment Without Commenting

When to use: Legitimately can't answer (confidential, legal, layoffs, safety).

How: Explain why you can't, then offer what you can. Never say "no comment."

Trade-offs: Comes "perilously close" to no-comment — transition smoothly.

Crisis Response Protocol

When to use: Any breaking crisis.

How: Communicate within the hour ("present in your own coverage"); focus on victims with genuine humanity; get all bad facts out at once (don't drip); apologize fully the first time (no "if/then"); choose the right-level spokesperson (err high); use social media within ~30 min; weigh legal vs. reputational cost.

Trade-offs: Speaking early with incomplete facts feels risky — state what you know, what you're doing, and when you'll update.

Crisis Preparation Drill

When to use: Before any crisis, ideally yearly.

How: Assemble a cross-department team → brainstorm via the 8 categories → reduce to the 5 most likely-and-damaging → write a response per crisis → run staged "real-time" on-camera drills (breaking news → reputation-forming → finger-pointing).

Trade-offs: Time-intensive; "once you hear the thunder, it's too late to build the ark."

Kill Verbal Filler (the 30-second object drill)

When to use: Habitual "uhhh," "ummm," "like," "you know."

How: Shout a random object, talk about it for 30 seconds with pauses but zero filler; record to verify.

Trade-offs: Filler only matters when it distracts — don't over-police the occasional "uh."

The Seven-Step Prep Workflow

When to use: Before every interview (do a "shortcut" version under deadline).

How: (1) Message worksheets → (2) File cards → (3) Interview the reporter → (4) Research both sides → (5) Small Q&A (≤12 Qs) → (6) Recorded practice interview → (7) Pick 3 improvement areas.

Trade-offs: Over-preparation paralyzes — keep the Q&A small; reduce to trigger words.

Reshuffle: Who Wins When AI Restacks the Knowledge Economy

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Reshuffle — Decision Cheatsheet

The one reframe

When you catch yourself asking "How smart is the AI?" or "What can we automate?", stop. Ask "What does this system look like once it adopts the machine's logic?" — because AI's economic impact comes from restructuring the system around a task, not from performing the task.

Diagnostic order (never invert)

1. Has the playing field (system/ecosystem) changed?

2. Has the basis of value creation moved?

3. Does the business model still hold?

4. What capabilities does the new game need?

5. Which roles and workflows still matter?

6. Only now — where does AI apply?

Starting at step 6 is the framing error. It produces motion, not direction.

Constraint router — where does my value come from?

Your value rests onAI's effectDo this
Scarcity (rare knowledge, gated access)Collapses fastest — expertise commoditizesExit; rebundle around risk or coordination
Risk (errors are costly, someone must be accountable)Grows — probabilistic outputs create accountability gapsOwn judgment, liability, and trust
Coordination (many misaligned moving parts)Grows most — AI extends coordination into new domainsOwn representation, decision, and execution

Is this task safe? — displacement test

  • Did it get cheaper? → economic displacement.
  • Did it stop mattering in the workflow? → contextual displacement.
  • Either one devalues the job. A task can feel meaningful (intrinsic value), still be done, and command nothing.
  • Typist effect tell: the task still exists but no one needs a person whose job is that task.

Reskilling: when it actually works

  • Works when the system still needs a human to execute that work.
  • Fails when the system has removed the need. Then only rebundling around the new constraint works.
  • Default: stop asking "what skill next?" and ask "where has friction moved?"

Tool vs. Engine

AI as a ToolAI as an Engine
RoleOptimizes tasks in the current modelDetermines core system performance
EffectCompetes better at the old gameChanges the rules of competition
Replaceable?YesNot without re-architecting

If your AI could be swapped out without redesigning the business, it's a tool — expect no durable advantage.

Am I becoming a wrapper? — the integration trap, 3 stages

1. Tools commoditize execution.

2. Tools absorb expertise.

3. You reorganize around the engine → performance-based lock-in.

Tells: you dropped internal processes because they "just add complexity"; your performance gains now arrive from the vendor's release notes; customers can't name what's yours.

Move: keep a layer the engine can't see — proprietary field data, risk absorption, decision rights, integrated delivery.

How far to climb the solutioning stack

ModelPaid forRequires
Work-as-a-serviceOperational delivery (hours, cycles)Tool performance ownership
Results-as-a-serviceMeasurable results to specDomain depth + deeper integration
Outcomes-as-a-serviceCustomer-specific strategic outcomesEnd-to-end control, liability, monitoring

Rule: climb only as far as you can absorb the risk. Liability without visibility, integration, and execution control is a loss engine.

Consensus or interpretation?

  • Participants can be made to adopt shared standards → coordination with consensus (CCC model): auditable, enforceable, slow to spread.
  • Participants won't ever agree on formats → coordination without consensus (Tractable model): AI interprets each actor's native inputs; standards become implicit. This is the domain AI newly opens.
  • Tell that you need the latter: repeated failed attempts to get everyone onto one platform.

Control point checklist (all three, or you don't have one)

  • Unified representation — shared source of truth everyone acts on
  • Unified decision — you resolve the decision they'd otherwise negotiate
  • Unified execution — workflows integrated so the decision actually happens

UI simplification alone never earns the right to coordinate. Power comes from dependence, not dominance.

Where the control point sits

  • Customers stuck on a hard choice → demand-side control point (own the decision moment).
  • Partners can't align on delivery → supply-side control point (own the coordination anchor).

Four strategic postures — pick one out loud

PostureMoveAdvantage
Reactive optimizerSpeed up today's tasksNone that compounds
Anticipator ("Gretzky")Spot value migration earlyIncremental; still the old game
Logic shifter ("Curry")Change where/how decisions are madeStructural, within the industry
Field reshaper ("Tiger")Restructure the ecosystemMost durable; you set others' rules

Rule: the deeper the reimagining of coordination, the greater the power shift and the more enduring the advantage.

Three traps when the ground keeps shifting

  • Chase transient advantage → wins evaporate, never compound (Chegg).
  • Build executional agility → faster at solving the wrong problem (Yahoo).
  • Perpetual experimentation → motion without commitment.

All three optimize within the old system and tether you to it.

Smells

  • "We need an AI strategy." → You need a strategy for the conditions AI creates.
  • AI pilots proliferating with no system thesis → execution bias.
  • Outputs that look impressive but lack rigor → vibe coding.
  • Task-level speedups + rising cross-team friction → coordination paradox; you fragmented the org.
  • "Humans stay in the loop, so we're fine." → human-in-the-loop illusion; check who actually decides.
  • Everyone's output suddenly looks alike → collapse of differentiation; the skill premium is gone.

glossary.md

Glossary — Reshuffle (Sangeet Paul Choudary)

Terms as the author defines them. Chapter attribution in parentheses.

A

Above-the-Algorithm vs. Below-the-Algorithm — Above: workers who use or build algorithmic systems for leverage. Below: workers managed by them, with little autonomy or differentiation. (Ch 3)

Accessibility — How easy it is for a customer to adopt and pay for a solution. (Ch 9)

Agentic Execution — Autonomous goal-driven agents that monitor systems, detect intent, and act across workflows without human prompting. (Ch 6)

AI as a Tool vs. AI as an Engine — Tool: optimizes tasks inside the existing model; doesn't change the basis of competition. Engine: drives core system performance and defines how the business operates. (Ch 12)

AI as Coordination Infrastructure — AI's transformational role is not automation but extending coordination into previously uncoordinated domains by structuring ambiguity and translating tacit cues. (Ch 6)

AI-Native Firm — An organization designed from the ground up around AI in core workflows and knowledge distribution, unlike incumbents layering AI on old systems. (Ch 6)

Algorithmic Management — Using algorithms to allocate, supervise, and evaluate work; compresses wages, standardizes output, strips decision control from workers. (Ch 3)

Assistive Execution — AI-supported workflows where humans still decide; the bridge to agentic workflows. (Ch 6)

Autonomy-Coordination Trade-off — The assumption that more team autonomy means less alignment. AI dissolves the trade-off. (Ch 6)

B

Barcode-Native Architecture — An organization built to fully exploit a coordination technology's data (Walmart with barcodes), not merely to adopt it. (Ch 1)

Behavior Graph — Preferences inferred from observed actions; replaces the social graph in AI-native experiences (TikTok). (Ch 10, 12)

Building Block — A discrete, modular capability that can be rented, reused, and recombined into a larger system. (Ch 7)

Building Block Economy — An economy of rentable modular capabilities; success depends on how well you rebundle them and manage constraints between them. (Ch 7)

C

Clockspeed — The relative pace of innovation across parts of a value chain; AI tools evolve faster than the businesses adopting them. (Ch 8)

Cold Start Problem — Participants won't join until value is visible, but value needs participants. (Ch 11, 12)

Collapse of Differentiation — When AI makes everyone's output look alike, expertise stops commanding a premium. (Ch 4)

Composable Business — A business that assembles third-party capabilities rather than building them. (Ch 7)

Composition Power — Control over how components and actors plug into a system. (Ch 1)

Constraints — System bottlenecks limiting performance: scarcity-based, risk-based, or coordination-based. (Ch 5)

Constraint Management — Identifying and designing around system limits to secure consistent performance and defensibility. (Ch 9, 12)

Contextual Value — The value a role holds because it resolves a critical constraint in a specific system — not because the skill is rare. (Ch 5)

Control Point — A chokehold others must operate through to create or deliver value; power by indispensability, not ownership. (Ch 11, 12)

Coordination — Aligning independent agents toward a shared outcome under fragmentation, ambiguity, or misaligned incentives. (Ch 1)

Coordination Gap — The space between what algorithms can coordinate (codified workflows) and what economic activity actually requires (judgment, context, tacit knowledge). (Ch 1)

Coordination Paradox — Narrow local automation fragments the organization and raises, not lowers, coordination costs. (Ch 6)

Coordination Tax — The hidden, exponentially scaling cost of keeping teams aligned: meetings, messaging, searching, manual handoffs. (Ch 6)

Coordination Technology — Technology that aligns fragmented system parts — barcodes, containers, and now AI. (Ch 1)

Coordination Without Consensus — AI-enabled coordination where actors need no prior agreement on formats or rules; AI interprets diverse inputs into shared understanding. (Ch 11)

Curation — Elevating relevant signal from noise and shaping context and narrative; rises in value as information commoditizes. (Ch 5)

Curiosity — The disciplined ability to frame high-leverage questions; an economic asset when answers are cheap. (Ch 5)

D

Data Flywheel — More usage → more data → better system → more usage. (Ch 11)

Decision Friction — The cognitive burden or uncertainty that stops customers choosing confidently. (Ch 10)

Dependence vs. Dominance — Ecosystem control now comes from being depended on, not from ownership or lock-in. (Ch 11)

Demand-Side / Supply-Side Control Point — Power from controlling customer decisions vs. power from coordinating how participants deliver. (Ch 10, 11)

E

Economic Collapse of the Task — A task still gets done but no longer commands a premium because AI made it cheap. (Ch 2, 4)

Economic vs. Contextual Displacement — A task can become cheaper (economic) or lose importance in the workflow (contextual). Either devalues the job. (Ch 4)

Economic Visibility — Whether the system recognizes and rewards a role's contribution; contextual value must be made visible to be captured. (Ch 5)

Ecosystem Flywheel — AI coordination attracts participants → more data → better coordination → more participants. (Ch 11)

Engine — The component that determines system performance; not replaceable without re-architecting. (Ch 8)

Execution Bias — Acting fast because execution is cheap, at the expense of strategic intent. (Ch 12)

Exponential Systems — One coordination breakthrough (containers, APIs) triggers layers of new capabilities, restructuring industries rather than just speeding outputs. (Ch 1)

F–H

Framing Error — Solving a problem with an obsolete mental model while the underlying structure has changed. (Ch 2)

Governance Power — The ability to set and enforce rules of participation. (Ch 3, 11)

Human-in-the-Loop Illusion — Believing humans stay central by supervising AI, while in fact being reduced to support roles in systems that make the decisions. (Ch 3)

I–L

Intrinsic / Economic / Contextual Value — A task can be meaningful, paid for, or workflow-critical; these come apart. (Ch 4)

Judgment — Making accountable decisions under uncertainty; gains value as AI outputs turn probabilistic. (Ch 5)

Knowledge as Capital — Knowledge as a rentable, scalable, recombinable asset rather than labor. (Ch 4, 7)

Learning Loop — AI improves from use, so unlike barcodes it changes the system as it learns from it. (Ch 1)

Leverage — Amplifying output without proportional input, via rented capabilities, AI, and platform orchestration. (Ch 7)

Local Optimization, Systemic Fragility — Isolated improvements in one part increase misalignment with the rest. (Ch 8)

M–P

Modularity — Discrete interchangeable components combinable into larger systems. (Ch 7)

Narrative Control — Power to shape meaning and action through framing and curation. (Ch 3, 5)

Network Capital — Distributed audience reach that enables outsized impact without infrastructure. (Ch 5)

Ownership of Outcomes — Accepting liability, which demands representation (visibility), integration (decision-making), and execution (delivery). (Ch 9)
