Performance Leverage — Leverage from owning a superior critical component (engine). (Ch 8)

Performance-Based Lock-In — Dependence created by superior component performance, not contracts. (Ch 8)

Pie-Slicing vs. Pie-Growing — Technology grows the pie but also reshapes who slices it; AI concentrates coordination power. (Ch 3)

Platform Tax — Fees or concessions an orchestrator extracts for access to decision moments or customers. (Ch 10)

Positive Constraint — A deliberately chosen boundary or design rule that improves coordination and creates differentiation, preserving judgment or diversity that pure speed would sacrifice. (Ch 9, 12)

R

Rebundling — Reassembling unbundled tasks and capabilities into new roles, workflows, organizations, or industry architectures around new constraints. (Ch 5, 6, 7)

Reliability — How consistently a solution performs in the field under real-world constraints. (Ch 9)

Reliability Leverage — Leverage from taking responsibility for consistent outcomes in unpredictable environments. (Ch 8, 9)

Representation Power — The power to define what is visible and measurable, and thus to set the frame for decisions. (Ch 3, 11)

Reskilling Fallacy — Believing new skills alone protect you when the system no longer needs human execution of the task. (Ch 4, 5)

Right to Coordinate — The earned ability to organize an ecosystem by removing friction in both decisions and execution; requires deep integration, not a nicer UI. (Ch 11)

Risk Absorption — Internalizing technical, financial, or operational failure risk so the customer doesn't bear it. (Ch 9)

S

Scarcity- / Risk- / Coordination-Based Constraints — The three constraint types that generate role value: limited access; high-consequence errors; misaligned moving parts. (Ch 5)

Showrooming — Customers explore in-store and buy online. (Ch 10)

Skill Premium — Extra income from a rare or difficult skill; shrinks when AI lets less-skilled workers match output. (Ch 4)

Skill-Biased Technological Change — The claim that technology rewards the highly skilled; breaks down when AI narrows the high/low performance gap. (Ch 4)

Solution — A complete offering delivering reliable outcomes by managing constraints, integrating complements, and absorbing risk. (Ch 8, 9)

Solution Bundle — Tools, services, financing, and guarantees that together make performance predictable. (Ch 9)

Standardization Risk — The more standardized and measurable the work, the easier for tools and insurers to absorb its performance and liability. (Ch 9)

System Builder — A firm that reengineers the system around a tool — financing, operations, integration, risk — not just the tool. (Ch 9)

System-Aware Adaptation — Tracking where constraints move as systems evolve and repositioning to solve new frictions, instead of chasing skills. (Ch 5)

System-Centric vs. Task-Centric View — Analyzing how technology reshapes the architecture of work systems vs. evaluating task-by-task substitution. (Ch 2)

T–W

Tacit Knowledge — Expertise in intuition and experience, hard to codify but essential under uncertainty. (Ch 5, 6)

Three-Circle Model — The task-level job nested inside the organizational system, nested inside the competitive ecosystem — AI reshapes all three. (Ch 2)

Tool Provider vs. Solution Provider — Supplies functional components vs. integrates and is accountable for outcomes. (Ch 8)

Typist Effect — Job obsolescence caused by system redesign rather than task automation: the task survives, the logic that justified the job does not. (Ch 2)

Unbundling — Breaking a job, product, or workflow into components once old constraints are removed; separates expertise from labor. (Ch 4)

Unified Representation / Decision / Execution — AI produces a shared view, aligned decisions, and coordinated follow-through across actors using different tools. (Ch 6, 11)

Vertical Encroachment — A tool provider moving into the solution layer and absorbing the customer experience. (Ch 8)

Vibe Coding — Karpathy's term for outputs that look impressive but lack rigor; symptom of performative execution. (Ch 12)

Wrapper — A solution provider reduced to an interface over someone else's engine: controls appearance, not substance. (Ch 8)

Work- / Results- / Outcomes-as-a-Service — Paid for operational delivery, for measurable results, or for customer-specific strategic outcomes — each step deepens integration and liability. (Ch 9)

patterns.md

Patterns — Reshuffle (Sangeet Paul Choudary)

System-First Diagnosis

When to use: Before any AI initiative, roadmap, or "AI strategy" request.

How: Work outside-in, not inside-out. (1) Has the competitive landscape changed? (2) Has the basis of value creation moved? (3) Does the business model still make sense? (4) What capabilities does the new game require? (5) Which roles and workflows still matter? Only then ask what AI should do. Never start from "what can we automate?"

Trade-offs: Slower to first visible win; leadership impatient for demos. But task-first programs produce motion without direction — Yahoo was agile in the wrong direction.

Three-Circle Analysis

When to use: Assessing exposure of a job, product, or firm to AI.

How: Analyze at three nested levels — the task-level job, the organizational system it sits in, the competitive ecosystem that system sits in. A task can survive at level 1 and still be eliminated at level 2 (typist effect) or level 3.

Trade-offs: Requires information about the ecosystem you may not own; but skipping it produces the framing error of defending tasks in a system that no longer needs the role.

Locate the Moving Constraint

When to use: Repositioning a role, team, or firm when AI erodes existing value.

How: Classify what your value currently rests on — scarcity-based (rare access/knowledge), risk-based (high-consequence errors), or coordination-based (aligning many moving parts). AI collapses scarcity fastest. Ask where friction has moved to in the new system, then rebundle capabilities around that new constraint. Re-run periodically: constraints move.

Trade-offs: You may have to abandon the skill that earned your reputation. Reskilling into an adjacent scarce skill is the trap this pattern replaces.

Unbundle-Then-Rebundle a Role

When to use: A job whose core task has been economically collapsed by AI.

How: (1) Decompose the role into tasks. (2) Mark each task by whether it lost economic value (cheap now) or contextual value (no longer matters in the workflow). (3) Identify the new constraint the workflow now has. (4) Assemble a new bundle of complements around that constraint. (5) Make the contribution economically visible so the system pays for it.

Trade-offs: Rebundled roles (RevOps manager, nurse navigator) often lack a title or budget line at first — visibility must be created, not assumed.

Audit the Coordination Tax

When to use: When local AI deployments are delivering task speedups without organizational gains.

How: Measure the friction between teams — meetings, status chasing, document search, rework from handoffs — not the time inside tasks. Then apply AI to the seams. Watch for the coordination paradox: automating locally while leaving seams manual makes fragmentation worse.

Trade-offs: Coordination cost is invisible in most metrics, so the business case is harder to build than a task-automation ROI case.

Unified Representation → Decision → Execution

When to use: Building coordination advantage across fragmented teams or ecosystem actors.

How: Layer 1 — build a shared, live representation (a digital twin / source of truth) all actors can align on. Layer 2 — use it to drive a unified decision the actors would otherwise negotiate over. Layer 3 — integrate workflows so the decision is executed reliably across tools. Own all three layers and you own the control point.

Trade-offs: Deep integration is slow and expensive; a UI layer is fast but earns no right to coordinate.

Coordination Without Consensus

When to use: Ecosystems too fragmented to ever agree on shared standards (construction, healthcare, multi-vendor supply chains) — exactly where consensus-based platforms have repeatedly failed.

How: Don't force participants onto a shared vocabulary. Let each keep its own tools and formats, and use AI to interpret unstructured inputs into structured, shared meaning. Standards become implicit (learned from data) rather than explicit (agreed in advance).

Trade-offs: Consensus models (CCC) are more auditable and defensible once established; interpretation models (Tractable) scale into new geographies and insurers without new integrations but depend on data volume and stay probabilistic.

Escape the Tool Integration Trap

When to use: Your differentiation increasingly comes from an AI engine you don't own.

How: Watch the three stages — tools commoditize execution, then absorb expertise, then become the gravitational center you reorganize around. Counter by keeping a proprietary layer the engine cannot see: field data, risk absorption, customer decision rights, or an integrated delivery system. Diversify engines before performance-based lock-in sets in.

Trade-offs: Refusing maximum engine performance costs short-term competitiveness. The alternative is becoming a wrapper.

Climb the Solutioning Stack

When to use: Deciding how much outcome liability to take on as a tool or solution provider.

How: Move deliberately along work-as-a-service (paid for operational delivery) → results-as-a-service (paid for measurable results) → outcomes-as-a-service (paid for customer-specific strategic outcomes). Each step requires more visibility (representation), more decision integration, and more execution control. Only climb as far as you can absorb the risk.

Trade-offs: Higher rungs earn more pricing power but demand liability, monitoring, and domain depth; climbing without them turns a margin story into a loss story.

Design for Indecision

When to use: Customers face abundant options and low confidence — where AI has made supply cheap and choice overwhelming.

How: Find the highest-friction decision in the customer journey, take responsibility for it, and rebundle the fragmented steps around it into a trusted path. Owning the decision moment is a demand-side control point; you can then charge a platform tax for access to it.

Trade-offs: Owning decisions means owning blame for bad ones; trust is slow to build and fast to lose.

Choose Your Strategic Posture Deliberately

When to use: Setting the ambition level of an AI program.

How: Name which of the four you are: reactive optimizer (speed up today's tasks), anticipator (spot value migration early but keep the old game), logic shifter (change where and how decisions get made), field reshaper (restructure the ecosystem itself). Deeper reimagining of coordination = more enduring advantage.

Trade-offs: Reshaping requires ecosystem access and patience; optimizing is safe, cheap, and non-compounding.

Set Positive Constraints

When to use: Designing an AI-native product or workflow where unbounded capability produces mush.

How: Choose a deliberate boundary that structures behavior and generates data — TikTok's 60-second limit forced fast signal for the behavior graph. Retire the constraint once it has done its job.

Trade-offs: Constraints look like self-imposed handicaps to competitors and internal stakeholders until the flywheel they enable becomes visible.

Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Radical Candor — Cheatsheet

The quadrant: where is your guidance landing?

Challenge Directly = NOChallenge Directly = YES
Care Personally = YESRuinous Empathy (most common mistake)RADICAL CANDOR (goal)
Care Personally = NOManipulative Insincerity (worst)Obnoxious Aggression (2nd best)

Decision rule: If you're withholding criticism to avoid discomfort → you're in Ruinous Empathy; just say it. If you're being harsh without showing care → add care, don't stop challenging. Prefer Obnoxious Aggression to silence, but aim top-right.

Tells you're in the wrong quadrant

  • You say "good job" with no specifics → Ruinous Empathy praise.
  • You're rehearsing how to soften it until you say nothing → Ruinous Empathy.
  • You're thinking "you're stupid/lazy/greedy" → Obnoxious Aggression / personalizing.
  • You reversed your position to be liked / avoid conflict → Manipulative Insincerity.
  • Nobody is ever mad at you → you're not challenging enough.
  • All praise, no criticism coming back at you → you're not soliciting well.

Order of operations (rollout sequence)

1. Share your stories — explain Radical Candor in your own words; show vulnerability.

2. Get criticism first — prove you can take it before dishing it out (go-to question + silence).

3. Career conversations — start with longest-tenured reports (life story → dreams → 18-mo plan).

4. Perfect 1:1s in parallel (report owns agenda; you listen).

5. Give impromptu guidance — and gauge it.

6. Assess — don't add more until guidance + relationships + 1:1s feel solid.

7. Staff / big-debate / big-decision meetings.

8. Encourage guidance between people; prevent backstabbing.

9. Fight meeting proliferation; think time.

10. Growth-management plans; reward rock stars.

11. Peer gauging; walk around; skip-levels (if manager of managers).

12. Radically Candid hiring, firing, promoting, reviews.

Giving guidance — HHIPP

Humble · Helpful · Immediate · In person · Praise in public / criticize in private · don't Personalize.

  • Say it in 2–3 minutes between meetings; don't save it for a 1:1/review.
  • Use SBI: Situation → Behavior → Impact.
  • Say "that's wrong," not "you're wrong." Never Reply-All criticism.
  • Worry more about praise (make it specific/sincere); for criticism, "just say it."

Rock star vs. superstar

Rock Star (gradual growth)Superstar (steep growth)
Wantsmastery, stabilitynew challenge, learning
Reward withrecognition, top ratings, guru/teaching roles, tenure honorsnew opportunities, stretch projects, mentors
Don'tpromote out of a loved roleblock or squash ambition

Both essential. No permanent labels — trajectories change with life.

When to fire (three questions)

1. Have I given Radically Candid guidance, repeatedly, over time?

2. Do I understand the impact on the rest of the team?

3. Have I sought a second opinion?

→ Yes + no improvement = it's time. The 4 lies that delay it: "it'll get better," "somebody > nobody," "a transfer is the answer," "it's bad for morale." Firing rules: don't wait too long · don't decide alone · give a damn · follow up.

GSD wheel (drive results)

Listen → Clarify → Debate → Decide → Persuade → Execute → Learn. Don't skip a step; don't get stuck on one. You're usually not the decider — push it to whoever's closest to the facts; get facts, not recommendations.

Persuade = Aristotle

Pathos (the listener's emotions — most neglected) · Ethos (expertise + humility, "we" not "I") · Logos (show your work).

Meeting rhythm

MeetingPurposeRule
1:1listen/clarifyreport sets agenda; never cancel
Stafflearn (metrics) / listen (snippets) / clarify (name debates)no decisions here
Big Debatewrestlenot deciding; decide-by date
Big Decisiondecidedecider named; decision is final
All-Handspersuade + hear dissentQ&A > presentation
Think Timethinksacred; no one schedules over it

Emotion first-aid (in a 1:1)

Acknowledge ("I can see you're upset") · ask questions · don't add your guilt · tissues a walk away · closed water bottles at hand · walk, don't sit · forgive yourself and step out if needed. Never say "don't take it personally / don't be sad."

Core self-check (when lost)

"Am I showing I care personally?" and "Am I challenging each person directly?" If both yes, you're doing fine.

glossary.md

Glossary — Radical Candor

Abrasive Trap — Gender bias whereby women who challenge directly get penalized as "abrasive/shrill/bossy"; a small rating bias compounds into far fewer female leaders (Ch 6).

Absentee Management — Hands-off, ears-off, mouth-off: no curiosity, no goals, unaware of problems. One failure mode opposite micromanagement (Ch 7).

All-Hands Meeting — Company/team-wide meeting to persuade people of decisions and hear/address dissent via Q&A (e.g., Google TGIF, Apple Town Hall) (Ch 8).

Big Debate Meeting — Meeting reserved for debating major issues, explicitly not deciding; lowers tension and builds a debate culture (Ch 8).

Big Decision Meeting — Meeting to make (final) decisions, usually following a big debate; led by the appointed "decider" (Ch 8).

Care Personally — First dimension of Radical Candor: giving a damn about people as whole human beings, not just their work (Ch 1).

Career Conversations — Russ Laraway's three 45-min conversations (life story → dreams → 18-month plan) to understand motivation and help people grow (Ch 7).

Challenge Directly — Second dimension of Radical Candor: telling people clearly when work isn't good enough (and when it is); often the best way to show you care (Ch 1).

Collaboration Tax vs. Investment — When GSD steps drag, collaboration feels like a tax; run well, it's an investment. The boss absorbs much of the tax (Ch 4).

Fundamental Attribution Error — Explaining behavior by personality traits ("you're lazy") instead of situation/behavior; inaccurate and unfixable (Ch 2, Ch 6).

Free at Work — The state people reach when the boss relinquishes unilateral authority and builds trust, so they bring their best selves (Ch 5).

Get Stuff Done (GSD) Wheel — Seven-step results process: Listen → Clarify → Debate → Decide → Persuade → Execute → Learn (Ch 4).

"Get it right" vs. "be right" — Great bosses care about reaching the right answer, not being right; they insist people tell them when they're wrong (Ch 4).

Gauge (guidance) — Having your team tag where your guidance lands on the quadrant, since Radical Candor is measured at the listener's ear (Ch 6).

Growth Management — Reframing "talent management/potential" as helping each person move along the growth trajectory they want (Scott Forstall's "growth" not "potential") (Ch 3, Ch 7).

Growth Trajectory — Whether someone is in a steep (rapid-change) or gradual (stability/mastery) growth phase right now; not permanent (Ch 3).

HHIPP — Principles for giving impromptu guidance: Humble, Helpful, Immediate, In person (Praise in public, criticize in private), don't Personalize (Ch 6).

Kanban Board — To Do / In Progress / Done board (Toyota/Ohno) making workflows and bottlenecks visible; measures activities, not just results (Ch 8).

Left-Hand Column — Argyris/Schön exercise: write what you said (right) vs. what you thought (left) to surface arrogant snap judgments (Ch 6).

Listen, Challenge, Commit — Andy Grove's mantra: humility to listen, confidence to challenge, wisdom to stop arguing and get on board (Ch 6).

Loud Listening — Stating a strong point of view and insisting people challenge it back ("strong opinions, weakly held") — Steve Jobs's style (Ch 4).

Manipulative Insincerity — Worst quadrant: neither caring nor challenging; fake praise/criticism for advantage or ease (Ch 2).

Micromanagement — Hands-on, ears-off, mouth-on: tells "how" without understanding, gets lost in details, hoards information (Ch 7).

Obnoxious Aggression — Challenging without caring ("front-stabbing"); the second-best quadrant — at least people know where they stand (Ch 2).

Partnership — The management target: hands-on, ears-on, mouth-off — curious, listens, asks why, removes obstacles (Ch 7).

Pathos / Ethos / Logos — Aristotle's persuasion elements: the listener's emotion, credibility (expertise + humility), and logic ("show your work") (Ch 4).

Personalizing — Making guidance about character/essence instead of a specific behavior; corrodes accuracy and the relationship (Ch 2, Ch 6).

Platinum Rule — Do unto others as they would have done to them (figure out their comfort), vs. the Golden Rule's own-preference default (Ch 5).

Radical Candor — Caring personally and challenging directly at the same time; also the top-right quadrant (Ch 1, Ch 2).

Rock Star — Person on a gradual growth trajectory; solid, has mastered and loves the craft, doesn't want the next job; reward, don't promote out (Ch 3).

Ruinous Empathy — Caring without challenging; withholding criticism to avoid discomfort; responsible for most management mistakes (Ch 2).

Situation–Behavior–Impact (SBI) — Feedback technique: describe the situation, the behavior, and the impact — keeps guidance humble and specific (Ch 6).

Skip-Level Meeting — Annual meeting with your reports' reports (without those managers) to help managers improve; "not for attribution" (Ch 6).

Snippets — Short written weekly updates in a shared doc, read in a staff-meeting "study hall" to avoid interminable verbal updates (Ch 8).

Spelunking — A boss occasionally diving deep into details / going straight to the source of facts to stay grounded (Ch 4).

Superstar — Person on a steep growth trajectory; needs constant new challenge; the source of a team's growth (Ch 3).

Think Time — Sacred blocked calendar time to think that no one may schedule over (Ch 8).

Whoops the Monkey — Dan Woods's stuffed-animal ritual: people self-report mistakes at all-hands for automatic forgiveness and shared learning (with a "Killer Whale" for peer praise) (Ch 6).

Work-Life Integration — Reframing "work-life balance" (zero-sum) so work and life give each other a "double bounce" (Ch 5).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Radical Candor

Concrete, reusable techniques from the book, with when/how/trade-offs.

Solicit criticism with a go-to question

When: Building a guidance culture; you get too little criticism.

How: Ask "Is there anything I could do or stop doing that would make it easier to work with me?" Then embrace the discomfort — count to six of silence, don't fill it, don't reassure. Ask again if needed. Reward whatever you get; never critique the criticism.

Trade-offs: Feels awkward at first; requires you to genuinely act on what you hear or trust evaporates.

Situation–Behavior–Impact (SBI)

When: Giving any praise or criticism.

How: State the situation you saw, the behavior, and the impact. ("In this morning's meeting (S), the way you talked through the objection (B) was persuasive because it showed you'd heard the other side (I).")

Trade-offs: Requires you to have observed specifics — a reason to give guidance immediately, before details fade.

Left-hand column

When: A frustrating conversation where judgment leaked out.

How: Draw a line down a page; right = what you said, left = what you thought. Question the left column's assumptions.

Trade-offs: Reflective, not in-the-moment; best as prep or debrief.

Gauge your guidance

When: You want to know how your guidance actually lands.

How: Explain the quadrant to the team; have them tag your praise/criticism by quadrant (stickers, or the Candor Gauge app). Track over time.

Trade-offs: Stickers cause pile-on/anonymity issues; anonymous tags signal low trust you must rebuild.

Reward candor visibly

When: Someone gives you hard, valid criticism.

How: Make a visible change (Kim's "radical bander" rubber band others could snap when she interrupted). If you can't change fast, show effort; if you disagree, agree with something, check understanding, then explain why.

Trade-offs: Gimmicks lose novelty; the point is the signal, not the prop.

Career conversations (3 conversations)

When: First thing to roll out on a team; yearly per report, in 1:1 slots.

How: (1) Life story — "from kindergarten, tell me about your life," note motivators at moments of change; (2) Dreams — ask for 3–5 dreams incl. a "crazy-ass dream," map dreams × skills × competence; (3) 18-month plan — what to learn, from whom, how the role can change, with action items.

Trade-offs: ~2.25 hrs/person over 3–6 weeks; respect discomfort and don't press personal topics.

Growth-management plan

When: Annually, to balance the team.

How: Put names in the growth 2×2 boxes fast (≤20 min), get an outside/peer check for bias, write 3–5 bullets per person. Calibrate with peers; ensure fairness by level.

Trade-offs: Boxes are temporary snapshots — never permanent labels.

Hiring process

When: Any hire.

How: Hiring manager (not recruiter) writes the job description defining fit as rigorously as skills; use blind skills assessments; a consistent 4-person diverse committee incl. someone off-team; casual moments reveal fit; write feedback within 15 min; bias toward "no" — if not dying to hire, don't.

Trade-offs: Slower; the cost of a bad hire (and firing) is far higher.

Firing well

When: Repeated Radically Candid guidance hasn't produced improvement.

How: Don't wait too long; don't decide unilaterally (boss/peers/HR, get documents edited); give a damn (follow gut over rigid legal advice when it reduces harm); follow up ~a month later.

Trade-offs: Emotionally and legally hard; reframe as freeing the person ("the job sucks for them").

GSD wheel

When: Any significant team decision/initiative.

How: Listen → Clarify → Debate → Decide → Persuade → Execute → Learn. Ensure each step happens; don't skip or stall. Push decisions to the person closest to the facts; collect facts, not recommendations.

Trade-offs: Feels slow, but skipping steps costs more later; you needn't be in every step.

Two listening styles

When: You want everyone heard.

How: Quiet (silence, neutral face — reassure sometimes) or Loud (state strong opinions weakly held, insist people push back). Pick the one natural to you.

Trade-offs: Quiet → people guess your view; loud → intimidates the marginal, so build their confidence.

Persuade with pathos/ethos/logos

When: Bringing along people who weren't in the decision.

How: Address the listener's emotions, establish credibility (expertise + humility, "we" not "I"), and show your logic ("show your work").

Trade-offs: The neglected one is usually the listener's emotion.

1:1 meetings

When: Weekly (5 reports) → biweekly (10–20); never cancel.

How: Direct report sets the agenda; you listen and clarify (not dump criticism). Use follow-up questions ("Why?", "How can I help?", "What wakes you up at night?", "What are you working on that you don't want to?").

Trade-offs: 1:1 time is the natural bottleneck on how many reports you can have.

Staff meeting (learn/listen/clarify)

When: Weekly.

How: Review key metrics (~20 min) → silent study-hall snippets in a shared doc (~15 min, no side chatter) → identify (don't make) key decisions/debates (~30 min), assigning owners to separate big-debate/big-decision meetings.

Trade-offs: Not the place for debates/decisions — split those out.

Split debate and decision meetings

When: Team > ~20; contentious topics.

How: Big Debate = wrestle, no decision, set decide-by date, switch roles halfway. Big Decision = decider (appointed) makes final call. Both: egos at the door, notes shared, anyone may attend.

Trade-offs: Looks like meeting proliferation but actually reduces it via self-selection.

Kanban board / measure activities

When: Making work visible; ensuring fair recognition.

How: To Do / In Progress / Done with color-coded Post-its; measure activities not just results.

Trade-offs: Visibility itself reduces bias and routes help to bottlenecks.

Walk around

When: ~1 hr/week, esp. as a manager of managers.

How: Talk to people you haven't seen lately; find and sometimes fix small problems yourself.

Trade-offs: Office hours attract the same cranks; walking reaches the quiet ones.

Prevent backstabbing / clean escalation

When: One person wants to complain to you about another.

How: Refuse; insist they talk directly. If unresolved, host a live three-way conversation (not email) and help them find a workable solution.

Trade-offs: Adds occasional mediation meetings but prevents political blowups.

Skip-level meetings

When: Once a year per direct report (manager of managers).

How: Meet reports' reports without the manager; explain-show-explain; get consent; do it for everyone; not-for-attribution; take & project notes yourself; share with the manager within ~8 min; ensure 1–2 concrete changes.

Trade-offs: Energy-intensive; guard against proliferation and gripe sessions.

Peer guidance: "Whoops the Monkey"

When: Building peer-to-peer candor.

How: At all-hands, people self-report mistakes (auto-forgiveness, shared learning) via a stuffed monkey; peers award a "Killer Whale" for great work.

Trade-offs: Culturally specific — inappropriate where mistakes are safety-critical or the design ethos is formal.

Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Seeing Like a State — Cheatsheet

1. Is this scheme headed for failure? (the four-element test)

Score each. All four present = Scott's recipe for disaster. Fewer than four = risky, not lethal.

#ElementPresent when…Mitigation
1Administrative ordering of nature/society (state simplification, legibility)A standard grid replaces diverse local practice; the metric will be enforced, not just observedKeep the old records; measure what you suppressed
2High-modernist ideologyConfidence outruns evidence; "rational design of social order"; visual/aesthetic order treated as proof of functionDemand a falsifiable prediction and a failure criterion
3Authoritarian executor willing to use coercive powerNo veto point; dissent is reframed as obstruction; emergency powersRestore a real veto held by someone who bears the cost
4Prostrate civil society unable to resistThose affected have no voice, no exit, no organizationFund/convene the affected before, not after

Scott's summary: legibility supplies the capacity, high modernism the desire, the authoritarian state the determination, an incapacitated society the terrain.

Elements 1 and 2 alone are ordinary and often benign. Under representative institutions, high modernism "could spur reform." The lethal ingredient is that nobody can say no.

2. Tells & smells

If you see…You're probably in…
The plan is judged by how it looks from above (grid, symmetry, aerial view)Aesthetic order mistaken for functional order (ch4, ch7)
A lavishly subsidized, closely supervised pilot cited as proof of scaleMiniaturization (ch7)
Practitioners' workarounds described as non-complianceSuppression of mētis (ch9)
One number now defines success for a many-purpose activityThin simplification / hegemonic metric (ch8, ch10)
First cycle exceeds forecast; second cycle collapsesThe monocropping signature — scientific forestry, Waldsterben (ch1)
The map is being enforced as lawFacts on paper remaking facts on the ground (ch1, ch2)
Nobody can explain how the system actually runs day to dayFormal order parasitic on informal process (ch9)
Rollout is nationwide, simultaneous, irreversibleScope has defeated foresight (ch10)

Fastest single diagnostic: run a work-to-rule thought experiment. If following the documented rules exactly would halt the work, the documentation is not the system — and any plan built from it is thin.

3. Designing interventions: Scott's four rules of thumb (ch10)

RuleDecision test
Take small stepsCan I stand back and observe before the next move? Haldane: a mouse survives the mineshaft, "a horse splashes."
Favor reversibilityIf this is wrong, what does undoing it cost? Leopold: "keep all the parts."
Plan on surprisesDoes the design admit uses I haven't imagined? Land that grows several crops; adjustable floor plans.
Plan on human inventivenessAm I assuming later participants will improve on my design — or that they'll degrade it?

4. Choosing between formal rule and local judgment

  • Environment repetitive, stable, predictable → fixed routines are legitimately efficient. Codify.
  • Environment mutable, indeterminate, particular → mētis governs. The harbor pilot outranks the captain inside the harbor.
  • Generic rule + local case → budget for translation. "The more general the rules, the more they require in the way of translation."
  • Rules of thumb are summaries of practice — teach them after competence, like grammar after speech.

5. The two maps test (ch10)

Draw Map 1 (routes the design provides) and Map 2 (time-lapse of everything unplanned people actually do). If Map 2 is doing load-bearing work your design doesn't represent, the design is not viable alone. "Planned Brasília is, in a thousand ways, underwritten by unplanned Brasília."

6. Institutional litmus test

Does this form enhance the skills, knowledge, and responsibility of those inside it?

  • "Canned" — self-sufficient, receives no input, permits no modification (Iwo Jima statue, Taylorist line, superquadra).
  • Mētis-friendly — completed by its users (Vietnam Memorial, common law, language, democracy).

Narrow environments produce a less resourceful population — which then genuinely needs supervision. The plan manufactures the subjects it assumed.

7. Guardrails against misreading Scott

  • He is not anti-state, anti-planning, anti-science, or anti-modernity. The state is "the ground of both our freedoms and our unfreedoms."
  • Legibility has legitimate uses he credits explicitly: public health, taxation fairness, rule of law, poverty relief, citizenship.
  • His target is precisely "an imperial or hegemonic planning mentality that excludes the necessary role of local knowledge and know-how."
  • He does not romanticize the local; mētis coexists with domination, monopoly, and exclusion.
  • Markets are not the escape hatch. Large-scale capitalism "is just as much an agency of homogenization, uniformity, grids, and heroic simplification as the state."

8. Transfers

DomainThe state simplificationThe suppressed mētis
Software architectureThe canonical model / schema / rewrite planOn-call intuition, undocumented workarounds, why that config exists
Org designOrg chart, job descriptions, levelling rubricWho actually gets things unblocked
Metrics / KPIsThe single north-star numberEverything the number had to exclude to be countable
Platform policyUniform global rule, enforced at scaleLocal context, edge cases, community norms

Design rule for all four: keep the intervention small, reversible, and diversity-preserving; and keep a channel open to the people whose knowledge the model excluded.

glossary.md

Glossary — Seeing Like a State

Abstract citizen — the standardized, interchangeable planning subject with no gender, tastes, history, values, or traditions; not an oversight but "the necessary first premise of any large-scale planning exercise" (Ch 10).

Appropriation and control — Scott's claim that legibility schemes typically optimize extraction and supervision rather than production (Ch 6, Ch 7, Ch 8).

Authoritarian high modernism — high-modernist ideology joined to a state willing and able to use coercive power against a society that cannot resist; the lethal configuration (Ch 3).

Bricolage — Lévi-Strauss's term for mētis's mode of innovation: recombining existing elements rather than inventing from first principles (Ch 9).

Brasília — Costa and Niemeyer's planned capital; Scott's central case of a city that works only because of the unplanned settlement surrounding it (Ch 4).

Cadastral survey — the parcel-by-parcel land map that assigns each holding to a single taxable owner; it does not describe a tenure system, it creates one (Ch 1, Ch 2).

Canned institution — a social form that is symbolically self-sufficient and permits little or no modification by its participants; opposite of mētis-friendly (Ch 10).

Cultivated natural capital — fish farms and tree plantations replacing wild stocks and old-growth; gains appropriability and short-run yield, loses "redundancy, resiliency, and stability" (Ch 10).

Epistēmē — universal, deductive, verifiable knowledge; with technē, the pole against which mētis is defined (Ch 9).

Facts on paper vs. facts on the ground — the gap between the state's record and lived reality; when the record is enforced, the ground is remade to match (Ch 1, Ch 2, Ch 6).

Four-element recipe for disaster — (1) administrative ordering of nature and society, (2) high-modernist ideology, (3) an authoritarian state willing to use coercive power, (4) a prostrate civil society unable to resist. All four are necessary (Intro, Ch 3).

Freehold tenure — individual, alienable, registered land ownership; a legibility technology that erases overlapping and common-use rights (Ch 1, Ch 2).

Grève du zèle — French term for the work-to-rule strike (Ch 9).

High modernism — muscle-bound faith in scientific and technical progress, mastery of nature, and rational design of social order. A faith that borrows science's legitimacy — "must not be confused with scientific practice" (Intro, Ch 3).

Institutional neurosis — the apathy, withdrawal, and loss of initiative that single-purpose, controlled environments produce in their inmates (Ch 10).

Kolkhoz / sovkhoz — Soviet collective and state farms; machines for grain requisition and control more than for production (Ch 6).

Landrace — locally adapted, open-pollinated crop varieties; the genetic reservoir on which modern hybrids silently depend (Ch 8, Ch 10).

Legibility — the state's rendering of complex local practice into a standard grid that can be centrally recorded, monitored, and manipulated. Scott's master concept (Intro, Ch 1, Ch 2).

Mētis — practical, local, experiential intelligence acquired by doing; Odysseus's quality. Most valuable where situations are mutable, indeterminate, and particular (Ch 9).

Mētis-friendly institution — multifunctional, plastic, diverse, adaptable forms that are completed by their participants and that renew their skill. Models: language, common law, democracy (Ch 10).

Miniaturization — the high modernist's retreat, after plans miscarry, into a controllable micro-order — model city, model village, model farm — then cited as proof the design scales (Intro, Ch 7).

Monocropping — single-species, even-age planting; the signature of thin simplification in both forestry and agriculture (Ch 1, Ch 8).

Normalbaum — the "standard tree" of German scientific forestry, an abstraction of usable timber volume that eventually reshaped the actual forest (Ch 1).

Polyculture / polycropping — mixed planting; less productive short-run, "demonstrably more stable, more self-sufficient, and less vulnerable to epidemics and environmental stress" (Ch 8, Ch 10).

Prostrate civil society — a population lacking the capacity to resist state plans; the fourth element, and "the leveled social terrain on which to build" (Intro, Ch 3).

Permanent surnames — fixed heritable names imposed for taxation, conscription, and property tracking; a canonical legibility case (Ch 2).

Standardized weights and measures — abstract universal units replacing relational local measures that encoded soil quality, labor, and yield in the unit itself (Ch 1, Ch 2).

State simplification — an abridged map representing only the slice of society that interests the official observer; the basic given of modern statecraft (Intro, Ch 1).

Synoptic view — the single at-a-glance perspective a common metric makes possible; what the "partially blind" premodern state lacked (Intro, Ch 1).

Taylorism — scientific management by decomposition of work into specified repetitive movements; "not just a strategy of production, but also a strategy of control and appropriation" (Ch 6, Ch 9).

Technē — codified, universal, hard-and-fast technical knowledge, deducible from first principles; settled knowledge, but incapable of explaining its own discovery (Ch 9).

Thin simplification — a schematic model too impoverished to serve as instructions for a functioning order; the thinner the formal scheme, the less resilient it is (Ch 9, Ch 10).

Two maps test — Map 1 traces the routes a design provides; Map 2 traces all unplanned activity. Map 2 usually supersedes Map 1 and does load-bearing work (Ch 10).

Ujamaa villagization — Nyerere's compulsory Tanzanian resettlement into gridded standard villages; well-intentioned, and Scott's clearest case of aesthetics and miniaturization overriding local agronomic knowledge (Ch 7).

Vanguard party — Lenin's conception of the revolutionary party as engineer and general staff of revolution; countered by Luxemburg and Kollontai (Ch 5).

Visual/aesthetic order vs. functional order — the high-modernist habit of reading rational order "in remarkably visual aesthetic terms," so that what looks regimented is presumed to work (Intro, Ch 3, Ch 4, Ch 7).

Waldsterben — "forest death"; the German term for the second-rotation collapse of scientifically managed monocrop forests (Ch 1).

Work-to-rule — following every rule and job description exactly until work halts; Scott's proof that formal rules depend on uncodified informal practice (Intro, Ch 9).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Seeing Like a State

Concrete moves Scott identifies: the state's techniques for producing legibility, the failure mechanisms they set off, and the counter-techniques he endorses.

---

State Legibility Techniques (Part 1)

Scientific Forestry

When to use: You need a single, countable output from a complex living system.

How: Define the abstraction (Normalbaum — the standard tree measured in cubic meters of usable timber); clear the "debris"; plant a single fast-growing species (Norway spruce) in even-age, straight rows; harvest on a fixed rotation.

Trade-offs: Spectacular first-rotation yields — the forest is now readable at a glance and the ledger balances. Second rotation collapses by 20–30%; German foresters coined Waldsterben ("forest death"). The recovery effort ("restoration forestry" — artificial nesting boxes, imported ant colonies, reintroduced spiders) is an admission that the cleared "debris" was the system. Canonical case for every thin simplification that follows.

Cadastral Survey & Freehold Tenure

When to use: The state must identify who owes tax on which land.

How: Map parcels; assign each to a single named owner; give the categories the force of law.

Trade-offs: Makes taxation assessable and titles enforceable — but it does not describe the tenure system, it creates one. Overlapping, seasonal, and common-use rights that the grid cannot render simply cease to exist legally. Facts on paper displace facts on the ground.

Permanent Surnames

When to use: The state needs to track individuals across time — taxation, conscription, corvée, criminal records, property.

How: Replace patronymics, occupational names, and locally sufficient naming customs with a fixed, heritable, officially registered surname.

Trade-offs: Foundational to citizenship, inheritance law, and public health registries. Also foundational to conscription lists and to rounding up designated populations — the same technique, opposite valence.

Standardized Weights and Measures

When to use: You need to compare, aggregate, or trade across localities.

How: Replace relational, purpose-bearing local measures (a journal = a day's work; a farm "of two cows") with universal abstract units.

Trade-offs: Enables markets and the synoptic view. Destroys information — local measures encoded soil quality, labor input, and yield expectation in the unit itself. The abstract unit is precise about less.

Haussmannization / The Grid City

When to use: The center wants a city it can see, supply, move through, and police.

How: Drive straight boulevards through the medieval tangle; standardize frontages; make the plan readable from above.

Trade-offs: Real gains in sanitation, circulation, and fire control. Also — explicitly — troop movement and the suppression of barricades. Legibility serves whoever holds the center.

---

High-Modernist Design Patterns (Parts 2–3)

Miniaturization

When to use: (Scott's warning, not endorsement) When a plan miscarries, its carriers retreat to a controllable micro-order.

How: Build a model village, model farm, or model city; subsidize and supervise it lavishly; display it as proof of concept.

Trade-offs: The demonstration succeeds because of the subsidy and supervision that cannot scale. Treating it as evidence for a national rollout is the mechanism by which pilots become catastrophes.

Taylorism

When to use: Output is single-purpose, measurable, and the environment is stable.

How: Decompose work into repetitive, specified movements; move knowledge from the floor to the planning office.

Trade-offs: Genuine efficiency in stable, repetitive settings. But it is "not just a strategy of production, but also a strategy of control and appropriation," and it degrades exactly the improvisational capacity the plant depends on when conditions shift.

Monocropping / Industrial Agriculture

When to use: Maximum bushels per acre at least cost, under controlled conditions.

How: One crop, uniform genetics, mechanized operations, one-variable-at-a-time trials on experimental plots.

Trade-offs: Yield gains are real. But the experimental plot's controlled conditions are themselves a simplification; hybrids persist only because of the diversity and immunities of antecedent landraces; and questions of soil structure, community, sustainability, and taste are excluded rather than answered.

Villagization / Collectivization

When to use: (Diagnostic) The state wants population and production it can count, supply, and requisition.

How: Move dispersed households into gridded, roadside, standard-plan settlements; consolidate holdings; set quotas centrally.

Trade-offs: Optimizes appropriation and control, not production. Ignores the soil, rainfall, and grazing knowledge that determined the original dispersed pattern. Survives, when it survives, on the private plots and informal economy the plan forbids.

---

Counter-Techniques Scott Endorses (Part 4)

Work-to-Rule as Diagnostic

When to use: To test whether documented process equals actual process.

How: Ask what would happen if everyone followed every rule and job description exactly and did nothing else.

Trade-offs: If the answer is "work halts," you have proven the formal scheme is parasitic on uncodified practice — and any plan derived from the documentation is thin. Cheap to run as a thought experiment; the real thing is a strike.

Small, Reversible Steps

When to use: Any intervention whose second- and third-order effects you cannot enumerate.

How: Take a small step → stand back → observe → plan the next small move. Prefer interventions that can easily be undone. "The first rule of intelligent tinkering is to keep all the parts" (Leopold).

Trade-offs: Slower and less impressive than a comprehensive rollout. Buys the ability to be wrong survivably — the thing every case in the book lacked.

Designing for Surprise and for Human Inventiveness

When to use: Whenever the future is contingent — i.e. nearly always.

How: Choose land that can grow several crops; housing with adjustable floor plans; factory layouts that admit new processes. Assume later participants will improve on the design.

Trade-offs: Costs option value up front; refuses the resolution that comes from fixing requirements.

The Two Maps Test

When to use: Assessing whether a designed system can stand alone.

How: Draw Map 1 (routes the design provides) and Map 2 (a time-lapse of all unplanned activity). Identify which Map 2 activities the system depends on.

Trade-offs: Surfaces the informal dependencies before they are inadvertently designed out.

Building Mētis-Friendly Institutions

When to use: Whenever quality depends on the engaged participation of the people inside.

How: Apply the litmus test — does this form enhance the skills, knowledge, and responsibility of its participants? Prefer multifunctional, plastic, diverse, adaptable forms over single-purpose ones. Models: language, common law, democracy, the Vietnam Memorial.

Trade-offs: Where the purpose is "narrow, simple, and invariable over time," codified hierarchical routines may well be adequate and most efficient in the short run — Scott concedes this explicitly, along with "the incontestable benefits either of the division of labor or of hierarchical coordination for some tasks."

Shift: Managing Your Emotions So They Don't Manage You

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Shift (Ethan Kross)

Is this emotion a problem yet? (two tests only — never valence)

  • Intensity — is the reaction proportional? If you exploded at the soccer coach or despaired over jeans, no.
  • Duration — has it kept running after delivering its message? Clinicians diagnose partly by duration; use the same marker.
  • Neither tripped → leave it alone. All emotions are functional; you're extracting information.

Which shifter? (decision tree)

  • Can you look away from the trigger?

- No (fire in the room, terminal diagnosis, declining parent) → Perspective shifters (Ch 5). Distanced self-talk first, then reframe.

- Yes → Is what you're currently doing working?

- Yes → keep doing it. Don't overthink.

- No, and you're approaching → switch to avoidance/distraction, or change category.

- No, and you're avoiding → switch to approach, or change category.

  • Are you depleted, flooded, or distracted? → Sensory shifter (Ch 3). It's the only category that works below the cognitive-control threshold.
  • Have you tried the internal three and nothing moves? → go external:

- Environment is the driver → Space (Ch 6): switch or modify.

- You need another mind → Relationship (Ch 7): an emotional adviser, not a venting partner.

- The group you're in is the problem → Culture (Ch 8): diagnose beliefs/norms/practices, then change or leave.

  • You know the tool and still don't use it → WOOP (Ch 9).

When feeling X, do Y, because Z

Feeling / situationDoBecause
Stressor outside your control (broken leg)Positive reframeReframing helps when the situation is fixed
Stressor inside your control (cheating partner, toxic job)Act, don't reframeSilver-lining a fixable problem predicts greater depression
Flooded, can't think straightDistanced self-talkCosts no prefrontal effort; works in seconds during the stress "brownout"
Intrusive image loopingStop the video / re-shoot itTrigger is uncontrollable; trajectory isn't
Post-incident anger at an email or a siblingWalk away, come back tomorrowTime is the active ingredient of the psychological immune system
Grief that ambushes you at bad momentsPre-set if-then with a 10-second future-projectionDeliberation is unavailable mid-emotion
Can't stop comparing on social mediaReframe the comparison, then cut frequencyComparison is reflexive; only frame and dose are controllable
Need a lift, no tool at handDo something small for someone nearbyProsocial acts match mindfulness/gratitude in effect size
Just took an emotional hitLook at a photo of someone you loveRestorative effect substantial; buffering effect nonexistent
Anxiety about a performanceRead your racing pulse as readinessReinterpretation of physiological cues speeds recovery

Tells & smells — which failure mode am I in?

TellDiagnosisMove
Circling the same thoughts, no progress ("traffic circle with no exit")Chatter — approach is failingSwitch to avoidance or perspective
Trying not to think about it, thinking about it constantlyAvoidance Warning Sign 1Psych immune system can't handle it alone; approach
Substances, compulsive sex/gambling/eatingAvoidance Warning Sign 2Bright red flag; different category of help
Endless research, unnecessary tests, re-checking locks, asking loved ones repeatedlyAvoidance Warning Sign 3 — counterfeit approachName the real fear; stop the reassurance loop
Rising "I / me / my" in your speech or writingZoomed-in immersionDistance before reframing
You're as wound up as the person you're advisingCo-ruminationPivot: "I have a thought on this, are you okay to hear it?"
Only surfaces when someone else raises itNothing. Already metabolized.Don't excavate

Trade-off matrix — internal shifters

EffortSpeedWorks when flooded?Main risk
SensoryLowestms–secondsYesCongruency drift; becomes a crutch (food, sex)
Attention (avoid)LowMinutes–daysYesChronic avoidance → anxiety, depression
Attention (approach)HighSlowNoChatter; dredging up settled things
Distanced self-talkNear zeroSecondsYesFeels awkward; not a substitute for acting
ReframingHighSlowNo — the brownout kills itNegative reframing; worry loops
Mental time travelMediumSeconds–minutesPartlyRumination/anxiety if uncorralled

Thresholds, durations & defaults the author commits to

  • Two questions for picking a sensory default: biggest punch / lowest cost. Kross's answer: music (immediate, effective, zero cost), playlists pre-loaded, one tap away.
  • Three "thens" per "if" — the SEAL contingency standard.
  • Ten seconds — the duration in the grief WOOP's future-projection plan.
  • The more intense the emotion, the longer before someone is receptive to perspective. Empathize first, always.
  • Get three phone numbers at every meeting and practice calling while stable (AA) — you follow through in crisis only if you rehearsed out of it.
  • A little emotional sharing and validation is healthy; a group-text spiral is contagion.
  • Success criterion: "not overtaken," never "not feeling." Fear in a threatening situation should stay.

Exact phrasings worth keeping

  • Self-talk: "Okay, [Name]. You've got to get going. You need to start acting."
  • Advising: "Tell me more about that. That sounds hard. I'm not surprised you feel this way."
  • Pivot request: "I have a thought on this, are you okay to hear it?"
  • Front-loading an advice-giver: "Can I just vent about this for a bit, and then maybe you have some ideas for me?"
  • Anti-catastrophizing (AA): "Where are your feet?"
  • Response vs. reaction: a response is intentional and constructive; a reaction is knee-jerk.

The four-question spaces audit

1. What can I do today to curate this space?

2. What can I remove to turn stress down?

3. What can I add to turn calm or joy up?

4. What local emotional oases exist, and when do I visit them this week?

WOOP template

W — what do I want? (challenging but feasible)

O — best thing about achieving it, and how will it feel?

O — the main obstacle within myself (never external)

P — IF ____(obstacle)____, THEN ____(specific action, named shifter, with a duration)____.

Culture: diagnose in three layers

  • Values stated but vague → make them concrete and spell out the specifics.
  • Norms absent or contradicting values → run a norms audit; change is easier than expected because people want to belong.
  • Practices missing → this is almost always the gap. Never issue a value as an instruction ("be vulnerable"); build the training for it.
  • Nothing fixable → leaving is a legitimate move. People opt out of toxic cultures every day.

The one rule above all

There is no one-size-fits-all solution. Experiment to find your combination, then use WOOP to make sure you actually deploy it.

glossary.md

Glossary — Shift (Ethan Kross)

ABCs — Adverse event → Belief → Consequence; change B and C follows. Taught to Kross by David Williams, 1999. (Ch 5)

Attention — the mental spotlight determining what enters awareness; usually automatic, but consciously steerable toward (approach) or away from (avoidance) a target. (Ch 4)

Beliefs and values — what the people in a group care about; the foundation layer of the cultural blueprint. (Ch 8)

Chatter — getting stuck in a negative thought loop; the shared alarm bell signaling that either approach or avoidance has stopped working. (Ch 4)

Cognitive control — the prefrontal capacity to modulate automatic responses, think abstractly, divert attention, and switch priorities. Works to amplify emotion as well as dampen it. (Ch 2)

Cognitive miser — the human default of conserving mental resources by taking low-friction, rutted paths. (Ch 3)

Cognitive support — helping someone work through a situation rather than only commiserating; the routinely missing half of emotional support. (Ch 7)

Collectivist vs. individualistic cultures — where social harmony is paramount (e.g., Japan) suppression is more common and viewed positively; where it isn't, expression is prized. Makes "suppression is unhealthy" a local verdict. (Ch 8)

Compensatory control — control gained from performing a ritual's prescribed steps, offsetting a situation that feels out of control. (Ch 8)

Co-rumination / venting — rehashing a problem together past the point of usefulness; good for bonding, bad for the problem. (Ch 7)

Distanced self-talk — silently referring to yourself as "you," by name, or in third person to gain perspective; Kross's stated go-to tool. (Ch 5)

Duration — how long an emotion persists after it has delivered its message; one of the two check-engine lights. (Ch 1)

Dwelling — fixating on obstacles so completely you can't see a path forward; counterproductive alone, essential when paired with a vision. (Ch 9)

Ecological intelligence hypothesis — cognitive control evolved partly to manage food-supply uncertainty (don't eat all the berries now). (Ch 2)

Emotion — a loosely coordinated response of feeling, thinking, and bodily reaction to events judged meaningful; an instrument for responding to a situation. (Ch 1)

Emotional advisers — the subset of your network who both validate and broaden your perspective; the people to call in real distress. (Ch 7)

Emotional congruency effect — when feeling bad, spontaneously choosing sensory input that perpetuates the mood. (Ch 3)

Emotional contagion — emotions spreading person to person like a virus, beginning with unconscious mimicry. (Ch 1, Ch 7)

Emotional oases — accessible restorative places; refilling stations along a marathon route. (Ch 6)

Emotional Stradivarius — the metaphor for your emotional apparatus: a priceless instrument nobody taught you to play. (Ch 1)

Emotion regulation — altering the trajectory of an emotional response by speeding it up, slowing it down, or changing its intensity. (Ch 1)

Feelings — the consciously accessible part of an emotional experience; the "fever" readout. (Ch 1)

Flexibility — the capacity to deploy attention both toward and away as context demands; Bonanno's best predictor of resilience. (Ch 4)

Foreign language effect — reasoning more objectively and with less emotional charge in a non-native language. (Ch 5)

Functional interdependence — a condition where people must cooperate to succeed, as in rice farming; shapes regional emotional culture. (Ch 6)

Garcia effect — a sensory-learned aversion acquired after a single experience, unlike most learning. (Ch 3)

Green space (Laurie Santos's sense) — the location of epiphany you decamp to for conceptual distance; needn't be green, only significant and restorative. (Ch 6)

Implementation intention — a rehearsed if-then link between a specific situation and a specific action (Gollwitzer). (Ch 9)

Indulging — fantasizing about a desired outcome without confronting obstacles; actively lowers goal attainment. (Ch 9)

Intensity — whether an emotional reaction is proportional to its circumstance; one of the two check-engine lights. (Ch 1)

Intrusive thoughts — spontaneous, often distressing thoughts arising outside control; reported by 94% of psychologically healthy people. (Ch 2)

Law of least work / least effort — organisms choose the path of least physical and mental effort; the main reason effortful tools go unused. (Ch 3, Ch 9)

Linguistic markers of immersion — overuse of "I," "me," "my" signaling absorption in a problem; the verbal zoomed-in selfie. (Ch 5)

Master switch — the metaphor for culture: one press governs many settings at once. (Ch 8)

Mental contrasting — pairing a vivid desired future with the crucial internal obstacle (Oettingen). (Ch 9)

Mental representation — the image, memory, or thought tagged as threat whose activation produces fear (Foa & Kozak). (Ch 4)

Mental time travel — deliberately recalling the past or simulating the future to gain distance and surface impermanence. (Ch 5)

Myth of universal approach — the belief that difficult feelings must always be confronted, expressed, and processed. (Ch 4)

Negative reframing — using cognitive control to construe a situation as worse; the engine of worry loops. (Ch 5)

Norms — spoken and unspoken rules that promote and maintain a culture's values; enforced by inclusion and exclusion. (Ch 8)

Norms audit — cataloguing a group's current norms and testing them against its stated values. (Ch 8)

Place attachment — an emotional bond to a specific place; about resonance with you, not the place's qualities. (Ch 6)

Practices — rituals, exercises, and teachings that let a group actualize its beliefs and adopt its norms. (Ch 8)

Propinquity effect — proximity as a leading determinant of whom you befriend and marry. (Ch 6)

Prosocial spending — spending resources on others; produces a happiness boost regardless of amount. (Ch 7)

Proust effect — a sensory cue unlocking an involuntary autobiographical memory and its original emotion. (Ch 3)

Psychological immune system — the built-in system metabolizing psychological threat; its key component is time. (Ch 4)

Reframing / reappraisal / reconstrual / cognitive change — four names for changing how you construe a situation to change how you feel; the foundation of CBT. (Ch 5)

Reframing paradox — worriers try to reframe and neurally fail, exerting more effort for less benefit. (Ch 5)

Ritual — a fixed, meaning-infused sequence of behaviors performed the same way each time. (Ch 8)

Self-efficacy — belief in your capacity to create change in an area of life; a "master belief," linked to a 28% performance increase. (Ch 2)

Sensory bundle — an immersive experience braiding several sensory channels together (baking, surfing, cooking, nature). (Ch 3)

Sensory shifter — a deliberate sensory input used to change emotional state; the lowest-effort tool in the book. (Ch 3)

Signal, not noise — treating each emotion as directional information rather than interference. (Ch 1)

Situation modification — deliberately altering your environment to remove emotional triggers or add emotional supports. (Ch 6)

Social intelligence hypothesis — cognitive control evolved to navigate group life, where unmanaged anger meant exile. (Ch 2)

Solomon's paradox — the asymmetry between wisdom dispensed to others and wisdom applied to one's own life. (Ch 5)

Space shifters — switching or modifying physical space to change emotional state. (Ch 6)

Trajectory — the ongoing arc of an emotion after onset; the controllable half of the equation. (Ch 2)

Trigger — the event that sets off an emotional reaction plus its automatic response; uncontrollable. (Ch 2)

Wise reasoning — open-mindedness, perspective-taking, and intellectual humility; increased by distanced language. (Ch 5)

WOOP — Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan; the merger of mental contrasting and implementation intentions. (Ch 9)

patterns.md

Patterns — Emotion-Regulation Techniques from Shift

Stop the Video

When to use: An intrusive image or catastrophic scenario starts looping (Luisa's what-ifs about her daughter).

How: Treat the scenario as a tape playing. Either hit stop — redirect attention to something small and available (a book, a magazine, a task, a person who needs you) — or re-shoot the scene: same setting, benign outcome (Ella at the same party eating a hot dog and leaping into the pool).

Trade-offs: Cheap and fast. Doesn't resolve the underlying fear, so if the image keeps returning (Warning Sign 1), the loop is beating the tool and you need approach or a different category.

Sensory Shifter Audit

When to use: Once, proactively, to establish your default low-cost tool before you need it.

How: Answer two questions. (1) Which one or two of the five senses pack the biggest punch for me? (2) Which comes with the lowest cost? Your go-to is the intersection. Then pre-load it — mood-specific playlists already on the phone, one tap away.

Trade-offs: The highest-punch channel is often high-cost (taste, sex). Naming the cost is what stops a shifter from becoming a crutch.

Sensory Bundle

When to use: A single sensory channel isn't moving a big, deep, sharp emotion.

How: Choose an activity that braids several channels — baking bread (touch, smell, taste, sight), cooking, gardening, nature immersion, surfing. Multiple pathways activate in parallel.

Trade-offs: Higher time cost than a song, and often requires setup. Pays back in depth of shift; Chayce Baldwin feels grounded within seconds of hands in dough.

Deliberate Difficult-Emotion Exposure

When to use: You want to process a hard emotion but on your own schedule rather than being ambushed by it.

How: Use sensation to open the door — the sad song you cry along to alone, the horror movie that supplies fear at no risk.

Trade-offs: Research here remains ongoing. Plausible benefit is feeling less ambushed later; the risk is drifting into passive emotional congruency.

The Working Question (Approach vs. Avoid)

When to use: Any time you're unsure whether to confront a feeling or turn away.

How: Ask "Is what I'm doing working? Is it making me feel better about the problem in front of me?" If yes, don't overthink it — keep going. If no, switch poles (approach ⇄ avoid) before switching tool categories. Note that approach can hurt now and still be working.

Trade-offs: Requires honest self-report, which distress degrades. Use the warning signs below as external checks.

Flexible Avoidance

When to use: A distressing situation you can't yet act on productively, or a recurring high-pressure role that needs counterbalance (Rodman's excursions, Bubby's selective disclosure).

How: Deliberately disengage — slam the laptop instead of replying, walk out of the escalating fight, let friends drag you out dancing — and give it enough runway for the psychological immune system's key ingredient, time, to flatten the peak. Then pivot back to expression when it's useful.

Trade-offs: Chronic avoidance is genuinely damaging (linked to anxiety, depression, more problems over a decade). What makes it safe is the pivot. If you can't pivot, it isn't flexible avoidance.

Distanced Self-Talk

When to use: Heat of the moment, before or after high-stakes events, or any negative loop. The author's stated default.

How: Silently address yourself as "you," by your own name, or in third person. "Okay, Jerry. You've got to get going. You need to start acting." / "Come on, Ethan, you can finish writing this chapter."

Trade-offs: Reduces negative emotion within seconds, and — uniquely — without activating the brain waveform that tracks effort, so it survives the stress-induced prefrontal brownout that kills ordinary reframing. Feels awkward at first. Not a substitute for action in situations requiring one.

Mental Time Travel

When to use: You're stuck in the present intensity of something and can't look away.

How: Backward — What similar things have I gone through? How did I get through them? What did I gain that I can use now? Forward — How will I feel about this in a week? A month? A year? At the end of my life, what will this mean? Give it a duration; the grief example uses ten seconds.

Trade-offs: Directly contradicts present-moment dogma, deliberately. Fails as a first move in acute crisis where action is required — Jerry needed the pronoun switch first.

Language Switch

When to use: Emotionally loaded reasoning, if you're bilingual.

How: Think or talk to yourself in your second language, where words carry less emotional charge and reasoning is measurably more objective.

Trade-offs: Only available to multilinguals. The transferable lesson is that small linguistic shifts reroute emotional relationships — which is what distanced self-talk exploits.

Switch Your Space

When to use: Internal shifters aren't moving, and the assumptions of your current environment have become invisible (Laurie Santos in New Haven, "like horse blinders").

How: Go somewhere that resonates — not merely away. Aim for the right effect. Check hyper-local options first: a reading nook, a backyard tree, your own bedroom. Sean's version was five days in his childhood home; Laurie's was a sublet in Cambridge.

Trade-offs: The full version (sabbatical, relocation) is neither easy nor cheap. Hometowns can also trigger regression, and for people in recovery, old places carry the wrong associations.

Situation Modification — Remove

When to use: Something in your environment is reliably producing an emotion you don't want, or setting up a goal failure whose emotional aftermath will be worse than the temptation.

How: Take it out. Box up the leftover pizza and force it on departing guests. Phone under the pillow. TV out of the bedroom. Do it preemptively, before the desire-guilt-shame cascade can start.

Trade-offs: Half of Kross's students insist this isn't self-control. He argues that's a narrow and incorrect view — self-control can be easy, and controlling the environment first is a legitimate and superior route. Duckworth's data: situation-modifiers beat willpower-instructed students.

Situation Modification — Add

When to use: Recovering from an emotional hit, not preventing one.

How: Put photos of loved ones in the spaces where you work and live. Look at one after a painful memory surfaces.

Trade-offs: Sharply asymmetric. In Kross's study the buffering effect was nonexistent and the restorative effect substantial — so this is a repair tool, not armor.

The Spaces Audit

When to use: Once per major space you occupy routinely; the cumulative environments matter most.

How: Look around and answer four questions. What can I do today to curate this space? What can I remove to turn the volume down on stress? What can I add to turn it up on calm or joy? What local emotional oases exist, and how do I fold pit stops into my week?

Trade-offs: Low cost, easy to defer indefinitely. Pair with WOOP if it keeps not happening.

Empathize-Then-Zoom-Out (as adviser)

When to use: Someone comes to you in distress.

How: Open with listening, empathizing, validating, normalizing — Tell me more about that. That sounds hard. I'm not surprised you feel this way. Watch for signs you're absorbing and amplifying their state. When an opening appears, gently broaden. If unsure, ask outright: "I have a thought on this, are you okay to hear it?" Accept "no."

Trade-offs: The more intense the emotion, the longer before they're receptive — rushing produces resistance. Validating only is the more common failure, but advice-first is the more damaging one to the relationship.

Redirect Your Own Support Conversation

When to use: You're the one hurting and the conversation is sliding into co-rumination.

How: Ask what they would do in your situation, or what it looks like from the outside. Or front-load with an advice-giver: "Can I just vent about this for a bit, and then maybe you have some ideas?" Or educate a co-ruminator: "I came across this thing about how venting doesn't help long term. I had no idea!"

Trade-offs: Requires enough presence of mind to notice mid-conversation. Disclosure is neurologically rewarding, so the pull to keep venting is real.

Emotional Advisory Board

When to use: Once, as an inventory; revisit as your network changes.

How: Two columns, personal and work. List everyone you go to about problems. Assess each on venting vs. zooming out. Circle only those who do both. Those are your emotional advisers.

Trade-offs: Not a purge. "Not everybody can be everything to us" — you can let people fully into your life without recruiting them to help you shift.

Reframe the Comparison

When to use: You catch yourself comparing — which you will, since the reflex is universal from preschool on.

How: Don't fight the comparison; set the frame. Upward → "If they can achieve that, so can I" (motivation), not "look what they have" (envy). Downward → "Things could be much worse; I'm doing great" (gratitude), not "that could happen to me" (fear). Also manage frequency — reserve comparison for when you need a perspective assist — and remember it's one data point, context-specific.

Trade-offs: Incessant upward comparison undermines well-being regardless of framing; at that point pull attention away entirely. Castigating yourself for comparing just stacks negative emotion.

Prosocial Action as a Lift

When to use: You need a mood shift and have no tool at hand.

How: Look around for who's nearby and do something small. Take lunch-making off a stressed partner's plate. Mow the reclusive neighbor's lawn. Spend a small amount on someone else rather than yourself.

Trade-offs: As effective as mindfulness and gratitude interventions in meta-analysis, across age, sex, and social anxiety, in rich and poor populations. Requires enough capacity to look outward, which acute distress reduces.

Build a Ritual

When to use: A recurring situation where you feel out of control, or a predictable emotional spike (bedtime anxiety, pre-performance nerves).

How: Fix a meaning-infused sequence you perform identically each time — candle, poem, journaling, meditation, LeBron's chalk toss. Stack levers where possible: a pre-dinner dance party (sensory + attention), a headphone-free morning walk. Do it with others for solidarity and social glue.

Trade-offs: The control is compensatory, not literal — it doesn't change the situation. That's the point, and also the limit.

The Cultural Blueprint (diagnose or change)

When to use: A group in your life is helping or hurting your emotional life and you can't tell why.

How: Decompose into beliefs/values → norms → practices. To diagnose: which layer is missing? (Usually practices.) To change: Rule 1 check the foundation and make values concrete and specific ("build with heart," "stand for safety" — with the specifics spelled out). Rule 2 run a norms audit against those values; norm change is easier than expected because people want to belong. Rule 3 customize practices so people can train for the new norms.

Trade-offs: Slower than any individual tool. If the culture forecloses the emotional life you need and won't change, leaving is the legitimate alternative.

WOOP

When to use: Any recurring emotional pattern you can see coming; the bridge from knowing to doing.

How: Wish (challenging but feasible) → Outcome (best thing about achieving it, and how it will feel) → Obstacle (the main challenge within yourself) → Plan (IF obstacle, THEN specific action). Pre-select which shifter the "then" invokes and give it a duration.

Trade-offs: Both halves are required — indulging without obstacles lowers attainment, dwelling without vision paralyzes. External obstacles break the tool. Give high-stakes "ifs" three "thens," as the SEALs do.

The Stacked Response

When to use: A live emotional emergency where no single tool is sufficient.

How: Run several in sequence and accept partial gains from each. Kross's 5 a.m. school-threat sequence: reframe/zoom out → refocus attention into work → resist mass venting while seeking one informed perspective → care for others → sensory break and change of space when chatter sets in.

Trade-offs: The target is "not overtaken," never "not feeling." Fear in a threatening situation is functional and should remain.

The Stimulated Mind: Future-Proof Your Brain from Dementia and Stay Sharp at Any Age

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Stimulated Mind

Where to start: the 3-S decision tree

  • Which node is weakest?

- Demanding job, constant problem-solving → stimulus is fine. Add supply or support: exercise, sleep, people.

- Unrewarding work, retired or near it → add stimulus: a class, a hobby, volunteering.

- Chronically time-poor → set-and-forget: water filter, air purifier, multivitamin, sardines at breakfast.

- Genuinely unsure → start with sleep. It's only the support arm, but it greases everything else.

  • Then pick exactly one. Two competing priorities usually produce zero.
  • Prefer multi-node activities: group/coordinative exercise, outdoor volunteering, in-person classes. These hit all three S's at once.

Decision rules

  • When you don't know the mechanism, act anyway — we still can't fully explain how exercise works, and that has never justified not exercising.
  • When a single counterexample appears ("she exercised daily and still got dementia") — you're stacking a deck, not buying immunity. At 80, ~20% of the 4–5 healthy-factor group was still diagnosed; that's still half the risk of the 0–1 group.
  • When a target feels unreachable, lower it and broaden it — setting lower goals with a wider definition of "counts" improves both adherence and how you feel about your health.
  • When you slept badly, still train — 20–30 min moderate aerobic improves nearly every cognitive domain and mood regardless of sleep, possibly more so after poor sleep.
  • When you're deciding whether to genotype — ApoE4, polygenic scores, and amyloid/tau blood panels change how serious you are, not what you do. ApoE4 amplifies other risks rather than replacing them.
  • When family history worries you — look for shared lifestyle, not shared DNA. That's the actionable overlap.
  • When choosing a cognitive activity — expect near transfer only. Train the function you refuse to lose.
  • When offloading to a device or AI — crutch (replaces a capacity) or orthotic (extends one you still exercise)?

Thresholds & defaults
