The five rules (apply to every decision)

1. Prepare for your own race — benefit × consistency, not benefit alone.

2. Never give up — accumulate; a missed week is noise across decades.

3. Don't go it alone — social makes it easier and better.

4. Everything counts — acknowledge what you already do.

5. Be kind to yourself (and others) — recovery is where adaptation happens.

Tells & smells

  • You're doing the "dead mouse" life — everything arrives without effort. Adult brains only rewire when given a reason: challenge or social engagement.
  • Retirement is the archetypal mismatch — often the point where decline accelerates, because work's cognitive and social stimulus was removed.
  • You believe you exercise less than your peers — associated with the highest mortality risk even after adjusting for actual activity. The belief is itself a risk factor.
  • You're holding a mental list of health tasks you're not doing — inherently stressful and possibly counteracting your good work.
  • The tracker became the goal — if the sleep score or glucose monitor is stressing you or keeping you indoors, it's a hindrance.
  • You're waiting for the drug — two decades of zooming inward have not delivered prevention or cure.
  • Intense exercise inside an hour of bed — delays melatonin, raises arousal, cuts REM. Move it to morning or afternoon.
  • You're optimizing two things at once — expect zero.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Stimulated Mind

3-S Model — Wood's capstone systems model: brain function is driven by Stimulus, Supply, and Support acting as an interconnected network. (Ch 14)

Active grandparent hypothesis — The idea that humans evolved to remain physically and socially active into old age, so continued contribution is the ancestral norm. (Ch 9)

Allostasis / allostatic load — Achieving stability through change; allostatic load is the cumulative cost of unresolved stress, which impairs the support arm. (Ch 11, 14)

Amyloid Cascade Hypothesis (ACH) — Model in which amyloid beta accumulation triggers inflammation, tau tangling, neuron death, and decline. Explains only 20–25% of cognition and decline. (Ch 2)

ApoB — Lipoprotein marker of cardiovascular risk; concerning above 118 mg/dL. (Ch 13)

ApoE4 — Most common genetic risk factor for dementia. Amplifies risk from other factors rather than changing which factors matter. (Ch 14)

Astrocytes — Star-shaped glia regulating fluid flow, sleep, injury response, and neuronal energy; one human astrocyte can contact up to two million synapses. (Ch 3)

Autophagy — Cellular housekeeping that recycles damaged proteins and components; impaired autophagy is a hallmark of aging. (Ch 3)

Brain reserve (brain maintenance) — The structural "hardware": how much brain tissue you have and how well it is preserved. (Ch 1)

Car Maintenance Model — Wood's metaphor: amyloid is rust, your brain is the car, and the brain is its own mechanic. (Ch 3)

Closed-skill vs. open-skill exercise — Closed = predictable, self-paced (running, cycling); open = reactive and unpredictable (tennis, martial arts), which adds cognitive stimulus. (Ch 7)

Cognitive Athlete — Framing daily cognitive work as training that requires programmed recovery, not just more stimulus. (Ch 12)

Cognitive efficiency — Doing more with less neural activation as a skill becomes practiced. (Ch 9)

Cognitive Gears (high / middle / low) — Hewitt & Hintsa's model for matching task type to available cognitive capacity across the day. (Ch 12)

Cognitive reserve — The "software": total cognitive capacity, and how much can be lost before impairment appears. (Ch 1)

Cognitive resilience — Redundancy: the ability to tolerate accumulated brain damage without losing function. (Ch 1)

Community connector / compassionate community — Frome model of embedding social connection into healthcare; ER admissions fell 14% while surrounding areas rose 28% over four years. (Ch 10)

Crystallized intelligence — The components of cognition that form wisdom; does not automatically decline and may peak in the sixth or seventh decade. (Ch 4)

Default mode network (DMN) — Medial parietal plus prefrontal regions active when not focused on a task; heavily affected by aging. (Ch 4)

Digital dementia — Cognitive decline attributed to offloading memory and navigation to devices. (Ch 9)

Digital twin — A data replica used to predict which intervention would most reduce your personal dementia risk. (Ch 14)

Exercise snacks — Very short bouts of activity (e.g., 15 squats every 20 minutes, 5 flights of stairs daily) that accumulate meaningful benefit. (Ch 7)

FINGER — Finnish multidomain trial (1,200+ adults 60–77) combining diet, aerobic + resistance exercise, cognitive training, and cardiovascular monitoring; improved cognition over two years. (Ch 5, 14)

Glia — Non-neuronal brain cells (astroglia, microglia, oligodendroglia); nearly as numerous as neurons and central to maintenance. (Ch 3)

Google effect — Failing to encode information you know you can look up. (Ch 9)

Headroom — The book's central prize: reserve cognitive capacity above daily demand, available when you need it. Composed of the Three R's. (Ch 1, 6)

Homocysteine — B-vitamin status marker; keep below 13, ideally below 10–11 μmol/L. (Ch 8)

Hormesis — Beneficial adaptation to a mild, recoverable stressor. (Ch 11)

Hypostress — Too little challenge; the understimulated end of the general adaptation syndrome. (Ch 11)

Last-in first-out hypothesis — Recently evolved brain regions decline fastest; Wood amends it to include the regions they connect to. (Ch 4)

Lazebnik's broken radio — Test case for whether component cataloging can repair a tunable system. It cannot. (Ch 2)

Mismatch — The gap between the environment the brain evolved for and the one it now inhabits; retirement is the archetype. (Ch 1, 4)

Movement Funnel — Wood's exercise hierarchy: Snack → Propel → Resist → Sprint → Coordinate. (Ch 7)

MHT (menopausal hormone therapy) — Symptom-guided hormone treatment; Wood's position is treat symptoms, not brains. (Ch 13)

Neurovascular coupling — Active neurons and astrocytes dilate local vessels, directing oxygen and nutrients where needed — the physical link between stimulus and supply. (Ch 3, 14)

NSDR (non-sleep deep rest) / yoga nidra — Deliberate waking rest protocol; 20 minutes daily for two weeks in the cited work. (Ch 12)

Nutrient Cascade — Prioritizing scarce nutrients toward short-term survival over long-term maintenance (see Triage Theory). (Ch 8)

Physiological sigh — Double inhale followed by long exhale; ~5 minutes/day for stress reduction. (Ch 11)

POINTER — US replication of FINGER in adults 60–79; gains in executive function and processing speed, equal across ApoE4 genotype and sex. (Ch 14)

PRIME information — The categories of personal knowledge that mark a genuinely close relationship. (Ch 10)

Primal Play — Darryl Edwards' approach to unstructured, playful movement. (Ch 7)

Reductionism — Understanding a system by isolating components; legitimate for mechanism discovery, insufficient for human cognition. (Ch 2)

Resolve — Wood's third R: shedding the expectation of decline and committing to lifelong engagement. (Ch 1)

Rule of thirds — Expect roughly a third of any pursuit to feel good, a third average, a third bad. (Ch 12)

Satiety per calorie — Choosing foods by how full they make you per unit energy. (Ch 8)

Stereotype-embodiment theory — Langer's finding that people age according to their stereotypes about older people. (Ch 4)

Stimulus / Supply / Support — The three nodes of the 3-S model: cognitive challenge; oxygen, energy and nutrients; and repair processes of rest and sleep. (Ch 14)

Striver's curse — The decline experienced by those whose identity rests on peak fluid-intelligence performance. (Ch 9)

Superagers — People whose cognitive function stays stable from their fifties into their eighties; most of us are capable of it. (Ch 14)

Tau tangles / tauopathy — Abnormal tau strands forming when neurons are injured; Alzheimer's and CTE are both tauopathies. (Ch 2)

Thirds-of-a-plate method — Wood's unnamed plate heuristic (he presents it as a recommendation, not a branded framework): divide a ten-inch dinner plate into thirds — lean protein, nutrient-dense veg and fruit, and a final third flexed to energy needs. (Ch 8)

Transfer (near / intermediate / far) — How far a trained skill generalizes; far transfer is rare, which is why brain-training games disappoint. (Ch 9)

Triage Theory — Bruce Ames' theory that under nutrient shortage the body sacrifices long-term maintenance for short-term survival. (Ch 8)

Tsimané — ~17,000 Indigenous Bolivians with the world's lowest estimated dementia rates and slower brain aging. (Ch 5)

WOOP — Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan — the behavior-change protocol Wood uses for dietary change. (Ch 8)

Yerkes–Dodson curve — Inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance. (Ch 11)

patterns.md

Patterns — Protocols & Techniques from The Stimulated Mind

The 3-S Diagnosis

When to use: Deciding where to intervene, with limited capacity for change.

How: Identify your weakest node. Busy demanding job (plenty of stimulus) → add supply/support: exercise, sleep, time with people. Unrewarding work or at/near retirement (low stimulus) → new hobby, class, volunteering. Chronically time-poor → set-and-forget items: water filter, air purifier, high-quality multivitamin, tin of sardines at breakfast. Then pick one change: "when you only have the capacity to do one thing, focusing on two makes it likely that zero will happen."

Trade-offs: You lose precision about which mechanism you improved — accept it. Working one risk factor usually improves several at once.

The Movement Funnel

When to use: Building an exercise practice from any starting point.

How: Progress through the tiers, adding rather than replacing. Snack — break sitting hourly; 15 squats every 20 min; 5 flights (50 stairs)/day; even 1–2 min of vigorous activity gives benefit, 7 min/day offsets sedentary risk. Propel — walk; 4,000 steps cuts dementia risk 25% vs. 1,500; each additional 1,000 steps = 7–8% lower dementia and 15% lower mortality, plateauing around 10,000 (Wood's working range 8,000–12,000); brisk = 2.5 mph or 100 steps/min. Resist — 1–3 sets of 5–15 reps, 1–3×/week; minimum effective dose 4 sets/week per body part; use Dan John's five movements (Push, Pull, Hinge, Squat, Carry). Sprint — Norwegian 4×4 (4 min hard / 3 min easy, ×4, 3×/week) or Tabata (20 s on / 10 s off ×8). Coordinate — open-skill and complex-coordination activity.

Trade-offs: WHO baseline is 150–300 min/week MVPA, but the funnel deliberately starts far below that so you actually begin. Keep intense sessions out of the hour before bed — they delay melatonin and cut REM.

The Hippocampus Walking Protocol

When to use: You want a documented structural brain change from the simplest possible intervention.

How: 40-minute brisk walks, 3×/week. Ramp in: start at 10 minutes, add 5 minutes per week until you reach 40. Associated with roughly 2% hippocampal growth per year.

Trade-offs: Slow-building; the payoff is structural rather than immediately felt.

Nutrients / Energy / Pattern

When to use: Any dietary decision, in place of arguing about diet ideology.

How: Evaluate three things separately. (1) Nutrients — are you getting the brain-critical ones? (2) Energy — are you in chronic excess? (3) Pattern — is the overall dietary pattern whole-food dominant? Governed by two rules: maximize nutrients and fuel for your own needs. Structure meals with Wood's thirds-of-a-plate recommendation: a ten-inch dinner plate divided into lean protein, nutrient-dense veg and fruit, and a final third flexed to energy needs.

Trade-offs: Deliberately agnostic about named diets, which frustrates people wanting a verdict.

Core Nutrient Targets

When to use: Auditing the supply arm.

How: Protein 0.55 g/lb minimum, 0.7–0.8 g/lb ideal (RDI is only 0.4; Tsimané intake ≈ 2 g/kg). Protein snack rule: grams of protein ≥ calories ÷ 10. Omega-3 2–3 g/day EPA+DHA, or 2–3 servings of 4-oz fatty fish per week. B12 500 μg, folate 700 DFE, B6 20 mg, B2 1–2 mg — verify via homocysteine below 13, ideally below 10–11 μmol/L. Vitamin D3 2,000 IU (deficient below 20 ng/mL; target 40–50). Magnesium 200–400 mg. Creatine 5 g. Berries 1–2 cups/day. Tea or coffee 2–4 cups. Chocolate at 80%+ cacao.

Trade-offs: Food first — sardines, mackerel, or herring deliver protein, omega-3s, vitamin D, most B vitamins, copper, selenium, and creatine at once, with lower contaminant load than large fish. Low omega-3 + low vitamin D + high homocysteine was associated with more than a four-fold increase in dementia risk.

Energy-Excess Screen

When to use: Checking whether the supply arm is compromised metabolically.

How: Flag any of — BMI >30; waist >35 in / 90 cm; waist-to-hip ratio >0.85 (F) or >0.90 (M); waist-to-height ratio >0.55; fasting glucose >100 mg/dL; HbA1c >5.6%; HDL <40 (M) / <50 (F); triglycerides >150; blood pressure >130/80; ApoB >118 mg/dL. A 10/4 mmHg blood pressure reduction is a meaningful target.

Trade-offs: These are screening thresholds, not diagnoses — they point to where to act, not what to prescribe.

Cognitive Stimulus Selection

When to use: Choosing an activity to load the stimulus node.

How: Prefer uniquely human stimuli — language, music, social interaction, coordinative movement — over generic brain-training. Documented doses: new language 2–5 h/week or 30 min/day via app; music 60-min lesson plus 30 min practice; dance 90 min ×2/week for 3–4 months; juggling 10–30 min/day for 6–12 weeks; video games ~30 min/day; olfactory training 2 h/night with 7 scents for 6 months.

Trade-offs: Expect near transfer only. ACTIVE (2,800 adults 65+, ten 60-min sessions over 5–6 weeks with boosters at 1 and 3 years) held gains for 5 years and reduced at-fault crashes — but showed no cross-domain transfer. Train the function you actually want to keep.

The AI Cognitive-Orthotic Test

When to use: Deciding whether to offload a task to a tool.

How: Ask whether the tool is a crutch replacing a capacity you want to keep, or an orthotic extending a capacity you're still exercising. Offloading navigation, memory, and reasoning wholesale produces the Google effect and digital dementia.

Trade-offs: Some offloading is genuinely freeing; the test is whether the underlying function still gets trained.

Stress Optimization

When to use: When stress is chronic rather than acute-and-resolved.

How: Crum's three steps — see the stress, own the stress, use the stress (measured by the Stress Mindset Measure). Layer DiTuro's four moves: Breathe, Prioritize, Change what you see, Change the narrative. Add Kross's distancing shifts and Pennebaker expressive writing (15 min × 4 days). Use a traffic light self-check: green, yellow, red.

Trade-offs: Reframing works on recoverable stress. Genuine hypostress needs more challenge, not better coping — the Yerkes–Dodson curve runs both directions.

Breathing & Downregulation

When to use: Sleep onset, acute stress, or between cognitive blocks.

How: 3:7 breathing (inhale 3, exhale 7) for 20 min before bed — cut sleep onset time by roughly two-thirds in the cited work. Alternatives: 4-7-8, or a 4-6-8 ramp. Physiological sigh ~5 min/day. Bedtime brain-dump list, 5 min. Transcendental-style meditation 10–20 min/day. Mindfulness 13 min/day for 8 weeks. Gratitude practice at least weekly.

Trade-offs: All low-cost; the constraint is consistency, not technique choice.

Sleep Programming

When to use: Building the support arm.

How: Target 7–9 hours (acceptable range 6–10). Subtract 30–60 min from time in bed to estimate actual sleep. Improve in 15-minute increments of sleep opportunity — even 15–30 extra minutes a day matters. Respect ~90-minute cycles. Caffeine cutoff 9 hours before bed. Bedroom 65–70°F. Judge on the three components: quantity, quality, regularity.

Trade-offs: Exercise partially rescues short sleep — in UK Biobank (400,000 people), the elevated dementia risk of ≤6 hours was offset by 15–20 min of brisk walking or 7 min of intense exercise daily. Seven hours gave the lowest dementia risk and the largest brains. Don't use this as license to under-sleep.

The Cognitive Gears Day

When to use: Structuring cognitively demanding work.

How: Assign tasks to high, middle, or low gear and match them to your capacity through the day. Use 6-step day planning plus Newport's shutdown ritual. Pomodoro 25/5; microbreaks of 5–10 min. Protect against interruption — email interrupts roughly 4×/hour and each costs 10–15 min of recovery; task switches average 50 seconds.

Trade-offs: A 20-minute exercise bout before a memory-demanding task is a legitimate substitute for another cycle of grinding.

Anti-Frailty Tool Kit

When to use: Older adults, or anyone protecting against the strength curve (muscle falls ~1%/year after 50; strength falls 2–3× faster).

How: Jumping/impact work, blood-flow-restriction (Kaatsu) training, and protein hacks to reach intake targets. Benchmarks: leg press ≈ 2× bodyweight; aim for the top third of strength for your group. Balance training daily.

Trade-offs: Falls are the most common cause of head trauma in adults over 65, so strength and balance work is dementia prevention, not just orthopedics.

Exposure Reduction

When to use: Auditing the support arm for things actively impairing repair.

How: Alcohol — more than 2 drinks/day is harmful; even 2 UK units/day (a UK unit is 8 g; a US drink is 14 g) associates with brain shrinkage. Nicotine 1–4 mg where used. Review medications against the Beers Criteria. Air quality: N95 and PM2.5 monitoring. Oral health: xylitol 2–3 g, 2–3×/day.

Trade-offs: Hormone therapy (MHT, testosterone) should be symptom-guided — treat symptoms, not brains.

AI for Good: How Real People Are Using Artificial Intelligence to Fix Things That Matter

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — AI for Good

The Empowerment Test (apply first, to any AI proposal)

Who does this empower? A teacher customizing lessons for thirty students ≠ a company eliminating teachers. A doctor spotting patterns in scans ≠ an insurer denying claims. Back the amplifier, resist the replacer.

Should you build it? — decision path

  • Is there a specific problem that matters, named by someone who lives with it?

- No → stop. Solution-in-search-of-a-problem is the book's most common failure.

- Yes ↓

  • Does a specific AI capability map to it (predict / classify / optimize / generate)?

- No → the answer is process or staffing, not AI.

- Yes ↓

  • Is there an owner whose reputation is staked on the outcome?

- No → find your Buffington first. Championless pilots die.

- Yes ↓

  • Can you standardize the data first?

- No → that IS the project (Perna: "see myself" before you optimize).

- Yes → build, quietly, on notional data if real data is blocked.

Consequence of being wrong → deployment posture

If wrong, the cost is…Posture
Trivial / reversibleShip; learn from usage
Wasted timeHuman reviews output
Clinical or legal harmHuman-in-the-loop mandatory; overrides logged as training data
Irreversible to a personDon't automate the decision; automate the surfacing

Vendor selection — tells

Green flagRed flag
Restates your problem more precisely than you didDemos before defining
Commits to a decision you'll makeCommits to a technology
Small enough that you have leverageYou are a rounding error to them
Works on your dataWorks on their slideware

Institutional-resistance diagnosis

SymptomName itMove
Good strategy, willing leadership, nothing changesFrozen middleFix incentives, not people
Rules nobody can explainGall's Law limitAudit unused authorities before seeking new ones
Six-month review for a routine stepBureaucratic tortureDe facto ban — route around or get cover
Sixteenth report, same findingsDiagnosis is doneWork ratification + execution, not analysis
Reformers vs. civil servantsCollaboration gate failureBuild with, or lose the institutional knowledge

Adoption sequence for professionals (clinicians, teachers)

1. Volunteers only — never open with a mandate

2. Bake-off — competing tools, usage data decides

3. Confidence first — let them win before you ask them to change

4. "You're the final check" — preserve authority explicitly

5. Mandate — only after voluntary adoption plateaus

Thresholds & numbers the book commits to

  • Prompt validation: 10+ runs, judge the worst output, not the best
  • Admin burden in US healthcare: 25–30% of spend
  • Federal acquisitions workforce: ~30,000 people
  • Prior military software studies since 1982: 15, same conclusions
  • Rule of thumb: four singles > one home run on politically exposed projects

Failure tells — you are in trouble if…

  • Evaluation is "vibes-based"
  • The pilot was announced before it worked
  • The champion is a title, not a person
  • Success is measured in transactions, not outcomes (transaction-count fallacy)
  • The model is fluent and nobody has checked whether it's right (Eliza effect)
  • It agrees with you when you push back (sycophancy)
  • The plan requires the frozen middle to volunteer for extra risk

Personal protocol (Epilogue)

1. Flirt with the tools — know capability vs. claim

2. Decline what feels wrong; non-use is the strongest feedback tech has

3. Price the swap: what data, what attention, worth it?

4. Say loudly where AI should go — money follows taxes, purchases, votes

5. Or build it yourself; most people in this book had no software expertise

glossary.md

Glossary — AI for Good

Accelerationists — camp arguing AI should be built as fast as possible to reap benefits and beat global competition (Ch 1)

Administrative burden — the 25–30% of US healthcare spending (~$5B at Cleveland Clinic scale) consumed by non-clinical work (Ch 8)

AGI (artificial general intelligence) — theoretical synthesis of AI capabilities surpassing human intellect across domains (Ch 1)

Alert fatigue — clinician desensitization from too many low-precision automated warnings (Ch 13)

Ambient scribe — AI that listens to a clinical visit and drafts the note, with doctor-in-the-loop review (Ch 11)

Bayesian Health — vendor whose sepsis model tiers alerts by probability rather than firing uniformly (Ch 13)

Bonini's paradox — a model detailed enough to be fully accurate becomes as hard to understand as the thing modeled (Ch 26)

Bullshit umbrella — senior cover that shields a team from bureaucratic interference during a crisis (Ch 16)

Case mix index (CMI) — severity-weighted measure of a hospital's patient population (Ch 12, 13)

Character.ai — companion chatbot platform built on an attention-based engagement model (Ch 22)

Classifier — AI that labels or sorts: images, email, tumors on an MRI (Ch 1)

Context stuffing — loading a model's context window with source material to constrain its answers (Ch 4)

Context window — the span of text a model can consider at once (Ch 3, 4)

Digital twin — a live data model mirroring a physical system, from a supply chain to a patient's anatomy (Ch 9, 15)

DOGE — initiative Tyrangiel treats as the cautionary counterexample: provocation over collaboration (Ch 21)

Doomers — camp arguing AI risks catastrophe or extinction and must be slowed (Ch 1)

Ed — the failed Los Angeles schools chatbot; shorthand for edtech deployed ahead of its competence (Ch 2)

Eliza effect — human tendency to attribute understanding to a system that merely reflects language back (Weizenbaum, 1966) (Ch 22)

Epic — dominant electronic health record system; its closed nature shapes what hospital AI can do (Ch 11, 13)

FASA (Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act, 1994) — statute requiring agencies to consider commercial products; the basis of Palantir's suit (Ch 17)

Frozen middle — the acquisition/program layer between leadership intent and execution, not incentivized to move (Ch 18, 20)

Gall's Law — every complicated working system evolved from a simple working system (Ch 18)

God view — a single synthesized real-time picture of a whole problem space (Ch 1, 15)

Hallucination — fluent, confident, false model output (Ch 2, 3)

Human-in-the-loop — required human review of AI output; also functions as legal and political cover (Ch 11, 20)

IMS (Integrated Master Schedule) — Operation Warp Speed's synchronized plan across all agencies and vendors (Ch 15)

Inherently governmental — legal category of work that may not be delegated to machines or contractors (Ch 20)

Iron triangle — the closed loop of agencies, incumbent contractors, and Congress that resists new entrants (Ch 17)

Notional data — placeholder data used to build and demo a system before real data arrives (Ch 16)

Ontology — Palantir's core abstraction: a shared model of an organization's entities and relationships (Ch 16)

Operation Warp Speed — the COVID vaccine distribution effort; the book's origin story (Ch 1, 14, 15)

Optimizer — AI making split-second decisions to improve logistics, pricing, or allocation (Ch 1)

p(doom) — self-reported probability of AI-caused human extinction (Ch 1)

POSIWID — "the purpose of a system is what it does" (Anil Dash) (Ch 21)

Productive struggle — the difficulty a learner must experience for learning to occur; the thing a tutor must not short-circuit (Ch 7)

Prompt drift — degradation of a tuned prompt when the underlying model is updated (Ch 3)

Red teaming — adversarially attacking your own system to find failures before users do (Ch 4)

Sepsis — fast-moving infection response; the canonical case for probabilistic clinical alerting (Ch 13)

SERT (Sepsis Emergency Response Team) — the human team an alert is designed to mobilize (Ch 13)

Sycophancy — a model's tendency to agree with the user under pressure, abandoning correct answers (Ch 2)

SWAP Study — Defense Innovation Board's Software Acquisition and Practices report; named the frozen middle (Ch 18)

Team Human — Tyrangiel's shorthand for AI that amplifies human judgment rather than replacing it (Ch 27)

Vibes-based evaluation — judging model output by impression instead of a repeatable test; the default failure (Ch 4)

Zero-shot translation — translating a language pair the model was never explicitly trained on (Ch 24, 26)

Zone of proximal development — the band just beyond current ability where learning happens; applied to device design (Ch 23)

patterns.md

Patterns — AI for Good

Techniques practitioners in this book actually used. Each is attributed to the person who ran it.

Hillis's Reframe

When: you cannot tell what AI is good for because vendor noise dominates.

How: "Try to imagine the tech without the tech companies." Ask what the capability enables for someone with a real problem, stripped of who profits from the answer.

Trade-offs: clarifies use, ignores cost and vendor lock-in — reintroduce those after.

Perna's "See Myself" Principle

When: coordinating anything across organizations that don't share data.

How: before optimizing, build one live standardized picture of positions, supplies, and flows. Reduce complexity to a single tracer material (Perna used plastic) to test whether the picture is real.

Trade-offs: data standardization is the expensive, unglamorous majority of the work.

The Definition-First Vendor Test

When: selecting an AI vendor.

How: give each an hour. Reject any who cannot state the problem back to you more precisely than you stated it. Hire the ones who commit to a decision you'll be able to make, not a technology.

Trade-offs: filters for clear communicators, which correlates with but does not guarantee capability.

The Ten-Run Prompt Test (DiCerbo)

When: validating any prompt before it faces users.

How: run the same prompt ten-plus times and inspect the spread, not the best output. Ship only if the worst run is acceptable.

Trade-offs: slow and manual; replaces vibes-based evaluation, which is worse.

The Role-Constraint Prompt Pattern

When: a model must refuse to do the user's work for them.

How: specify role, what it must never do, and the recovery move when pushed. Khan's tutoring script: ask what the student thinks first, never give the answer, decompose into the next smallest step.

Trade-offs: constraints erode under adversarial pressure and after model updates — retest on every version bump.

Context Stuffing

When: you need answers anchored to your material, not the model's priors.

How: load authoritative source content into the context window and instruct the model to answer only from it.

Trade-offs: bounded by window size; does not eliminate hallucination, only reduces it.

Zubovic's Pilot-Site Selection Rule

When: choosing where to run a first deployment.

How: pick the site with a leader who will personally champion it and whose reputation is staked on the outcome — not the easiest or largest site. "Get Buffington."

Trade-offs: success may not generalize to sites without a champion; plan the second site deliberately.

Quiet Pilot Containment

When: piloting anything that could be politically destroyed by early failure.

How: keep the pilot small and unpublicized until the failure modes are known. Announce after it works.

Trade-offs: limits learning volume and can read as secrecy if discovered.

The Voluntary Bake-off (Boose)

When: introducing a tool into a professional workforce that resents mandates.

How: let clinicians volunteer, run competing vendors side by side, let usage data pick the winner. Escalate to a mandate only after voluntary adoption plateaus (Mihaljevic's Mandate Threshold).

Trade-offs: volunteers self-select as enthusiasts; ghosting is common, so recruit more than you need.

The Sepsis Alert Triage Ladder

When: an automated alert system is being ignored.

How: tier alerts by probability instead of firing uniformly; route each tier to a different response. Treat every clinician override as training data (the Override-as-Training-Data Loop).

Trade-offs: tiering requires a calibrated model; miscalibration moves harm rather than removing it.

Build-With, Don't Buy-Out-of-the-Box (Pappas)

When: deploying into a workflow whose practitioners must trust the output.

How: co-build with the people who will use it; ship the reassurance that they remain the final check.

Trade-offs: slower than procurement, and the result is harder to resell elsewhere.

Four Singles Instead of a Home Run (Jaffe)

When: the full problem is too large or too political to solve at once.

How: ship four small, independently useful wins rather than one transformative system. Start on notional data so building begins before real data clears.

Trade-offs: risks a pile of tools with no coherent ontology unless the data model is planned up front.

Werfel's Five-Degree Turn Doctrine

When: reforming an institution that cannot survive visible upheaval.

How: make small course corrections continuously, keep the work below the threshold of political attention (the Invisibility Shield), and let compounding do the rest.

Trade-offs: invisibility forfeits the credit and the mandate that would let you move faster.

Pandya's "Why You Should Care" Rule

When: pitching technical work to non-technical stakeholders.

How: lead with the consequence for the listener's constituency, never the architecture.

Trade-offs: none; the omission is the common error.

The Collaboration Gate for Public-Sector AI

When: judging whether a government AI effort will help or damage.

How: ask whether the team is building with the civil servants who run the system or against them. Provocation-first efforts (Ch 21) destroy the institutional knowledge they need.

Trade-offs: collaboration is slower and dilutes the reformer's narrative.

Johnson's Burden-Side Rule

When: designing for someone who cannot easily self-report.

How: put the sensing and interpretation burden on the technology and the caregiver's observations, not on the person being helped. Meet him at the what — start from observed behavior, not a diagnostic label.

Trade-offs: caregiver-labeled signal carries the caregiver's interpretation; validate against outcomes.

Shah's Rope-and-Car Principle

When: a system must survive real-world conditions it wasn't trained on.

How: design the protocol so it can be perturbed and still function, rather than optimizing for clean-condition accuracy.

Trade-offs: costs benchmark performance to buy field robustness.

Tyrangiel's Four-Step Civic Protocol

When: you are a non-expert deciding how to engage with AI.

How: (1) flirt with the tools enough to know real capability vs. claim; (2) decline features that feel like a solution seeking a problem — non-use is the strongest feedback signal; (3) price the swap (data, attention) and read the terms; (4) back AI that amplifies human judgment, oppose AI that replaces it.

Trade-offs: individually slow; the mechanism is aggregate, not personal.

The Unaccountability Machine: Why Big Systems Make Terrible Decisions — and How The World Lost Its Mind

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Decide & Diagnose

The two laws everything reduces to

  • Fundamental law of accountability: your ability to change a decision = your accountability for it. If you can't change it, you can't be blamed for it — and neither can anyone else.
  • Ashby's Law: only variety can absorb variety. If regulator variety < environmental variety, the system cannot be controlled. No amount of effort, funding, or good intentions substitutes.

Decision rules

WhenDoBecause
No information from the affected person could change the outcomeName it an accountability sink; stop arguing with the operatorThe operator is not a decision-maker; the decision was made elsewhere and is unappealable by design
A regulator's variety is plainly below the environment'sKill the project or attenuate the environment — don't add staffRequisite variety is a hard constraint, not a resourcing problem
A division bounces crisis to crisisGive it its own internal Systems 2/3/4/5It's an unrecognised viable system, not a badly-supervised one
Leadership attention runs only to this quarterRebuild System 4 before anything elseThe organisation is decerebrate and coasting on a stable environment
Algedonic signals are frequentLook down, not at the signallerEmergencies escalating means lower levels can't absorb their own variety
Algedonic signals are zeroCheck the channel existsSilence is more often a missing channel than health
Stated purpose ≠ delivered outcomeApply POSIWID; ask what structure makes this systematicDissolves conspiracy-vs-cock-up, which is the wrong question
Someone says "however you look at the numbers"Read it as "however I look at these numbers"The modelling choices did the work, not the data
A model is settling a real decisionRun the four-condition checkFailing any one means you're watching the Ricardian Vice
Reusing a metric outside its originAsk what decision it was collected forLearn the numbers by looking at the business, never the reverse
About to outsource or cutTrace one signal across every boundary it crossesIf the contract carries only "OK"/"stopped", you've bought decerebration
Tempted to write a new ruleLocate where feedback is amplified, attenuated, or removedRules add variety to the regulated side; feedback adds it to the regulator
Designing any maximising systemPair it with a higher-level supervisor and a red handleThe top level of an autonomous system must never itself be a maximiser

Diagnostic tree — "why does this system keep making terrible decisions?"

  • Does the information reach a decision-maker at all?

- No, no channel → missing channel. Build it.

- No, channel exists but signal arrives unusable → missing translation capacity. It's data, not information.

- Yes, but too late to act → arrival timing failure; same as no channel.

- Yes, in time and actionable → continue.

  • Can the receiver absorb that much variety?

- No → requisite-variety mismatch. Attenuate incoming, amplify regulatory, or accept the system is uncontrollable.

- Yes → continue.

  • Is there a System 4 watching what isn't in contact with operations yet?

- Only extrapolative forecasting → System 4 absent (forecasting ≠ intelligence).

- Nothing → decerebrate organisation.

  • Does System 5 rule the relevant information out of scope?

- Yes → identity failure. The most common root cause; no amount of lower-level fixing survives it.

Tells & smells

An accountability sink: "that's the policy" with no named owner · an exceptions process that exists but is never used · a crumple zone (the rule absorbs the blame that would have hit a manager) · the affected party has facts nobody is authorised to receive.

A variety mismatch: controls with fewer dimensions than the environment's degrees of freedom · observation frequency slower than the rate variety is generated · a regulator that keeps being "surprised" by things insiders already knew · "we just need better data" as the standing answer.

A decerebrate organisation: excellent quarterly execution, no one owns the five-year question · forecasts are the current model extended · System 4 was the first thing cut · performing beautifully right up until the environment changes structurally.

Ideology wearing a lab coat: a phrase cited to a source that doesn't contain it (the "fiduciary duty to maximise shareholder value" attributed to Friedman) · legal jargon used outside its legal context · "ad hoc" deployed to disqualify habit and rules of thumb · semantic drift from increase to maximise, from profits to shareholder value.

A system about to fail: targets demanding the impossible (you will get the unethical) · quarterly beat institutionalised as the primary filter · redundancy threat swamping middle-management judgement · costs prioritised over revenues because they're what management directly controls · volatility suppressed by using unemployment as the attenuator.

Defaults the author commits to

  • Prefer viability over maximisation as the corporate objective.
  • Management by exception: push variety-handling to the lowest level that can absorb it; size the manager to the residual variety, not the total.
  • Resource bargain: grant autonomy up to the point of jeopardising the wider system — no further, no less.
  • Retain limited liability only for small, non-controlling investors; no further levels of it.
  • The single private-equity reform worth making: any entity taking control of an operating company must guarantee its debts. Do not try to regulate "excessive" borrowing — requisite variety says that's doomed.
  • Economists demoted to competent technicians (Keynes' dentists), toolkit retained.
  • Accept unaccountable, robotic decision-making — give up the demand for a human to blame — and compensate by repairing feedback and attending to red handles. "I blame the system" becomes a literal statement.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Unaccountability Machine (Dan Davies)

Cybernetics vocabulary first: get variety, requisite variety, accountability sink, and System 1–5 exactly right; the rest hangs off them.

Accountability sink — A structure that severs the link between a decision's outcome and any human who could be answerable for it; its defining test is that no information from the affected person could change the result (Ch 1, 3). Not merely "nobody is responsible" — it is a variety-amplification device, "a solution as much as a problem" (Ch 4).

Ad hoc — In economics, a disqualifying insult; it rules habit and rules-of-thumb out as explanations (Ch 6).

Algedonic signal / "red handle" — A channel letting any level signal directly to the top, across intervening levels, that something threatens viability and needs immediate action; modelled on a train's emergency brake (Ch 5, 10).

Ashby's Law (Principle of Requisite Variety) — Only variety can absorb variety: a regulator must have at least as many states as the system it regulates (Ch 4).

Ataxia / purpose tremor — Feedback too weak (response trails the target) vs. too strong (oscillating overcorrection) (Ch 4).

Attributability test — A cost is attributable exactly to the extent it would be avoided by not producing that output; the accountants' version of the fundamental law of accountability (Ch 7).

Black box — A system defined by its behaviour, not its composition, because its internals cannot be safely or usefully known; respecting its integrity is management cybernetics' signature move (Ch 2, 3). Contrast clear box (directly controllable) and muddy box (analysable, but at disproportionate effort).

Business hallucination — Acting on a picture generated by reporting conventions rather than the real process (Ch 7).

Complexity — Defined operationally as that which must be treated as a black box (Ch 2); complex vs. complicated = treatable "only as a whole" vs. traceable by maths (Ch 3).

Control fraud (Black) — A criminal captures a bank and installs incentives that produce fraud via legitimate-looking cash transfers. Self-organising control fraud (Davies) — a system so criminogenic that banks organise themselves into fraud with no boss-to-crook link (Ch 1).

Criminogenic organisation — One whose incentives are structurally designed to ensure crimes (Ch 1).

Crumple zone — A policy's function of absorbing impact to shield a manager from a disastrous decision (Ch 1).

Cybernetics — The abandoned science of decision-making systems; management cybernetics is Beer's applied branch (Ch 0, 2).

Cybersyn — Chile's system: Cybernet (telex network, System 2), Cyberstride (statistical filter distinguishing blip / trend change / new normal), the Operations Room (System 3), Checo (System 4) (Ch 7i).

Decerebrate organisation — Still operates, but has lost intelligence and identity, so cannot act purposively; coasting on a stable environment (Ch 5i, 9).

Decided-upon, the — Those affected by decisions who have no person to address (Ch 0).

Decision-making system — Any arrangement producing decisions from standardised information rather than a human reacting to circumstances; Davies' replacement term for "artificial intelligence" (Ch 0, 3).

Deep politics / parapolitics (Scott) — The part of government where accountability is intentionally diminished and kept out of public discourse (Ch 1).

Financialisation — Not a parasite on the real economy but the growing weight of the financial aspects of the whole system (Ch 8).

Fundamental law of accountability — Your ability to change a decision equals your accountability for it. Corollary, the principle of diminishing accountability: the more decision-making is industrialised, the less accountability survives (Ch 1, 3).

Homeostasis / homeostat — The state a system returns to under feedback, with no implication that it is optimal; Ashby's homeostat was four veto-capable needles with 810,000 states that rapidly re-stabilised (Ch 2, 4). Homeostatic forces are the subsystem links pulling an organisation back to existing behaviour (Ch 2, 7).

Management accounting vs financial reporting — Process control and cost allocation tied to specific decisions, vs. a periodic convention-based summary for financiers that attenuates variety (Ch 7).

Management by exception — Push variety-handling to the lowest level that can absorb it; escalate only what that level cannot handle (Ch 5, 7i).

Metasystem — Beer's term for the part of a viable system responsible for its internal organisation (Systems 3–5) (Ch 5).

Microfoundations / homo economicus / representative individual — The requirement that phenomena be derived from individual optimising decisions; an agent valuing only price and quantity, perfectly informed; and the aggregation that removes heterogeneity and strategic interaction (Ch 6).

POSIWID — "The purpose of a system is what it does." Not cynicism: a description of how System 5 preserves viability (Ch 2, 5, 10).

Polycrisis (Tooze) — Structurally similar 21st-century crises whose common feature is loss of control by the existing hierarchy (Ch 1).

Rank and yank — Annual bottom-10% firing, retained mainly for its threat value (Ch 9).

Recursion / embedding — Every viable system contains all five systems and is itself a System 1 inside a larger one (Ch 5).

Residual variety — What is left after Systems 1 and 2 absorb theirs; the volume System 3 must be sized to (Ch 5).

Resource bargain — Autonomy granted up to the point of jeopardising the wider system: what a unit gets, and what it is accountable for delivering (Ch 2, 5, 10).

Reversing the polarity — The shift by which the working class came to insure the corporate sector against the business cycle instead of the reverse; restoring the polarity is Ch 10's core prescription (Ch 9, 10).

Ricardian Vice (Schumpeter) — Proving something in a stripped-down model, then acting as if it were proved about the world (Ch 6).

Status syndrome / social gradient (Marmot, Whitehall) — Loss of control over one's work is physiologically lethal (Ch 9).

Survival set — The output ranges corresponding to the regulated thing continuing to exist (Ch 4).

Systems 1–5 (Viable System Model) — 1 Operations (makes change in the world); 2 Regulation (stops operations clashing); 3 Integration (coordinates the 1s, strikes and polices resource bargains); 3* audit; 4 Intelligence ("there and then", watching the environment not yet in contact with operations); 5 Philosophy/identity (balances 3 against 4 by fixing what kind of organisation this is) (Ch 5).

Technostructure (Galbraith) — The managerial class maintaining overall system stability (Ch 10).

Translation capacity / transduction — Capability at each end of a channel to render a signal into a form the receiving box can act on; without it, variety stays "data" and never becomes information (Ch 4, 5, 9).

Ultrastability (Ashby) → viability (Beer) — The ability to find a steady state under conditions the designer never anticipated; viability is the potential to persist as an independent entity (Ch 4, 10).

Variety — The number of states a system can be in. Not intrinsic — a property of how you choose to describe it (Ch 4). Variety engineering = deliberately attenuating incoming variety and amplifying regulatory variety until Ashby's Law is satisfied.

patterns.md

Patterns — Diagnostic Techniques

The Sink Test

When to use: You suspect a policy, algorithm, or process is an accountability sink rather than a decision.

How: Ask the defining question — is there any information the affected person could supply that would change the outcome? If no, it is a sink. Then run the override test: who, by name, can overrule this? If the answer is "nobody" or "the policy", the sink is complete. Check whether an exceptions mechanism exists and is actually used — an unused exceptions process is decoration.

Trade-offs: Sinks are not automatically bad. They are variety-amplification devices — a solution as much as a problem. The good ones (Davies' common-law test) retain slow reputational feedback and can be revised; the bad ones are unappealable and unrevisable.

The Requisite-Variety Audit

When to use: Assessing whether any regulator — a manager, a regulator, a control system, a project plan — can possibly do its job. Davies flags this in a footnote as the most useful advice in the book.

How: For each regulatory link, compare rather than measure: is the regulator's variety greater or less than the variety arriving from the environment? Use the vehicle-controls test as a quick dimensional check (a train has one control dimension, a car two, a plane three — match the controls to the environment's degrees of freedom). Then check observation frequency against the rate at which the system generates variety.

Trade-offs: Gives you a clean verdict on impossibility-in-principle, and distinguishes "fails for lack of resources" from "cannot work at all" — but it tells you the mismatch exists, not which of attenuation or amplification is the cheaper fix.

Hunt the Three Model Defects

When to use: A control system exists and is well-resourced but keeps being surprised.

How: Treat the control system as a model of its environment and look for exactly three defects: (1) sources of environmental variety the model omits entirely; (2) regulatory variety that is overestimated; (3) information assumed to be transmitted that is not actually transmitted. Then ask the complementary question: what does the control system not monitor? (Pre-2008, deficits were watched; private-sector debt was not.)

Trade-offs: Requires knowing the domain well enough to name the missing variety sources; the method won't generate them for you.

VSM Role Audit

When to use: Diagnosing a chronically dysfunctional organisation, division, or programme.

How: Name which actual component performs each of Systems 1–5. Map functions, not org-chart boxes — the functions exist whether or not anyone holds the title. Check both directions: the larger system this unit is embedded in, and the organisation inside its own operations. A missing role is a predicted failure point.

Trade-offs: Tempting to force five labels onto existing boxes; resist. Stopping at one level of recursion is the most common error.

The System 2 / System 3 Test

When to use: Working out whether a management layer is coordination or control.

How: System 2 is the management everyone agrees is necessary (timetables, scheduling, the quartermaster). System 3 is the management people complain about. The tell: System 3 managers routinely disguise themselves as System 2 — presenting control as harmless coordination.

Trade-offs: Useful for reading org politics, but the distinction is functional, so the same person can do both.

The Decerebration Check

When to use: An organisation is performing well but you suspect it has cut away its own brain.

How: Ask what the leadership's attention actually runs to. If it runs only to this quarter's revenue and current staffing, System 4 is absent and the organisation is coasting on a stable environment. Distinguish forecasting from System 4: if the forecasts are extrapolations of the current model, they are here-and-now extended, not intelligence.

Trade-offs: Decerebrate organisations look fine — sometimes excellent — until the environment changes structurally. The check has no short-run confirming evidence.

Red-Handle Frequency as Diagnostic

When to use: Judging the health of levels below you.

How: Count algedonic signals. Frequent emergency escalations mean systems further down are missing, misidentified, or dysfunctional — the signal is doing work that should have been absorbed lower. Also resource the receiving end: an algedonic channel with no translation capacity delivers noise.

Trade-offs: Zero red handles is not health; it may mean the channel doesn't exist.

The Problem-Child Diagnostic

When to use: One division bounces from crisis to crisis while others don't.

How: Treat it as an unrecognised System 1 — a unit that could in principle exist independently but has been denied its own internal 2/3/4/5. Give it the missing internal functions rather than more supervision from above.

Trade-offs: Occasionally the unit genuinely isn't a viable system and should be merged or dissolved instead.

Boundary-Crossing Audit Before Cuts

When to use: Before any restructuring, outsourcing, or headcount reduction.

How: Trace a real signal end to end. Identify every organisational boundary it crosses and what capacity translates it at each crossing. Then run the channel-state test for outsourcing: if the contract can only carry "OK" and "stopped working", there is no bandwidth for "conditions are changing" — you have bought a decerebration.

Trade-offs: Slow, and it makes cuts look more expensive than the accounting does. That is the point.

POSIWID Divergence

When to use: A system's stated purpose and delivered outcomes disagree, and you are being invited to argue about intentions.

How: Ignore stated purpose. Read the purpose off the outputs. Then ask "what structure made this the systematic output?" — which dissolves the conspiracy-versus-cock-up question entirely.

Trade-offs: Reads as cynicism if stated aloud; it is actually a claim about System 5, not about anyone's motives.

The Four-Condition Check Before Trusting an Optimisation Model

When to use: An economic or quantitative model is being used to settle a real decision.

How: Confirm all four: commodity good; observable marginal cost curve; spot markets independent of later periods; negligible strategic interaction. If any fails, you are watching the Ricardian Vice. Separate the assumptions made for tractability from those equivalent to assuming the conclusion. Translate "however you look at the numbers" as "however I look at these numbers."

Trade-offs: Beating a Ricardian requires either data collected for a different purpose or a flaw internal to their model — the four-condition check tells you which fight you're in.

Ask What Decision the Number Was Collected For

When to use: Reusing any metric, report, or dataset outside its original context.

How: Trace the number to the decision it was designed to support. Apply the attributability test to costs: a cost is attributable exactly to the extent it would be avoided by not producing the output. Rule of thumb — learn the numbers by looking at the business, never the business by looking at the numbers.

Trade-offs: Most available numbers fail this test, which leaves you with less data and better judgement.

The Feedback-Location Method

When to use: Designing a fix, instead of writing another rule.

How: Don't specify behaviour. Ask where feedback is currently amplified, attenuated, or removed — then restore the missing loop. Corollary target-regime diagnostic: demand the impossible and you get the unethical.

Trade-offs: Harder to audit than a rulebook, and it produces no compliance artefact.

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Unspoken Rules

Decision rules and tells to keep beside you. The judgment, not the vocabulary.

The master test: the Three Cs

Before any move, ask: does this show competence, commitment, AND compatibility? Each fails two ways:

CUndershoot (reads as…)Overshoot (reads as…)Aim
Competenceclueless, sloppy, slowknow-it-all, makes others look baddo it fully, accurately, promptly
Commitmentapathetic, clock-watcherdoormat, burning out, fakepresent and eager, with boundaries
Compatibilitycold, hard to be aroundposer, sucking up, inauthenticcomfortable to work with, still yourself

Managers judge the perceived version of your work, not just the actual output. Make progress visible.

Should I act / ask / push? (curiosity vs. entitlement)

  • Imagine getting a flat "no." Honest reaction "just thought I'd ask" → ask, it's curiosity. Reaction "outrageous!" → don't, it's entitlement.
  • Worst case is almost always a "no," not danger. Fear is of judgment, not safety → give it a shot.
  • Got an unearned edge? Be less entitled. Habitually wait for permission? Be more.

Is this a good question to ask? (three circles)

  • I already know it → don't ask.
  • I could figure it out (Google, the wiki, 5 min) → figure it out, don't ask.
  • Only learnable by asking → ask — and show your homework: "Here's what I know, here's what I don't."

New here — which mode am I in?

  • Learner mode (new): expected to ask. Always have a good question ready; "Any questions?" is a yes-question.
  • Leader mode (established): expected to know and contribute. Don't ask what you should already own.

How urgent / important is this task?

  • Urgency = proximity + scrutiny + anxiety + time-sensitivity.
  • Importance = centrality + scrutiny + criticality.
  • Triage: urgent+important → do now · important not urgent → schedule · urgent not important → timebox/delegate · neither → delete.
  • Force-rank ties. Default: under-promise, over-deliver; no surprises.

Receiving a task — clarify before you start

1. What / How / By When — get all three up front.

2. RACI — who's Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed?

3. Work backward from the deadline; ask for interim check-ins.

4. Repeat it back to catch misunderstandings.

5. Stuck? Propose A or B + a recommendation, never an open "what do you think?"

Before you hit Send (digital signals)

Typos? · Caught up on the thread? · Right time? · Tone matches intent? · OK if this gets forwarded?

  • Match the room: email-first vs. IM-first; monochronic (time = blocks, be prompt) vs. polychronic (time = fluid).
  • You're judged on impact, not intent — over-clarify in writing.

Appearance: how much to conform

  • Mirror coworkers at your level; unsure → default more formal.
  • Sort each element: Sacred (protect) · Negotiable (weigh by situation) · Indifferent (give away freely).
  • Tactic: bend — conform first, reveal your authentic self once trust is built.

Reading a new team (tells)

  • Power ≠ title. Watch who decisions route through → the influencer: Gatekeeper / Veteran / Expert / Socialite / Adviser.
  • Friendly ≠ loyal to you. Note first loyalties before confiding.
  • Swimlane rigid? → ask permission first. Loose? → act, then inform. In doubt → ask.
  • Don't overshoot your zone of commitment — it reads as threatening.

Decoding feedback (two axes)

VerbalNonverbal
IndirectSubtle hints (softened)Behavior changes (avoidance, micromanaging)
DirectUncensored comments (blunt)Blunt actions (work redone/reassigned/rejected)
  • Separate substance (what they mean) from delivery (how they said it). Ask the root cause.
  • Remember negativity bias — one criticism outweighs three compliments; don't spiral.
  • Ask: "What should I start / stop / keep doing?" Apply fast, report back (coachability = commitment).

Something's wrong — fix it / live with it / leave it

1. Diagnose root cause: is it People / Position / Place? (Use the "Why?" exercise.)

2. Strip emotion with 10-10-10: best in 10 minutes / 10 months / 10 years?

3. Choose the path of least regret, not the fastest relief.

4. Leaning toward leaving? Run the ten-question leave-it test — more "yes" = more sense to go. Protect your last impression.

Positioning for promotion

  • Nine-box: aim top-right = do today's job well AND show you can do the next one / lead.
  • Claim an unoccupied swimlane — what can I do / fix / bridge / know / share that no one owns?
  • Contribution counts only if noticed AND reported, and better (not merely different), on a mission-critical problem.
  • Asking for a raise: data + one-page summary + a specific number + appreciation.

Build relationships (when you know no one)

  • Answer bids (small connection requests) — don't let them drop.
  • Can't relate? Fall back to EAR: Engage, Ask, Repeat. Use "Yes, and…"
  • First move by audience: casual chat (nearby) / double opt-in intro (warm) / customized cold email (stranger).
  • Be an energy giver, not a complainer. Relationships compound — start early.

glossary.md

Glossary — The Unspoken Rules

Accountable — the person whose reputation is on the line for a deliverable; only one per task (Ch 8).

Ask-for-permission vs. beg-for-forgiveness spectrum — how rigid a team's swimlanes are; rigid → clear it first, loose → act then inform (Ch 10).

Authentic — true to who you are, as opposed to the average of your coworkers (Ch 6).

Bare-minimum rule — outcomes scale with the initiative you put in; doing only what's asked caps your results (Ch 2).

Bid — a small request for connection (a comment, question, gesture); relationships are built by noticing and answering bids (Gottman) (Ch 11).

Big picture / the eight blanks — understanding how your org and role fit the whole; the senior-leader mindset that turns a workhorse into a thought partner (Ch 3).

Blunt actions — direct + nonverbal feedback: reassigning, redoing, or rejecting your work (Ch 13).

Behavior changes — indirect + nonverbal feedback: avoidance, micromanaging, going quiet (Ch 13).

Boomerang employee — someone who leaves an organization and later returns, often at the same level (Ch 14).

Call to action — the specific response a message asks for; every message should make the next step obvious (Ch 8).

Coachability — visibly applying feedback; reading as coachable signals commitment (Ch 13).

Cold email — outreach to a stranger, customized enough that it can't be mistaken for spam (Ch 11).

Comfort zones — the topics and behaviors a given person treats as appropriate vs. taboo (Ch 10).

Commitment — being fully present and eager to help the team hit its goals; one of the Three Cs (Ch 1).

Compatibility — making others comfortable and glad to be around you, without seeming inauthentic; one of the Three Cs (Ch 1).

Competence — doing your job fully, accurately, and promptly without micromanagement or making others look bad; one of the Three Cs (Ch 1).

Curiosity vs. entitlement test — imagine getting a "no"; if your honest reaction is "just thought I'd ask," the ask is curiosity, not entitlement (Ch 2).

CYA ("cover yourself") — because digital messages are permanent and forwardable, communicate so a forwarded copy never hurts you (Ch 7).

Double opt-in intro — connecting two people only after both have agreed to be connected (Ch 11).

EAR (Engage, Ask, Repeat) — conversation fallback: engage, ask a question, repeat; default to questions when you can't relate (Ch 11).

Eight blanks — see Big picture: the gaps you fill to understand how everything fits (Ch 3).

Eisenhower Matrix (adapted) — triage by urgency × importance: do / schedule / timebox-or-delegate / delete (Ch 9).

Energy givers vs. energy vampires — people who add energy to a room vs. those who drain it with complaints; be the former (Ch 11).

External narrative — the audience-tailored version of your story that proves the Three Cs; lead with this, not the internal "me, me, me" version (Ch 5).

Feedback ranges — feedback mapped on two axes, verbal↔nonverbal and direct↔indirect (Ch 13).

Fire drill — a sudden, urgent demand that disrupts planned work (Ch 9).

First loyalties — who someone is loyal to first; friendly toward you ≠ on your side (Ch 10).

Fix it / live with it / leave it — the three responses to any bad situation (Ch 14).

Gatekeepers / Veterans / Experts / Socialites / Advisers — the five informal-influencer types who hold power beyond their title (Ch 10).

Good question — one you genuinely can't answer on your own; only learnable by asking (Ch 3).

Hero of your own journey — others are too busy with themselves to scrutinize you, so act (Ch 2).

Hero's journey (Past, Present, Future) — frame your story as origin → present → goal in about two minutes (Ch 5).

High-context vs. low-context — cultures/people who communicate through the unspoken vs. at face value (Ch 13).

IC (individual contributor) — someone who does the work directly rather than managing others (Ch 15).

Importance (three factors) — centrality, scrutiny, criticality: how much a task matters (Ch 9).

Indifferent zone — appearance/identity elements you can abandon without any felt loss (Ch 6).

Influencer — someone with leverage to sway decisions without formal authority (Ch 10).

Intent vs. impact — what you mean vs. how you come across; close the gap, especially in writing/remote work (Ch 7, Ch 13).

Internal narrative — your private "why I do this" story; build it first, but rarely lead with it (Ch 5).

Learner mode vs. leader mode — the two expectation states: new → expected to ask questions; established → expected to know and contribute (Ch 4, Ch 12).

"Let's give this a shot" — the mindset of trying things you might fail at but might succeed at (Ch 2).

Mental fridge — a stocked set of talking-point "ingredients" you can pull from to answer unexpected questions (Ch 5).

Mirroring — inferring the unspoken norm from coworkers at your level and matching it (Ch 6).

Monochronic vs. polychronic — cultures that treat time as fixed blocks vs. fluid and flexible (Ch 7).

Nine-box matrix — performance × potential grid; aim for the top-right box to position for promotion (Ch 15).

Negativity bias — criticism registers more strongly than praise; weight feedback accordingly (Ch 13).

Nonpromotable tasks / office housework — note-taking, lunch orders, event-planning: work that rarely advances a career and disproportionately falls on women and people of color (Ch 9, Ch 11).

Ownership — treating a task as if your reputation depends on it, including knowing when to ask for help (Ch 8).

Path of least regret — choose the option best for the long term, not the one that relieves discomfort fastest (Ch 14).

Pattern of behavior — your "whenever… always…" reputation; managed by being predictable (Ch 9).

People / Position / Place — the three root sources of a conflict; diagnose which before acting (Ch 14).

Perceived vs. actual — managers judge the perceived version of your work (visible progress, confidence), not just the actual output (Ch 1).

Performance vs. potential — effectiveness in your current job vs. ability to do the next one / lead (Ch 15).

Pre-day-one research (15 strategies) — a ~45-minute prep routine to "see the big picture" before any role, call, or meeting (Ch 3).

Preread / prework — materials circulated before a meeting; mining them yields your one comment + one question (Ch 12).

Promotable tasks — visible, valued work that advances your career; seek these over office housework (Ch 9).

Puddle (locality) — the scope of a problem: small, medium, or large; sets how far you must go to escape it (Ch 14).

RACI — Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed: clarify roles on any task (Ch 8).

Reject / embrace / bend the rules — three stances when your appearance doesn't "fit" the norm (Ch 6).

Sacred / negotiable / indifferent zones — three concentric circles for sorting which identity elements to protect, weigh, or give up (Ch 6).

Seen and heard / seen but not heard / neither — the three roles you can hold in a meeting; calibrate by size, attendees, topic (Ch 12).

Skip manager — your boss's boss (Ch 10).

Swimlane — what a person owns and when, regardless of their title (Ch 10, Ch 15).

Subtle hints — indirect + verbal feedback: softened, diluted messages (Ch 13).

Ten-ten-ten (10-10-10) — strip emotion from a decision by asking how each option feels in 10 minutes / 10 months / 10 years (Ch 14).

Three Cs — competence, commitment, compatibility; the book's central lens, needed all at once (Ch 1).

Three circles of question quality — what you know / what's figure-out-able / what's only learnable by asking; ask only from the outer circle (Ch 3).

Thought partner vs. workhorse — perceived as someone who grasps the big picture vs. someone who just executes (Ch 3).

Transferable skills — capabilities from a past role bridged explicitly to the new one (Ch 5).

Trade-off triangle (people/position/place) — you rarely get all three good at once; know which you're trading (Ch 14).

Uncensored comments — direct + verbal feedback: blunt, unsoftened criticism (Ch 13).

Undershooting vs. overshooting — each C fails in two directions: too little (clueless/apathetic) or too much (overbearing/poser) (Ch 1, Ch 5).

Unoccupied swimlane — an unclaimed but valuable need you can own to show potential (Ch 15).

Uptalking — rising intonation at the end of statements that undercuts perceived confidence (Ch 5).

Voluntelling — a higher-up framing an assigned task as if it were optional (Ch 4).

Virtuous circle — early relationships and opportunities compound into more of both (Ch 11).

What / how / by when — the three things to clarify the moment you receive any task (Ch 8).

"Why?" exercise — repeatedly asking "why is this happening?" to drill from symptom to root cause (Ch 9, Ch 14).

Zone of commitment — the scope you're authorized to act within; overshooting it reads as threatening (Ch 10).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — The Unspoken Rules

Concrete, repeatable methods from the book. Each: when to use, how, trade-offs.

The Three Cs

When: As a diagnostic lens on any workplace move, message, or decision.

How: Before acting, check that you're showing all three at once — Competence (do the job fully/accurately/promptly), Commitment (be present and eager for the team's goals), Compatibility (make others comfortable). For each, avoid undershooting (too little → clueless/apathetic) and overshooting (too much → overbearing/poser).

Trade-offs: Optimizing one C can dent another (e.g. over-asserting competence can hurt compatibility); balance, don't maximize.

"Let's Give This a Shot" + Curiosity vs. Entitlement Test

When: Facing an opportunity you might fail at, or unsure whether to ask for something.

How: Ask "what's the worst that can happen?" (usually a "no"). Then run the entitlement test: imagine the "no" — proceed only if your honest reaction is "just thought I'd ask," not outrage. Then act and let others say no.

Trade-offs: Some people need to be less entitled (got an unearned edge), some more (habitually wait for permission). Calibrate to which you are.

Pre-Day-One Research (15 strategies)

When: Before any new role, first call, big meeting, or interview.

How: ~45 min of higher-priority moves — skim Wikipedia/company About + News, recent Google news, memorize key faces, LinkedIn the people CC'd, confirm dress code + logistics (arrive 15 min early), set a Google Alert, accept intro chats — plus lower-priority depth (competitors, Glassdoor/Reddit, "anyone else I should speak with?"). Goal: see the big picture and fill "the eight blanks."

Trade-offs: Time-box it; research is prep, not a substitute for showing up and asking good questions.

Three Circles of Question Quality + "Do — and Show — Your Homework"

When: Before asking anything as a newcomer.

How: Sort the question — inner circle (you already know) / middle (figure-out-able → don't ask) / outer (only learnable by asking → ask). When you ask, narrate your work: "Here's what I know, here's what I don't" or "Here's my question and why I'm asking."

Trade-offs: Asking good questions early earns credit that buys leeway for naive questions later.

Twelve "Yes!" Onboarding Questions + Find Your Job

When: Starting a role, especially with weak onboarding.

How: Self-check you can answer "Yes!" to all twelve (paperwork, reporting lines, role expectations, check-in cadence, intros, priorities, tools/access, routine…). Where the answer is "no," ask the scripted question. If given tasks but no real role: observe & take notes, ask & learn, volunteer for work.

Trade-offs: Think like an owner — the gaps are yours to close even when no one hands you a map.

Tell Your Story: Internal vs. External Narrative (5 steps) + Mental Fridge

When: Any "tell me about yourself / why are you here" moment.

How: Build the internal narrative (your real why), then the external one (audience-tailored, proves the Three Cs), add structure (Past/Present/Future hero's journey), finesse style (no uptalking/overshooting), and practice. Stock a "mental fridge" of talking-point ingredients to answer the unexpected.

Trade-offs: Lead external, not internal — the "me, me, me" version reads as self-absorbed.

Manage Appearance: Mirror, then Reject/Embrace/Bend + Sacred/Negotiable/Indifferent

When: Deciding how much to conform your look/identity to a workplace.

How: Infer the unspoken norm by mirroring coworkers at your level (default more formal when unsure). Choose to reject, embrace, or bend (conform first, reveal authentic self after building trust). Sort each element into sacred (protect), negotiable (weigh), indifferent (give away freely).

Trade-offs: Over-adapting wastes energy on things coworkers never noticed; protect what's sacred.

Send the Right Signals: Five Questions Before Send + Intent vs. Impact

When: Before sending any message; calibrating remote/written presence.

How: Before send, check — typos? caught up on the thread? right time? tone matches intent? OK if forwarded? Match the team's email-first vs. IM-first culture, and its monochronic (time = blocks) vs. polychronic (time = fluid) rhythm.

Trade-offs: You're judged on impact, not intent; permanent digital signals mean over-clarify rather than assume.

Take Ownership: What/How/By When + RACI + Give Others Something to React To

When: The moment you receive any task.

How: Clarify what, how, by when immediately; map RACI (who's Responsible/Accountable/Consulted/Informed); work backward from the deadline with interim check-ins. For non-urgent questions: search first, bundle them, escalate one rung with context. When stuck, propose option A/B with a recommendation instead of asking an open "what do you think?"

Trade-offs: Repeating the task back feels redundant but catches costly misunderstandings early.

Manage Workload: Urgency × Importance Triage

When: Too much to do; deciding order.

How: Score urgency by four factors (proximity, scrutiny, anxiety, time-sensitivity) and importance by three (centrality, scrutiny, criticality). Triage on the adapted Eisenhower Matrix: do / schedule / timebox-or-delegate / delete. Preempt predictable patterns (Friday updates, post-holiday clearing, templates) and report problems at root cause via the "Why?" exercise.

Trade-offs: Seek promotable work over office housework; under-promise and over-deliver to avoid surprises.

Read between the People (5 steps) + Five Influencer Types

When: Joining any new team.

How: Map (1) the chain of command, (2) the influencers, (3) swimlanes, (4) loyalties, (5) comfort zones — by observing behavior and language, not titles. Spot the five influencer types (Gatekeepers, Veterans, Experts, Socialites, Advisers) by who decisions route through. Gauge swimlane rigidity on the ask-permission ↔ beg-forgiveness spectrum.

Trade-offs: Friendly ≠ loyal; don't mistake an early ally's warmth for first loyalty.

Spark Relationships: Spark → Play → Sustain + Bids + EAR

When: Building a network from zero.

How: Respond to others' bids for connection; keep conversation flowing with EAR (Engage, Ask, Repeat) and "Yes, and…"; tailor the first move to the audience (casual chat / double opt-in intro / customized cold email); sustain ties over time. Be an energy giver.

Trade-offs: Relationships compound (virtuous circle) — small early investment pays outsized later returns.

Master Meetings: Seven Questions + Three Roles + One Comment + One Question

When: Before, during, and after any meeting.

How: Run the seven prep/participation/follow-up questions, scaling depth to the meeting's importance. Calibrate your role — seen and heard / seen but not heard / neither — by size, attendees, and topic. With prep time, mine the preread for one thoughtful comment + one thoughtful question (what's missing/confusing/wrong/unexpected).

Trade-offs: Every meeting has a hidden goal and two unspoken duties — to learn and to represent your team.

Manage Feedback: The Feedback Ranges + Intent Behind Impact + Feedback Meeting

When: Receiving or soliciting feedback.

How: Locate the feedback on two axes (verbal↔nonverbal, direct↔indirect) → subtle hints / uncensored comments / behavior changes / blunt actions. Separate substance (what they mean) from delivery (how they said it). In a feedback meeting, ask "what should I start / stop / keep doing?", apply fast, and report back.

Trade-offs: Negativity bias makes criticism sting; coachability (visibly applying it) is itself a signal of commitment.

Resolve Conflicts: Fix it / Live with it / Leave it

When: Any persistently bad work situation.

How: Diagnose root cause via People / Position / Place (and the "Why?" exercise). Strip emotion with 10-10-10 (how does each option feel in 10 min / 10 months / 10 years). Then fix it tactfully, live with it, or leave graciously — choosing the path of least regret. Use the leave-it ten-question test when weighing quitting.

Trade-offs: The people/position/place trade-off triangle means you rarely fix all three; your last impression matters as much as your first.

Show Your Potential: Nine-Box + Unoccupied Swimlane + Ask-for-It

When: Positioning for a raise or promotion.

How: Aim for the top-right of the performance × potential nine-box (do your job well and show you can do the next one). Claim an unoccupied swimlane via the five questions (what can I do / fix / bridge / know / share?). Prioritize contributions that are noticed and reported, and that are better (not just different). To ask for a raise: bring data, a one-pager, a specific number, and appreciation.

Trade-offs: Different-but-unnoticed work doesn't count; aim for better-and-visible on a mission-critical problem.

Cheatsheet — The Big Book of NLP

Decision-ready rules. Pick the right pattern, apply it the way Vaknin would. Keep beside you while working.
