Core decision rules

  • Before any change, run an ecology check. Unaddressed secondary gain or system impact silently sabotages the result. (Ch 1, Ch 2)
  • Resistance = lack of rapport. If you meet resistance, stop pushing and rebuild rapport. (Presupposition #16, Ch 3)
  • The meaning of your communication is the response you get — calibrate to the response, not your intention. (Presupposition #12)
  • Change at the highest relevant logical level. A problem felt at Identity won't yield to a Behavior fix; a behavior issue doesn't need an identity overhaul. (Ch 12)
  • Find the positive intention before removing any behavior or belief — removal without it relapses or leaves a void. (Ch 6, Ch 7)
  • Edit the driver submodality, not the content. The charge lives in size/brightness/location/light — find that knob first. (Ch 5, Ch 8)
  • Pace before you lead — match the person's world (3 verifiable facts / their physiology / their values), then move them. (Ch 3, Ch 10)
  • Chunk UP for agreement, DOWN for solutions. Vague is undisputed; specific is actionable. (Ch 9)
  • Phrase suggestions positively — the mind can't process a negation ("non-smoker" cues smoking). (Ch 10, Ch 12)
  • Anchor at the PEAK with a unique, dedicated trigger — peak + purity + uniqueness = the strongest anchor. (Ch 4)
  • Accept and use whatever happens (utilization) — interruptions, resistance, and odd responses are raw material, not derailment. (Ch 1, Ch 10)

The 21 Presuppositions — the decisive ones for change-work

  • #8 Every behavior has utility in some context → look for the gift inside the problem.
  • #12 The meaning of communication is the response you get → own the outcome.
  • #14 There is no failure, only feedback → mine every miss.
  • #15 The most flexible element controls the system → expand your choices.
  • #16 Resistance signals lack of rapport → back up and reconnect.
  • #17 People have the internal resources they need → your job is to direct, not supply.

Meta-Model quick reference (recover the deleted/distorted)

Hear thisViolationAsk
"never / always / everyone"Universal Quantifier"Never? Not once?"
"I can't / I must"Modal Operator"What stops you?" / "What if you did?"
"they / people / it" (vague)Lack of Referential Index"Who, specifically?"
"the relationship / my fear"NominalizationTurn it back into a verb — "relating how?"
"she makes me angry"Cause–Effect"How does what she does cause your anger?"
"I know he doesn't care"Mind Reading"How do you know?"
"It's wrong to…"Lost Performative"According to whom?"

Safety & ethics tells

  • Refer clinical cases (phobia, trauma, addiction, severe grief) to licensed professionals — NLP is not a treatment substitute. (Ch 8, Ch 13)
  • "Poor participant" is often a brain shutdown, not stubbornness — Think Physiology and consider referral. (Ch 13)
  • All communication should increase choice (Presupposition #19) — use Milton patterns to expand options, never to coerce. (Ch 10)
  • Stay the formal authority, one outcome at a time — don't befriend early or work 10 issues at once. (Ch 1)

glossary.md

Glossary — The Big Book of NLP

Key terms with definitions, alphabetical. Chapter references in parentheses.

Alternating bilateral stimulus — Side-to-side eye movement, sound, or touch that triggers the reprocessing state shift (Ch 13).

Anchor — A stimulus conditioned to trigger a particular state; learned, not innate. Firing an anchor activates the state (Ch 4).

Associated — Experiencing from inside your own eyes (1st position) with full felt charge; opposite of dissociated (Ch 5, Ch 8).

Calibration — Linking an observed behavioral cue to a person's internal cognitive/emotional state (Ch 3).

Characterological Adjective (CA) — A single word naming a relationship role; implies its counterpart (victim↔victimizer) (Ch 13).

Chunking up / down — Moving to more abstract/general (up) or more specific/concrete (down) levels; up wins agreement, down enables solutions (Ch 9).

Congruence — Alignment of words, tone, body, and outcomes; root of charisma and effective change (Ch 1, Ch 12).

Conversational (covert) hypnosis — Producing trance through ordinary-seeming talk with no formal induction (Ch 10).

Core state — The centered, expanded peace reached by chaining outcomes inward (Ch 6).

Criteria — Values that drive decisions; ranked in a hierarchy where higher override lower (Ch 7, Ch 11).

Deep structure — The fuller internal experience that words derive from; what the Meta-Model recovers (Ch 9).

Dissociation — Observing yourself from outside (3rd/meta position) with little felt charge (Ch 5, Ch 8).

Double bind — A choice between two options that both fulfill the same presupposition/outcome (Ch 10).

Double dissociation — Two layers of separation (watching yourself watch a movie, from the projection booth); for highly triggering memories (Ch 8).

Downtime — A light internal trance with awareness turned fully inward; uptime is outward awareness informed by inner awareness (Ch 4, Ch 10).

Driver (driving/critical) submodality — The submodality whose change most shifts a state's intensity; the highest-leverage edit point. Find it first (Ch 5, Ch 8).

Ecology / Ecology check — The systemic impact of a change across the whole person/system; verifying no part or life area objects before locking in a change (Ch 1, Ch 2, Ch 6).

Embedded command — A directive inserted and marked out (via tone/tempo/gesture) inside a larger sentence or question (Ch 10).

Evidence procedure — How a person knows an outcome has been achieved (Ch 2, Ch 11).

Extinction — Decay of an anchor from overuse or staleness (Ch 4).

Frame — The boundary on what you consider; "the one who sets the frame controls the action." A reframe changes it (Ch 6, Ch 1).

Imprint / Re-imprinting — A belief installed during a developmental window (imprint); returning to that source to supply missing resources rewrites it (re-imprinting) (Ch 7).

Law of Reversed Effect — The harder one consciously tries, the harder the result becomes; demands indirect suggestion (Ch 10).

Law of Requisite Variety — "Only variety can destroy variety"; more options/positions weaken a rigid belief and increase influence (Ch 7, Ch 1).

Limiting belief — A non-resourceful generalization that blocks goals; treated as loosenable structure, not truth (Ch 7).

Logical Levels — Dilts's hierarchy: Environment, Behavior, Capability, Beliefs/Values, Identity, Spirit/Purpose; higher levels organize lower (Ch 12).

Map vs. territory — Your internal model is never the reality it represents; always improvable (Ch 1).

Matrixing — Strategic case planning across four categories: Meaning, Context, Behavior, Physiology (Ch 13).

Meta-program — A context-dependent, continuum-based tendency in how attention is sorted (toward/away, etc.); never a fixed label (Ch 11).

Meta-position — A dissociated observer stance above a conflict, used to negotiate (Ch 6, Ch 8).

Meta-state — A layered meaning/value stacked on top of another state (Ch 12).

Milton-Model — Artful, deliberately vague language (Meta-Model violations on purpose) to induce trance and bypass conscious resistance; inverse of the Meta-Model (Ch 10).

Modal operator — The word (must/can't/should/could) revealing a mode of necessity, possibility, or impossibility (Ch 9).

Modeling — Extracting another's strategy or state of excellence so it can be reproduced (Ch 11).

Nominalization — A process/verb frozen into a static noun (relationship, fear); fails the "put it in a wheelbarrow" test (Ch 9).

Pacing and leading — Match the person's verifiable experience first (pace), then shift your state to move theirs (lead) (Ch 3, Ch 10).

Part — A largely subconscious cluster of motives/attitudes acting like a sub-personality (Ch 2, Ch 6).

Perceptual positions — 1st (self/associated), 2nd (the other's shoes), 3rd (detached observer/meta) (Ch 6, Ch 8).

Positive intention — The constructive purpose underlying even a harmful behavior; respond to it, not the symptom (Ch 2, Ch 6).

Presupposition — A useful operating belief acted on without proof; the 21 NLP presuppositions are NLP's core beliefs (Ch 1).

Priming — Triggering a state conducive to a way of thinking or acting; broader and vaguer than a command (Ch 10, Ch 13).

Reframe — Changing the frame for a better outcome: content (what it means) or context (where it fits) (Ch 6).

Rep systems (representational systems) — Channels through which experience is coded: Visual, Auditory, Kinesthetic, plus auditory-digital/olfactory-gustatory (Ch 1, Ch 4).

Reprocessing — Re-encoding a poorly stored overwhelming experience so it integrates and symptoms resolve; shared mechanism behind EMDR, EFT, Time Line Therapy, and the NLP phobia cure (Ch 13).

SCORE — Symptom / Cause / Outcome / Resource / Effect; a framework for shaping any problem (Ch 8).

Secondary gain — A hidden benefit a problem behavior delivers that sabotages change until addressed (Ch 1, Ch 2, Ch 6).

Self-sabotage — A negative pattern sustained by a hidden payoff; addressed via its positive intention (Ch 12).

Sensory acuity — Trained ability to notice involuntary micro-changes (skin color, muscle tone, breathing, pupils) (Ch 1, Ch 3).

Somatic / bottom-up — Changing thought by working through body, state, and nervous system rather than cognition (Ch 13).

State — The combined mind-body condition at a given moment; functional or dysfunctional (Ch 4).

Strategy — An ordered sequence (syntax) of internal representations that produces a result; e.g. spelling = visual recall then kinesthetic check (Ch 11).

Submodality — A quality within a sense (visual: size, brightness, color, distance, location, movie-vs-still; auditory: volume, pitch; kinesthetic: location, temperature) (Ch 5).

Surface structure — The spoken words; a compressed, deleted/distorted/generalized output of the deep structure (Ch 9).

Swish — The signature submodality pattern: a big/bright associated trigger image is rapidly swapped for a small/dim dissociated desired-self image (Ch 5).

Thought virus — A toxic, self-propagating belief (Dilts); inoculated against and quarantined (Ch 7).

Time Line Therapy — Processing memory along the timeline via Source Event, Echo Events, and Future Success (Tad James) (Ch 13).

TOTE — Test–Operate–Test–Exit; the feedback loop inside every strategy (Ch 11).

Transderivational search (TDS) — The mind's fuzzy hunt for meaning in vague input; itself produces brief trance (Ch 10).

Trance — A focused, inward, suggestible state; can be light and momentary (Ch 10).

Universal quantifier — Totalizing words (never/always/everyone) signaling over-generalization (Ch 9).

Utilization — Accepting and turning whatever the person presents — even a symptom or resistance — into a resource (Ch 1, Ch 10).

V-K dissociation — Changing a memory's visual viewpoint to break its kinesthetic (felt) charge; engine of the Phobia Cure (Ch 8).

Values hierarchy — Your most important values, ranked, giving higher-level decision direction (Ch 11).

Well-formed (well-defined) outcome — A goal that is positive, specific, self-actionable, context-bound, sensory-rich, and ecological (Ch 2).

patterns.md

Patterns Catalog — The Big Book of NLP

Concrete techniques, when to use them, how, and trade-offs. Grouped by theme. For full steps and worked examples, open the linked chapter.

Outcomes, Feedback & Ecology (Ch 2)

Well-Defined Outcomes

When: Starting any goal or change, before spending resources. How: State it positive → ability-framed → contextualized → in the senses → chunked → resourced → ecology-checked → milestoned → written → tested. Trade-off: Over-specifying can cause analysis paralysis.

Failure Into Feedback

When: A belief makes you feel defeated about a capability or goal. How: Sort the failure's VAK into eye positions, build the goal image up-right, normalize the memories, anchor a positive reference and fire it at the goal. Trade-off: Needs comfort with eye-position/submodality work.

Ecology Check

When: Before committing to any change. How: Dissociate to 3rd position; ask who benefits/is hurt, short- and long-term; use Cartesian questions ("What would happen if you did / didn't?"). Trade-off: Skipping it invites self-sabotage.

Finding Positive Intention / Secondary Gain

When: Self-sabotage or a stalled change. How: Address the part; ask what it wanted to accomplish; recycle answers up to the core value. Trade-off: Relies on accepting the "parts" frame; hidden gains rationalize away easily.

Rapport, Pacing & Mirroring (Ch 3)

Pacing and Matching / Mirroring

When: Building rapport, sales, coaching, modeling. How: Subtly match cadence, predicates, posture, breathing; then test by leading. Trade-off: Obvious imitation breaks rapport and offends.

Satir Category Rapport-Building

When: Pacing a difficult communicator (Blamer, Placater, Computer, Distracter, Leveler). How: Pace each style without triggering its defense, then lead; default to Leveler (congruent, factual) if unsure. Trade-off: Styles are situational, not fixed labels.

When NOT to Mirror

When: Aggression, suffering, or intense-need states. How: Use same-team posture; mirror only general comforting cues. Trade-off: Mirroring distress induces overwhelm.

States & Anchoring (Ch 4)

Anchoring / Self Anchoring

When: You want a resource state on demand. How: Pick a unique trigger, elicit the state strongly, set the anchor at the PEAK, test. Trade-off: Anchors decay if reused or unreinforced.

Collapsing Anchors

When: A situation triggers an unwanted state. How: Anchor the negative and a stronger positive; fire both; release the negative first; test. Trade-off: Needs the positive clearly stronger.

Chaining States / Circle of Excellence

When: A target state is too far to reach in one jump (chaining); or you want a peak state at will (Circle). How: Bridge through intermediate anchored steps; or load a stepped-into spatial circle with the state and future-pace. Trade-off: Tedious; the spatial cue must stay dedicated.

Physiomental State Interruption

When: A stuck/dysfunctional state won't shift. How: Exaggerate its driving submodality to absurdity; test. Trade-off: Fails if you target the wrong submodality.

Submodalities & the Swish (Ch 5)

The Swish

When: An unwanted habit with a clear trigger. How: Big/bright associated trigger image ↔ small/dim dissociated desired-self image; swap fast with a whoosh; repeat 5–7× with break states; test. Trade-off: Needs a real trigger; generalizes only when aimed at a self-image, not a behavior.

Godiva Chocolate

When: Low motivation for a worthwhile behavior. How: Hide a craving image behind the behavior image; open/shrink a hole 3+ times. Trade-off: Requires ecology check; over-talking kills it.

Compulsion Blow-Out / Spinning Icons

When: A compulsion or recurring negative state. How: Overdrive its two strongest submodalities (or orbit negative + antidote icons) to extreme until boring/blended; break state. Trade-off: Refer clinical cases; start with weak states.

Reframing & Parts Work (Ch 6)

Six Step Reframe

When: A habit you "can't stop." How: Signal the part → elicit its positive intention → creative part makes 3 alternatives → part accepts → future-pace + ecology. Trade-off: Needs a cooperative unconscious signal.

Content / Context Reframing

When: A limiting interpretation (content), or a behavior bad only in some settings (context). How: "What else could this mean?" / "Where would this serve you?" Trade-off: Can feel like denial if facts are ignored.

Parts Negotiation / Advanced Visual Squash

When: Two parts at war. How: Elicit each part's outcome and meta-outcome; broker a non-interference treaty (negotiation), or merge a part in each hand after sharing resources (squash). Trade-off: Needs honest meta-outcomes; abstract if parts won't image.

Beliefs & Belief Change (Ch 7)

Re-Imprinting

When: A deeply imprinted childhood belief or symptom. How: Float to the source imprint; give the past self and role models the missing resources; rewrite forward. Trade-off: Heavyweight; overkill for small issues.

Belief Chaining (Basic / Advanced) & Belief Out-Framing

When: Shift a belief from un-resourceful to resourceful. How: Walk spatial steps with reframes; or view the belief from a 3×3 grid (Past/Present/Future × Self/Other/Observer) and gather alternatives. Trade-off: Advanced versions need a partner/guide.

Hierarchy of Criteria

When: Procrastination from a values conflict. How: Tie the stalled behavior to a higher Identity-level criterion. Trade-off: Requires a grasp of logical levels.

Phobias, Trauma & Emotional Healing (Ch 8)

Phobia Cure (Fast Phobia / V-K Dissociation)

When: An irrational fear or single-event trauma. How: Double dissociation; watch a black-and-white movie from the projection booth; then run it backward fast in color, associated; repeat; test. Trade-off: Can re-traumatize — refer clinical cases to professionals.

Change Personal History

When: Recurring button-pushing memories. How: Set an exit cue, chain to the earliest instance, collapse adult-resource anchors onto the memories. Trade-off: Needs flexible real-time adaptation.

SCORE / Dancing SCORE

When: A stuck multi-faceted problem. How: Gather Symptom/Cause/Outcome/Resource/Effect (statically, or spatially with movement); loop effects as feedback; add the missing resource. Trade-off: Analytical; needs space/privacy for the Dancing version.

The Meta-Model: Precision Language (Ch 9)

Meta-Model Challenging

When: Gathering accurate information or loosening a limiting belief. How: Map the words to a sensory representation; spot the deletion/distortion/generalization; ask the recovery question; test back. Trade-off: Over-use feels like interrogation and breaks rapport — use softeners.

De-Nominalizing

When: Someone is stuck/disempowered by a "thing" (a nominalization). How: Find the frozen process; turn the noun back into a verb with an actor in the driver's seat. Trade-off: Dissolves the easy agreement that vague nouns create.

Persuasion by Chunking Up / Down

When: Negotiating (up) vs problem-solving (down). How: Chunk up to vague generalities for agreement; chunk down to specifics to solve. Trade-off: Chunking up is near-hypnotic — wrong for solving.

The Milton-Model & Conversational Hypnosis (Ch 10)

Pace–Link–Lead

When: Inducing light trance in conversation. How: State 3 verifiable facts, join with "and/as," then lead with a suggestion. Trade-off: Needs genuine rapport or feels manipulative.

Embedded Commands / Double Binds

When: Implanting a directive past resistance, or increasing cooperation. How: Mark a short command inside a quote/question with intonation; or offer two choices that both serve the same presupposition. Trade-off: Over-marking becomes obvious; sophisticated listeners spot the non-choice.

Nested Loops

When: Delivering suggestions inside story. How: Open 5 stories, embed the suggestion in #5, close 5→1 in reverse. Trade-off: Requires skill and engaging stories; long.

Strategies, Meta-Programs & Modeling (Ch 11)

Spelling Strategy

When: Poor spelling or rote recall. How: View the word up-left from a calm anchored state; write it from the image; write it backward; loop. Trade-off: Visual-heavy; resists non-visual learners.

Walt Disney Strategy

When: Developing a plan or idea. How: Anchor Dreamer, Realist, and Critic in three separate spots; cycle through them; the Critic asks questions, not attacks. Trade-off: Needs space and discipline to keep states clean.

2nd / 3rd Position Modeling

When: Copying someone's excellence. How: Take 2nd position for the feel, 3rd position for the structure/syntax; extract the strategy and state. Trade-off: Self-report can be inaccurate; needs practiced observation.

Self, Identity & Logical Levels (Ch 12)

Logical Levels Alignment / Co-Alignment

When: Reclaiming direction on a goal (self) or aligning a team. How: Walk the issue through all six levels; build bottom-up carrying each state upward; find overlaps and integrate down. Trade-off: Slow; needs group buy-in for teams.

Loving Yourself / Inner Hero / Assertiveness Installation

When: Low self-worth, acting-out, or passivity. How: See yourself through a loving person's 2nd position and anchor the state; or pace the person's highest identity-level values, then lead; build a state + boundary "force-field." Trade-off: Fails if recognition is artificial; needs a genuinely safe model figure.

Advanced & Newly Introduced Tools (Ch 13)

Reprocessing

When: Trauma, anxiety, or intrusive symptoms. How: Target the memory → state shift via alternating bilateral stimulus → optional cognitive work → body scan / future pace → recovery. Trade-off: Needs training/supervision; refer severe trauma.

Matrixing

When: A complex, multi-issue ("twilight"/subclinical) client. How: Mind-map across Meaning, Context, Behavior, Physiology into actionable items. Trade-off: Requires psychopathology knowledge; slower than single techniques.

Vision Communication Protocol

When: One partner overwhelms the other in relationship talks. How: Single issue → vision → values → steps → one tiny ask, framed in the partner's language. Trade-off: Only for functional relationships; can suppress serious issues if misused.

Smart Eating Pattern

When: Stress eating vs real hunger. How: Felt-sense hunger check → imagine eating → contrast → future-pace. Trade-off: Relies on honest interoception.

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Think Like a Rocket Scientist

Decision rules and tells for reasoning under uncertainty, generating ideas, testing them, and learning from outcomes.

If / Then decision rules

If you're…Then…
Paralyzed by a scary leapName the worst and best case in writing; turn unknown unknowns into known unknowns
Justifying something only with "we've always done it this way"You've found an invisible rule — question it; the best way to expose a rule is to violate it
Copying a competitor's playbookStop — you're in a "smartness contest with everyone who came before"; reason from first principles or invert
Stuck on HOW to solve itQuestion the WHAT — reframe the problem; ask "What problem is this tactic here to solve?"
In love with your first solutionBreed multiple conflicting hypotheses; you're probably solving the wrong problem
BrainstormingDiverge first (be the fly, "What could we do?"), converge second (be the bee) — never reverse the order
Aiming for 10% improvementAim 10x instead — force a new approach, not an incremental tweak
Starting an audacious projectDo the monkey first (hardest part); set kill metrics now, while clearheaded
About to trust a test that "passed"Test to fail — hunt the breaking point; exaggerate the flaw you found
Feeling the dopamine of being proven rightTry to prove yourself wrong — every "no" carries more information than a "yes"
On a winning streakAssume you're slightly behind; run a postmortem on the success
About to act on a big decisionRun a premortem — assume it failed, list why, assign probabilities
Relying on a safety net (redundancy, deadline extension, ABS)Pretend it isn't there (risk homeostasis)

Idea generation (separate from judgment)

  • Generate before you evaluate. Idea generation and idea evaluation are different modes — don't let "we've tried that / no budget / won't be approved" kill ideas before generation finishes.
  • Be the fly, not the bee: flutter freely first; the bee dies bumping the light.
  • Ask "What would a science-fiction solution look like?" and "What could we do?" (not "should").
  • Compare apples and oranges — collect diverse inputs, then connect them.
  • Get bored on purpose — the answer arrives when you walk away.

Tells of the certainty trap (Ch 1)

  • You're "looking for keys under the street lamp" — choosing the familiar/safe because that's where the light is.
  • You're forcing a definite conclusion onto genuinely ambiguous evidence.
  • You feel a story clicking into place (narrative fills the vacuum of understanding).
  • You're ignoring the anomaly that doesn't fit ("That's funny…" is the entrance to discovery — don't discard it).
  • Antidote: say "I don't know"; be "uncomfortably uncertain over comfortably wrong."

Tells of the success trap (Ch 9)

  • "We got away with it last time, so we can lower the standard a bit" (normalization of deviance).
  • A recurring flaw has quietly become an "acceptable risk."
  • You're calling something "routine"; you've stopped running postmortems.
  • Near misses feel like wins — you treat "no harm" as "no foul."
  • Dissenters are being branded downers; the burden has shifted to prove danger rather than prove safety.
  • Antidote: stay in "Day 1"; treat yourself as a permanent work in progress; fix the cause behind the cause.

Testing (test as you fly)

  • Make the test mirror flight; then fly as you tested. Any gap can be catastrophic.
  • Test the assembled system, not just the parts ("understand the 'and'"); retest the whole after any change.
  • Observe behavior, don't self-report — put the iPhone in their hands; watch people grimace.
  • Diversify testing instruments and calibration targets — never rely on one.

Failure (learn fast, not fail fast)

  • Ask both "What went wrong?" and "What went right?" — keep the good inputs (Amazon's Fire → other tech; failed angina drug → Viagra).
  • Judge inputs, not outputs — avoid "resulting" (a good decision can produce a bad outcome).
  • Reward excellent failures, punish mediocre successes.
  • Leaders advertise their own failures to build psychological safety.
  • A single failure ≠ final defeat; breakthroughs are evolutionary ("solve one problem, then the next").

The three stages (map)

StageMoveCore principles
LaunchIgnite thinkingDance with uncertainty · first principles · a mind at play · moonshots
AcceleratePropel ideasReframe the question · prove yourself wrong · test as you fly
AchieveLearn from outcomesIntelligent failure · guard against the success trap

glossary.md

Glossary — Think Like a Rocket Scientist

Antelopes vs. mice — Go after the big prize, not the sure small one; a lion burns more energy catching a mouse than it yields, while an antelope feeds it for days (Ch 4).

Backcasting — Starting from an imagined future and working backward to the steps, letting vision drive resources instead of forecasting forward from current resources (Ch 4).

Beginner's mind (shoshin) — Approaching a problem as an outsider with no stake in the status quo; "in the beginner's mind there are many possibilities; in the expert's mind there are few" (Ch 3).

Breaking point (test to fail) — Designing tests for the worst case to find where a thing breaks, before reality breaks it; exaggerate a flaw rather than dismiss it as an outlier (Ch 7).

Certainty fetish / certainty trap — The compulsion to make ambiguous things appear definite, leading us to "look for keys under the street lamp" (Ch 1).

Combinatory play — Recombining ideas from unrelated fields ("compare apples and oranges"); "to create is to recombine" (Ch 3).

Confirmation bias — Overvaluing evidence that confirms our beliefs and undervaluing what contradicts them; coined by Peter Wason (Ch 6).

Connoisseur of uncertainty — Someone exhilarated rather than frightened at the edge of the known; they "dance" in the dark room (Ch 1).

Convergent thinking (the bee) — Narrowing to the seemingly obvious solution; useful for evaluation but deadly if used first (the bees die bumping the light) (Ch 4).

Dance with uncertainty — Treating the unknown as friend not foe; "first chaos, then breakthrough" (Ch 1).

Divergent thinking (the fly) — Free, open-ended idea generation without judging constraints; the flies find the exit by fluttering (Ch 4).

Einstellung effect — A fixed mental set: once a familiar solution is known, we stop seeing better alternatives (Ch 5).

Falsifiability — A hypothesis has value only if it can be proven wrong (Popper); separates science from pseudoscience (Ch 6).

Family of hypotheses — Generating multiple, ideally conflicting, working hypotheses so you can't fall in love with one (Ch 6).

First-principles thinking — Stripping a problem to its irreducible fundamentals and reasoning up from there, instead of by analogy (Ch 2).

Flip-flopping (as a virtue) — Changing your mind when the facts change; "I'd rather be right than consistent" (Ch 6).

Frankenstein's monster / Frankenstate — Individually benign components turning catastrophic in combination; why you must test the assembled system ("understand the 'and'") (Ch 7).

Functional fixedness — A mental block against using an object in a new way (Duncker's candle-box problem); dissolved by seeing form over function (Ch 5).

How fascinating! — A curiosity ritual that strips the drama out of a failure and creates emotional distance (Ch 8).

Intelligent failure — A failure from exploring the edges and solving unsolved problems; an investment and teacher, unlike sloppy failure (Ch 8).

Inputs over outputs — Judging decisions by their quality, not by outcomes you don't fully control; avoids "resulting" (Ch 8).

Invisible rules — Habits that have rigidified into rules without anyone deciding they should ("tie the cat to the pole") (Ch 2).

Inversion ("What if we did the reverse?") — Flipping a question or best practice on its head; "invert, always invert" (Ch 5).

It remains Day 1 — Treating every success as a fresh start; "Day 2 is stasis… followed by decline" (Bezos) (Epilogue).

Kill metrics — Predefined go/no-go criteria set while clearheaded, so you can quit a moonshot before sunk cost distorts judgment (Ch 4).

Kill-the-company / red teaming — Playing the antagonist trying to destroy you, then switching back to defend the weak points (Ch 2).

Learn fast, not fail fast — The goal is the lesson, not the crash; celebrate the learning, never failure itself (Ch 8).

Margins of safety — Building stronger/thicker than the minimum required, sized to the stakes and the irreversibility of the decision (Ch 1).

Medici effect — The creative explosion when people from different disciplines are combined (Ch 3).

Monkey first — Tackling the hardest, riskiest part of a project before the easy "pedestal" work (Ch 4).

Moonshot (10x not 10%) — An audacious goal so big the status quo has to go, forcing first-principles solutions (Ch 4).

Near miss — An incident that could have been a hit; masquerades as success because luck held, and breeds complacency rather than urgency (Ch 9).

Normalization of deviance — Repeated success with a known flaw turning an anomaly into an "acceptable risk" (O-rings, foam-shedding) (Ch 9).

Occam's razor — Given two hypotheses that explain the data equally well, prefer the simpler — a guiding principle, not an absolute rule ("seek simplicity and distrust it") (Ch 2).

Observer effect — Being watched changes behavior; mitigate with double-blind tests and real-world observation (Ch 7).

Path dependence — What we've done before shapes what we do next (the shuttle's engine width traced to Roman roads) (Ch 2).

Permanent work in progress — Never declaring a project or yourself finished or "routine"; train like you're #2 (Ch 9).

Premortem — Before acting, assuming the project failed and working backward to why; the inverse of backcasting; assign probabilities (Ch 9).

Problem finding (reframe the question) — Searching for a better question instead of a better answer; "a problem well defined is a problem half solved" (Ch 5).

Psychological safety — A climate where "no one will be punished or humiliated for errors, questions, or requests for help" (Edmondson) (Ch 8).

Redundancy — A backup that prevents a single point of failure from killing the mission; must be independent to work ("fail without failing") (Ch 1).

Resulting — Equating the quality of a decision with the quality of its outcome (Annie Duke) (Ch 8, Ch 9).

Risk homeostasis (the unsafety of safety) — Safety measures offset by riskier behavior; "pretend the crosswalk isn't marked" (Ch 9).

Risking your significance — Abandoning the identity story that constrains you (Steve Martin quitting stand-up at his peak) (Ch 2).

Steel man — Articulating the strongest version of an opposing argument before rejecting it; the opposite of a straw man (Ch 6).

Strategy vs. tactics — Strategy is the objective; tactics are the actions serving it — "What problem is this tactic here to solve?" (Ch 5).

Success is a lousy teacher — Success seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose; a wolf in sheep's clothing (Ch 9).

Test as you fly, fly as you test — Making tests mirror real "flight" conditions, then operating as you tested (Ch 7).

Thought experiment (Gedankenexperiment) — Running a fictional scenario in "the laboratory of the mind" to disprove or illuminate (Ch 3).

Two-way vs. one-way doors — Reversible vs. irreversible decisions; keep the door two-way when you can (Ch 1).

Unknown knowns — Self-delusion: thinking we know what we know but don't; the land of false confidence (Ch 1).

Working hypothesis — A testable, disposable work-in-progress belief, held "for the sake of the facts" — the opposite of an opinion (Ch 6).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Think Like a Rocket Scientist

Concrete, reusable methods Varol draws from rocket science for work and life.

Name Your Fear (Worst-Case / Best-Case on Paper)

When to use: Before a scary, paralyzing leap into the unknown.

How: In writing, ask "What's the worst that can happen, and how likely given what I know?" AND "What's the best that can happen?" Turn unknown unknowns into known unknowns.

Trade-offs: The naming defangs fear (usually worse than the fact), but forces you to confront things you'd rather not see. Pair with redundancies and margins of safety for irreversible one-way decisions.

First-Principles Teardown

When to use: A high-leverage problem where the conventional answer is expensive, stuck, or inherited without reason.

How: Break the thing to its fundamental components/physics ("What is a rocket made of?"), find the true cost/constraint of those fundamentals, then rebuild up from there instead of copying a template.

Trade-offs: Effortful; deploy where it matters most, not on every daily decision. Reason by analogy for the trivial.

Question Your Assumptions ("What if this weren't true?")

When to use: To expose invisible rules governing your work or life.

How: Spend a day questioning each commitment, budget line, and process: "Why am I doing it this way? Can I get rid of this or replace it?" The best way to expose a rule is to violate it. Be suspicious when you list multiple reasons to keep something.

Trade-offs: Not everything should be questioned constantly — routines free you from decision fatigue.

Kill-the-Company / Red Teaming

When to use: To surface blind spots invisible from the inside; before a big strategic bet.

How: Play the competitor trying to put you out of business; generate the attacks; then switch back and defend the weak points. Personal version: "Why is this employer justified in not hiring me?"

Trade-offs: Emotionally uncomfortable; requires genuinely inhabiting the adversary rather than humblebragging.

Thought Experiments ("What if?")

When to use: Testing an idea, disproving an assumption, or finding a path before any physical experiment.

How: Construct a fictional world where things work differently, run it in imagination, follow the logic to its extreme to surface contradictions. The word experiment lowers the stakes — if it fails, nothing bad happens.

Trade-offs: The goal is to ignite inquiry, not to be immediately right; some experiments lead nowhere but still shake you off autopilot.

Deliberate Boredom / Incubation

When to use: When a hard problem won't yield to direct effort.

How: Schedule distraction-free unstructured time — walks, showers, a "Think Week," a daydreaming chair. Switch the brain from focused to diffuse mode and let the subconscious connect ideas.

Trade-offs: Feels unproductive and underwhelming in an instant-gratification culture; creativity arrives as a whisper, not a bang.

Combinatory Play (Compare Apples and Oranges)

When to use: A creative jam or the need for a genuinely novel solution.

How: Collect diverse inputs across disciplines, then connect the dissimilar. Ask "What other industry has faced this before?" Recruit cognitively diverse people (the Medici effect); cycle between solitude and collaboration.

Trade-offs: The fit is rarely perfect, but the act of comparing sparks new lines of thought.

Moonshot Framing (10x not 10%)

When to use: When you want a breakthrough, not a marginal gain.

How: Set a goal so large the status quo can't reach it (eliminate all accidents, not improve safety). The bigness forces first-principles solutions and clears the crowded center where competitors chase mice.

Trade-offs: Requires tolerating a portfolio where most bets fail; must be paired with pragmatic execution.

Diverge Then Converge (Fly, Then Bee)

When to use: Any idea-generation problem.

How: First be a "fly" — generate wildly, "This could be done if…," ask "What could you do?" and "What would a science-fiction solution look like?" Only then switch to the "bee": rapid evaluation, kill metrics, business plans. Never let judgment kill ideas before generation finishes.

Trade-offs: Order matters — converging first ("we've tried that, no budget") strangles originality.

Backcasting & Monkey First

When to use: Planning toward an audacious goal.

How: Work backward from the imagined future (or happy customer — Amazon's pre-written press release) to the steps. Then tackle the hardest, riskiest part first (train the monkey before building the pedestal) and set kill metrics up front.

Trade-offs: Don't treat the plan as a bible ("detailed dreams blind you to new means"); the pedestal is satisfying busywork that postpones the real risk.

Reframe the Question (Strategy vs. Tactics, Function vs. Form, Inversion)

When to use: When stuck, or before committing to solve any problem.

How: Spend more time in problem definition. Ask "What problem is this tactic here to solve?" to find the strategy. Describe tools function-free to defeat functional fixedness. Ask "What if I did the reverse?" to beat stronger competitors.

Trade-offs: Feels slower than jumping to answers, but the framing of the question determines the answer.

Prove Yourself Wrong (Falsification)

When to use: Testing any belief before you commit.

How: Hold working hypotheses, not opinions (change your vocabulary). Breed multiple conflicting hypotheses. Generate cases that would break your rule (like the 2-4-6 game), not confirm it. Ask "What's missing? What fact would change my mind?" Seek dissent and steel-man opponents.

Trade-offs: Self-falsification is genuinely unpleasant (no dopamine hit), but every "no" carries more information than a "yes."

Test as You Fly, Fly as You Test

When to use: Before any launch, speech, interview, or high-stakes performance.

How: Recreate real conditions (jittery, in an unfamiliar room, with a stranger throwing curveballs). Test to fail — hunt the breaking point and exaggerate flaws. Test the assembled system, not just parts. Observe real behavior instead of self-reports; diversify testing instruments and calibration targets.

Trade-offs: Harder and less comfortable than a friendly dress rehearsal, but any gap between test and flight can be catastrophic.

Celebrate Intelligent Failure & Near-Miss Reporting

When to use: Building a team that must take risks and surface problems.

How: Reward excellent failures, punish mediocre successes. Leaders advertise their own failures repeatedly to build psychological safety. Focus on inputs, not outputs. Keep a "black box" and a "Flight Rules" catalog so lessons endure. Mine near misses — frequent, cheap, predictive.

Trade-offs: Requires distinguishing intelligent from sloppy failure; hold people accountable for failing to learn, not for failing.

Guard Against the Success Trap

When to use: After success and hot streaks.

How: Treat everything as a permanent work in progress; drop "routine." Run postmortems after wins ("What went wrong with this success? What role did luck play?"). Run premortems before acting (assume failure, list causes, assign probabilities). Fix the cause behind the cause. Distrust the safety net (risk homeostasis) and protect dissent.

Trade-offs: Wanting less uninterrupted success feels irrational, but regularity signals hidden fragility.

Scale: The Universal Laws of Life, Growth, and Death in Organisms, Cities, and Companies

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — Scale (Geoffrey West)

Exponent Reference

The magic number 4 = 3 spatial dimensions + 1 from the fractal network → all biological exponents are multiples of ¼.

Key Invariants & Thresholds

Heartbeats per mammalian lifetime~1.5 billionhumans ~2.5B, the great outlier

Decision Rules — "How should this quantity scale?"

  • Is it infrastructure or a supply network? → expect sublinear (0.75–0.9). Bigger should be cheaper per unit. If it isn't, your network is not optimized.
  • Is it a genuinely individual quantity (a house, a tap, a job)? → expect linear (~1.0). Per-capita comparison is legitimate here and only here.
  • Is it produced by people interacting? → expect superlinear (~1.15). Wages, ideas, crime, disease. Per-capita comparison is invalid.
  • Do the terminal units stay the same size as the system grows? → yes ⇒ sublinear network scaling applies.
  • Does supply scale sublinearly while maintenance scales linearly? → growth will stop. Sigmoidal, then death.
  • Does supply scale superlinearly? → growth is open-ended and faster than exponential, with a finite-time singularity.

Decision Rules — "What if it doesn't scale as expected?"

ObservationRead it asDo
Above the curvegenuine overperformancestudy it; check it persists over decades before crediting management
Below the curvegenuine underperformancelook for structural cause, not recent policy
High raw value, zero residualjust bigstop congratulating; it's size
Exponent nearer 1.0 than 0.85 on infrastructurenetwork not optimized / not space-fillinglook for redundancy or fragmentation
Company sales exponent drifting downeconomies of scale beating innovationdimensionality is contracting → decline ahead
Doubling time shrinkingsuperexponentiala wall exists with a date; plan a paradigm shift
Doubling time constantexponentialunbounded but not singular; manageable
Growth still exponential after 20 yearsyou forgot to detrendremove inflation and market expansion

Tells & Smells

  • Someone ranks cities or companies per capita → the ranking is measuring size. 7 of the 20 largest US cities are top-20 on per-capita GDP; none are top-20 on scale-adjusted indicators.
  • A leader claims credit for a size effect (New York's low per-capita carbon, Santa Fe's high) → it's the exponent, not the policy.
  • A composite index built by linear combination (WEF, Forbes, Fortune, The Economist) → naive; recompute on residuals.
  • A 1:1 scale model offered as evidence → aesthetics, not dynamics. Demand the dimensionless number.
  • A dose, load, or capacity scaled per kilogram → the LSD-elephant error. Use the ⅔ or ¾ law.
  • A metaphor doing the work of a theory ("the DNA of the company", "the ecology of the marketplace") → evocative, predicts nothing.
  • A narrowing product line described as "focus" → contracting dimensionality; the reliable precursor of corporate death.
  • R&D spend cited as evidence of innovation → tax-driven label; R&D share falls with size. Measure output diversity.
  • A smooth EKG or a rigid, low-variance system called healthy → in fractal systems, rigidity is fragility; variance is resilience.
  • Gaussian statistics applied to city sizes, incomes, or crashes → power laws have fat tails. Caveat emptor.
  • Comparing cities across national systems (Osaka vs. Chicago) with within-system laws → invalid without an anchor.

The Punchline

Companies scale sublinearly like organisms, not superlinearly like cities. So they mature, stop growing, and die on a ~10.5-year half-life — while cities almost never do. The lever, if there is one, is keeping dimensionality expanding against the bureaucratic contraction that size makes inevitable.

glossary.md

Glossary — Scale (Geoffrey West)

Allometric scaling — scaling in which shape changes with size, so exponents are not simple multiples of ⅓; term coined by Julian Huxley. Contrast isometric. (Ch 2, 3)

Anthropocene — the ~10,000 years since agriculture, when human effective metabolic rate began rising. (Ch 5)

Area-preserving branching — network geometry in which the summed cross-section of daughter branches equals the parent's, eliminating wave reflections; noted by Leonardo da Vinci in trees. (Ch 3)

Central place theory — Christaller's static hexagonal lattice of nested settlements; space filling and self-similar, but untested against data. (Ch 7)

Coarse-grained theory — a zeroth-order model predicting system averages (why human life span is ~100 years) rather than individual outcomes. (Ch 1, 3)

Coastline paradox — measured length depends on ruler size; a length quoted without its resolution is meaningless. (Ch 3)

Compustat — S&P database of US publicly traded companies since 1950; 28,853 firms over 1950–2009 underpin the mortality analysis. (Ch 9)

Censored companies — firms alive at the end of the data window; must be corrected for (Kaplan–Meier) or life expectancy is biased downward. (Ch 9)

Dimensionality (of a company) — the breadth of its product and idea space; contracts with age, unlike a city's, which expands. (Ch 9)

Dimensionless number — a unit-free ratio identical for model and original when they are dynamically similar; e.g. the Froude number. (Ch 2)

Doubling time — time to double at the current rate. Constant under exponential growth; shrinking under superexponential growth. (Ch 5, 10)

Dunbar's number — ~150 stable social relationships, part of a nested hierarchy 5 / 15 / 50 / 150 / 500 / 1,500 with branching ratio ~3. (Ch 7)

Economy of scale — sublinear scaling: the bigger you are, the less you need per capita. (Ch 1, 3)

Effective / social metabolic rate — energy throughput per person including technology. Biological ~100 W; global average >3,000 W; US ~11,000 W. (Ch 1, 5)

Emergent behavior — collective properties not present in, nor predictable from, the individual components. (Ch 1)

Entropy — the inevitable disorder produced whenever energy is transformed (Clausius, 1855). "Entropy kills." (Ch 1, 4, 5)

Essential singularity — the accumulated limit of infinitely many increasingly frequent finite-time singularities. (Ch 10)

Finite time singularity — growth reaching infinity at a finite time; the signature of superexponential growth and the core of West's sustainability argument. (Ch 1, 10)

Fourth dimension of life — fractal, space-filling networks make organisms behave as if four-dimensional, turning Euclidean ⅓ exponents into ¼. (Ch 4)

Fractal dimension — a measure of crinkliness; equals the log-log slope plus 1. Cities cluster near ~1.2, up to ~1.8. (Ch 3, 7)

Froude number — v²/(Lg); matching it between model and full scale makes motion dynamically similar, so speed scales as √length. (Ch 2)

Increasing returns to scale — the economists' term for superlinear scaling. (Ch 1, 7)

Invariance of terminal units — network endpoints (capillaries, alveoli, leaves, electrical outlets, people and houses) stay the same size across all system sizes. Second network postulate. (Ch 3, 7)

Isometric scaling — shape preserved; areas ∝ length², volumes ∝ length³. Galileo's case. (Ch 2)

Kaplan–Meier estimator — survival analysis method (1958) correcting for censored observations. (Ch 9)

Kleiber's Law — metabolic rate ∝ mass^(3/4); holds across ~27 orders of magnitude of mass. (Ch 1, 3)

Krogh radius — maximum oxygen diffusion distance from capillary to cell; sets an upper bound on body size. (Ch 4)

Liability of adolescence — the acute vulnerability of a young firm once seed capital is spent without profit. (Ch 9)

Log-log plot — logarithmic axes on which a power law appears as a straight line whose slope is the exponent. (Ch 1, 2)

Marchetti's constant — ~1 hour per day of total travel, ~half an hour each way commuting; invariant across city size, mode, country, and era. (Ch 8)

Metabolic theory of ecology (MTE) — mass scaling combined with Arrhenius temperature dependence (ATP activation energy ~0.65 eV). (Ch 4)

Mortality rate (constant) — the age-independent death probability that produces exponential survivorship and a well-defined half-life. (Ch 4, 9)

Ontogenetic growth model — derivation of bounded, sigmoidal growth from sublinear supply (M^¾) against linear maintenance (M¹). (Ch 4)

Optimization (minimization of energy dissipation) — third network postulate: evolution selects the space-filling network that minimizes cardiac output. (Ch 3)

Pace of life — decreases with size in organisms (quarter-power laws); increases with size in cities (15% rule). (Ch 4, 8)

Power law — y ∝ x^α; the mathematical form of every scaling relation in the book. (Ch 1, 2)

Preferential attachment (Yule–Simon) — new items added in proportion to existing abundance; "the rich get richer." Generates Zipf-like distributions. (Ch 8)

Quarter-power scaling — the family of biological exponents built on ¼: life span +¼, heart rate −¼, metabolic rate ¾. (Ch 1, 3, 4)

Scale-Adjusted Metropolitan Indicator (SAMI) — a unit's residual deviation from its size-predicted value on the scaling curve; the correct replacement for per-capita ranking. (Ch 8)

Self-similarity / scale invariance — the same structure or ratio repeating at every magnification. (Ch 3)

Sigmoidal (bounded) growth — the S-curve produced when sublinear supply meets linear maintenance. (Ch 4, 9)

Space filling — first network postulate: the network must reach every locally active subunit. (Ch 3, 7)

Square-cube law — Galileo's argument that area ∝ length² while volume ∝ length³, so strength ∝ weight^(2/3). (Ch 2)

Sublinear scaling — exponent < 1; economies of scale. Organisms 0.75, city infrastructure ~0.85, companies ~0.9. (Ch 1, 7, 9)

Superexponential growth — faster than exponential; doubling time shrinks; leads to a finite-time singularity. (Ch 5, 8, 10)

Superlinear scaling — exponent > 1; increasing returns. Socioeconomic city output ~1.15. No biological analog. (Ch 1, 7)

Terminal units — see invariance of terminal units. (Ch 3, 4, 7)

The 15 percent rule — per doubling of city population, ~15% more socioeconomic output per capita and ~15% less infrastructure per capita. (Ch 1, 7, 8)

Urbanocene — West's coinage for the post-Industrial-Revolution epoch dominated by cities. (Ch 5, 6)

Zipf's law — a city's rank is inversely proportional to its size; also word frequencies. West treats it as phenomenological, without fundamental significance or an agreed mechanism. (Ch 7)

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — Scale (Geoffrey West)

Fit the Scaling Law

When to use: before any comparison, forecast, or benchmark across entities of different size.

How:

1. Choose the size variable (body mass, population, employees, revenue).

2. Plot the quantity of interest against it on log-log axes.

3. Read the slope — that is the exponent β.

4. Classify: β < 1 sublinear (economies of scale), β ≈ 1 linear (genuinely per-capita), β > 1 superlinear (increasing returns).

5. Only then interpret levels.

Trade-offs: needs many entities spanning at least 2–3 orders of magnitude; noisy for small samples and for companies, which have much higher variance than cities or organisms.

Scale-Adjusted Metrics (Residual Analysis)

When to use: whenever you want to know whether a unit is genuinely performing rather than merely being large. The book's single most actionable technique.

How:

1. Fit the scaling law across all comparable units within one system (one country's cities; one exchange's companies).

2. For each unit compute the residual — the log-deviation of its actual value from its size-predicted value.

3. Rank by residual, not by raw value or per-capita value.

4. Interpret: positive residual = overperformer; negative = underperformer.

Trade-offs: only valid within a single system; residuals persist for decades, so they measure structure rather than recent management. Requires the correct exponent — using 1.0 reproduces the per-capita error you were trying to avoid.

Doubling-Time Diagnosis

When to use: assessing whether a growth trajectory is safe, exponential, or headed for a wall.

How: measure the time to double at successive points in the history. Constant doubling time ⇒ exponential (unbounded but harmless in finite time). Shrinking doubling time ⇒ superexponential ⇒ a finite-time singularity exists and has a date.

Trade-offs: needs a long, clean series; the singularity date is highly sensitive to fit and should be treated as an order-of-magnitude estimate.

The Three-Postulate Test

When to use: deciding whether network scaling theory should apply to a new system at all.

How: check for (1) space filling — does the network reach every active unit? (2) invariant terminal units — are the endpoints the same size at all system sizes? (3) optimization — is there a quantity (energy, time, cost) that competition or evolution has minimized? All three present ⇒ expect a clean power law.

Trade-offs: qualitative judgment; the third postulate is the hardest to establish and the easiest to assume.

Dimensionless-Number Modeling (Similitude)

When to use: extrapolating from a small model, pilot, or prototype to full scale.

How: identify the dimensionless group governing the behavior (Froude number v²/Lg for hulls); match it between model and full scale; derive the required scaling of the other variables (speed ∝ √length).

Trade-offs: if you cannot construct a dimensionless number, do not extrapolate. A geometrically faithful 1:1 miniature transfers appearance, not dynamics.

Detrend Growth for Market Expansion

When to use: evaluating any company's growth story.

How: divide out inflation and overall market/sector expansion before plotting the growth curve. What looks exponential and open-ended usually turns sigmoidal.

Trade-offs: choosing the right market baseline is contestable; do the analysis under two or three baselines and check robustness.

Find the Invariant

When to use: looking for conserved quantities and hidden design constants in a scaling system.

How: multiply a rate that scales as x^(−α) by a duration that scales as x^(+α). The size dependence cancels. Example: heart rate (mass^−¼) × life span (mass^+¼) = ~1.5 billion heartbeats for every mammal.

Trade-offs: the invariant is an average with real spread; humans are a 2× outlier on heartbeats. Do not treat it as a personal budget.

Weight the Network by Flow

When to use: when a real network looks non-fractal (a road grid, an org chart) and you suspect the theory still applies.

How: redraw each edge with thickness proportional to the flow originating from the hub of interest. Hierarchical, branching, fractal structure typically emerges from an apparently rectangular grid.

Trade-offs: requires flow data, which is often the hard part.

Constant-Mortality Survival Analysis

When to use: estimating life expectancy for a population of firms, products, or projects.

How: build the survivorship curve, correct for censored (still-alive) units using the Kaplan–Meier estimator, and test whether survivorship is exponential. If it is, the mortality rate is age-independent and a half-life exists.

Trade-offs: age-independence is a strong empirical finding for US public companies but should be re-tested, not assumed, in a new domain.

Track Dimensionality as a Health Metric

When to use: diagnosing organizational decline before it shows in financials.

How: measure the breadth of the product and idea space over time — number of distinct lines, share of revenue outside the core, genuine R&D breadth. Contracting dimensionality plus a finely balanced cost structure means reduced resilience.

Trade-offs: R&D spend is a poor proxy (tax-driven labelling, and its share falls with size). Prefer output diversity to input spend.

Innovation-Interval Planning

When to use: career, R&D portfolio, and long-horizon strategic planning.

How: estimate the historical interval between paradigm shifts in your domain, note that it is shrinking, and plan for a working life spanning several of them rather than one.

Trade-offs: intervals are estimated from a handful of hand-picked events; directionally reliable, numerically soft.

The Making of a Manager: What to Do When Everyone Looks to You

3 markdown file(s)

cheatsheet.md

Cheatsheet — The Making of a Manager

Decision rules and heuristics for acting the way Zhuo would. Keep beside you.

The one thing to never forget

Your job = get better outcomes from a group of people working together. If an action doesn't improve the team's outcome (via purpose, people, or process), it's probably not your job.

Should I even be a manager? (decide before saying yes)

If you…Then…
Are more motivated by an outcome than by a specific role/craft✅ strong fit (covers most weaknesses)
Would say "No problem!" to 70% of your day in meetings✅ you get energy from people
Can stay steady through others' emotional crises✅ fit
Want the title, freedom to call shots, or feel obligated⚠️ wrong reasons — "I should/can" ≠ "I want to"
Have one craft you can't give up⚠️ consider the IC track — it's a transition, not a promotion

Diagnosing poor work (in order)

1. Are expectations aligned? (does "great" mean the same?) → if no, set them.

2. Is it motivation? (unclear picture / aspiration mismatch / no consequences) → address it.

3. Only then: is it a skills gap? → train or hire. (Skills gaps don't close in months.)

The trust test — you're doing well if all three are true

1. Reports bring you their biggest challenges unprompted.

2. You exchange critical feedback without it being personal.

3. They'd gladly work for you again. (Unsure? It's probably a no.)

→ Multi-week "everything's fine"? Prod further. Aim for 1:1s that feel a little awkward.

Feedback decision rules

  • Give more than you think — reports' #1 ask is "more feedback"; aim ≥50% positive.
  • Before the work → set expectations. Same day → task-specific. Across patterns → behavioral (in person, with examples). Few times/yr → 360.
  • Critical feedback → direct + dispassionate: "When I observed [X], I felt concerned because…" No sandwich. No disguised "questions." Never when upset ("Let's talk later").
  • Bad-news decision → state the decision first; don't fake a joint discussion.
  • Feedback failed? Check in order: often enough? → heard? (make it safe) → actionable? (specific + what-success-looks-like + next steps).

People moves — act fast

  • ~80% of the time, pep talks for a fundamentally mismatched report fail. Drawn-out "help" is worse for them.
  • Test: "If they weren't already here, would I recommend another team hire them?" / "Would I rehire them if the role were open?" If no → move them (better role) or let them go — respectfully, decisively, not up for debate.
  • Never tolerate a brilliant jerk — the team is better off when they leave.

Meetings — the ruthless-efficiency rules

QuestionRule
Why meet?Define the great outcome first, then pick ONE type: Decision / Info / Feedback / Ideas / Relationships
Who's invited?Only those needed for that outcome + decision-maker + affected stakeholders. Cut the rest.
Prepared?Send agenda/materials the day before (curse of knowledge)
Ideas?Solo silent writing (Post-its) then discuss
Airtime?Cover interruptions, open doors for the quiet, cap overtalkers
End?Agreed next steps + recap (decision, owners, next check-in)
Do you need to be there?If the right outcome happens without you → skip it, get notes. Cancel meetings good for no one.

Hiring rules of thumb

  • Frame it as building the future, not filling holes. It's your job, not the recruiter's.
  • Interviews predict poorly → de-bias: past work + honest references + multiple independent interviewers + prepared identical questions.
  • Reject weak hires (unanimous but unenthusiastic) and anyone toxic (bad-mouths past employers, blames others, arrogant).
  • Bet on a passionate advocate. Hire people capable of more. Prioritize diversity.
  • Leadership hire? Go slow, do homework — bad ones are disproportionately disruptive.
  • Recruiting is a funnel — effort reliably pays off. Ask: "If hiring were the only thing that mattered, what would I do differently?"

Execution rules

  • Vision must be concrete (5 people repeat it identically) — kill help/improve/enhance.
  • 80/20: rank every list; do #1 before #2; "if only one goal, which?"
  • Every problem gets one owner; every task a who + by when.
  • Break big goals into milestones (defeat Parkinson's Law).
  • Reversible decision? Move at ~70% info (Bezos). Then disagree and commit.
  • Prize execution over strategy — a fast runner beats a slow one who knows the path.

Delegation dial (calibrate constantly)

Micromanager ————————————|———————————— Absentee
 (stifling, talent      SWEET SPOT      (no support,
  leaves)          dive in AND step      overhead)
                    back per person
  • Keep only work at the intersection of most important to org AND only you can do best.
  • Delegate anything a report can do as-well-or-better; giving big problems = a sign of trust (declare ownership publicly).
  • Rule of thumb: double your leadership capacity every year; aim to put yourself out of a job.
  • People trump projects — "Do we have the right people on the right problems?"

Culture levers (all four, or it won't stick)

1. Talk about what matters — 10 times, 10 ways (repetition ≠ condescending).

2. Walk the walk — a say/do gap is the fastest trust-killer. (Don't state a value you won't live.)

3. Align incentives — watch for traps (individual-over-team, short-over-long, rewarding no-conflict, the squeaky wheel).

4. Invent traditions that make values concrete.

→ Real culture = what you'll give up for your values, not the slogan.

Self-management defaults

  • Everyone feels like an imposter — normal. Choose the growth mindset (feedback = fuel, not verdict).
  • In the Pit: don't pay the "double tax," assume your story is irrational → seek the truth, keep a Little Wins journal, ask for help.
  • Treat your manager as a coach, not a judge. Ask "how can I be twice as good?"
  • Training worth it? Ask "One year from now, will I be glad I did this?"

glossary.md

Glossary — The Making of a Manager

360-degree feedback — Feedback aggregated from multiple colleagues for a more objective, complete view; gathered a few times a year (Ch 4).

Absentee manager — The over-delegating extreme: little support, no hard calls, lost credibility as "overhead" (Ch 9).

Additive vs. multiplicative — Doing the work yourself adds a fixed amount; improving purpose/people/process multiplies the team's output (Ch 1).

Apprentice — Transition path where your manager's growing team is split and you take a portion; the easiest, most-supported route (Ch 2).

Behavioral feedback — Feedback on themes/patterns across many tasks; personal, needs specific examples, given in person (Ch 4).

Bench (great bench) — A layer of leaders strong enough to run things without you; tested by the "extended vacation test" (Ch 7).

Brilliant jerk / divider effect — A talented person who belittles others and makes the whole team less effective (opposite of a multiplier) (Ch 3).

Calibration — Making your self-view (or your read of a report) match reality by seeking others' honest input (Ch 5).

Compliment sandwich — Burying criticism between praise; Zhuo rejects it as insincere and diluting (Ch 4).

Concrete vision — A bold, measurable, easily-repeated statement of the outcome (not the how); five people should repeat it identically (Ch 8).

Context switching — Rapidly shifting focus across many topics; a defining reality of managing large teams (Ch 9).

Culture — The norms and values that govern how things get done; revealed by what a team will give up for its values (Ch 10).

Curse of knowledge — Experts forget what it's like to see material fresh; fixed by sending materials in advance (Ch 6).

Debrief (retrospective / postmortem) — A blameless review of what went well/badly and what to change; learnings written down and shared (Ch 8).

Delegation — "The art of knowing when to dive in yourself and when to step back and entrust others" (Ch 9).

Disagree and commit — Backing a decision fully once made, even if you argued against it (Bezos) (Ch 6, Ch 8).

Dream-manager questions — First-1:1 questions a New Boss asks reports to learn their ideal manager (Ch 2).

Dunning-Kruger effect — Cognitive bias where the less-skilled overrate themselves; a reason calibration matters (Ch 5).

Fixed vs. growth mindset — Fixed: actions governed by fear of judgment; Growth: feedback is fuel and ability can improve with effort (Dweck) (Ch 5).

Funnel (recruiting funnel) — Viewing hiring as consistent conversion rates (emails → meetings → interviews → offers → accepts) (Ch 7).

Imposter syndrome — The universal feeling of being a fraud; hits managers hard because they're looked to for answers and constantly do new things (Ch 5).

Managing is caring — You can't fake respect; care means helping reports succeed and telling them the truth, unconditionally (Ch 3).

Micromanager — The over-involved delegation extreme: stifling, distrustful, drives talent away (Ch 9).

Multiplier effect — The leverage a manager creates by improving the team rather than personally producing (Ch 1).

New Boss — Transition path: hired to lead an established team; gets a "newbie window" and blank slate (Ch 2).

Newbie card — The ~3-month window where a New Boss is expected to ask everything; use it to ramp fast (Ch 2).

Output vs. activity — Measure results (orders won), not busyness (calls made) (Grove) (Ch 1).

Parkinson's Law — "Work expands to fill the time available"; beaten by smaller milestones (Ch 8).

Pareto / 80/20 principle — Most results come from a minority of causes; focus is identifying which (Ch 8).

Pioneer — Transition path: founding member now responsible for a growing team; most autonomy, least support (Ch 2).

The Pit — The low point where imposter syndrome and self-doubt peak; escaped with a six-tactic toolkit (Ch 5).

Playbook — A codified checklist for a repeated task (run a meeting, close a hire) others can execute (Ch 8).

Portfolio approach — Splitting the team's work across short/medium/long time horizons (thirds) (Ch 8).

Purpose, People, Process — The why/who/how; the three buckets every managerial task sorts into (Ch 1).

Successor — Transition path: taking over your departed manager's entire role (Ch 2).

Survival mode — When the org is "on fire," you abandon long-term investment and do whatever it takes now (team hierarchy of needs) (Ch 1).

Task-specific feedback — Same-day feedback on a concrete action; focused on the what, not the who — the easiest type to give (Ch 4).

Trust test (three statements) — Reports bring you their biggest challenges; you exchange critical feedback without it being personal; they'd gladly work for you again (Ch 3).

Twice as good ("How can I be twice as good?") — The frame for on-the-job self-improvement (Ch 5).

Weak hire — A unanimous but unenthusiastic "hire"; Zhuo says reject it — bet only on passionate advocacy (Ch 7).

Would-I-rehire question — "Assume the role were open — would I rehire this person or gamble on someone else?"; used for struggling reports/managers (Ch 3, Ch 9).

patterns.md

Patterns & Techniques — The Making of a Manager

Concrete, reusable methods from the book. Each is a thing you can do.

The Purpose/People/Process Audit

When to use: any time your team's outcomes are lagging and you're unsure where to intervene.

How: sort the problem into why (purpose), who (people), or how (process). Ask which lever most improves the collective outcome, and act there rather than on symptoms.

Trade-offs: in survival mode, skip this and fight the fire directly.

Diagnosing Poor Work (skill vs. motivation)

When to use: a report's work isn't great.

How: run a series of conversations — (1) Are expectations aligned (does "great" mean the same to both)? (2) Is it motivation (unclear picture, aspiration mismatch, no consequences)? (3) Only then, is it a skills gap? Fix the earliest failing link.

Trade-offs: skills gaps rarely close in a few months; be honest about timelines.

The Weekly 1:1

When to use: with every direct report, ≥30 min weekly.

How: focus on the report, not status. Prepare questions each morning. Use Identify → Understand → Support question banks; let the report lead. Never use it for status updates (use another channel).

Trade-offs: at ~8+ reports the math breaks — that's the signal to develop managers beneath you.

Setting Expectations Up Front

When to use: before any project, promotion timeline, or launch commitment.

How: agree on what great/mediocre/bad looks like, offer starting advice and pitfalls, and state how you'll be involved. Readjust the instant reality shifts.

Trade-offs: none — "every major disappointment is a failure to set expectations."

Delivering Critical Feedback

When to use: something isn't working and must be addressed.

How: deliver directly and dispassionately. Template: "When I [observed] your [output], I felt concerned because… I'd like to understand your perspective and resolve this." Be specific, clarify what success looks like, suggest next steps. Ask "Does this resonate? Why or why not?" No sandwich; don't disguise concerns as questions; don't engage while upset.

Trade-offs: for a decision (not feedback), state the decision first and don't open it to debate.

The Four Feedback Types (cadence ladder)

When to use: building a complete feedback practice.

How: (1) expectations before work; (2) task-specific, same-day, ≥50% positive; (3) behavioral, in person with examples; (4) 360 a few times/year (ask: what should X do more of? what should X stop?).

Trade-offs: task-specific is easiest but insufficient alone — reports also want career/behavioral feedback.

The Brutal-Honesty Self-Inventory

When to use: understanding how you manage (esp. new managers, or in the Pit).

How: list strengths (3-word descriptions from loved ones; proudest qualities; success traits; common praise) and weaknesses/triggers (inner-critic complaints; wished-for gifts; triggers; common improvement feedback). Then calibrate with your manager and 3–7 close colleagues.

Trade-offs: asking for feedback is uncomfortable; frame it as growth, not a worthiness test.

Escaping the Pit (six tactics)

When to use: peak self-doubt/imposter syndrome.

How: (1) don't beat yourself up (no "double tax"); (2) assume your story is irrational — seek the truth; (3) visualize success/past wins; (4) ask people you can be real with; (5) keep a Little Wins journal; (6) set boundaries and self-care.

The Five-Type Meeting Design

When to use: before scheduling any meeting.

How: define the great outcome, then pick one type — Decision / Sharing Information / Feedback / Generating Ideas / Strengthening Relationships — and design for it. Don't make one meeting do two jobs.

Trade-offs: decision meetings make poor idea-generation forums (and vice versa).

Meeting Preparation & Follow-up Ritual

When to use: any meeting, especially recurring or large.

How: send agenda/materials the day before (beats curse of knowledge). End with agreed next steps; send a recap (decision, action items + owners, next check-in).

The Calendar Audit

When to use: feeling overwhelmed/behind.

How: for one week, log every meeting — did you participate, were you critical, did you get value? Drop the "no"s; ask for pre/post notes instead. Cancel meetings valuable to no one.

The Future Org Chart

When to use: every January (or planning cycle).

How: map expected headcount, level per role, needed skills/strengths, gaps, and diversity additions. Use it as the rubric that stops you from hiring the next available person.

Smart-Bet Hiring

When to use: every hire (interviews are unreliable predictors).

How: examine past work (portfolios/teach-a-class); get honest references; use multiple interviewers who record rationale independently before debrief; prepare identical questions; reject weak hires and toxic candidates; bet on passionate advocacy; hire people capable of more; prioritize diversity.

Trade-offs: leadership hires are disproportionately disruptive — slow down and do homework.

Concrete Vision Test

When to use: writing any team goal or roadmap.

How: strip squishy words (help/improve/enhance); make it bold, measurable, repeatable. Ask five people who heard it to repeat it — they should match.

Break-It-Down (defeat Parkinson's Law)

When to use: any big goal with a far deadline.

How: split into near milestones; give each a who and a by when; buffer for the planning fallacy; work backward from the target date.

Debrief / Retrospective

When to use: after a project, on a cadence, or after any error.

How: 1–2 hrs; what went well / badly / to change. Blameless — collective language ("our process failed"), objective timeline. Write down and share learnings.

Delegating a Hard Problem

When to use: growing a report and freeing your own time.

How: confirm you truly believe they can solve it; hand it over; publicly declare them the owner (empowers them); stay "on the boat" coaching — don't walk away.

Put-Yourself-Out-of-a-Job Rule

When to use: continuously, as the team grows.

How: spend your energy only at the intersection of "most important to the org" AND "what you're uniquely best at." Delegate everything a report can do as well or better. Aim to double leadership capacity yearly.

The Would-I-Rehire Test

When to use: a report or manager is persistently struggling.

How: ask "Assume the role were open — would I rehire this person or gamble on someone new?" If no, make the move (help them find a better role or let them go), respectfully and decisively.

Culture-Building Loop

When to use: shaping how your team works.

How: (1) map current vs. aspirational culture; (2) talk about what matters ten times, ten ways; (3) walk the walk; (4) align incentives and address violations; (5) invent traditions that make values concrete.
